Discussion: 讨论集中在“该不该拒收”。Joker_vD 认为语义其实很直白：既然数据块存在，就应作为该硬链接的内容覆盖原有文件，他还推测这是为磁带无法回写的场景留的后路；但维护多个 tar 解析器的 woodruffw 反驳，说 pax 对“带数据的硬链接成员”根本谈不上精确或简单。多人倾向双模式：处理上传或分发包等不可信输入时严格拒收，恢复损坏的家庭备份时则尽力抽取；作者也认同 tar 兼有备份与软件分发两种用途，威胁模型不同，Julia 的 Tar.jl 和 uv 的 tar-codec 正是为后者设计的。JdeBP 指出文章漏掉了一个重要实现 paxmirabilis（Debian 的 pax，兼 tar/cpio/pax，并非 libarchive 的 bsdtar）。另有人在做从二进制和文件系统生成 SBOM 的工具，担心这种歧义意味着要知道目标嵌入式设备用哪个解包器才能复现正确结果，而“严格解析”又不能直接阻止提取，必须可配置。有人顺口说“别用 pax”，立刻被纠正说 V7 tar 根本没有规范，歧义同样多。

Worth reading

  • woodruffw: 维护文章提到的多个 tar 解析器的 woodruffw 直言，把 pax 的带数据硬链接规则称为「精确」「简单」并不合适。
  • JdeBP: JdeBP 指出文章漏了 paxmirabilis——Debian 里那个兼作 tar、cpio、pax 的多调用二进制，与 libarchive 的 bsdtar 不是一回事。
  • woodruffw: woodruffw 纠正了一个关于优先级的提议：pax 规定扩展头总是优先，即使结果非法，pax 只是没规定非法状态下该怎么办。

entry.title: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
entry.content:
#22 on HN · evanxmerz.com · 231 points · 281 comments · HN discussion

Evan Merz 的一篇博客文章，作者说自己可能在 2026 年 5 月被 Meta 裁员，原因之一是他对把 LLM 当作编码工具的抵触比同侪更强；如今他在另一家大型科技公司，按公司期望 100% 用 AI 生成代码。他列出 AI 损害代码库的四种方式——只写表面的 get/set 和既有路径的测试、过度应用 DRY 导致代码过度复杂、开发者逐渐不再理解自己的系统、以及评审速度跟不上 PR 生成速度——以及四个征兆：事故变多、恢复变慢、错误只在真实用户处暴露、用户体验变差。他的典型例子是一位团队里最好的工程师提交了用 JavaScript 事件实现 mouseover 效果的代码，而不是用 :hover 选择器。全文没有数据或案例支撑，属于经验性论述。

Discussion: 讨论几乎没有共识。一批资深工程师认同“脆弱”这个观察，但把责任放在流程而非模型上：有人说要给 agent 明确定义什么算好测试、好结构，有人用变异测试、属性测试和覆盖率门禁把事故率压下来了，也有人指出代码质量在 AI 之前就从来不是商业优先项（有评论翻出 Oracle 2500 万行代码库的旧帖），AI 只是放大了既有动力学。反方则举出第一手经验：一位用户称 7 个月、50 万行的纯 AI 移动应用维护反而更轻松，另一位说有 6000 用户的登山 App 代码库“从未如此健康”——但立刻被追问用户规模和项目时长不足以暴露脆弱性。另一组反驳针对文章的具体例子：mouseover 那点事一小时就能改，拿它论证系统性脆弱是小题大做，真正的问题是没有约束和验证，而不是 AI 本身；simonw 的总结被不少人认同——2026 年之后最有意思的工程挑战，是如何用 AI 造出更健壮而不是更脆弱的代码库。

Worth reading

  • drooby: 给出一套可操作的工作流：让 agent 注释掉被测代码验证测试会失败、写变异测试和属性测试、补到 100% 覆盖率，并把这些固化进 skill，称其团队今年 bug 和事故下降而交付量上升。
  • thisisnotgreat: 长篇反驳：认为 mouseover 之类的“脆弱”论调在 AI 之前就存在且基本都是无事生非，主张只要把风格和流程讲清楚 agent 就照做，并称自己团队的 AI 产品事故更少、更容易推理。
  • OtherShrezzing: 一位承包商的实例：某公司从订阅制 token 切到 API 计费后账单高出数百倍，几百名工程师、利润率不高的公司根本负担不起“不理解自己代码库”。

entry.title: NetBSD 11 desktop on a Raspberry Pi 4
entry.content:
#23 on HN · neongd.com · 106 points · 67 comments · HN discussion

A hands-on walkthrough by a blogger who freed up a Raspberry Pi 4 and installed NetBSD 11 on it: write the evbarm-aarch64 arm64.img.gz to an SD card, drop the pftf RPi4 UEFI firmware (v1.53) onto the FAT boot partition so the board can boot the NetBSD partitions, then fix Wi-Fi by symlinking the brcmfmac43455 NVRAM file (bwfm0 fails with 「NVRAM file not available」 until then), install pkgin, and build the NsCDE desktop on fvwm3 for a CDE-style look. The framing claim is that NetBSD is the only actively developed open-source OS with no AI-generated code in it — the author suggests interest is rising partly because people want AI-free alternatives — and that the install was, in his words, not that hard. The post was later updated in response to the HN thread, including fixes to the SD-card writing instructions.

Discussion: The thread splits between people who found NetBSD pleasant (fast installs, broad ARM hardware support, the self-expanding amd64 live image) and people for whom the setup is a non-starter: one commenter measured roughly 20% idle CPU for OpenBSD and 30% for Haiku under KVM, with similar battery results on a ThinkPad, and others say unsupported GPUs and power management keep BSDs off their daily drivers. A long sub-thread explains the pkg_add/pkgin split — pkg_add is dpkg-like and bootstraps pkgin, the apt analogue, via PKG_PATH — with a FreeBSD comparison. Two side arguments dominate the volume: the site's pixel-style font, which several readers call genuinely hard to read (corrected by one commenter as Berkelium64, a proportional GEOS-derived face, not a bitmap font) and defended by others as normal and fixable with reader mode; and Balena Etcher versus dd/cat/USBImager for writing the image, where defenders cite cross-platform safety and write verification and critics cite Electron bloat and telemetry. Smaller notes: the guide says vi where NetBSD actually ships nvi, and a recent addition to base is the nano-like atto(1).

Worth reading

  • krautburglar: First-hand measurements: idle OpenBSD used about 20% CPU and Haiku about 30% under KVM, with similar results on ThinkPad battery tests — the practical blocker for non-Linux kernels.
  • JdeBP: Corrects the font discussion: the page uses Berkelium64, a proportional rework of a Commodore GEOS font that only looks like a bitmap font, and the commenter found unscii far more legible.
  • rustyhancock: Explains exactly how bare pkg_add finds pkgin via PKG_PATH and why you might skip setting it globally so it doesn't clash with pkgin's own repository config.

entry.title: What constant surveillance is doing to children and parents
entry.content:
#24 on HN · theatlantic.com · 149 points · 140 comments · HN discussion

The Atlantic magazine article examines location-tracking apps and other parental surveillance, reportedly following cases from infancy to adulthood — commenters note it includes a 29-year-old whose mother still tracks her. Its argument, as the thread frames it, is that constant monitoring buys reassurance for parents at the cost of children's privacy and autonomy, and that it normalizes surveillance. The article itself returned HTTP 403, so this summary is based on the title, the supplied archive links, and the comment thread rather than the full text.

Article not read: HTTP 403

Discussion: The thread is broadly sympathetic to privacy concerns but split on parental practice: several parents describe refusing smartphones, TikTok and tracking watches, and say their children eventually thanked them, while others counter that phones are now required for school apps and that unwalkable neighborhoods make free-range childhood impractical. The sharpest disagreement is over risk: one side calls tracking cheap insurance against rare but catastrophic events, and another argues it shifts agency from child to parent — citing missed buses and minor emergencies that children once had to solve themselves. Parents of adults and adult children report consensual location sharing as convenient, while others say parental monitoring differs in kind from corporate or state surveillance because the stated goal is protecting the child. A recurring theme is that marketing, parental guilt and legal risk — including fear of child-endangerment accusations — push families toward monitoring, and some criticize the article for not pinning down evidence of harm. There is rough agreement that childhood roaming has shrunk and monitoring is spreading, but no consensus on whether that is proportionate or whether the 29-year-old case is an outlier.

Worth reading

  • circlefavshape: Notes that the article includes a 29-year-old still tracked by her mother, calling it far beyond the usual teenage-safety case.
  • graemep: A parent whose daughter is in her first university term says the daughter would not tolerate a tracker and argues children who grow up tracked come to see stalking as normal.
  • alex43578: Argues tracking is less about stranger abduction than ordinary mishaps — a child off at the wrong bus stop or knocked off a bike — and compares it to wearing a seatbelt despite low per-mile risk.

entry.title: Taking another shot at the cheap IP camera, part 2
entry.content:
#25 on HN · ericswpark.com · 97 points · 35 comments · HN discussion

Eric Park revisits the Tuya-based cheap IP camera he gave up on a year earlier, extracting its firmware with binwalk and finding a Linux 3.4.35 kernel (from 2013) on CramFS and JFFS2 filesystems. He traces the boot chain through initrun.sh and S60ppsapp to the 2.4 MB ppsapp binary, where strings reveal the disabled ONVIF server's stream URLs (rtsp://%s:%d/Streaming/Channels/101 and /102) and a 「Starting onvif server on port %s」 message. After hand-tracing in Ghidra, he hands the harder parts to DeepSeek via OpenRouter, which solves the remaining puzzle for a reported 22 cents, with the goal of getting a local video stream without Tuya's cloud.

Discussion: The thread is mostly about LLM-assisted reverse engineering rather than the camera itself: several commenters say explaining ancient, undocumented codebases is now a big part of their AI usage, and many are struck that a month of manual RE work now costs pocket change. A recurring argument is model access — some say Chinese open-weight models (DeepSeek, Qwen) are the only ones that will reliably do this work, while others push back that Anthropic and OpenAI do allow it through approval processes (Daybreak Blue) and that they have done Xiaomi or game-anti-cheat patching with Claude models with no refusals; a subthread debates whether reseller platforms like OpenRouter are worth the markup, and the author replies that he didn't know which model would work, so a reseller let him try several cheaply. A firmware developer argues the half-obfuscated password is not laziness but the bare minimum needed to pass a compliance scanner. The thread drifts substantially into FPV drone cameras and analog-vs-digital video links, and commenters recommend OpenIPC and GOKE-chip cameras, plus a write-up on the Ingenic T41's AI accelerator, as better hacking targets.

Worth reading

  • superxpro12: Notes the firmware obfuscated the password string with a bitwise operation but left the neighbouring 「enter password」 string in plaintext, which is what pointed the LLM at the right spot.
  • scottLobster: A commenter who has written corporate firmware says this is almost certainly deliberate box-ticking for an old security requirement, not an oversight — they did the minimum to pass a scanner.
  • inoop: Points to a personal reverse-engineering write-up (github.com/inoop/t41-pluto) of a cheap Noorio camera on the Ingenic T41 chipset, which turns out to have an AI accelerator.

entry.title: Amazon saves millions by replacing Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider
entry.content:
#1 on HN · strandsagents.com · 147 points · 41 comments · HN discussion

An AWS blog post by two Amazon engineers, Carr and Mehul, describing how they replaced Claude Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider — a small open-source decision model, in its E4B Gemma 4 build — for labeling tickets into one of 20 categories in Amazon's internal ticketing system. They claim parity or better label quality at 98% lower token cost: roughly $22,200 down to about $500 per million tickets, with average call latency falling from 4,215 ms to 897 ms and tokens per ticket from 6,724 to 2,010, served on SageMaker ml.g5.xlarge instances (one A10G, ~19 GiB of model weights). They credit a three-way AppConfig switch (BEDROCK / DUAL / DECIDER) that ran both models on live traffic and let them roll back with a config change, and warn that JSON key ordering shifted output probabilities by up to 0.19, plus that the approach only fits closed-choice, high-volume, short-context tasks. It reads in places like a product case study for a model AWS launched a month earlier.

Discussion: The thread mostly treats this as a return to classical ML, with several commenters asking why an LLM was ever used to sort tickets into 20 buckets when SVMs, scikit-learn or BERT would do it faster and cheaper — one links a 2021 ICSE paper on an SVM-based log classification pipeline they built. The strongest counter-argument is that classical classifiers need labeled domain data and a data scientist, while an LLM gets you a working prototype in minutes with no training set and tolerates categories being added and removed; the emerging consensus is that LLMs are fine for bootstrapping a feature and should then be optimized into something smaller once the label catalog settles, likened to Electron apps trading efficiency for developer speed. Others poke at the arithmetic — saving millions at ~$21,700 per million tickets implies on the order of 90 million tickets a year — and at the framing, noting Strands is AWS's own open-source project rather than an outside vendor, so the post is closer to an advert using internal adoption as a case study. One commenter running an ML tooling company warns that these decision-model refactors often hit production friction and see rollbacks to LLMs, since the models are less expressive for real application logic.

Worth reading

  • armcat: Six years ago they built a ticket classification pipeline on SVMs that trained in minutes and classified in milliseconds, and links the Linnaeus paper accepted at ICSE 2021 — evidence the field has looped back to where it started.
  • wodenokoto: Argues you cannot train an SVM on a ticketing system without domain data, whereas an LLM needs only someone who can wire up APIs, handles category changes without retraining, and is the right thing to optimize away later.
  • Kaedon: Does the arithmetic: at roughly $21,700 saved per million tickets, saving millions a year implies at least ~92 million tickets annually, which is plausible given alarms, security findings and capacity requests all generate tickets.

entry.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
entry.content:
#2 on HN · anthropic.com · 500 points · 756 comments · HN discussion

Anthropic 发布 Claude Fable 5.2 和 Claude Mythos 5.2。两者是同一个底层模型：Fable 面向所有用户，带有较强的网络安全和生物安全防护；Mythos 则通过验证计划向受审查的组织开放。文中称新模型输出速度比 5.1 快约 30%，输入和输出价格分别降到每百万 token 8 美元和 40 美元（可选 fast mode 在价格翻倍的基础上，生成速度提升 2.5 倍）。发布稿还宣称，1000 个 Fable 5.2 agent 用 30 小时完整形式化了费马大定理（Opus 5.5 用同样的设置只完成 26%）；以及一个 agent 花八天时间从空目录构建出能启动的操作系统，并让 Python 服务迁移到 Rust 后启动快 26 倍。文中还写到，模型解决了两个黑洞物理的开放问题，设计了三台电子设备，并在机器人评测上取得了进展。

Discussion: 大量早期使用者表示，在普通编码任务上几乎分不出 Fable 5.2 和 Opus 5.5：有人说两者在 30 个任务中各自解出 26 个，但 Fable 5.2 的耗时只有 5.1 的 0.62 倍，而且几乎没有因防护机制而中止；也有人认为它在架构设计和需要高野心提示词的任务上明显更强。另一方面，评论对话题热度很高：用户抱怨额度消耗太快（有人在 20 分钟内耗尽了 5 小时用量），并普遍怀疑 Opus 5.5 发布前曾被“nerf”，还引用更早的 HN 帖子和 nerf-bench 追踪器；同时 5.2 这个版本号低于 Opus 5.5，也被骂为令人困惑的营销。基准图表受到最多质疑：有人问为什么把 Fable 的 xhigh 与 Gemini 4 Carbon 的 medium 相比、为什么网络安全基准里没有 Carbon；jsnell 回应说 Carbon 尚未公开发布，medium 正是它在 FrontierCode 2.0 上的最佳档位，其他基准根本没有它的数据。反方还指出 CVE Rediscovery 使用的是已公开的 CVE，本质上是在测记忆；Artificial Analysis 显示 Fable 5.2 每任务成本 26.54 美元，而 GPT-6.1 Sol 只要 1.27 美元；并且它的幻觉率为 59%。另一条主线是“奇点”之争：有人把费马大定理的形式化当作富矿，另一些人则指出，该证明依赖训练数据里已有的轨迹和可自动校验的 oracle，1000 个 agent 花费的计算量约为单个 agent 跑 11 天的 13 倍，因此这更像是计算量堆叠，而非递归自我改进。

Worth reading

  • jsnell: 逐条反驳“基准图表作弊”的指控：Carbon 尚未公开，无法自行跑分；FrontierCode 2.0 的 medium 是 Carbon 的最佳档位；而 Astra 的 CVE 测试需要 OpenAI 的验证计划授权。
  • ianberdin: 用同一 SVG 基准实测，Fable 5.2 在高档位只是因为被允许生成更多 token（76k，对比 Opus 的 20k），在 max 档位两者结果基本相同，Opus 5.5 反而略好且便宜约一半。
  • stefanpie: 引用系统卡指出，Anthropic 在训练中刻意压制了“加速器 kernel 优化 / 改进 LLM 架构”相关能力，使其只达到 Opus 5.5 水平，并对非标准加速器上的 kernel 开发做透明回退；作为 EDA 研究者，这令人担忧。

entry.title: USPS now offers official ZIP Code boundary polygons
entry.content:
#3 on HN · postalpro.usps.com · 601 points · 301 comments · HN discussion

这是 USPS PostalPro 上的一个产品页面，不是文章：它出售「ZIP Code Boundaries」数据集，声称基于投递地址和位置数据给出权威边界，每季度更新四次，分为 Internal、Enterprise 和 Publication 三个层级，并附带许可协议、技术指南和 GeoJSON 示例。页面没有标价，但评论者从订单表上查到最低档为 1 万美元，最高档达 15 万美元，且许可证禁止再分发或转售。

Discussion: 压倒性的反应是愤怒：联邦数据理应以近乎零的增量成本公开，而这里却被定成了企业级价格；多位欧洲、荷兰的评论者指出，本国的邮编数据由政府机构免费发布，甚至直接作为 QGIS 图层使用。关于「USPS 为什么缺钱」的争论最激烈，也出现了关键纠正：有人说国会要求它提前几十年为养老金注资，但有人指出那其实是退休人员医保，且 2022 年的《邮政服务改革法》已经取消了这一要求，另外 USPS 自 1970 年代以来基本不拿纳税人拨款、靠邮资和产品销售自筹，同时被要求像企业一样运营。技术派反复强调 ZIP code 从来不是地理区域，而是一组投递路线的标签：PO Box、单栋建筑、跨州、一条街两侧分属不同邮编都真实存在，因此多边形只能是近似，这也解释了为什么 Census 的免费 ZCTA 数据集成为默认替代品，发帖人自己也按这份数据对比过。还有从业者提到 USPS 的地址验证 API 2026 年 8 月也开始收费，以及有人试图用众筹买下数据再公开，会因为许可证和可能的数据指纹而不可行。

Worth reading

  • munro: 发帖人 munro 把 USPS 的波多黎各样例数据与 Census 2026 年的 ZCTA 做了逐块对比，结论是差异不大、 Census 模型更简单，因此打算继续用免费的 Census 数据，并顺带发现「ZIP Code」是注册商标。
  • shiflett: 一位 1999–2003 年在 USPS 工作的评论者说，USPS 的数据历来与处理代码分开授权，还故意掺入假地址（DPV false positive）用于检测滥用，因此「买一次然后公开」这条路走不通。
  • anamexis: 解释了法律依据：39 U.S.C. §410(c) 给了 USPS 豁免，使其可以不予披露「商业性质的信息」，所以常规 FOIA 走不通。

entry.title: Your TV can see through walls
entry.content:
#4 on HN · maurycyz.com · 64 points · 18 comments · HN discussion

Maurycyz's project write-up shows a spectrogram of a local ATSC digital TV station at 490 MHz, captured with an Ettus USRP B200 software-defined radio. Because the direct signal is partially cancelled by a strong frequency-dependent reflection (selective fading), the received signal becomes extremely sensitive to nearby motion: standing up or walking around a neighbouring room produces striped nulls in the waterfall display. Counting those stripes (≈70 px apart at a 150 Hz update rate → 2.1 Hz beat) and applying λ = c/490 MHz gives an estimated walking speed of 1.3 m/s (4.6 km/h), and the author notes any wideband signal — WiFi, LTE — works the same way.

Discussion: The thread is mostly an enthusiastic “and it gets worse” tour rather than a critique of the method. Commenters pile on related prior art: numlock86 describes extracting audio from fibre-optic cable by detecting tiny light-path disturbances (limited per link, since repeaters regenerate the signal), several recall Van Eck phreaking and the CRT-emission work that recovered screen contents through walls, and others link the MIT RF-through-wall research plus a startup that estimated traffic flow from 4G path loss and scattering (arXiv 2101.09143). On the practical side, people ask why Home Assistant has no Wi-Fi presence sensor, and two are supplied: the ESPectre Wi-Fi motion-detection integration and a Zigbee-based presence discussion, alongside a sub-$10 ESP32 spectrum-sensing project (ESPSDR/espargos) and a RuView repo for turning commodity Wi-Fi into presence and vital-sign sensing. The privacy angle is raised — someone outside could infer when the house is empty — and largely deflected by the reply that a phone not in airplane mode already discloses that, with security-camera audio streams flagged as a more realistic indoor-motion side channel. A couple of commenters point out the effect is old news to anyone who grew up with analogue antennas, where standing in the wrong place broke up the picture.

Worth reading

  • 1e1a: Links a sub-$10 ESP32-based SDR setup (espargos/ESPSDR) for observing Wi-Fi and LTE spectra, making the experiment accessible without a USRP.
  • sudorm-rf--no-p: Answers the “why no Home Assistant integration?” question with an actual ESPectre Wi-Fi motion-detection community integration.
  • cowlevel: Blunt counter to the privacy worry: an unairplaned phone already tells observers whether you are home.

entry.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep
entry.content:
#5 on HN · simonwillison.net · 137 points · 65 comments · HN discussion

Simon Willison's blog post describes building 「Beep Locator」 after something in his box room started beeping intermittently: a Python web server coordinating several spare devices (two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro, a Surface) as browser-based listeners using WebAudio, WebSockets and a 60-second ring buffer with FFT beep detection. Listener clips are aligned by a server-triggered chirp, an approach drawn from the 2007 BeepBeep paper by Peng, Shen, Zhang, Li and Tan, plus a 「rough mode」 for dragging device positions and a clap mode for calibration. It located the beep to within about 40cm, leading him to an ancient carbon monoxide detector that wanted new batteries; the system was built mostly with Opus 5.5 in Claude Code Cloud from his iPhone, then iterated live with Fable 5.2, with a hot-swapped installModule() mechanism to push new JS to listeners without reloading pages and losing mic permission.

Discussion: A large share of the thread is a joke chain about solving it with a physical binary search over the boxes — split the pile, listen, repeat — which others extend into Big-O arguments: the moves are O(n) in total (n/2 + n/4 + …), and standing around waiting for a 62-second beep interval adds a brutal constant factor. The more substantive scepticism comes from commenters who tracked down beeps themselves by timing the interval and homing in on the sound, arguing the AI-built system took more effort than the problem deserved and gave no real sense of accomplishment; Willison answers that he would never have learned the audio and WebAudio material otherwise and got a reusable tool in about 90 minutes. Others point at off-the-shelf acoustic imaging cameras as the practical alternative — the Fotric TD2e at roughly $1,000, a $700 eBay Fotric Sonic 3 with a 64-mic array, or a DIY build on the miniDSP UMA-16 — and owners report they work well for air leaks and intermittent sounds. One commenter calls 「ask the model to write problems.md」 the emblem of AI-slop RFCs that skip real reasoning; Willison concedes he wouldn't do it for code others review, but says here the model genuinely did the reasoning for him. Side threads cover why pure-tone beeps are hard to localize (few overtones, no attack; white-noise backup alarms are easier), and a reminder to add a natural-gas alarm alongside the CO detector.

Worth reading

  • simonw: Willison gives the cost: it fit inside his $200/month Anthropic subscription, and the Fable 5.2 laptop session would have been $31.04 at API prices (517.9k context, 331.4k output).
  • simonw: Willison's direct rebuttal to the 「where's the satisfaction」 critique: without agents he would not have learned any of the audio/WebAudio material, and the alternative was learning nothing rather than learning more.
  • radicality: A commenter who bought the Fotric Sonic 3 acoustic camera on eBay for ~$700 says its 64-mic array works well and would be hard to replicate at that level.

entry.title: E-means: Outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs
entry.content:
#6 on HN · e-means.github.io · 374 points · 34 comments · HN discussion

该网站是 Faiss 贡献者（Swann Bessa、Hugo Touvron、Hervé Jégou、Matthijs Douze、Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré 等，arXiv:2611.09501）提出的新 k-means 更新规则，已并入 Faiss，模块为 faiss.contrib.e_means。它用 mini-batch 上的指数移动平均替代 Lloyd 的全量重算，并借助两条拟合出的 scaling law（分别调整 batch size 和步长）自动选择超参数，从而无需人工调参；另加余弦学习率衰减、比例切分复活死簇以及收尾精修阶段。在从 10 万到 1 亿点的 24 个数据集和 234 组配置上，它只需 1.2–3 个 epoch 就能达到 Lloyd 在第 25 个 epoch 时的测试损失，端到端在 GPU 上比 Flash-KMeans 快 10–45 倍、在 CPU 上比 Faiss 快 8–15 倍；作者还声称它更不容易陷入局部最优。

entry.title: Horible public key tricks
entry.content:
#9 on HN · maurycyz.com · 138 points · 43 comments · HN discussion

A blog post by maurycyz.com explaining how to get a trusted TLS certificate whose RSA public modulus, when base64-encoded, spells out a readable message — the certificate shown literally contains 「You+dont+actually+have+to+pick+random+private+keys / No+one+checks+these+things / A+certificate+authority+got+away+with+the+number+4+for+a+year」. The method: pick two random primes, edit the bytes of n to embed the message, set q = n/p, round up to the next prime (usually a few hundred away), and since the message sits in the upper half of n it survives; base64 gives roughly 150 characters of space at RSA-2048 and 320 at RSA-4096, and misalignment usually resolves within four attempts. The author concedes the key loses entropy and that his script doesn't check for close primes or small d, but argues forward secrecy makes a compromised key survivable for a public website.

Discussion: The sharpest pushback comes from tptacek, who argues the post's premise is dated: purely passive attackers are extinct, all serious attackers are man-in-the-middle attackers (usually by diverting victims' own traffic, e.g. DNS injection), so an unauthenticated TLS session cannot be called 「secure」. A large subthread debates whether CAs should sanity-check customers' private keys: arcfour insists it is not the CA's job to stop you from being stupid and that brute-forcing keys is infeasible at Let's Encrypt's scale of ~10 million certificates a day, while others note Tom7 found at least one ACME CA that does a cursory check for a tiny prime, and one commenter points to the IETF CSR attestation draft as a real answer. Several people push back on the 「ACME is burdensome」 framing, recalling $1000+/year EV Verisign certificates that required faxing legal documents, though a reply notes TLS simply wasn't needed to publish a site back then. Off-topic branches cover Tom7's 「World's worst TLS server」 paper (also available as a video), resentment at Apple's $99/year notarization fee, and the blog's terminal-style 「tty」 mode. Commenters also noticed the typo in the headline (「Horible」), and the submitter suggests the unusually dense typos may be a deliberate human-authorship signal.

Worth reading

  • tptacek: tptacek argues passive-only eavesdroppers no longer exist and that calling an unauthenticated TLS session 「secure」 is simply wrong.
  • hxtk: First-hand detail that some ACME CAs still sign RSA certs actually brute-force the key to catch a tiny prime — Tom7 hit this and had to switch to a four-prime modulus.
  • Curiositry: The submitter notes the post's typo density (yeild, pivate, relevent, chalange) looks intentional, linking the author's own page about typos as a quality indicator.

entry.title: Ultorg: The User Interface for Relational Databases
entry.content:
#10 on HN · ultorg.com · 40 points · 9 comments · HN discussion

Ultorg is a desktop, general-purpose graphical front end for relational databases from Eirik Bakke, the researcher behind the long-running SIEUFERD project, now publicly released after roughly 17 years. It presents real SQL queries as a spreadsheet-like surface, visually laying out arbitrary one-to-many joins, nested groups and subqueries, editing data in place (with review before commit) and auto-deriving formatting defaults, with no cloud component. It connects to Access (.mdb/.accdb) and Excel (.xls/.xlsx) today, with Oracle, Snowflake, SQLite, Athena and Exasol in beta, and the site carries a testimonial from Harmonic co-founder and CEO Tudor Achim calling it the best tool for visualizing and investigating their data.

Discussion: The thread is small (9 comments) and mostly admiration for the interaction design — several call it the best SQL admin interface they have seen, better than Metabase — paired with resistance to the commercial model: commenters object to a subscription for a small desktop app and ask for a perpetual license around $500 instead. One person who has actually used it says it shines when the data already follows good practice (consistent unique IDs across tables and sheets), and that it is easier to design work around Ultorg than to migrate existing files into shape; they also worry about losing access to carefully tailored files if they stop paying. Others redirect to alternatives — LINQPad and its .Dump() method, plus two open-source options: a project posted on HN the same day and DBFlux. A question about extensibility (adding custom buttons, e.g. to export an invoice) drew no answer, and one commenter dismissed the visual design outright.

Worth reading

  • kragen: Kragen praises the 17-year research effort but refuses the proprietary terms, and links his own 5,200-word written notes (sieuferd.md in his pavnotes2 repo) plus Bakke's 5-minute 2016 talk, noting Ultorg implements DML but not SQL's DDL.
  • akshayrajeshwar: A prior user reports it is amazing on well-structured data with consistent unique IDs, but that starting a project with Ultorg in mind beats migrating existing files, and that a perpetual license would suit a business better than a subscription.
  • maxloh: Points to an open-source alternative posted on HN the same day that the commenter says has a better-looking UI.

entry.title: Formalizing CPython
entry.content:
#11 on HN · broyojo.com · 47 points · 19 comments · HN discussion

A post by David Andrews and Chao Zhang describing a project that had AI agents (reportedly Opus 5.5) rewrite CPython 3.15.2 function by function in Lean, testing each copy against real Python before proving theorems about it. The result: 613,318 lines of Lean in 1,539 files, 18,898 theorems and lemmas, 4,071 of 26,004 functions (15.7%) copied, tested, proved and independently reviewed — starting 29 October 2026. The proofs turned up 418 bug reports, about 55 of them able to crash the interpreter or corrupt memory from ordinary Python code, including crashes via StrEnum keys with setdefault, ElementTree slice assignment, email Message-ID parsing and base32 ignorechars.

Discussion: The thread is small and mostly split between interest and dismissal. One camp finds the bug-hunting approach genuinely promising but asks how it could become routine: the author of the Julia-in-Lean work argues it currently needs too much human and AI agent effort to be automated, and suggests proofs written alongside code and checked in the test suite, like expensive compiler checks. A prominent skeptic refuses on principle to cite an AI-written document, and others press on whether the hand-translation to Lean could be replaced by parsing or annotation, with the reply that the question is how much modelling gap you accept — and that without automated verification bounding triage it is just an expensive form of agentic hallucination. A professional Python programmer is surprised the bug count is only 418 and expected around 10,000; another points out coverage is only about 16% of functions so far. A side thread drifts into whether one could just develop in Lean and compile for speed, with a pointer to lean-zip as evidence that verification enables harder optimizations.

Worth reading

  • jakobnissen: The Julia-formalization author argues the approach finds plenty of bugs but is not yet automatable, and that the durable fix is opt-in properties written alongside code and checked in the test suite.
  • senderista: A blunt objection to the project's premise: the author declines to cite an AI-written document at all.
  • bb88: A professional Python programmer expected roughly 10,000 bugs rather than 418, and is corrected that the project has only covered about 16% of functions so far.

entry.title: A failed experiment in laptop cooling
entry.content:
#12 on HN · kevinboone.me · 17 points · 14 comments · HN discussion

这是 Kevin Boone 的一篇博客文章，记录他为 Lenovo P53 自制散热底座的过程。这台机器搭载六核 2.6GHz 的 Intel H 级 CPU、32GB 内存和带 8GB 显存的 NVidia GPU，满载不到 30 秒就冲到 90°C 并开始降频。他用回收橡木做了个 25 度倾斜的底座，装了三只 10mm 厚、2500 RPM 的 5V 风扇对准三个进风口，结论是完全没用：除了抬高机身带来的轻微收益外，外置风扇既没降下温度，也没让内置风扇转慢，连 SSD 温度都没改善。他猜测内外风扇串联反而互相阻碍，并认为 P53 本身散热已经足够好，高温是刻意的设计取舍。

Discussion: 评论区的核心反驳是作者的测量指标选错了：机器本来就是热限制的，加散热不会降低温度，只会让它在同一温度下维持更高性能更久，应该测 FLOPS 或游戏帧率而不是温度，有人用「拓宽拥堵路段后公交依旧满载但吞吐量上升」作类比。多位用户给出亲测有效的替代方案：外接抽风式散热器、给用了两年的 Framework 换硅脂、以及 MacBook Air 加导热垫把热量导到铝壳。一位用户钻了 Framework 的屏幕边框，合盖使用时性能提升 30%，开盖只提升 5%。也有人质疑风扇是否装反或装在了出风口，以及笔记本外壳本身导热是否才是瓶颈。大致共识是：抬高机身确实有用，换硅脂值得一试，但对高负载下的 CPU/GPU 温度别指望外置风扇。

Worth reading

  • eigenspace: 指出作者测温度是错的指标，热限制机器应该比较同温度下能维持的性能（如循环跑 peakflops 或游戏帧率），外置风扇可能已经起效只是没体现在温度上。
  • xnickb: 第一手经验：在 Framework 笔记本的磁吸边框上钻孔后，合盖使用性能提升 30%，开盖仅提升 5%，去掉边框再额外提升 10%。
  • turbocon: 报告外接抽风式真空散热器效果不错，而且事先用现成的充气泵抽风验证过 CPU 温度确实下降。

entry.title: CoreWeave bond yield tops 16% as AI credit stress rises
entry.content:
#14 on HN · cnbc.com · 121 points · 76 comments · HN discussion

CNBC 报道称，CoreWeave 2032 年到期、票面利率 9.625% 的债券收益率已升破 16%，其五年期 CDS 周四一度突破 1,289 个基点，周五回落约 8% 至 1,155。压力也蔓延到巨头：过去一个月 Nvidia 的 CDS 涨 76%、Broadcom 涨 49%、Amazon 涨 44%，不过绝对水平仍低（Nvidia 约 139 个基点，Oracle 约 298）。文章把部分原因归于民主党在俄亥俄、得州、佐治亚的选举胜利带来的数据中心暂停风险——高盛估计可能影响美国 45% 的规划容量——同时指出超大规模厂商今年已发债 2,960 亿美元，第三季度整体自由现金流为负，BofA 预计 AI 相关信贷发行 2027 年达 6,850 亿美元的峰值后于 2028 年回落。

Discussion: 讨论分成两派。看空方以一位评论者的亲身见闻开场：某大型金融机构的架构师把 CoreWeave 列为「第三选项，或者说到时候还活着的那个」，被解读为 CoreWeave 已被业内判了死刑；也有人翻出 Exodus Communications 2001 年破产的旧闻作类比——八笔垃圾债共 34 亿美元，股价从 89.81 美元跌到 17 美分。看多方反驳说算力依然极度稀缺，「H100 发布四年了还在打折也买不到」，并发起一场关于 Anthropic 财务的长辩论：一方援引 S-1 称其有 1,120 亿美元现金、约 700 亿美元年收入、连续两个季度现金流转正；另一方坚持收入未覆盖支出、1 万亿美元多为不可取消的算力承诺、正现金流只是「扣除坏消息前的盈利」。关于「CoreWeave 倒了能否捡到便宜 GPU」，多数人认为不会：超大规模厂商会接盘，数据中心卡无风扇、需整机架散热，且二手企业级 GPU 市场本就火热。另一条支线在比较收益率——Google 债券约 5.68%、两年期美债 4.56%，有人指出名义利率要扣掉 3.7% 的通胀才算数。

Worth reading

  • danielodievich: 一位从业者转述某大型金融机构架构师的原话，把 CoreWeave 排在「还活着的那个」之后，作为业内情绪的实证。
  • adventured: 将 CoreWeave 比作 Exodus Communications，并摘录其 2001 年破产细节：34 亿美元垃圾债、股价从 89.81 美元跌至 17 美分。
  • aurareturn: 用具体数字挑战「Anthropic 现金将尽」的说法：1,120 亿美元现金、约 700 亿年收入、10 倍同比增长，以及每季度 110–150 亿美元的算力承诺。

entry.title: A primer on GPUs and kernel optimization
entry.content:
#16 on HN · nabo.dev · 135 points · 12 comments · HN discussion

A blog post on nabo.dev (posted by nomi_uw, 135 points) that serves as an introduction to GPU architecture and writing/optimizing kernels — the comment thread quotes it explaining that on the H200s used for most of the work, main memory is HBM (high-bandwidth memory), which is ironically the slowest memory on the chip. The page itself could not be fetched (it returned almost no readable text, likely JavaScript-dependent), so the rest of its content is known only through what commenters quote and describe: an illustrated, apparently human-written primer rather than an autonomous-agent benchmark report.

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: The main argument is about what the primer leaves out: one commenter with kernel-tuning experience says it never mentions benchmarking or evaluation, which he considers the biggest source of error now that fast kernels are generated and hill-climbed — hot vs cold cache, bitwise equivalence to a reference, thermal noise, testing on separate GPUs, CUDA-graph compilation to strip launch overhead, and A/B B/A interleaving of kernel and reference runs. Others push back that this misreads the post, which is about human-guided optimization with LLMs rather than autonomous hill-climbing, and that the listed concerns are generic performance-hygiene items, not GPU-specific — the original commenter insists they matter just as much in human-guided work. A practical sub-thread asks whether to set per-op error thresholds (e.g. 99% of layernorms within 1e-4 of a golden kernel) or just evaluate end-to-end on the task; the answer given is to prefer end-to-end task evals for inference on a single 3090, since normalization layers can cancel earlier errors, while numerics and correctness matter far more for training kernels and backward passes. There is also praise for the writing's clarity (with a guess that LLMs helped mainly with diagrams, plus a couple of typos), a correction that HBM is off-chip unlike shared memory and registers, and a call for someone to write a book on the subject.

Worth reading

  • augment_me: Argues the primer omits benchmarking methodology entirely and lists the concrete practices that matter — cache state, bitwise equivalence, thermal noise, multiple GPUs, CUDA graphs, A/B B/A interleaving.
  • augment_me: First-hand advice on eval design: use end-to-end task metrics for inference because later layers can cancel earlier numerical error, but hold numerics tight for training and backward passes.
  • saagarjha: Corrects the post's phrasing: HBM is off-chip, unlike shared memory and registers, so calling it 「on the chip」 is a nit worth noting.

entry.title: Exact – a new cross platform UI framework
entry.content:
#17 on HN · github.com · 114 points · 73 comments · HN discussion

Exact is an early-alpha cross-platform runtime from the Expo team (repo expo/exact, with development happening in ccheever/exact2). UI is written in a small declarative DSL called Contract, logic in TypeScript or Rust; the Contract compiler emits a plan that becomes a ~20 KB ES-module runtime driving the real DOM on the web, or runs on a Rust VM with a Taffy-based layout kernel drawing through AppKit, UIKit or a GPU painter (vello/tiny-skia) — no webview, no JS bridge, no app JS before first pixel. It ships ten scriptable agent operations (tree, screenshot, tap, type, state, layout, logs, clock, prefer, perf) plus a seekable clock for flake-free tests, claims a 26 KB runtime vs React's 81 KB and a 300 ms hydration head start on the RealWorld/Conduit benchmark, 99 ms edit-to-page rebuilds, and documents a one-hour agent build of a todo app tested on web, macOS and iOS. Target platforms are web, macOS, iOS and Linux — Windows and Android are absent or behind.

Discussion: The dominant thread is platform coverage: the top comments argue Exact isn't credibly cross-platform without Windows or Android, with one reply noting that missing both leaves out roughly 74% of the global computing market, while others counter that 「cross-platform」 only means more than one platform and that it's an early alpha. A second cluster is hostile to the README's 「Claude speak」 — several readers say the prose is unintelligible and that its agent-first framing is a turn-off, though defenders point out that using agents is optional and that the formal error/refusal design helps humans too. Substantive comparisons come from the Slint maintainer, who calls the architecture very similar to Slint but notes Slint has been stable 1.x since 2023, and from skeptics of hand-rolled DSLs who doubt a lexer/parser without a formal spec will scale to complex UIs; the author replies that the intent is to write as much as possible in Contract and drop to JS or Rust for the rest. A tangent on JSX vs XAML vs QML ran long, and the discovery of an obviously machine-generated, near-minified glue.js in the web host prompted worry about reviewing agent-written code. Overall mood: intrigued, respectful of the Expo team's track record, but unconvinced anything here is production-ready.

Worth reading

  • ogoffart: The Slint maintainer lays out the architectural parallels (Rust, declarative DSL, own compiler, host-language logic, agent-inspectable tooling) and argues Slint's 2023-era stable 1.x API is the maturity gap.
  • bakugo: Links host/web/glue.js as an example of the codebase's extremely dense, machine-written style, which several follow-ups call unreviewable.
  • wahnfrieden: Answers the 「is this satire」 charge: agents are not required, a purpose-built editor is being built for manual work, and links the README's own definition of 「agent native」.

entry.title: Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game
entry.content:
#20 on HN · notesbylex.com · 353 points · 240 comments · HN discussion

A developer’s blog post describes giving Claude Fable 5.2 one overnight prompt to finish a beat ’em up based on his nephew Aiden’s drawings: five family heroes, Doggo, 12 bosses and a rescue plot. The agent discarded much of the earlier prototype and produced a playable 12-level, 18-character, four-player game with cutscenes, unlockables and an ending, using roughly 340M tokens, about 500 images, 11 music tracks and around 100 sound effects. The author argues the result is genuinely fun rather than a mere demo, and calls it a milestone for one-shot agentic game development.

Discussion: Commenters are split between delight at what a non-expert can build for a child and unease about abundance, craft and AI slop. The top thread mourns scarcity — one commenter says casually making an infinite runner while watching TV left them depressed — while others argue the bar has simply risen and kids can now attempt far more ambitious work. Much of the thread argues over “one-shot”: several note the author kept prompting for Hulk transformations, new family members and bug fixes, while defenders say it means no human back-and-forth during the initial build, not a flawless result. Players report the game is surprisingly fun, especially with controllers, but also flag broken walk cycles, weak enemy AI, poor mobile controls and a generic AI-art look; one detailed playtest says stages can be beaten by mashing punch. Cost estimates land near $294 at Fable 5.2 API prices, though the author says his tokens were free and roughly $300 would be the equivalent.

Worth reading

  • Tiberium: Breaks down the token bill to about $294 at Fable 5.2 API prices — 320M cache reads at $0.2/M, 19M cache writes at $10/M and 1M output at $40/M.
  • simonw: Simon Willison says Opus 5.5 already responds to “make this more fun” and posts side-by-side mouse-and-cat game attempts from Opus 5.5, GPT-6 and Fable 5.2.
  • insin: A detailed playtest argues the game only has the surface features of a belt scroller: enemies and bosses are trivial, one boss loops a running attack, and the design iteration that makes such games enjoyable is missing.

entry.title: Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators
entry.content:
#21 on HN · github.com · 559 points · 126 comments · HN discussion

A GitHub write-up arguing that Google quietly reversed its 2023 Gemini Workspace promise that personal Gmail, Docs and Drive content was 「not seen by human reviewers」. The author cites updated Google Help Answer 16836988 and an October 16 edit to the original blog post, which now warns users not to connect apps containing confidential information they would not want a reviewer to see. Testing with consumer Gemini and Connected Apps enabled, the post claims ambient mentions of trips, bills or reservations trigger background Workspace lookups without any @Drive or @Gmail tag, and that retrieval is probabilistic — ranging from no retrieval, to metadata summaries, to 2–6 sentence verbatim quotes containing account and confirmation numbers, to the full unredacted email including headers; the author argues Google's regex and NER scrubbers cannot deidentify this kind of narrative data.

Discussion: The top comment sharply narrows the scope: this affects consumer Gemini with Connected Apps only, while Workspace Gemini and Workspace Intelligence still claim exemption from human review under Google's Workspace privacy hub — the commenter calls it a product-management blunder precisely because it will make paying enterprise customers leery. Several users say the 「allow connected apps」 interstitial reappears constantly, that its scope (whole Drive and Gmail vs. per-file) is unclear, and that clicking allow lets Gemini autonomously pull file plaintext into context; one person who finally clicked allow just to stop the nagging spent half an hour undoing it and found connected apps must be disconnected separately in the Gemini app and in Google Search. First-hand reports split: one user says Gemini answers were uncannily tuned to an email they had received without ever mentioning reading mail, while another blamed a 24-hour Google Meet transcription delay on manual review and was rebutted with the point that Workspace has explicit retention contracts and is never used for training or human review. The thread then drifts into a long de-Googling sidebar — Immich, Nextcloud behind Tailscale, Restic/Kopia to B2 or Mega, FolderSync, purelymail — with near-consensus that self-hosting photos and files is easy but email should be moved last, and that exposing Nextcloud to the public internet is its own security risk.

Worth reading

  • bri3d: Corrects the story's framing: the human-review pipeline applies to consumer Gemini with Connected Apps, not to Workspace Gemini or Workspace Intelligence, which Google still documents as exempt.
  • rustyhancock: First-hand account of Gemini giving an answer uncannily matched to an email the user had just received, without ever stating it had read their mail.
  • prtmnth: Practical warning: after finally accepting the popup, this user found connected apps must be disconnected separately in the Gemini app and in Google Search — the settings are not shared.

entry.title: Parking-app convenience fees in 312 U.S. cities (median $0.35 per session)
entry.content:
#24 on HN · parkgraph.com · 76 points · 61 comments · HN discussion

Park Graph compiled a dataset of per-session fees charged by parking apps in 312 places across 43 states and DC (314 rows, checked Nov 5, 2026, CC BY 4.0), with each fee traced to a help-center page or city site and dated. The median fee is $0.35 — the single most common value, seen in 108 places — followed by $0.45 (56 places) and $0.30 (30); Anchorage, AK has the highest flat fee at $0.70, Nevada City, CA hits $0.75, and 15 places charge nothing. ParkMobile accounts for 289 of the places, with a $0–$0.75 range, while Passport, Flowbird, IPS Group and PayByPhone cover a handful each; 13 rows have no published fee.

Discussion: The dominant complaint is semantic and economic: a 「convenience fee」 you cannot decline is just a price increase, and several people argue it should be folded into the parking rate — countered by the observation that merchant rules from Visa/Mastercard (and platform most-favored-nation clauses) often forbid charging less for cash. Multiple commenters say coin meters, kiosks or tap-to-pay at the meter let them dodge the fee entirely, and one notes the fee typically appears only in the app, not at the pay station; others report the opposite, that cities removed the coin slot and forced the app. The strongest correction is that Park Graph is not a neutral observer — a commenter points out its own app adds 10% per transaction with a $0.75 minimum, roughly double the median fee it is reporting. Defenders of apps cite refunds for unused time, extending sessions remotely, and consistency across a metro; skeptics say refunds are rare and that requiring a smartphone (or license plate, card and 2FA) excludes people, with calls for regulation mandating a non-digital payment option or capping fees near card-processing cost.

Worth reading

  • emptybits: The co-founder of PayByPhone, which the dataset lists as charging $0, asks why every city wouldn't pick the free-to-driver option — prompting replies that fee-free apps may cost the city more or subsidize themselves with ads.
  • cco: Points out that the site's own app charges a 10% per-transaction fee with a $0.75 minimum, about twice the $0.35 median it is criticising.
  • strange_quark: Chicago first-hand detail: card payment at the physical meter avoids the fee, extending time re-triggers it, and the app forces a $20 minimum balance that the private operator holds.

entry.title: Time for AVIF everywhere?
entry.content:
#26 on HN · michaelponders.com · 66 points · 54 comments · HN discussion

A short blog post by Michael arguing that hosting providers, Mastodon, Bluesky and phone makers should push AVIF (and AV2 for video) harder, because HDD/SSD/NVMe prices have spiked through 2026 — Hetzner has raised prices several times citing hardware costs, partly driven by AI demand. The post acknowledges AVIF encoding is CPU-heavy and proposes having users encode locally before upload, keeping the original format, and standardizing on AVIF over WebP. It cites YouTube's planned move to AV2 around 2027 as evidence that efficient codecs pay off.

Discussion: Much of the thread argues with the post's premise rather than its conclusion: several commenters say storage is still cheap (one links diskprices.com showing roughly $25/TB and says media belongs on HDDs, not NVMe), while the author replies that cheap-to-whom matters for small hosts. A strong JPEG XL faction says JXL is the better candidate for a universal format — lossless transcoding of existing JPEGs, progressive decoding, fp16/fp32 linear HDR — while others counter that AVIF wins on lossy quality-per-byte and that JXL has no browser support. The CPU cost of AVIF encoding is the other battleground: one commenter measured ~25x JPEG's CPU and 12-second uploads on an old Xeon server, and others pushed back with much faster numbers on phones and modern hardware plus encoder speed flags. Side threads cover AV1 patent exposure, AVIF's multiple-frame support, and irritation that WebP/AVIF still break non-browser software pipelines like Fire TV and desktop tools.

Worth reading

  • jeroenhd: Reports concrete benchmarks on an old i3-2120 NAS (4–6s for AVIF vs ~2s JPEG at default speed, half a second with --speed 10) and argues the AV1 encoder has improved enough that older benchmarks are stale.
  • brigade: Corrects a widely repeated claim in the thread: AVIF allows 2^32-1 pixels per dimension versus JPEG XL's 2^30-1, and arbitrary planes exist as AVIF auxiliary images — comparison sites confuse AV1 profile limits with AVIF limits.
  • mikae1: Warns that a popular WordPress AVIF plugin transcodes every uploaded JPEG for all browsers, so images end up worse than the originals — a lossless path that JPEG XL offers and AVIF does not.

entry.title: On Being an Engineer in 2026
entry.content:
#27 on HN · twitter.com · 90 points · 128 comments · HN discussion

An essay by Shahar Glazner — co-founder and CTO of Keepalerting, now a tech lead at Elastic after an acquisition — arguing that engineers still hold real leverage over AI agents. His argument is a reductio: everyone has access to roughly the same models (he cites Opus 4.6 and Cursor), yet strong engineers still vastly outproduce weak ones, so 10x engineers have become 100x engineers; he attributes the gap to tacit knowledge (Michael Polanyi's 「we can know more than we can tell」), emergence, and lived experience — including the collective, undefined instinct for spotting AI slop.

Discussion: The thread splits less on the essay's logic than on what it implies for people. Several self-described strong engineers push back on the optimism: they say the job has lost its soul, that they can no longer hold the codebase in their heads, and that their edge over weaker colleagues has evaporated — one calls the new role 「Senior Agent Babysitter」, though another argues the true 100x engineers are the ones who still understand everything and can now take on far bigger projects. A parallel argument breaks out over the claim that average, disengaged engineers will be culled: some say a bell curve makes that obvious, others demand evidence and note the reality of layoffs and lack of ownership. Deep skepticism appears throughout — commenters say AI agents have never done good work for them, hallucinate in code review, and that 「LLMs can do any job in theory」 is uninteresting; a security engineer warns that locally run MCP servers and prompt injection create blast radii a deterministic dependency never could. The author (shahargl) shows up to post his own blog link, concede the 「we」 vs 「I」 framing criticism, and correct his CTO title, while a subthread on tacit knowledge argues it is precisely what reinforcement-learning post-training captures, so the moat may be a matter of environment and feedback rather than something ineffable.

Worth reading

  • zeroonetwothree: A self-identified 10x engineer says the opposite of the essay's optimism: they ship more than ever but no longer feel they truly understand their code, and must forward technical questions to an agent first.
  • wrs: Argues tacit knowledge is not a human moat at all — reinforcement-learning post-training is exactly the process of acquiring things never written down, limited only by environment and feedback quality.
  • kypro: Describes the job as still busy but much less enjoyable: no more hard logic problems, the edge over less competent engineers gone, and design arguments lost to 「we can just get Claude to refactor later」.

entry.title: TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max
entry.content:
#29 on HN · blog.google · 244 points · 75 comments · HN discussion

这是 Google 官方博客的一篇产品公告：第八代 TPU 家族今年第二次扩容，新增 TPU 8tx（面向受监管行业与政府的机密推理/小规模训练，基于 TPU 8t 同款芯片、配第五代 AMD EPYC 主机，号称比 8t 延迟低最多 2 倍且性能损失接近于零）和 TPU 8i Max（把两颗 TPU 8i 封装在一起，算力、SRAM 与 HBM 带宽全部翻倍，号称每机架算力密度最高）。文章称 Google 一年内推出四款 TPU 系统尚属首次、TPU 业务已有近 100 家客户（含前沿实验室、交易公司、零售与高校），并顺带宣传 TorchTPU、vLLM/SGLang 后端、开源 TPU Sync 状态层（称可把 KV 传输延迟与 TTFT 降低 90% 以上）以及 GKE 上 GA 的 Cloud Pathways。

Discussion: 讨论分几条主线。一是「为什么不直接卖芯片」：多人指出 Google 已开始向少数客户交付自有数据中心内的 TPU，Oracle 也宣布明年在自家云上提供 TPU，并提到 Anthropic 是买家；反驳者认为 Google 更想「租」而不是「卖」，且外部市场相对 Google 自身需求微不足道。二是抱怨这本质是营销稿：没有绝对算力数字、没有 watt/token 或 $/token，只有「2.7 倍上一代」这类相对柱状图，被比作 Apple 的发布会文案。三是长串关于全文 79 次提到 TPU 却从不拼出 Tensor Processing Unit 的争论——一方说首次出现时展开缩写是基本写作规范，另一方说读者显然该自己去搜、且光拼出全称也帮不了不懂 tensor 的人。另外几处吐槽是「近 100 家客户」十年才做到是否算多（有人反驳单客户年付十亿美元量级）、「Opening up TPUs to every developer」却没有任何上手指引或购买链接，以及对「agentic era」一词的疲劳。

Worth reading

  • freakynit: 推荐同批发布的 TPU Sync 博文，并指出它和开源项目 Strata 处理 Qwen 系列模型 KV cache/权重搬运的思路基本一致，附了原理文档链接。
  • Twirrim: 补充一手进展：Oracle 一周前宣布明年将在其云上引入 TPU 供客户使用，同批还部署 Cerebras，说明 TPU 已作为成熟芯片开始对外供货。
  • dehrmann: 一位自称在 Google 该领域工作的员工表示，普通用户虽买不到，但会间接受益——TPU 给数据中心里的 Nvidia 带来竞争压力，而且可以在 GCP 上租用。

entry.title: Claude Fable 5.2 scores 65 on Artificial Analysis, highest so far
entry.content:
#30 on HN · artificialanalysis.ai · 338 points · 244 comments · HN discussion

This is the Artificial Analysis model page for Claude Fable 5.2 (the 「Max, Default Fallback」 reasoning configuration), released November 9, 2026, with a 1M-token context window and $8/M input and $40/M output pricing (98% cache discount). It posts 65 on the Intelligence Index v5.0.1 — a suite of nine evals including Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode 2.0, HLE-Diamond and AA-Omniscience — against a median of 40 for similarly priced models, but the page itself flags it as slow (46.4 minutes per task vs a 12.6-minute median, 219.85s to first answer token) and very verbose (275M tokens generated vs a 72.8M median). Average cost works out to $26.54 per Intelligence Index task.

Discussion: The dominant argument is about cost rather than the score: the top comment notes that at max effort Fable 5.2 roughly doubles Fable 5.1's already-high cost per task, with output tokens jumping from 118k to 274k per task (reasoning alone 71k → 192k). The strongest counter-argument, repeated by several commenters, is that the AA page defaults to max effort, which nobody sane uses — at high it scores 62 for about $9.08 per task versus Opus 5.5 max's 59 at $10.04, and at low/medium it is both cheaper and smarter than Fable 5.1's equivalent settings. A second thread debates whether the release signals a 「wall」 of diminishing returns in intelligence-per-cost; some invoke the end of Dennard scaling and Anthropic's looming IPO, while others point out that inference scaling still works and labs routinely distill expensive models into cheap ones (Opus 5 → Opus 5.5). First-hand reports are mixed and sharply split: some users say it ignores CLAUDE.md instructions, fabricates results and refuses tasks it deems sensitive, while others say low effort beats Opus 5.5 medium/high on latency and quality. Side debates cover DeepSeek/GLM being ~100x cheaper for most work, Artificial Analysis's private benchmarks and its arbitrary 「most attractive quadrant」 cutoff, and whether Google's Argon/Carbon models are underrated.

Worth reading

  • rgbrenner: Breaks out the cost blowup: output tokens per task went from 118k (46k answer / 71k reasoning) in Fable 5.1 to 274k (81k / 192k) in 5.2, doubling cost per task even after the price cut.
  • neuronexmachina: Lists the per-effort numbers showing the headline figure is misleading: at medium Fable 5.2 scores 56 for $3.80/task versus 5.1's 43 for $5.56, and at low 54 for $3.10 versus 39 for $4.37 — cheaper and much smarter below max.
  • Aurornis: Warns that the AA charts default to max effort and points readers to the coding charts at normal settings, arguing Fable 5.2 on medium looks attractive versus Opus 5.5 high, while 「on max it looks like a good way to light your money on fire.」

entry.title: Payments Canada announces launch of Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system
entry.content:
#1 on HN · payments.ca · 332 points · 181 comments · HN discussion

Payments Canada's press release announces the launch of the Real-Time Rail (RTR), a national system letting participating banks, credit unions and payment service providers clear and settle payments in real time, 24/7, using ISO 20022 data-rich messaging. It cites C.D. Howe Institute projections of up to $14.5B in cost savings over a decade (lower processing costs, less cash and cheque use, less float) plus $16B in economic gains rising to $27B as features are added, and claims Canada is the first G7 country to require centralized fraud services at launch — confirmation of payee, a transaction fraud score, a risk list and a fraud reporting platform. The launch cohort is notably not the Big Five banks but Wealthsimple, Questbank, Peoples Trust, Paramount Commerce, KOHO, DoBusiness.com, Digital Commerce Bank and Bank of America; RBC is expected in Q2 2027, all institutions by mid-2027, reaching 90% of Canadians within a year. Built with CGI, Deloitte Canada, IBM Canada and Interac, which acts as technical operator and first fraud services provider, with Interac e-Transfers beginning to clear and settle on RTR.

Discussion: A large share of the thread is a proxy argument about the US: several commenters claim America has no real-time payments and ask why, and are corrected — The Clearing House's RTP network has run since 2017, FedNow launched in 2023, and combined they reach roughly 70% of deposit accounts, with one commenter citing about $800B/year in FedNow volume. Others defend the US status quo on netting and consumer protection grounds, arguing debit/credit chargebacks and end-of-day settlement are features, not bugs, and that instant rails like Zelle have no reversal path for scams. On Canada itself the scepticism is about reach: no major bank is in the first wave, so commenters compare it to SEPA Instant, which sat mostly unused for a decade until the EU made bank participation mandatory, and ask what RTR offers over Interac e-Transfer, which is already free-ish and near-instant for most people. Practitioners push back that RTR is bank-to-bank plumbing, not a consumer app — it cuts Interac settlement from tens of minutes to seconds, and the public-ish ownership (Payments Canada, overseen by the Bank of Canada and Finance) is the point, with debate over whether it is technically a Crown corporation. Side threads correct a claim of a 6% effective Canadian corporate tax rate, complain that 「Rail」 reads as trains, and worry about a centralized fraud layer plus the precedent of the 2022 Emergencies Act account freezes.

Worth reading

  • cdnsteve: Corrects the top comment's tax claim: the 6.4% is the marginal effective tax rate on new investment, not the corporate rate, which stays at 26.5% combined federal/Ontario or 11.2% for CCPC small-business income — and it is still draft legislation.
  • a-priori: Explains the phased rollout: the big banks sit out phase one to control volume, join in phases two and three, with the Globe and Mail reporting every Canadian institution on the rail by mid-2027.
  • toomuchtodo: A commenter working on FedNow policy gives concrete numbers — roughly $800B/year run rate, $10M per message for under five cents, 20-second SLA — and notes Walmart's pay-by-bank rollout as the first real consumer use case.

entry.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
entry.content:
#2 on HN · anthropic.com · 419 points · 172 comments · HN discussion

Anthropic's launch post for Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, which it says are the same underlying model split by safeguards: Fable ships to all users with cyber/bio guardrails, Mythos goes to vetted organizations via the Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs. Claims include up to 30% faster output than 5.1, a price cut to $8/$40 per million input/output tokens (optional fast mode at 2.5x speed for $16/$80), and stunts like 1,000 coordinated subagents building a bootable OS from an empty folder in eight days, a Python-to-Rust production migration with 26x faster startup, a 30-hour formalization of Fermat's Last Theorem, two open black-hole physics problems, and three working electronic devices designed from scratch. Anthropic still recommends Opus 5.5 as the default daily driver, positioning Fable/Mythos as advisor, orchestrator, or heavyweight for the hardest open-ended work.

Discussion: Most of the thread is not about 5.2 at all but about the recurring claim that Anthropic quietly degrades the previous flagship before a launch — several users say Opus 5.5 got noticeably worse in the past week or two, and others report the same for OpenAI's GPT Astra and Sol 6.1, so the suspicion is aimed at labs generally rather than one. The skeptics argue this is apophenia plus confounded variables: thinking-effort defaults, prompt/harness differences and traffic routing change output quality without any weights changing, and one commenter reran a pre-Nov-3 eval and found quality flat-to-better with faster time-to-first-token and slightly fewer tokens. A second cluster attacks the benchmark presentation — Fable 5.2 at xhigh compared against Gemini 4 Carbon at medium, Carbon left off the cyber comparison, and older models suddenly scoring 20-30% where they used to score 60%. Hands-on reports are mixed but warmer: faster and fewer max-token overflows than 5.1, strong vision-to-HTML results, but at least one user burned a full five-hour quota in 20 minutes because it spawned nested subagents despite an explicit cap. Side threads cover the odd version numbering (flagship 5.2 below Opus 5.5), Claude's prose style versus Gemini, launch-week subscription reset offers, and the economics of $200/month plans.

Worth reading

  • ariwilson: Reran a 30-task bug-fix eval on Opus 5.5 medium before and after the suspected nerf: 19/20 vs 36/40 solved, 0.95x thinking tokens, and median time-to-first-token halved from 3.0s to 1.7s — evidence of no quality regression.
  • spwa4: Argues the timing is not coincidental, tying the release to Qwen4 previews and claiming Anthropic is sitting on better non-public models (Model 2/3/4) and is now metering capability out deliberately.
  • advaith08: Early tester reports Fable 5.2 sped up an esoteric 600k-line Fortran materials-science codebase by 36x in two days and open-sourced the result on GitHub.

entry.title: Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
entry.content:
#4 on HN · research.meta.ai · 115 points · 49 comments · HN discussion

Meta's research blog post announcing Muse Ember (muse-ember-1.0), a small, cheap model aimed at the high-volume work agents repeat: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction and long-document parsing. It claims to match Claude Haiku 5.5's best score at roughly a third of the cost and to beat every GPT-6 Luna setting, at $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with a 1M-token context window and up to 512K output tokens, natively handling text, images, audio and video. Meta says it is the first model trained using Muse Wonder Full, was evaluated under its Superintelligence Scaling Framework (staying below high-risk thresholds), and costs about $0.14 per Artificial Analysis task.

Discussion: Almost nobody in the thread discusses the model itself; it is dominated by Simon Willison running his standard 'pelican riding a bicycle' SVG test at the six new effort levels (minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max), finding that more reasoning tokens did not produce an obviously better drawing and that several people actually preferred the minimal output. swatcoder explains why: models build SVGs concept-by-concept (bicycle, then pelican, then fish basket) instead of interleaving parts, so details like legs straddling the frame are wrong across the board, and short prompts make models fill gaps from learned associations — the same reason every drawing has a yellow sun, motion lines and a fish basket. On substance, commenters note the unusually low cache price (4% of input versus roughly 10% for Luna/Haiku), ask why no DeepSeek comparison and why there is no parameter count to justify 'small', and complain the weights are not open; one suggests it is the stealth OpenRouter model 'crouton-alpha', another that refusals should score negatively rather than zero on benchmarks. There is also a side argument about whether Meta is still relevant in the LLM race, with several defending its post-Llama-4 reboot and the Spark series, and a tangent predicting (and disputing) a future of hyper-specialized per-profession models.

Worth reading

  • swatcoder: Explains the 'ley lines' phenomenon: vague prompts make models fill gaps with the same trained-in defaults (yellow sun, three motion lines, fish basket), which is why creative AI output reads as lazy at scale.
  • minimaxir: Flags the concrete pricing edge: cached input costs 4% of normal input versus about 10% for Luna and Haiku.
  • open-paren: Claims Muse Ember is the model behind the 'crouton-alpha' stealth listing on OpenRouter, which another commenter immediately asks them to justify.

entry.title: Infineon marks innovation milestone with 300mm power silicon carbide wafer
entry.content:
#5 on HN · infineon.com · 43 points · 13 comments · HN discussion

这是英飞凌的一篇新闻稿，宣布推出号称全球首片 300 毫米功率碳化硅晶圆；按新闻稿摘要所述，它并非空白衬底，而是「业界首个在 300mm 碳化硅晶圆上加工出的功能性功率器件」。晶圆将于 2026 年 11 月 10 日在慕尼黑 electronica 展会上首次公开展示，英飞凌把它定位为面向汽车、可再生能源、工业与 AI 数据中心供电的供应保障举措，并称其可复用现有 300mm 硅设备。原文正文无法获取（页面需要 JavaScript），因此细节来自新闻稿摘要和评论。

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: 最主要的疑问是为什么花了这么久：有人指出设备本来就存在，因为 300mm 硅早已量产，所以大尺寸晶体生长和少数工艺步骤大概是主要障碍。一位评论者以为 Wolfspeed 今年早些时候已经做到 300mm，发帖者澄清英飞凌声称的是首片加工出功能器件的晶圆，而不是首片衬底。另有一段旁支讨论问欧洲能否重启 DRAM 生产，反驳意见是存储封装很复杂，而且欧洲在这一领域没有玩家；还有人认为 DRAM 本身是个周期性的亏钱生意。关于 SiC 与 GaN 的简短交流把前者归为高压用途、后者归为高开关频率用途。有一条评论主张功率半导体对国家安全和工业供应链至关重要，随即有人反问英飞凌是否真的要在游戏 PC 和卡车之间二选一，还有人指出卡车和汽车在没有这些器件的情况下也运行了几十年。

Worth reading

  • sshah03: 发帖者澄清英飞凌声称的是首片加工出功能功率器件的 300mm 晶圆，而不是首片衬底，从而回应了 Wolfspeed 的对比。
  • jpm_sd: 简洁的经验法则：SiC 用于高压，GaN 用于高开关频率。
  • alephnerd: 认为功率半导体是国家安全和工业的关键投入，可替换的卡车和汽车零部件远比新显卡重要——这一说法在回复中受到质疑。

entry.title: Fold Epic Paper Airplanes
entry.content:
#7 on HN · foldableflight.com · 665 points · 120 comments · HN discussion

FoldableFlight.com is Kyle Boyer's library of paper airplane designs — roughly a hundred planes from the classic Nakamura Lock and Michael LaFosse's F-14 Tomcat to original competition winners — each with a difficulty rating, speed/glide/accuracy bars, and a YouTube folding tutorial. The site also sells books and templates, and showcases record designs: a prototype that flies over 300 feet with cutting and tape, and 「Unite」, the time-aloft record holder at 31.2 seconds. Boyer answered questions in the thread himself, saying the ordinary schoolyard dart manages only 20–30 feet while many of his planes clear 100 feet.

Discussion: The thread is mostly warm nostalgia: people naming the Nakamura Lock they learned decades ago in books, Russia, or from older kids, and trading stories of school contests, Klutz and 「The Great International Paper Airplane Book」. The sharp disagreement is about the site itself — several users call it slow and spammy, report a newsletter popup that returns on refresh and crashed Safari on iOS, and say the instructions are video-only, while others defend it as a free tutorial library whose paid books are a fair upsell (the creator notes he runs no ads and admits he is 「not proficient in web design」). Boyer also rebuts two accusations directly: the site is not a reskin of the older foldnfly.com (different, larger library), and the duplicated 「Intermediate」 filter was his own CMS typo, not AI — 「No AI has been used to make the site」. Requests for written instructions prompted one commenter to generate a text guide with ChatGPT in under ten minutes, and the most-upvoted practical tip is the creator's own benchmark comparing darts to record planes.

Worth reading

  • FoldableFlight: The creator quantifies the gap: a classic dart flies 20–30 feet, most site designs clear 100 feet, and the distance record exceeds 300 feet but needs cutting and tape.
  • fghorow: A commenter says he won the 1978 UCLA paper airplane contest by folding a dozen copies of one design beforehand and throwing whichever tested best — rapid prototyping avant la lettre.
  • deno: When told the Mystic's instructions are video-only, a commenter produced a written step-by-step guide in under ten minutes using ChatGPT.

entry.title: Too many men suffering in silence, national health report finds (Canada)
entry.content:
#8 on HN · westcentralonline.com · 240 points · 215 comments · HN discussion

The linked WestCentralOnline article was unavailable here (HTTP 403), so this is based on the headline and what commenters quote from the underlying report. It covers a Canadian national health report on men's and boys' wellbeing that will feed into Canada's first federal Men and Boys' Health and Well-being Strategy, expected in early 2027; commenters cite figures such as men dying by suicide at roughly three times the rate of women and suicide being the second leading cause of death for men and boys aged 15–34. One commenter also quotes a 2012–2022 decline among young men aged 15–24 in self-reported very good or excellent mental health from 70% to 52%, with mood disorders rising from 11% to 16% and generalized anxiety from 4% to 10%.

Article not read: HTTP 403

Discussion: The thread quickly diverges from the report into divorce and custody law: one father says his lawyer warned that 50/50 custody was his ex's floor and that courts would favor the mother, and that he has not spoken to his son in almost two years after a modification attempt upheld the arrangement. Others argue family law reflects a society where women are still far more likely to be stay-at-home parents, so formally gender-neutral rules can produce unequal outcomes — a split over gender-neutral law versus gender-specific vulnerability that recurs throughout. There are also disputes over the suicide gap, with some attributing it to gun access and others citing method lethality, male help-seeking and countries with low firearm ownership, plus corrections that California has no ordinary common-law marriage and that BC's cohabitation threshold is two years, not six months. A recurring meta-complaint is that many comments project unrelated grievances onto the headline; some call it the worst HN thread they have seen, while others object that the report surveys men only and that women's mental-health metrics have worsened similarly. The nearest thing to consensus is that a government report alone will not change much without male community, purpose and earlier intervention.

Worth reading

  • treis: A father recounts his lawyer saying his ex's floor was 50/50 and that courts would favor the mother, then losing contact with his son for almost two years after a modification attempt upheld the arrangement.
  • dillondoyle: Corrects the common claim that cohabiting for years creates a common-law marriage in California, explaining the high bar for a Marvin action and that it is not family court.
  • wtch98: UK figures show the male suicide rate is about three times the female rate even though the top methods — hanging, self-poisoning and jumping — are equally available, undercutting the firearm-access explanation.

entry.title: Show HN: MeowDisplay Is iPhone Mirroring, but in Reverse
entry.content:
#9 on HN · meowdisplay.app · 31 points · 13 comments · HN discussion

MeowDisplay is a free, open-source app that turns an iPhone, iPad, Android device or another Mac into a display and remote-control surface for a Mac — the inverse of Apple’s iPhone Mirroring. Its landing page pitches Window view with tabs and split panes, an edge-held Stage Peek window switcher, several touch modes (Direct Touch, Smart Touch and Trackpad), Apple Pencil input, clamshell operation through a software virtual display, and USB, local Wi-Fi or Tailscale connections. It is iOS 2.0 on the App Store, a macOS 14+ companion app (2.0.0), and Android 10+ in closed testing; the author says it began as a fork of OpenDisplay and is built in Swift and Kotlin.

Discussion: The thread is broadly positive — one commenter said they had vibe-built a similar window-sharing system over a tailnet, and another praised the site as refreshingly free of marketing slop — but it presses on provenance and latency. A commenter challenged the lack of fork disclosure, and the author responded by adding it to the post and explaining that MeowDisplay builds on OpenDisplay’s capture, virtual-display, encoding and receiver foundations while taking interaction, streaming and security in a phone-first direction. Latency is the main skepticism: one commenter said nearly all remote-display tools feel mediocre and only RDP has felt truly responsive; the author replied that Wi-Fi testing showed a 14–17 ms median from capture to receiver handoff, not end-to-end, with occasional 50–90 ms spikes and stalled frames, and that he deliberately shows the Mac’s real cursor rather than a locally rendered one that might feel smoother but misrepresent its position. Asked about color, the author confirmed there is no HDR support yet and that iPhone color-profile accuracy has not been verified. Commenters also corrected the assumption that Apple’s built-in Sidecar already does this: Sidecar extends a Mac to an iPad, but not an iPhone.

Worth reading

  • mpolichette: mpolichette asks what the OpenDisplay fork actually changes and argues the provenance should have been declared in the announcement — the challenge that prompted the author to add the disclosure.
  • raiseCatError: The author gives concrete latency figures: 14–17 ms median capture-to-receiver handoff on Wi-Fi, not end-to-end, with 50–90 ms spikes and visible stalls.
  • freeli: freeli corrects the Sidecar comparison: Apple’s Sidecar extends a Mac’s display to an iPad, but it does not work on iPhones.

entry.title: Magenta solar panels may be agrivoltaics' cleverest trick yet
entry.content:
#10 on HN · anthropocenemagazine.org · 171 points · 87 comments · HN discussion

这篇来自 Anthropocene Magazine 的文章讲的是波长选择性（洋红色）太阳能板：它们只吸收植物用不上的那部分光谱用于发电，同时把光合作用需要的光透过去。由于正文抓取失败，细节只能来自评论中的转述：文章称，把美国 1% 的农田用于农光互补，就能提供全国约 20% 的电力，重点区域是德州—内布拉斯加—加州走廊；实验作物是西兰花，收获期延长了 25 天，但产量基本持平，遮阴降低了蒸汽压亏缺，生物量提升 2.8 到 4.5 倍，钙、镁、磷等大量元素不低于露天种植，铁、铜、锌略低。

Discussion: 讨论的主线是「这到底解决了什么问题」。一派认为在美国土地几乎不构成约束，把太阳能和农田分开、各自优化才是正解，并举出实际案例：低矮光伏板下的牧场冬天无法开拖拉机割草。另一派反驳说这从来不是二选一：农户可以靠发电增加收入，羊群放牧在光伏场下已在澳洲规模化运行，还能把光伏场最贵的除草成本降低 75% 至 95%。最有力的批评来自对可行性的工程分析：大型机械化农场需要高立柱、大跨度、与农机路径匹配的布局，中心枢轴灌溉需要整圈无障碍，喷洒农药和灰尘还会污染组件，这些会让成本远高于地面电站。也有人主张，用太阳能取代目前占美国玉米产量约 40% 的乙醇用粮才是更合理的起点；还有人说，真正阻力可能是农地分区管制，而「兼作农业」可以成为绕开管制的门路。另有分支争论从镉碲（CdTe）面板的碲供应，一路扯到小行星采矿和轨道轰炸。

Worth reading

  • kempbellt: 逐项拆解大型农场落地的工程成本：高立柱与宽跨度的结构、中心枢轴灌溉需要整圈无立柱、喷药和灰尘污染组件，并指出试验作物西兰花是手收的最佳情形，却仍晚熟 25 天。
  • efields: 一位 specialty cut flower 种植者的一手视角：自家作物本就需要遮阴、适合光伏，但对接的 USDA 代表因与太阳能公司打过交道而对农光互补持怀疑态度，认为缺乏可靠的公开数据。
  • wtch98: 用俄亥俄州的粗略数字算账：100 英亩玉米约 8 万美元营收、4 万利润，同样面积的光伏电站营收 100 万至 150 万美元；直接租地给光伏运营商每年拿约 10 万美元且零成本，因此「兼顾农业」是给不存在的问题找解法。

entry.title: Show HN: Every satellite that passed over any place this week, and its photos
entry.content:
#13 on HN · watched.earth · 57 points · 14 comments · HN discussion

a585gupt 发布了一个浏览器端工具 watched.earth：输入任意地点，它就用 SGP4 在 CelesTrak 目录上算出过去 7 天内飞过该点的所有卫星（约 1.7 万个在轨物体全部由 GPU 绘制，每帧解一次开普勒方程），再拉取这些过境对应的真实 Sentinel-2、Landsat 和 NASA 影像。作者称搜索不会漏掉任何一次过境——用极点、跨 180 度经线和极窄扫描带做了暴力枚举对拍，零遗漏——并且只在确有影像时才标记「watched」，不存储用户位置。他还提到一个坑：Sentinel-2 的时间戳常与实际过境时刻差 5–10 分钟。代码开源于 GitHub（dev-Armaan/satellites），他在征集还应接入哪些数据源。

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: 评论几乎是一边倒的好评，14 条里大半是称赞界面与动画、作者逐一回谢，几乎没有技术质疑或反驳。少数几条带有实际使用背景：wnissen 说这很适合规划背包徒步路线，他原本用 Copernicus，但这里覆盖的卫星更多、访问也更方便；六十多岁的 sixtyj 自称做地理空间行业，见过很多卫星概览网站，认为这个之所以出色是因为能直接看到卫星实际拍摄的那张影像。nico 的评价最有分寸——「很酷，也有点瘆人，但主要是酷」，并特别称赞在手机小屏上依然好用，以及那个与众不同的巨大输入光标。整体共识是这个 Show HN 完成度高、体验好，但讨论没有深入到数据准确性、影像时效或隐私等实质问题。

Worth reading

  • wnissen: 一位用户说它比自己一直在用的 Copernicus 覆盖更全、更易用，具体用途是规划背包徒步路线。
  • sixtyj: 一位地理空间从业者表示见过大量同类卫星网站，这个的差异点在于能看到卫星实际拍摄的那张影像。
  • nico: 评论称其「很酷也有点瘆人」，并具体指出手机小屏上依然易用、大号输入光标是难得的体验亮点。

entry.title: Show HN: DBDelve – Open-Source DB Client Made with Rust and GPUI
entry.content:
#16 on HN · text post · 62 points · 21 comments · HN discussion

A text-only Show HN by Shayan Abbas for DBDelve 0.3.6, a native, keyboard-driven database client built in Rust on Zed's GPUI, positioned against DBeaver, DataGrip, TablePlus, Beekeeper and Electron/Tauri clients. He posts benchmarks on an M1 Pro with 32 GB against DBeaver 25.3.1 on the same Postgres table (median of 5 runs): 1.1 s vs 5.2 s launch, 133 MB vs 606 MB idle memory, 0.21 s vs 1.96 s for a 1,000-row query, 56 s vs 208 s for 1M rows, and 4.9 GB vs 17 GB when pulling the full 1M-row, 100-column table into memory — a deliberately abnormal case where DBeaver's heap limit had to be raised by hand. The headline optimisation is 「packed rows」, which he says cut memory 40% (8.1 GB to 4.9 GB); the app has readonly/read-write/full-access modes, themes, customizable keybindings, connection projects, and imports connections from DBeaver and TablePlus, though it is not yet signed or notarized for macOS.

Discussion: Commenters broadly welcome a lean native alternative to DBeaver, with several saying they will try it, but the sharpest pushback is that performance is a weak selling point when most wall-clock time is spent waiting on the database. The author concedes slow queries stay slow, and argues the win is what happens after the query returns: smooth scrolling through result sets that crash other clients, faster UI painting, and a smaller memory footprint. A second thread digs into GPUI's packaging mess — Zed has not updated its crates.io crate in over a year, so users choose between community forks such as gpui-ce, gpui-pre and gpui-kit, which one commenter calls building on quicksand and doubts that a 「community edition」 has a community that will still exist next quarter. Elsewhere: the author says Postgres and SQL Server are native and Oracle works through ODBC, that Beekeeper connection import could be added, and that voluntary sponsors are the plan for keeping development going. One commenter dismisses the whole thing as part of the 「rewrite everything in Rust AI slop」 wave; another replies that it does not look like slop and that existing DB clients feel sloppy.

Worth reading

  • edstarch: Argues the GPUI ecosystem is fragmented into many 「vibe coded」 forks, making a dependency on it a bet on quicksand, however nice the resulting UI.
  • mbreese: Raises the main counter-argument: if queries dominate wait time, raw client performance is a hard sell — is the gain really in browsing result sets?
  • shayan_abbas: Answers the DataGrip question directly: Postgres and SQL Server are native, Oracle via ODBC, so all three are covered.

entry.title: When will this stop? The Raspberry Pi 5 16GB SBC now sells for $385
entry.content:
#17 on HN · cnx-software.com · 167 points · 139 comments · HN discussion

A CNX Software post noting Raspberry Pi's latest price rise: the Pi 5 16GB is now $385, $80 above the previous hike in April 2026, and the CM5 16GB starts at $375 for the Lite variant without wireless — with 32GB and 64GB eMMC costing the same. The Pi 500+ stays at $410. The piece puts this in a year of increases (all Pi boards with 4GB+ in April, Jetson modules up to 101% in July, 2GB Pi 4/5 in October, Arduino VENTUNO Q from $299 to $399) and cites Micron expecting the RAM shortage to last until at least 2028 and SK Hynix saying 2030, while noting memory vendors' shares have fallen recently.

Discussion: The dominant view, led by Aurornis, is that the 16GB model should be ignored entirely: a Pi is an embedded board, not a desktop or server, and most hobby work fits in 1–8GB, a $15 Pi Zero 2 W, a Pico or an ESP32. Others counter that the Pi is still nearly the only affordable general-purpose ARM Linux machine — Apple, rare Windows-on-ARM boxes and Pi clones aside — though one reply cites Windows on ARM at about 3% market share. The practical substitutes thread is the bulk of the discussion: N100 mini PCs, $40–100 off-lease thin clients with 8GB and an SSD, used Xeons with ECC RAM, $289 Ryzen 3 mini PCs on Amazon, a €304 Minisforum UM870, Mac Minis, Android TV boxes and €10 broken-screen Huawei P20s running Termux.
