A key correction: aleph_minus_one notes that reballing more RAM onto a Pi is blocked by firmware, linking the Jeff Geerling write-up and Raspberry Pi forum/EEProm issue threads — which splits the thread again, with some calling it greed and others saying it protects against arbitrage and counterfeit boards. On duration, vannevar predicts a crash within 12 months when the data-centre bubble bursts, which airspresso calls cope, arguing compute demand will absorb everything built.

Worth reading

  • aleph_minus_one: Points out that swapping in more RAM via reballing is blocked by Raspberry Pi firmware, with links to the forum thread, GitHub issue and Jeff Geerling's post on the RAM lockdown.
  • wmchen: First-hand warning that three Huawei P20 Pro units all developed swollen batteries within two years, and replacements swelled again in 6–9 months — a direct caution on the cheap broken-screen-phone suggestion.
  • Aurornis: Aurornis argues the real entry point is the $15 Pi Zero 2 W with more RAM than the original Pi, and says he owns a 16GB model but wishes the 16GB SKU had never been announced.

entry.title: What is malloc doing, anyway?
entry.content:
#19 on HN · benmandrew.com · 176 points · 38 comments · HN discussion

A hands-on walkthrough that builds a toy allocator to explain how glibc malloc works: brk/sbrk grow the heap, chunk headers sit before returned pointers, free lists allow reuse, and neighbouring free chunks are split and merged. It measures an empty syscall at 575 ns and finds malloc(16) about 22.7x faster than sbrk(16), then covers page faults, RSS, trimming the top of the heap, and using mmap for allocations of 128 KiB or more. The result is explicitly a teaching allocator, not a production one.

Discussion: The thread splits in several directions: some readers use the article as a springboard to stack-only and lexically scoped languages such as Goose, with some calling Goose exciting and others challenging its benchmark claims and pointing out its preallocated stacks and internal pool allocator. Several commenters push back on the article's framing, saying the toy allocator is far slower than glibc — roughly 20–150x — and that the material is essentially an undergraduate systems-programming exercise; others recommend mimalloc and writeups on dlmalloc, tcmalloc and jemalloc. A side argument concerns brk: some call it obsolete and prefer mmap, while others defend it as a useful pedagogical bridge into kernel memory management. One subthread corrects a claim about musl's brk return value by distinguishing the raw Linux syscall from the libc wrapper. There is rough agreement that malloc is mostly userspace bookkeeping over coarse kernel mappings, even if C is not truly low level.

Worth reading

  • i2talics: Argues the 「malloc has so much overhead」 takeaway is misleading: glibc malloc is 20–150x faster than the toy implementation, and production allocators heavily optimize frequent small allocations.
  • roelschroeven: Corrects the brk discussion: musl's raw Linux syscall returns the current break on failure, while the glibc wrapper converts that to the familiar 0/-1 result.
  • senderista: Recommends mimalloc as a reasonably approachable codebase for studying modern allocator design, noting it uses neither brk nor boundary tags.

entry.title: Zebkit – Chromium as an embeddable library
entry.content:
#20 on HN · github.com · 96 points · 36 comments · HN discussion

A GitHub project by ikey4u (Riiiiichard) that packages Chromium's Content layer, Blink, V8, PDFium, FFmpeg, Skia and HarfBuzz as a single library — libzebkit.so.1, Zebkit.framework, zebkit.dll — that a host app links into its own process, keeping its own main(), event loop and windows, with a C API plus Rust, Python and Node-free JS bindings. It is built from Chromium 157.0.8103.38 with 60+ patches, exports about 7,490 C functions from bundled dependencies under zebkit_vendor_* (SQLite, BoringSSL, ICU, zstd, dav1d, Opus), and claims versus Electron 45.2.1: 34% smaller, 2.3 s cold start instead of 6.6 s, 29% less page memory, and a native in-engine Playwright API that is 3–10× faster than Playwright over CDP (a click in 2–5 ms instead of 33).

Discussion: The thread's first question is simply how this differs from CEF, and the author answers with a candid list: easier install (cargo/pip), your own event loop, a plain C API, offscreen rendering, a full PDFium API and native Playwright — but CEF wins on maturity, platform coverage (mac Intel, ARM Linux) and missing pieces like printing, Web Bluetooth and Widevine. Skeptics are blunt, calling it 「slop」 and AI-generated (a long author comment was auto-flagged as AI-written, which one commenter defended as an agenda-driven accusation), and several push alternatives instead: Sciter's author notes his DLL is 18 MB and starts in ~60 ms versus zebkit's 171 MB and 2.3 s, while others say WebKit/WPE is the genuinely lightweight embeddable option. Security is the recurring technical objection — a shared library in-process seems to forfeit Chromium's sandboxing — but the author and a clarifying reply say the sandboxed renderer helper processes, Mojo channel and shared memory are all still there; he also confirms the library is shared but per-app runtime memory is not. The most concrete practitioner feedback comes from a CEF shipper who warns about notarizing helpers and FFmpeg/Blink license compliance, prompting the author to admit the release archives ship no license or notice files; separately, a GoNix developer got a ~20 MB cgo proof of concept running on macOS within the thread. A side note argues Google already heuristically detects Chromium embedders and blocks Google sign-in, so popularity would invite the same treatment.

Worth reading

  • netshade: A developer shipping CEF in production (ZShot) details the real distribution pain — notarizing every helper binary on macOS and choosing the right GPL/LGPL FFmpeg build — and the author concedes the archives contain no license files.
  • c-smile: Sciter's author gives a concrete counter-datapoint: an 18 MB Windows DLL and ~60 ms cold start, roughly 10× smaller and 38× faster to start than zebkit's 171 MB and 2.3 s.
  • prologic: A GoNix developer reports a working proof of concept within the thread — a ~20 MB Go binary on macOS via cgo, despite there being no official Go binding yet.

entry.title: Going back two years on Hacker News is like entering another, better universe
entry.content:
#21 on HN · news.ycombinator.com · 187 points · 100 comments · HN discussion

这个链接并不是一篇文章，而是 HN 自己的首页存档页面（news.ycombinator.com/front?day=2024-11-08）：2024 年 11 月 8 日的 30 条上榜故事，包含分数和评论数——Mitochondria Are Alive（638 分）、多个新的 macOS 沙箱逃逸漏洞（582 分）、稳定 Obra Dinn 的 1-bit 抖动（527 分）、FDA 提议下架口服去氧肾上腺素（303 分、508 条评论）、Rust 用于分词与解析、Show HN 的 Asterogue 和 Draw.Audio 等。发帖者提出的隐含主张是：那一页读起来比今天的首页更好——AI 内容更少，话题更杂。除了排名之外，该页面没有正文。

Discussion: 讨论把怀旧情绪一分为二。许多人认同原地踏步的感觉：抱怨“红迪化”、讽刺挖苦和 AI 内容泛滥已经淹没其他一切，有人说他们现在要一天屏蔽 100–200 个帖子，或者干脆离开去 lobste.rs。反对意见同样强烈：HN 的官方指南明确要求不要发“HN 正在变成 Reddit”的帖子，并链接了大约九条同类抱怨——其中一些已有近 20 年历史——而 dang 本人指出，2025 年 11 月 8 日，甚至一个月前的存档首页看起来也差不多，这种感知早在网站得名 HN 之前就存在了。关于 AI 还有更具体的分歧：一位自称支持 AI 的知名评论者承认，首页上 AI 内容多到令人遗憾，而且很难干预，因为 AI 对技术的影响可与“互联网”比肩；另一位则反驳说，默认首页 25 条里只有约 5 条是 AI 内容，这还算合理。实际建议包括给帖子加标签或过滤（unslop.news、一个自动隐藏标题含 AI 关键词帖子的浏览器扩展）、用 PGP 签名来证明作者身份（被批评者认为行不通），以及逐渐转向邀请制社群。也有不少人认为，真正的问题是政治、愤怒和“空洞的冷笑”越来越多，而不是 AI 本身。

Worth reading

  • dang: dang 指出，一年前和一个月前的首页看起来相似，而且这些抱怨早在网站还叫 Hacker News 之前就已存在，并链接到 2007 年的一条评论。
  • tptacek: tptacek 自称是软件开发中 AI 的坚定支持者，但他同意首页上 AI 内容多到令人遗憾，并说这不容易修复，因为 AI 对技术的影响可与互联网相提并论。
  • pc86: pc86 引用了 HN 的官方指南，其中禁止发“HN 正在变成 Reddit”的抱怨，并链接到九条约 20 年前的此类评论。

entry.title: Pigshell: Unix the Web
entry.content:
#22 on HN · pigshell.com · 41 points · 16 comments · HN discussion

Pigshell v0.6.4 is the linked page for an old experiment in bringing a Unix/Plan 9-style shell to the web, apparently exposing online resources in a filesystem-like way. The page itself would not render without JavaScript, so the submission provides little direct detail; commenters fill in the picture by describing it as a web shell built around 9p-style access to web resources.

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: The thread initially drifts into browser security: Chrome shows a generic 「Not Secure」 warning, but commenters correct the diagnosis — the site redirects from HTTPS to plain HTTP, so there is no certificate for Chrome to inspect. A side argument compares Chrome and Firefox over HSTS bypasses, with one side praising Firefox for loading the page anyway and the other noting Chrome’s hidden thisisunsafe escape hatch. The more substantive discussion is about Plan 9, 9p and mapping the hierarchical web onto a filesystem, with references to Plan 9’s webfs, a mkfifo.com pipe-building project and IBM CMS pipes. Several commenters like the style and the idea but see little practical use; the project’s GitHub repository has not been updated since 2015, which also explains some of its rough edges.

Worth reading

  • pred_: Corrects the SSL complaint: the certificate is fine, but the site redirects from HTTPS to HTTP, leaving no certificate for Chrome to report on.
  • somat: Connects Pigshell to Plan 9’s webfs and notes that webfs actually fetches web resources rather than mapping HTML’s hierarchy onto the filesystem.
  • mbreese: Points out that the GitHub repository was last updated in August 2015, giving useful context for the site’s age and security warnings.

entry.title: Cryptocurrency lawsuit: Ethereum Foundation required "suicide pledge"
entry.content:
#23 on HN · denverpost.com · 128 points · 134 comments · HN discussion

A Denver Post report on a lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado by Kayleen Fulton, a Boulder resident fired from the Ethereum Foundation after organizing resistance to a 38-page document called 「The Ethereum Foundation Mandate」. Sent to roughly 250 staff in March, the mandate gave employees until Monday to commit to its principles or take severance and leave; page 11 carried an illustrated 「Source Seppuku License」 vowing that authors and maintainers would 「take his or her own life with a sword」 if they failed to uphold its pledges. About 80 employees voted to remove the clause, but leadership kept it (moving it into an illustration), co-executive director Bastian Aue called it 「part of the artwork」, and Fulton — who had just been diagnosed with cancer — was fired along with the colleague who co-organized a letter signed by 53 staff; she earned $195,000 and sues for disability discrimination, retaliation, FMLA interference and related claims.

Discussion: The thread splits sharply on whether a joke in an employment document is harmless or disqualifying. One camp (embedding-shape, glerk, andai, anonymous908213) argues the anime illustration is self-evidently not literal, is unenforceable anyway, and functioned as a culture-fit filter — with one commenter calling the plaintiff a 「litigious loser」 for suing over an obvious joke. The larger camp insists that anything in a signed document is part of the document: nostrademons recounts asking about the Crockford License's 「Good, not Evil」 clause only to be told 「Google is Evil」, making the point that vague terms are left to a jury, and several others argue that if a clause is meaningless you strike it rather than trust the employer. Commenters note the bind — you cannot simultaneously claim the mandate is so mission-critical that dissenters must leave and that parts of it are jokes — and that 「we put jokes in our contracts」 invites scrutiny of every other provision. Side threads cover jury duty disillusionment, whether severability clauses save the rest of the document, the DAO hard fork as evidence the foundation does exercise authority, and corrections from practitioners: tromp notes the difficulty bomb was a PoW-to-PoS migration tool retired in 2022, and tancop argues real Ethereum control sits with execution and consensus client teams, not the foundation.

Worth reading

  • nostrademons: A former Google engineer's first-hand story about the Crockford License's 「Good, not Evil」 clause illustrates why vague or jokey language in a legal document is a real liability — and why a jury, not the author, gets to interpret it.
  • Heliodex: Links the actual published mandate at ethereum.org/foundation/mandate so readers can check the seppuku text themselves, with follow-ups noting it survives in the HTML version, just without the art.
  • tancop: A detailed correction on Ethereum governance: the foundation has influence but little hard power, and execution/consensus client teams decide what enters a hard fork — the EF deliberately declined to build its own consensus client.

entry.title: Try Gleam
entry.content:
#25 on HN · nchagnet.eu · 90 points · 100 comments · HN discussion

博主 nchagnet 的一篇热情推介，对象是 Gleam——一门语法简洁的函数式语言，既能编译到 BEAM（Erlang VM），也能编译到 JavaScript。他围绕三个「吉祥物特性」展开：|> 管道操作符、use 模式（用于处理回调、避免回调嵌套）以及尾调用优化（因为 Gleam 根本没有循环，需要递归）。他还介绍了代数数据类型、process.spawn_unlinked 和进程消息传递，并主张 OTP 的 actor 与监督者模型可以替代他团队所用那种偏重、昂贵的 Kubernetes 控制器与 Pod 式配置；同时指出 Gleam 能在前端与后端共享类型。文末他列出了一些保留意见（原文在这一处被截断）。

Discussion: 讨论主要分裂成两个方向，另有一条很长且容易跑题的支线。一个使用 Claude 的开发者说，他用 Claude 维护一个前后端都用 Gleam 的全栈应用，几乎不用手写代码，并称赞它的类型安全和共享类型，能免去全 TypeScript 技术栈所需的大量配置；另一些人则质疑，既然让 AI 写代码，为什么要选冷门语言。这里出现了纠正：有人引用腾讯的一项 agentic 编码研究（Elixir 表现第一），指出这项研究给冷门语言分配了更简单的问题；回复者则建议参考 OpenAI 的 SQLite 复现实验，它显示差距不大。对实际语言的抱怨包括：与 Elixir 互操作要靠 mix_gleam 外加自定义绑定，而不是原生互操作，这被拿来与 Clojure 无缝使用 Java 作对比；缺少自动柯里化（作者澄清，Gleam 确实支持 _ 部分应用，只是不支持柯里化）；工具链有用，但没法只跑单个测试，只能跑整套。评论中占篇幅最大的一条支线围绕社区行为准则及语言主页上的政治表态，有人认为这是拒绝采用这门语言的理由，其他人（包括作者）则反驳说，日常使用中从不会遇到这些，准则只是标准的反骚扰表述。

Worth reading

  • sczi: 认为常被引用的腾讯 agentic 编码研究不可信，因为冷门语言拿到的是更简单的问题，并指向 OpenAI 的 SQLite 复现研究作为更现实的对比。
  • whalesalad: 主张 Gleam 缺少 Elixir 原生互操作是大问题，将它与 Clojure 无缝使用整个 Java 生态的能力作对比。
  • nchagnet: 作者纠正了一条常见误解：Gleam 支持 _ 部分应用，能与管道配合使用；缺少的只是自动柯里化。

entry.title: Children of Men: The future is a mirror for the present
entry.content:
#28 on HN · reactormag.com · 121 points · 94 comments · HN discussion

A Reactor essay arguing that Alfonso Cuarón's 2006 Children of Men — loosely adapted from P.D. James's 1992 novel — is both great science fiction and a pointed political allegory, and has only grown more resonant in the twenty years since release. It traces the production history (Paul Chart's draft, then Mark Fergus and Hawk Ostby, then Cuarón and Timothy J. Sexton, who pitched it as 「Y tu mamá también, but in the future」), the deliberate refusal to explain the global infertility, the narrowed focus onto refugees and internment camps in a 2027 Britain that has closed its borders, and the filmmaking craft — Battle of Algiers-style documentary realism and long takes — that the piece credits for elevating it.

Discussion: Almost nobody argues about the film itself: the thread is near-unanimous praise, with people describing it as one of the best films of the century and swapping favourite long takes — the car ambush, the immigrant-camp battle, the ceasefire scene — and correcting each other that the famous 「single take」 is really several seamlessly stitched shots. The debate instead drifts into demographics: several commenters say the infertility premise stopped feeling like science fiction once real fertility rates fell, which sparks a long argument over whether the crisis is economics (housing, education, opportunity cost of time), culture and later/rarer partnering, or a global trend that only bites in affluent places — with pushback that 171 countries were below replacement in 2024 and that 「a handful of countries」 is wrong. Others object that fertility has collapsed in poor and rich countries alike, that crisis-driven baby booms are a myth, or that below-replacement fertility is desirable given earlier overpopulation fears; a few note that no government policy has reversed the trend. Separately, some readers complain the essay ignores the film's heavy Christian/nativity symbolism, which they say is close to being the point, and one long comment recalls seeing it in Australia with zero buzz and walking out shellshocked.

Worth reading

  • Joeri: Says podcast and data research point away from both 「children are precious」 and male-fertility explanations, and toward later and less frequent partnering; notes every government attempt to reverse the trend has failed.
  • haunter: Kills the alternate-ending rumour: the rescue ship was always there, there are no alternate versions — though a cinematographer reportedly argued for the fog-only ending during production.
  • thrownawaysz: Flags that the essay never mentions the film's inverted Christian allegory, which is barely subtle on screen and even more explicit (a makeshift baptism) in P.D. James's novel.

entry.title: Fun things to do with your VM/370 CE machine – Fun with big computers
entry.content:
#30 on HN · rbanffy.github.io · 92 points · 27 comments · HN discussion

Rui Carmo (rbanffy) walks through booting VM/370 Community Edition — the patched, license-unencumbered descendant of IBM's VM/370 Release 6, capped at one CPU and 16M of “storage” — with a single Docker command (rbanffy/vm370ce, port 3270) plus the x3270 emulator. From there it's a hands-on tour: log on as CMSUSER with password CMSUSER, edit PROFILE EXEC in the EDIT editor, write and run a BASIC hello world, compile a FORTRAN IV (G) program, and discover its output landed in a file called FT06F001 before FILEDEF redirects ddname 6 to the terminal. He also wonders aloud why the first character of each Fortran output line vanishes.

Discussion: The thread is largely old-mainframe hands trading lore: CMS Pipelines, REXX and XEDIT macros, minidisk letters as a reorderable command search path, sparse minidisks that let you put 100 MB on a 5 MB disk, and a trick for reading file-mode-0 files by patching the access command. The article's Fortran mystery gets authoritatively corrected: JdeBP explains the missing character is the Hollerith H field descriptor in FORMAT (the string is read as “ELLO WORLD”), not just line-printer carriage control — and that the author is doubly wrong because the first column of formatted output also controls vertical spacing; wrs points to “Fortran carriage control” as the search term and recalls a student printing 132 underscores with overprint control until the printout fell off the printer. Several commenters push back gently on the Unix-centric framing, wishing for more non-Unix OS coverage, while practitioners note z/VM 7.5 keeps these rituals alive commercially — coolkil says a US z/VM career is plausible but Europe has little demand, and suggests KVM if you want Linux on a modern mainframe. Others report the beginner's wall: jsrcout fired up Hercules and had no idea what to do, which is exactly the gap the guide fills.

Worth reading

  • JdeBP: JdeBP delivers the definitive correction on the dropped first character — it's FORTRAN's Hollerith H field descriptor swallowing the 'H' in HELLO, compounded by carriage-control column one — and links native REXX implementations (Regina, ObjectREXX) for Unix.
  • j_seigh: j_seigh lists period CMS hacks from inside IBM: REXX XEDIT macros, minidisk search-order linked lists, sparse-file abuse, and a diagnose command that dumped 3270 screens (with field attributes) as documentation markup.
  • wrs: wrs gives the right search term, “Fortran carriage control” (+ overprint, 0 double-space, 1 form feed), and a story of using 132 overprinted underscores to cut a printout off inside the printer.

entry.title: Starship Flight 15 on 11/13 plans to catch both booster and ship
entry.content:
#31 on HN · spacex.com · 146 points · 101 comments · HN discussion

The linked SpaceX mission page was not readable, but a commenter pasted the mission plan: Flight 15 is targeted for Nov 13, 2026, with a 75-minute window opening at 4:45 p.m. CT, and would be the first attempt to return both Super Heavy and Starship to the launch site for catch. The ship would coast for more than 22 hours and about 14 orbits at roughly 275 km while deploying 26 Starlink v3 satellites, about 52 t, or around half of Block 3’s advertised 100 t capacity.

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: The main argument is over the light payload: tristanj calls 26 Starlink v3 satellites a disappointing half-load for Block 3 and worries about Raptor 3 thrust shortfalls, while others reply that 52 t would still be the third-heaviest orbital payload ever, that SpaceX is deliberately avoiding extra variables during a test campaign, and that risking fewer $1.2M satellites on a failed insertion is prudent. The exchange sharpens when tristanj asks for a technical reason rather than vibes; testing22321 says outsiders are only speculating and points to SpaceX’s record of iteration, while imtringued argues Starship has abandoned Falcon 9’s make-it-work-first philosophy. On the catch itself, commenters note that the same chopsticks handle both vehicles, and the unusually long 22-hour coast is seen as a deliberate boil-off and data-gathering exercise with multiple deorbit bailout points. Later subthreads drift to whether SpaceX is approaching a launch monopoly through vertical integration and its Falcon 9 wind-down, to HLS and Artemis cost and schedule criticism versus SLS, and to a side argument about orbital data centers, where one commenter says space cooling is physically doable and another argues the economics and terrestrial bottlenecks are the real issue.

Worth reading

  • metalman: Pastes the mission plan: Nov 13, 2026, a 75-minute window from 4:45 p.m. CT, about 275 km and 14 orbits over more than 22 hours, and the first dual booster-and-ship catch attempt.
  • m4rtink: Says Raptor 3 is cleaner and lighter but cannot safely run at higher thrust than Raptor 2, so system-level performance estimates assuming more thrust need to be revised.
  • skew-aberration: Offers the strongest critical counterpoint: Starship has received $3B of a $5B HLS contract while being optimized for commercial LEO, and compares its cost and schedule with Saturn V and six lunar landings.

entry.title: KetchUp – Open-source SketchUp alternative built with Rust and WebGPU
entry.content:
#1 on HN · ketchup3d.github.io · 426 points · 116 comments · HN discussion

链接页面现在把该项目标为 BenchUp（标题仍写作 KetchUp）：这是一个免费的 MIT 许可 3D 建模器，面向木工和家具设计，用 Rust 编写，可在桌面浏览器中运行，需要 WebGPU 或 WebGL2 支持，也有 Windows、macOS 和 Linux 原生版本。它支持画线、推拉、精确尺寸输入、组和组件，模型自动保存在本地，可导入 SketchUp .skp 几何体（不含材质和场景），导出 OBJ/STL，没有账号和云存储。它的卖点是「用 SketchUp 的工作流程来规划一张架子、桌子或工作台，然后再动手制作」。

Discussion: 讨论大体分成两派。一些人称赞这是对 SketchUp 的用户友好工作流程的继承，因为这个流程变得越来越难以获得：Trimble 砍掉了免费桌面版，取消了永久许可，并把开发重心转向网页版，许多人抱怨每年要支付数百美元订阅费。另一派主要的怀疑意见来自直接试用：画一个矩形就会提示你给对象命名，推拉需要先选取面，默认不吸附到网格，不支持触控板，菜单栏行为也不对——批评者说，它只达到 80% 的完成度，缺少真正让 SketchUp 易用的最后打磨，而且「AI 写不对，大概也修不对」。更广泛的争论是，用 LLM 构建自己的工具是否值得：支持者说，花几个小时就能得到一个可用的工具；反对方说，工具会变成项目本身，只靠一个人维护会陷入大量的边界情况，一个类似 Lightroom 的 vibecoded 克隆做了 5000 次提交后仍然漏洞百出。另外还提到了功能缺口和替代品：SketchUp 的 3D Warehouse 资源库被认为对普通用户是必不可少的价值，FreeCAD、Blender、SolidCraft、hew3d 和 ingetrazo 也被提到是替代品，而且作者已经同意改名，以避免与 KetchUp、SketchUp 发生商标纠纷。

Worth reading

  • LinguaBrowse: 详细的第一手可用性批评：推拉需要先用箭头工具选中，默认不吸附到网格，每个矩形都要求命名，菜单栏「File」「Edit」「View」的行为也不对——结论是，它没通过成为 SketchUp 所需的打磨测试。
  • sergio: 一位 SketchUp 老用户认为，对偶尔做家居改造的人来说，关键的缺失功能是 3D Warehouse——在建模时直接从 SketchUp 里下载现成的电视、家具、椅子模型，比单独拥有一个建模器方便得多。
  • dcoulmbe: 作者 dcoulmbe 回应商标担忧，表示会把这个应用改名为 Dovetail3D；另一位评论者随后指出，仓库现在显示的名称是 BenchUp。

entry.title: Unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world
entry.content:
#2 on HN · shubs.io · 278 points · 92 comments · HN discussion

这是一篇由 Shubs（infosecau）与 Sam Curry 合著的安全研究文章，作者为保护厂商而以「the automaker」代称，但文中视频与评论基本认定是 Toyota/Lexus。作者反编译安卓 App，顺出一条链条：车牌 → VIN（澳洲各州注册查询站）→ subscriber GUID → 用户在 ForgeRock OpenIDM 身份平台上的邮箱等 PII；又从厂商前端 vendor JS bundle 里找到硬编码的 OpenIDM 管理员凭据。真正的突破在于 WAF 只挡 /openidm/，用 /static%2f..%2fopenidm/ 路径遍历（由 GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra 跑了约六小时找出，作者手动试过 /XUI%2f..%2f 被 403）即可 PATCH 任意用户密码，再配合可跳过多因素验证的 IDTokenROPC 换取移动端 token，从而远程解锁/上锁、鸣笛、启动引擎。

Discussion: 评论区的第一条主线是「猜车」：多人从视频里的后视镜、大灯和引擎盖认出第五代 RAV4（XA50），并据「both brands」推断是 Toyota/Lexus；也有人从开源客户端 lexy 的 API 文档反推，还有人拿视频里管理面板配色当线索。第二条主线是威胁模型之争：一派认为这属于需要数周、多人协作的定向攻击，普通窃贼只会拉车门或砸窗，车主不必恐慌；另一派反驳说真正的危害是批量泄露的客户 PII，作者自己也只是顺带提到，而数据泄露正是多数网络犯罪的源头。关于披露，有人质疑文中没写是否上报，随即被指出 Sam Curry 的配套文章（samcurry.net/forgerock）说明两个厂商约两小时内修好并轮换了凭据；也有评论引用该文，指出此前已攻破 Honda、Nissan、Hyundai、Ford、Porsche、Kia、Subaru 等，而这两家此前从未被远程控制过。第三个话题是「联网车本身该不该存在」，从「我 2022 年的车是最后一辆新车」到「远程启动、诊断、事故呼救很有用，问题在控制权而非联网」两派对峙。整体共识大致是：错误很蠢（前端硬编码凭据、生产与非生产共用凭据），但安全本身确实很难。

Worth reading

  • defrost: 引用 Sam Curry 配套文章原文：上报后两家厂商约两小时内修复并轮换受影响凭据，不过完整攻击链只在美国账号和车辆上验证过；他还怀疑原文有过一句解释为何隐去厂商名的「忍者编辑」。
  • jaza: 指出厂商其实没自研认证或密码学、大部分做得不错，只违反了两条无需专家也能执行的基本规则——硬编码凭据（尤其在前端代码里）和跨环境共用凭据，而前者本可用静态分析强制检查。
  • avianlyric: 称把文中出现的 API 拿去问 LLM，它依据开源第三方客户端 lexy 的文档不到两分钟就判断出是 Toyota/Lexus，并亲自核对无误，觉得这有点吓人。

entry.title: I'm not convinced the AI bubble exists
entry.content:
#4 on HN · matteoraso.github.io · 217 points · 300 comments · HN discussion

A blog post by Matteo Raso arguing that the case for an AI bubble is weaker than the internet assumes. His core claims: the roughly $5 trillion in AI spending is mostly one-off data-centre capex rather than operating cost; Anthropic's S-1 shows $2.08 of revenue per $1 of compute and revenue growing from $41M in 2023 to $16.3B in the first half of 2026; Alphabet, Meta and NVIDIA trade at P/E ratios in the 20s; and a lack of moat doesn't prevent profit, as with the chicken sandwich wars. He also argues AI firms have barely tapped public markets and debt, and dismisses local/open-weight models as something ordinary users will never bother with.

Discussion: The strongest pushback is that the article's central premise is wrong: GPUs and networking gear have a 2–5 year useful life, so infrastructure is recurring capex, not a one-off — one commenter recalculates the debt payback over 5–6 years instead of 20 and gets roughly 4x the required revenue. Commenters also attack the $2.08-per-$1-compute figure as cherry-picked (it excludes training and other costs, and Anthropic's losses are reportedly widening), and note 16% yields on CoreWeave/neocloud bonds as the market's own verdict. Several argue the P/E defence is circular because the earnings are themselves funded by debt and equity from AI investors, and that open-weight models plus DeepSeek-style price competition will strip the labs' margins. Defenders of the piece — including a camp arguing bubble talk is motivated by nostalgia and 「SchadenFraud」 — say the utility is undeniable and that bubbles are about timing and overcapitalisation, not whether the tech works; even those concede that a correction with real casualties among model-layer companies is likely while the hyperscalers survive.

Worth reading

  • keybored: Argues the piece never engages the actual bear case, links Dan Luu's point-by-point rebuttal of Ed Zitron, and notes you can believe AI is useless yet still fear the fallout of a bubble popping.
  • wmf: Corrects the 20-year amortisation: most of the cost is GPUs, not buildings, so spreading it over 5–6 years quadruples the revenue needed to service the debt.
  • vannevar: Turns the article's own lines against it — 「if you ignore the cost of building cars, they are also very profitable」 — and argues the P/E earnings are circular, derived from debt- and equity-funded AI spending rather than end-user demand.

entry.title: Chimera Vocal Synth
entry.content:
#5 on HN · chimera-vocal-synth.vercel.app · 183 points · 25 comments · HN discussion

A browser-based 3D vocal synthesizer (the linked page is a JavaScript app, so only the title and comment reports describe it): you drag anatomical parts — glottis, tongue, false vocal folds, mouth — to shape a vocal tract and hear the resulting vowel or overtone. Commenters describe it as a modern, three-dimensional successor to Pink Trombone, and the submitter points to the source at github.com/jamesondh/chimera-vocal-synth.

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: The dominant reference point is Pink Trombone: several commenters call it the obvious ancestor, and one traces the lineage back to Bell Labs' Voder, demonstrated by Homer Dudley in 1939. The most interesting reports are from throat singers — one learned to throat-sing to put his baby to sleep and is now trying to reproduce his own mouth and throat shapes in the synth; another says that by tuning the false vocal folds he got a genuine Khoomei overtone and a decent Sygyt, though he could not find the Kargyraa range. A trans commenter raised voice-affirmation training, singing and language learning as uses, and got some hostile downvotes before others thanked him for the perspective; the thread's tone is otherwise playful. Practical notes: the submitter posted the GitHub repo alongside an earlier tweet, one user reports only noise on a phone with the engine loading past 100%, and another says it works on iOS.

Worth reading

  • EA-3167: A throat singer reports reproducing a real Khoomei overtone by adjusting the false vocal folds, and a passable Sygyt, but no Kargyraa — strong evidence the model is anatomically credible.
  • ks2048: Traces the idea back nearly a century to Homer Dudley's 1939 Bell Labs Voder, with a video link.
  • nmstoker: The submitter links the GitHub repo (jamesondh/chimera-vocal-synth) and an earlier HN post about the project.

entry.title: Declarative Dragging
entry.content:
#6 on HN · declarative-dragging.github.io · 497 points · 63 comments · HN discussion

A UIST '26 paper and project page by Joshua Horowitz, Andrew Blinn and Jeffrey Heer describing D2, a model-driven approach where an author specifies which future model states dragging an element should lead to, and the engine speculatively renders those states to view trees, extracts the dragged element's position in each, and synthesizes a smooth drag interaction. Behaviors are composable, with modifiers for floating, snapping and transitions, implemented in a library called Dragology for SVG on the web. Demos include twisted trees (order-preserving maps between trees), a permutation lab with linked parallel representations, and a revived 2022 math game prototype.

Discussion: The thread splits between admiration for the demos and a long argument about how hard drag-and-drop really is. A front-page war story about a non-technical PM who could not believe 「just drag-and-drop」 would take a week set off a debate: several commenters (including one who did it in 2010-era browsers and another who built a JS CMS) insist the state machine, ghost element, stacking contexts, touch vs mouse and browser quirks genuinely justify the estimate, while a gamedev commenter argues most apps need only hit-test-on-down and hit-test-on-up and that devs over-engineer beyond business requirements. On the research itself, skeptics ask what is novel given Sketchpad, ThingLab, Juno-2 and Apparatus (which already did speculative rendering), and note D2 requires you to supply the valid transforms rather than deriving them; others worry speculative rendering will blow up with 1000 drop targets or many elements, which a commenter counters by noting lifting one of n items yields only n next states. Andrew Blinn answers as author: transitions are history-independent, which rules out springy/physics-y animations for now, and continuous numeric parameters are handled by a 「vary」 operator. Several people praise the incidental discovery of the Hazel programming environment, and one commenter reports a working HTML prototype built on Solid using the FLIP technique.

Worth reading

  • gobdovan: Argues the paper omits Sketchpad, ThingLab and Juno-2 from its lineage, credits Apparatus for prior speculative rendering, and notes D2 does not discover valid transforms itself — inverse rendering would have been the more interesting research.
  • edflsafoiewq: Reverse-engineers the twisted trees demo into a concrete recipe: write the UI as a function of continuous parameters, compute the cursor's barycentric coordinates between the three nearest drop zones, and interpolate the parameters between their values at those zones.
  • disconcision: A commenter says they already have a basic HTML version running on Solid, using the FLIP technique for measurements, though generalizing it across existing frameworks is awkward.

entry.title: A Critique of GPUI
entry.content:
#8 on HN · blog.zortax.de · 77 points · 43 comments · HN discussion

这是 zortax 博客上一篇长文，把 Rust 原生 GUI 框架的状态模型本身当作问题：它认为 GPUI 和 egui 的状态模型对于复杂桌面应用都是死路，因为一次写操作无法告诉框架「什么变了、谁依赖它」。作者给出的基准测试数据是：3,000 行列表里改一个标签，在每行都带 cached view 的情况下要 8.4 ms，把行写成普通元素则要 92 ms，成本随树规模线性增长（每千行约 3 ms），而手写相等性检查可把「写入相同值」从 7.9 ms 降到 0.9 µs；Longbridge 的 gpui-fast 只能把前者降到 3.4 ms，因为帧仍然要遍历整棵树。文章还比较了 Elm/Iced（一个改动要重建整个 view，39,023 个 widget、7.3 ms）并主张 signals 模型（Floem、Solid、zgui）才是出路——作者同时披露自己在做 zgui，并移植了 GPUI 的 Linux 渲染器到 wgpu。

Discussion: 相当一部分评论火力集中在写作本身：多人指认文章是 AI 生成、表格「What a write runs / Who finds the change」难以理解，认为真正思考过这个问题的人应该自己动笔。最实质的反驳是利益冲突指控——有人指出 zgui 上月才发布 0.1.0、只有三个月开发史和唯一一个版本，而 GPUI 的 crates.io 版本也停在一年前的 0.2.2，因此这是披着批评外衣的软文。技术层面的争论集中在即时模式上：一位自称职业做 GUI 工具包的开发者说即时模式「绝不」更容易扩展，每次状态变更都重新求值并布局整个 UI 本质上不可扩展，egui 有时还要多次布局才能收敛；反方则说可以缓存布局，且当大量组件同时更新时 retained mode 的优势会消失，并强调无需在 UI 框架里复制一份状态这一概念上的收益。也有人举 Adobe 类应用（文章评论区提到的 Artcraft 系列，如 vectorcraft、photocraft）作为复杂 UI 成功的例子，随即被反驳其界面本身并不复杂、卡顿投诉多来自后端引擎而非 GUI，还有人说自己跑的 Photocraft 在虚拟机里只有 3 fps。此外有人指出 GPUI 强制手动 notify 是个 footgun，egui 的即时变更模式会造成半个界面显示旧状态、半个显示新状态的撕裂。整体没有形成共识，但「文章论证可信度存疑」的怀疑占了上风。

Worth reading

  • x-complexity: 指认这是 zgui 的软文：zgui 上月才发布 0.1.0、只有三个月历史和唯一一个版本，并强调框架成熟度是选择移植目标时无法回避的因素。
  • ben-schaaf: 一位职业 GUI 工具包开发者直接反驳即时模式更易扩展的说法：每次状态变更都要重新求值并布局整个 UI 本质不可扩展，egui 有时还需多次布局才能达到稳态。
  • slopinthebag: 对上述反驳的回应：即时模式也能缓存布局，在大量组件同时更新时 retained mode 的优势会减弱甚至反转，且不必在 UI 框架内复制状态本身就消除了一整类工作。

entry.title: Dux: Free, open-source Wayland desktop shell with file manager and theming
entry.content:
#9 on HN · duxlabs.dev · 264 points · 86 comments · HN discussion

Dux（前身为 Dank Material Shell，DMS）是一个基于 Quickshell/QML 的 Wayland 桌面 shell，可与 niri、Hyprland、Sway、labwc、mangowm 和 MiracleWM 搭配使用，提供状态栏、启动器、原生主题（用其 dank16 调色板为 GTK/Qt 应用生成配色）以及配套工具，如键盘优先的带标签页文件管理器、系统监视器和日历、任务应用。该站点还宣传基于 Fedora 的不可变发行版 Zirconium 以及带 MiracleWM 的官方 Fedora Miracle Spin。最新发布版本为 DMS 2.1「Stormborn」，新增了系统监视器、视频壁纸和经过改进的媒体播放器，而 v2.0 发布博客解释了从「Dank」到「Dux」的品牌更名；该项目免费且开源，并由 115+ 名 Ko-fi 支持者资助。

Discussion: 大多数评论来自长期使用 DMS/Dux 搭配 niri 的用户，他们报告称其稳定、无需维护，而且足够精致，可帮助 niri 走进主流，并称赞它最近支持了 Bazzite 等原子化发行版。反复出现的争论是把 Dux 与 Noctalia（现已脱离 Quickshell）比较：几位评论者说 Noctalia v5 更轻量，而 Dux 更全、更可扩展，不过实测内存使用被认为可以接受（约 90 MB 的 dms 加 330 MB 的 quickshell，而 niri 约 49 MB）。一些批评包括：它越来越「什么都有」，而不只是一个极简栏；与原生 niri 相比有功耗开销；以及设计上表明它大量借用了 Android/ChromeOS 的 Material Design。许多评论者抱怨使用 `curl | sh` 安装器：有人说这从来不是好做法，也有人反驳说真正的问题是卸载，而不是安全性，并指出十年来一直在进行同样的 HN 辩论。还有相当一部分争论围绕「Dux」这个名字，指出意大利法西斯曾用这个词称呼墨索里尼（「Il Duce」），而其他人辩护说它只是拉丁语中「领袖」的意思，在英国学校里也用于指「最优等学生」。

Worth reading

  • epihelix: 指出项目 AI 贡献政策（「使用 LLM 帮忙写代码可以，未经阅读就提交其输出不行」）以及 79 个版本和 321 名贡献者，反驳了那种认为它全靠 vibe coding 的猜测。
  • cowlevel: 认为反对 curl|sh 的情况关乎可卸载性和打包，而不是安全性，并称安全性担忧只是对太小的包进不了包管理器的势利看法；另一位评论者则举出 CI 安装脚本被劫持的真实事件。
  • vrotaru: 给出实际内存占用（quickshell 330 MB，dms 90 MB，niri 49 MB），以回应关于 Quickshell 开销的抱怨。

entry.title: Ask HN: What are you working on? (November 2026)
entry.content:
#10 on HN · text post · 198 points · 663 comments · HN discussion

This is the recurring monthly Ask HN check-in thread, posted by david927, carrying 198 points and roughly 660 comments; the entire post is two questions — what are you working on, and what have you been curious about lately. There is no linked article, so the content is the comment thread itself: a self-reported census of side projects, micro-SaaS launches, agent tooling and hobby research from HN users.

Discussion: The thread has no argument so much as a shared mood: the largest cluster is agent infrastructure — harnesses and orchestrators for steering many parallel coding sessions, agent-to-agent messaging, token-efficient browser control, agent memory layers and PR-review bots — with several people saying they are optimising token spend because prices are rumoured to be rising. The second cluster is people who were laid off recently and converted the time into small businesses: jzig built a field-service CRM with Google Local Service Ads integration to rescue his father's carpet-cleaning company (now near 3x ROAS), while others report honest, unglamorous numbers such as €2,000 MRR, about 50 paying customers, or 1,300 users. Pushback against the AI current is mild but present — joewhale calls bolting LLMs onto budgeting apps 「such a bad idea」 and keeps his own AI opt-in and stripped of identifiers, and wagslane frames boot.dev's new C, Terraform and bash courses as a bet that being genuinely good at things still matters. Deep systems work draws the most attention: a mainline kernel running on a Samsung Exynos phone, Fil-C's GNOME port, and a from-scratch Rust compiler, alongside a long tail of curiosity projects (knitting-stitch algebra, mains-frequency monitoring as a space-weather proxy, 6502 assembly, fountain-pen nib widths, coconut-water reviews). There is little real disagreement anywhere in the thread; it is mostly people showing work and asking for beta testers.

Worth reading

  • leobuskin: leobuskin describes replacing the entire stack on a Samsung A54 (Exynos 1380, Mali-G68): booting a custom Linux 7.3 kernel with Wayland and WPE WebKit and no Android layer, writing a thin mac80211-based firmware to replace the vendor blob, and reconstructing the LK-based S-Boot with byte-identical verification.
  • pizlonator: pizlonator gives a status update on Fil-C: GNOME is starting to work with some features disabled, Rust is about a third of the way to compiling to the Fil-ABI so Rust and Fil-C can interoperate without weakening either language's guarantees, and the SaRCAsm memory-safe assembler already runs OpenSSL.
  • vishvananda: vishvananda claims an agent-built C++ compiler that compiles about 4x faster than GCC and Clang, and is now applying the same approach to a brand-new Rust compiler aimed at Rust's compile times — early results promising but far from self-hosting.

entry.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's letter to staff about affair
entry.content:
#11 on HN · nvidianews.nvidia.com · 580 points · 601 comments · HN discussion

The linked post is the verbatim text of an email Jensen Huang sent NVIDIA employees: he admits he was unfaithful to his wife, takes full responsibility, asks for privacy for his family, and confirms that NVIDIA's board has opened an independent investigation into the 「national security concerns raised in news reports」, which he says he will cooperate with fully. The HN submission attaches Axios, NYT and CNN coverage reporting that the woman involved had ties to Chinese intelligence — a suspected honey trap — and that US officials had flagged the relationship to the company.

Discussion: The biggest cluster of comments is about timing: why the story broke days after the midterms, with theories ranging from a market-correction distraction to a deliberate leak by officials frustrated that the administration had known since May and done nothing, to administration infighting in which Rubio and others distance themselves from Trump and Huang is collateral damage. A second cluster asks whether Huang is load-bearing for NVIDIA: employees posting as Nvidians say he is the single most important person there, while others argue the company was simply in the right place twice (crypto, then AI) and that a decade of unprofitable CUDA investment shows founder-mode judgement rather than luck. On the affair itself, most argue the board and shareholders care only about blackmail and export-control exposure, and a sizable minority push back that character and judgement are the actual issue; several note that US CEOs are rarely fired for infidelity absent a subordinate or security angle. The letter itself gets grudging praise as textbook crisis communications — no deflection, no blaming the alleged spy — paired with cynicism that it was drafted by specialist PR advisers and that the board investigation will be slow-walked to a conclusion of nothing. A recurring counter-current doubts the spy framing entirely, noting Singapore's denial, no charges, and the lack of hard evidence on chip diversion through Malaysia.

Worth reading

  • icegreentea2: Argues the leak is less about Huang than Trump-administration infighting, timed just after the midterms with follow-up reporting naming Rubio as author of the internal warning memo.
  • ksec: Counter to the 「right place, right time」 line: CUDA was a money-losing, silicon-wasting bet for over a decade and most CEOs would have killed it — the case for founder-mode leadership.
  • jpgvm: A self-identified Nvidian says Jensen is the single most important part of the company, that his professional judgement has been stellar, and that pushing him out over this would be a travesty.

entry.title: RIP, Harvest
entry.content:
#15 on HN · aphyr.com · 312 points · 91 comments · HN discussion

Kyle Kingsbury's (aphyr) post saying goodbye to Harvest, the time-tracking and invoicing service he used for years, after its acquisition by Bending Spoons and the move to usage-based pricing. The article itself returned HTTP 451 at fetch time (commenters note it is blocked under the UK Online Safety Act; an archive.org copy is linked in the thread), so the details here come from commenters quoting it: a bill that went from about $13.32/month to $133.98/month, with the new plan also skimming roughly 2% of billings on top of card fees. Kingsbury asks freelancers what system they use instead.

Article not read: HTTP 451

Discussion: The thread is dominated by near-identical first-hand reports: Bending Spoons moved Harvest customers from flat per-seat pricing to usage billing that charges per project, client, task and invoice plus a percentage of gross billings, producing 10x to 100x increases. Concrete cases include a decade-long customer whose ~$1,500/year bill became a $20,000 charge on the company card, a renewal quote of $40 to $586.50/month for the same seats, and a 146x jump on the unlimited plan; several say support was unreachable. The main disagreement is over the replacement strategy rather than the grievance: some engineers warn that vibe-coding invoicing and payments is risky and that correctness and maintenance costs eventually arrive, while consultants who have already done it (Claude/Codex plus Beancount, SQLite, bank-statement reconciliation) say a small internal tool covering only their workflow took days and pays for itself. A smaller camp defends the private-equity arithmetic — 10x revenue while losing half the customers can still multiply profit — and argues trust and non-technical buyers remain a moat, but the rough consensus is that Harvest's brand is damaged and small consultancies are leaving. A correction subthread rebuts the claim that Harvest's advertised $9/$14 prices contradict the article: those are seat base rates that exclude the new usage charges, as Harvest's own support docs and renewal emails show.

Worth reading

  • boie0025: boie0025's consultancy, a Harvest user for over a decade at roughly $1,500/year, was moved to an 「enterprise」 plan and charged $20,000 on its card, could not reach anyone, executed a chargeback, and now runs an internal vibe-coded time tracker.
  • Digory: Digory quotes Harvest's renewal email directly: Basic at $40/month for 5 seats scheduled to renew on Enterprise Unlimited at $586.50/month for the same product, working out to about $75/month per seat after dropping spare seats.
  • Centigonal: Centigonal gives the opposing economic logic: if an acquirer 10xes revenue, loses half the customers and holds margins steady, it has still quintupled the acquired company's profits.

entry.title: When a language's creator and its owners strongly disagree [pdf]
entry.content:
#20 on HN · isocpp.org · 115 points · 110 comments · HN discussion

A PDF paper (P4454R0, widely attributed in the thread to Herb Sutter) about the C++26 draft failing its ISO vote, framed as a conflict between Bjarne Stroustrup — the language's creator, who opposes the contracts design — and the committee that owns the standard. Per the commenters, it summarizes Stroustrup's objections diplomatically and lays out roughly six paths forward, including dropping contracts and shipping C++26, re-voting, or The text itself was not readable here (it is a PDF), so this rests on the title and on what commenters describe.

Article not read: not a web page (application/pdf)

Discussion: Most commenters side with Stroustrup: they find his objections sensible and see contracts as a solution to a problem that plain assert does not have, though a few defend contracts as useful precisely because you can write assertions that stay live in production and in hardened libraries. Several people argue the post-mortem overweights Bjarne's personal opposition, pointing to broader committee fatigue with big half-baked features shipped before implementers can handle them — modules being the standing example — and note earlier incarnations of contracts were pulled from C++20 and C++23. A side thread accuses the paper's prose of being LLM-written, citing phrasing like no shipping production codebase uses contract_assert and the em dashes. The rest of the thread drifts into perennial ground: C++'s cognitive load versus Python and Rust, which pointer or reference to use, whether the committee model or a BDFL serves a language better, and the claim that C++ is on its way out now that LLMs can both exploit and rewrite it.

Worth reading

  • StellarScience: Lays out the paper's six options as concrete choices, from folding contracts into C++29 to publishing C++26 as national standards or leaving ISO for ANSI/INCITS.
  • aw1621107: Quotes the follow-up proposal P3911R2 to explain what 'guaranteed enforcement' would mean, arguing some national bodies consider the trade-off worth it, and notes codebases that keep asserts on in production.
  • digitalPhonix: Pushes back on the framing: Bjarne's opposition may have tipped the vote, but the real driver is accumulated wariness of large features left as exercises for implementers.

entry.title: The Web Is More Than Enough, by Paul Ford
entry.content:
#21 on HN · ftrain.com · 127 points · 74 comments · HN discussion

Paul Ford's post about tinylittleoffice.com, an office suite that stores document data in the URL, which he launched and watched max out the free Cloudflare plan before a couple hundred thousand visitors showed up on $0 hosting (after he added a credit card). His claim: the browser is a very powerful application platform and the cost of reaching that power is falling fast — Web Crypto, WebAssembly, WebGL, Web Audio, PDF.js — and he shipped the tool in 21 languages. He points to Simon Willison's browser-based 3D multiplayer RTS Battle Drones as proof that a non-game developer can now build such things, and speculates that if 100x more people start making software, the app-store economy and the current tech economy get reshaped.

Discussion: Commenters split between people who say the browser has become a startlingly cheap, capable app platform and people who say the web is too much — a monopoly-shaped, security-poor pile of complexity. Simon Willison says he now builds features on three.js, offline storage, SSE, WebAudio and WebAssembly multiple times a week rather than once or twice a year; he was immediately challenged with 「You mean the LLM is?」, and a long subthread argues over whether delegating to an agent counts as building, with the tech-lead-and-junior-engineer analogy as the common framing. The biggest fight is web versus native: one camp calls the browser merely user-interface tech locked into Chromium and WebKit, controlled by Google and Apple, and wants installable programs; the other camp says native distribution is the real trap, citing app-store review delays, yearly developer fees, Apple rejecting apps outright, and the browser sandbox being a genuine security win. Practitioners also push back on the hype — WebGPU, JavaScript and WASM still trail desktop APIs, background threading is awkward, and one commenter insists Visual Basic was easier for whipping up UIs than modern web development. Where people land seems to depend on whether they value distribution and sandboxing more than platform diversity, and whether their daily work is already client-server.

Worth reading

  • simonw: Simon Willison takes the 「drop three.js」 challenge, has Claude port a 3D nudibranch Fabergé egg from Three.js to vanilla WebGL, and links both versions plus the transcript — concluding it works fine, though the Three.js code is easier for him to read.
  • palata: palata argues the web is too much: you can assemble your own OS but not your own browser, since Chromium is Google's and Apple forces WebKit, so pushing web apps pushes lock-in to Big Tech engines.
  • jauntywundrkind: jauntywundrkind details how hostile native shipping is — Apple fees, queued reviews, the OpenCode iOS app reportedly held for weeks as an 「internal app」, and a tarot app Apple refused to even evaluate.

entry.title: Show HN: JavaScript web apps with WASM layout and GPU rendering in 280 KB
entry.content:
#23 on HN · github.com · 25 points · 11 comments · HN discussion

Uniform is a year-long solo project by rkaehn that packages a UI stack developers can ship with their app instead of inheriting the browser's HTML/CSS: a layout and rendering engine written in C, compiled to WASM for the web and to native code elsewhere, with a JavaScript API whose calls forward directly into the core. A native runtime under 2 MB runs the same JS on macOS and iOS (more platforms planned) and can package store-ready apps, and hot reload works on all platforms — including editing an app's JS on an iOS device with no computer or internet connection, with changes visible on the next display refresh. The post claims a 280 KB footprint and links a live demo that needs WebGPU; the GitHub README was unavailable (HTTP 504) when this was fetched, so the article's own detail beyond the post text could not be read.

Article not read: HTTP 504

Discussion: The thread is skeptical. Several commenters argue the project solves a problem nobody has: the browser is already a layout and rendering engine, and rebuilding it forfeits the platform integration users depend on — password-manager autofill, the user dictionary, CJK input methods and other IMEs, text selection, meaningful right-click menus, and normal trackpad scrolling and pinch-zoom. One commenter who ran the HN demo reports seeing rows paint in like a dial-up connection, no text selection, a right-click menu limited to Open/Open in New Tab/Copy Link on items, no scroll rubber-banding, and no pinch zoom, concluding he would hate to be asked to use an app built on this. The most common request is a demo of something that is actually impossible in HTML/CSS, since cloning Hacker News only advertises the drawbacks (slower, bigger, no native browser features). Defenders treat it as a worthwhile experiment toward sub-1 MB cross-platform UI without Tauri's system-webview baggage, and the author's hot-reload-on-iOS capability drew genuine praise. Practical complaints: Firefox on Android doesn't support WebGPU by default, the demo felt slow on Chrome Android, and the name 「Uniform」 is unsearchable and already shared by several other web projects. A cynical subthread predicts the approach's real market is unblockable ads and fully closed-source websites where inspect-element does nothing.

Worth reading

  • bschwindHN: First-hand report from the demo: items visibly paint in row by row, no text selection, broken context menus, no scroll rebound or pinch zoom —「as an end user I would hate if I was asked to use an application built on this」.
  • socalgal2: Lays out the concrete OS-level losses — password-manager autofill, user dictionary, and IME support for CJK and other languages — and cites Google Earth as a high-end WebGL/WASM app that still can't copy a name or right-click one.
  • onion2k: The central critique: a Hacker News clone proves nothing, because it only shows the approach is slower, bigger and missing browser features; what's needed is a demo of something HTML/CSS simply cannot do.

entry.title: Is Opus 5.5 nerfed? Thinking patterns changed on November 3
entry.content:
#25 on HN · twitter.com · 12 points · 5 comments · HN discussion

This is a short X post by Shane Melaugh claiming that Opus 5.5 was quietly altered on November 3. He says he had Gemini 4 Argon analyze 1,400 Claude Code sessions and found the model name unchanged but its reasoning behavior sharply different, with the amount of reasoning done at the 「high」 setting dropping significantly. In a quick test on a real bug, he says Opus 5.5 high jumped in too fast, got confused and failed to find a fix after three hours, while Opus 5.5 xhigh thought briefly and fixed it in minutes — so he argues the popularized 「use high for everything」 advice no longer holds.

Discussion: The thread is small and almost entirely anecdotal, with nobody reproducing the 1,400-session analysis or citing independent evidence. A heavy Opus 5.5 high user agrees the change was noticeable and says it felt like 「downgrading to the old version of deepseek」, though things have improved somewhat since. One commenter dismisses the claim outright, saying only the summarizer changed and model performance is unchanged, while another says the 「dumbing down」 is real and ties it to the company's IPO. Others speculate about timing — that such regressions often precede a new model launch, and that Anthropic may be racing a release around Qwen4 — but this is guesswork rather than measurement. The rough mood is shared suspicion of a silent change, with no consensus on cause.

Worth reading

  • terminalcommand: A daily Opus 5.5 high user says they independently felt the regression, comparing it to the older DeepSeek, and reports partial improvement since.
  • sunaookami: A direct counter-argument: only the summarizer changed, and model behavior and performance are unchanged.
  • Retro_Dev: Quotes another user reporting the same thing and speculates the change is timed to a new model launch, possibly around Qwen4 and the company's IPO.

entry.title: How I Fight AI Brain Fry
entry.content:
#26 on HN · sergeykuhne.com · 227 points · 164 comments · HN discussion

A short personal blog post by Sergey Kuhne about the exhaustion of juggling a dozen Claude Code and Codex terminal sessions at once. His fix is a priority queue that lives in git: every ticket is a markdown file next to the code (he uses the open-source board.md), an agent works the board in cycles — researching tickets, building ones a human has tagged as safe, running tests and browser checks, branching and asking first for sensitive code, never deploying to production — and anything needing human judgment lands in a single prioritized 「owner inbox」. An HTML page rebuilt from git on each cycle serves as the only reading surface; he takes one item, decides, and closes it back into the queue, which is what keeps his context from accumulating.

Discussion: The thread splits three ways. One camp argues the real fix is simply doing less: run one to three sessions, accept being idle, take the break that xkcd 303 always prescribed for compiles. A second camp has already built similar systems and swaps notes — 32 fanout agents producing up to 20 PRs a day, kanban boards over markdown notes, git-bug, kata, OpenSpec, per-issue chats, and agent 「grilling」 sessions that front-load design questions. A third and very large group dismisses the post as AI slop, quoting telltale lines like 「Then comes the part that matters most」 and 「That closing is the whole trick」; the author concedes he dictated and approved the text with Claude but insists the thought is his and he does not care. Two substantive counter-arguments recur: that the bottleneck is not idle waiting but reviewing 10k-line change lists from agents, and that inference speed, not process, is what would actually let people single-task. One commenter notes he has seen no study showing amortized net productivity gains from agentic coding above 30%.

Worth reading

  • sollewitt: Argues the real bottleneck is review, not idle time: parallel agents produce three 10k-line CLs to review on top of colleagues' code, and diluted context makes review slower than working serially.
  • rbehrends: An experienced commenter says he treats agents as virtual pair programmers and has yet to see evidence of amortized agentic-coding productivity gains above 30%, warning about tech debt.
  • mr_roboto: Describes an industrial-scale version: days of architecture planning and Jira cards, then fanout to up to 32 agents generating roughly 20 PRs per crunch day, followed by one to two weeks of testing and review.

entry.title: Air holes turn silicon wafers into flat UV focusing mirrors for compact optics
entry.content:
#28 on HN · phys.org · 50 points · 6 comments · HN discussion

A phys.org write-up of a University of Stuttgart study in Advanced Photonics (DOI 10.1117/1.AP.9.1.016002) that sidesteps the lack of UV-transparent metasurface materials by etching elliptical air voids — about 470 nm long and 100 nm deep — into bulk silicon instead of building solid pillars. Because the resonant field sits mostly in the air cavity, silicon's strong UV absorption is largely avoided, and the absorption-induced index change actually raises interface reflectivity and tightens confinement. Illuminated at 45° with 325 nm light, the half-millimeter-scale surface acts as an off-axis parabolic mirror, bending the beam 90° and focusing it to spots near 1 µm with focal lengths from 5 mm down to 1.25 mm, close to the diffraction limit up to NA 0.15; fabrication is a single lithography-plus-etch step on standard wafers, and the authors argue the approach can extend to deep and vacuum UV and support orbital-angular-momentum beams.

Discussion: The thread is tiny — six comments, mostly curiosity rather than debate. One commenter calls the idea 「genius」 and asks whether the voids can be resized for other wavelengths and whether the same trick could steer RF; the same person also asks whether the holes themselves cost a percentage of the light, and no one in the thread answers either question. The most substantive reaction is that extending this to EUV/XUV matters because those wavelengths are valuable for photolithography — a forward-looking application the paper only gestures at. Another commenter supplies the direct DOI link, and one points readers toward 「optical sieves」 as related prior art on hole-and-light physics. There is no disagreement and no first-hand practitioner report; treat the thread as pointers, not evaluation.

Worth reading

  • pfdietz: Flags EUV/XUV photolithography as the application that would really matter, beyond the demonstrated 325 nm result.
  • jacquesm: Points to optical sieves as relevant background for anyone interested in how holes manipulate light.
  • ranger_danger: Raises the obvious efficiency objection — that the air holes must themselves scatter or lose some light — which nobody in the thread answers.

entry.title: Playing with the STM32MP2
entry.content:
#29 on HN · serd.es · 57 points · 33 comments · HN discussion

A hardware engineer's writeup of bending the STM32MP257 — a dual Cortex-A35 (1.5 GHz) plus Cortex-M33 (400 MHz) applications processor with a 5 Gbps SERDES — into acting like a plain fast microcontroller: built only with upstream aarch64/arm g++ and binutils, no vendor SDK or HAL, no external DDR, no TrustZone or u-boot, everything in on-die SRAM running an event loop in EL3 from a hand-rolled FSBL flash image at fixed offsets (0x0e08_0000 in RETRAM, A35 image at 0x0008_0000). The end goal was PCIe gen1/2 x1 to an FPGA over two differential pairs. The author also mentions discovering a silicon bug with security implications that he sat on until ST could publish an advisory.

Discussion: Most of the thread is an argument about the name, not the project. The first commenter asks why a "full-desktop-capable" A35 ships under the STM32 label and calls it brand dilution, which pulls in a wave of embedded engineers insisting the Linux-core-plus-realtime-MCU combination is completely normal (NXP i.MX, TI AM355x, Xilinx Zynq, ESP32, even RP1 in the Pi 5) and is how you get hard realtime without paying for VxWorks. The pushback is about audience rather than technology: one commenter argues it's niche in terms of who actually does the work — first prototypes, hobby boards, open-source targets — since these parts come with eight-page databriefs and a 'contact sales' page, and shared-memory mailboxes between Linux userspace and an RT core are only 'very easy' to people already deep in the trenches. Elsewhere commenters correct the article's framing with pricing: the EV1 board is $425 at Digikey, but the Discovery Kit is around $103 and is where most people would start, though it drops PCIe. A side thread notes Cortex-A35 dates from 2015 and is still barely challenged by newer small application cores, and a small aside questions whether locked-down crypto-accelerator docs are export control or just ST avoiding vulnerability reports.

Worth reading

  • zwieback: First-hand report of using an STM32MP257 internally to build a quadrature-encoder logger: register-level SPI/I2C/GPIO on the M33 with Linux for UI and networking, exactly the split the part is designed for.
  • ACCount39: Strong counter-argument to the 'this is mainstream' consensus — shared-memory machine mailboxes are easy only for seasoned developers, and the average SBC user will avoid them entirely.
  • kvemkon: Price correction: the STM32MP257F-DK is $103 versus the $425 EV1 board, though it has no PCIe, and the commenter wishes small boards like this shipped 2 GB+ RAM and gigabit Ethernet.

entry.title: Edward Hopper's Iconic Painting, "Nighthawks
entry.content:
#36 on HN · lithub.com · 88 points · 28 comments · HN discussion

A LitHub excerpt from Louis Shadwick's book on Hopper, tracing how Nighthawks (1942, oil on canvas, 33⅛ × 60 in., Art Institute of Chicago) came together: begun by late November 1941 from nineteen preparatory sketches, with Hopper sketching coffee urns and salt shakers at the Dixie Kitchen diner in Midtown, modeling the two suited men himself in a full-length mirror and using Jo for the auburn-haired woman. Shadwick argues the wartime context is central — Pearl Harbor, New York blackout fears and Jo's frantic December 1941 letters — with Hopper finishing the canvas in about six weeks on 22 January 1942, absorbed enough to ignore the war news. He also weighs candidate real diners on Greenwich Avenue (Riker's, a wedge-shaped stand at 70 Greenwich Avenue, and Carter Foster's 2013 pick, Crawford Lunch), concluding Hopper probably amalgamated several buildings plus the Flatiron's glass prow.

Discussion: The thread is mostly appreciation rather than debate: the top comment notes the Art Institute of Chicago owns Nighthawks alongside Grant Wood's American Gothic and Seurat's A Sunday Afternoon, all bought for trivial sums (Hopper's for $3,000, Seurat's for $20,000). A long comment ties Nighthawks and the Seurat to Ferris Bueller's Day Off and reads the painting as an early signal of postwar urban isolation; several others report seeing it in person, one noting it was recently back on display and that the fluorescent interior glow doesn't survive digital reproduction. Recommendations cluster around explainer videos, the Hopper-vignette film Shirley: Visions of Reality, and jokey music pairings (Bob Seger's Night Moves and Turn the Page). A visible side thread is anger at the hosting site — one reader counted four pop-ups in a row over the painting on mobile, another noted Firefox mobile reduces it to a single dismissible cover, and a third suggested disabling JavaScript outright. Smaller notes: a joke that the man on the left is looking at his phone, nostalgia for the 1970s board game Masterpiece, and a Guardian cartoon (Shite Hawks) riffing on the title.

Worth reading

  • jmyeet: Lays out the Ferris Bueller museum scene in detail — Cameron's extreme close-up on Seurat's dots and the motherless child — and argues Nighthawks reads as a bellwether for postwar urban isolation.
  • nickhalfasleep: First-hand report that the painting is back on display at the Art Institute, and that the fluorescent-lit interior's color richness isn't captured by digital scans.
  • bartread: Blunt complaint that the article page throws four consecutive pop-ups over the painting on mobile, with a follow-up noting Firefox mobile cuts it to one and JS-disabling as the general workaround.

entry.title: Playing Zork 1 on a CP/M emulator on Linux (2021)
entry.content:
#38 on HN · kevinboone.me · 38 points · 14 comments · HN discussion

Kevin Boone 的一篇 2021 年教程，讲述如何用 z80pack 这个 Z80 模拟器在 Linux 上跑 CP/M 3，再从 CP/M 提示符启动 Infocom 1982 年的 Zork 1。步骤包括编译 z80pack 1.37 的 cpmsim 与 srctools、用 cpmtools 的 mkfs.cpm/cpmcp 制作并填充 4MB 硬盘镜像（z80pack-hd 参数）、把 ZORK1.COM 和 ZORK1.DAT 拷进同一张盘，以及为解决 Zork 只认 ctrl-h 退格键而修改终端设置。作者一开始就承认这件事毫无实用价值，唯一理由是借此熟悉 CP/M、为自建 Z80 复古机做准备；文中还提到 Infocom 游戏版权归属不明，以及 WordStar、Turbo Pascal 等 CP/M 软件。

Discussion: 评论区的共识是：想玩 Zork 根本不用这么麻烦。skx 推荐自己写的 Go 版 CP/M 模拟器 cpmulator，直接用本地文件夹代替磁盘镜像，一条 docker run 加 ZORK1 命令几分钟就能玩，还配了包含 Turbo Pascal 和 Zork 1-3 的软件合集；另一位补充了同样基于文件夹的 RunCPM。其余大半是怀旧：有人在车库里留着 Kaypro II 专门给人看绿色小屏幕上的 Zork，有人回忆在 MIT NE43 的 DECSYSTEM-2060 上用 MDL 跑 Zork、以及在自己搭的 RC2014 上玩。也有人提醒 frotz 这类 z-machine 解释器才是 Linux/BSD 上的正路，并给出 Infocom 游戏归档链接。唯一实质性的批评针对评论里推荐的网页版「AI 配图 Zork」：从房子往北再往北爬树时，配图显示的却是起始位置的白房子，而且建筑风格完全对不上。

Worth reading

  • stevekemp: 作者自己写了 Go 版 CP/M 模拟器 cpmulator，用本地文件系统代替磁盘镜像，附 docker 一行命令和含 Zork 1-3、Turbo Pascal 的软件合集仓库。
  • vunderba: 实测网页版 AI 配图 Zork，爬树场景的插图错配成游戏开头的白房子，质疑这个 vibe-coded 项目根本没测试过。
  • bogometer: 亲历者回忆：本科时在 MIT NE43 的 DECSYSTEM-2060 上通过 TOPS-20 的 MDL 玩 Zork，卡在难题时比 hack 或 rogue 解压多了。

entry.title: How to prove equations using diagrams, part 1
entry.content:
#41 on HN · epatters.org · 71 points · 8 comments · HN discussion

A Topos Institute blog post, cross-posted, that asks what an e-graph — an equality graph maintaining a congruence on expression trees — really is once you strip away union-find and the egg/egglog implementation. The author (epatters), who works on CatColab, introduces initial functors — functors whose pullback preserves limits — as the categorical tool explaining which diagram manipulations preserve the solution set of the equations a diagram presents; part 1 treats ordinary categories, corresponding to unary function symbols only. It cites Nelson and Oppen’s 1980 e-graphs, Willsey et al.’s egg (2021), Zhang et al.’s egglog (2023), and recent categorical-semantics proposals, and promises a finite-products generalization next.

Discussion: The eight-comment thread is mostly a terminology correction: henearkr says the domain J of a diagram should be called its index category or scheme, not its shape. JadeNB replies that the article does mention index category and that shape is common while scheme is not, and the author epatters agrees, pointing to nLab; henearkr concedes. Beyond that, boldslogan asks for pointers on functors and non-symbolic logic, and fn-mote notes that this is a category theory post subtitled initial functors, so readers can save themselves a click; no one disputes the mathematics.

Worth reading

  • epatters: The author confirms that shape is a standard name for a diagram’s domain and links to the nLab entry on diagrams, settling the terminology thread.
  • fn-mote: A blunt reader summary: this is a category theory post about initial functors, which tells casual readers whether to click.

entry.title: Goldman Sachs Is Pulling Claude Code from Its Bankers and Traders
entry.content:
#1 on HN · thestateofai.com · 220 points · 142 comments · HN discussion

A State of AI write-up (aggregating a Bloomberg report) saying Goldman Sachs updated internal guidance in October to restrict Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to its ~12,000 engineers out of ~47,000 staff, cutting off traders and bankers who had used the agents to watch client flows, model positions and build decks. It notes Goldman's CIO Marco Argenti had praised trader 'vibe coding' in July, that Goldman restricted Claude in Hong Kong in April, and that Goldman is a lead underwriter on Anthropic's IPO (S-1 filed October 26, expected Nasdaq listing as ANT before end of November). The piece argues the risk logic — unreviewed code with the user's own entitlements, information barriers, token costs — was sound but that the bank went about it badly by yanking access with no replacement.

Discussion: The largest thread is about cost and contracts, not capability: several commenters say Anthropic caps subscription/Team plans at 150 seats and forces larger orgs onto API-rate billing, so consumption overages are structural, not misuse; one says Google's flat-rate Gemini billing with throttling is winning non-engineering staff as a result, others defend the pricing as what the models are worth. A second camp reads the timing as IPO-motivated — Goldman is underwriting Anthropic — though several push back that underwriting and internal tooling decisions sit in separate, deliberately walled-off groups, and one argues a real operational incident (an agent placing or booking an order under a trader's account) is the likelier trigger, noting strats kept access. Bank-domain commenters say the real issue is stale, unsupported trader-built tools crossing the wall: missing source control, no deployment path, entitlement and Chinese-wall violations (a script that summarizes proprietary email and serves it to the desk), and engineer teams stuck 'improving' thousands of prototypes. Others are sympathetic to the traders, arguing the right answer is a sandboxed/abstracted environment rather than a ban, with a side debate over whether such environments inevitably collapse back into 'take it or leave it' software. There's also a correction thread: the Bloomberg original and fa-mag mirror are the real sources, and State of AI is characterized as an AI-written SEO site.

Worth reading

  • legitster: Claims their org is clawing back Claude access over chronic billing overages, that Anthropic won't offer a normalized rate, and that Gemini is displacing it by offering flat billing with throttling instead of overage bills.
  • steveBK123: Walks through the concrete compliance failure modes of trader/banker-built apps: an unmonitored channel across the Chinese wall, or an 'summarize my email' app that quietly breaks data entitlements — a huge use case among finance non-engineers.
  • MallocVoidstar: Says the actual source is Bloomberg (mirrored on fa-mag.com), and that State of AI is an AI-written site run by a spam company — a useful caveat on the linked page's credibility.

entry.title: Outlook.com Is Quietly Rejecting Email from Domains Without DMARC
entry.content:
#2 on HN · mailroute.net · 24 points · 12 comments · HN discussion

A post by Thomas A. Johnson, founder and CEO of the mail-relay vendor MailRoute, reporting that since November 5, 2026 Outlook.com, Hotmail, Live and MSN have been intermittently rejecting mail from domains that publish no DMARC record — including ordinary low-volume senders, not just the 5,000-messages-a-day bulk senders covered by Microsoft's May 2025 rule (550 5.7.515). Affected senders get a terse 「550 5.7.1 Message rejected: Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC Auth Records」 bounce with a per-message AS number, even when SPF and DKIM are fine, and delivery is inconsistent — one message lands, the next bounces. The proposed fix is a single TXT record, 「v=DMARC1; p=none」, which changes nothing for other receivers; the piece ends in a pitch for MailRoute's own relay.

Discussion: Nobody disputes that the problem is real: the poster says domains he manages with valid SPF and DKIM but no DMARC started bouncing over the weekend, and several others report the same. The main complaint is the silence — Microsoft published no postmaster notice or service-health entry, and one admin grumbles about having to mitigate it for hundreds of customers on a weekend. A recurring objection is that a p=none record proves little when SPF and DKIM are already aligned, and that requiring it adds pure busywork; a sharper version argues that two corporations should not get to decide who may send email, and that unclassified mail should be marked as spam rather than refused outright. Countering that, some commenters say misconfigured email DNS is astonishingly common and that authentication is now simply the cost of doing business, and one long-time self-hoster adds that his clean setup's mail to Hotmail addresses has been vanishing with no bounce at all.

Worth reading

  • xmddmx: The submitter confirms first-hand that domains with proper SPF and DKIM but no DMARC record began bouncing this weekend.
  • anonymous908213: Argues the real issue is policy: two corporations shouldn't control who can send email, and unauthenticated mail should be spam-filtered, not refused.
  • daneel_w: Reports weeks of mail to Hotmail recipients silently disappearing with no bounce from an otherwise clean, self-hosted setup.

entry.title: Llama-modchip: 284B DeepSeek on 64GB RAM, no GPU
entry.content:
#5 on HN · github.com · 281 points · 99 comments · HN discussion

llama-modchip 是一组针对 ggml/llama.cpp 的内核补丁、量化转码器和运行时工具，目标是让稀疏 MoE 模型完全跑在系统内存里。它宣称把 DeepSeek-V4-Flash（284B 总参数、13.17B 激活）从 76.87 GiB 压缩到 56.56 GiB（1.71 bpw），从而连同 256K KV cache 一起锁进 64GB Linux 机器的约 62.5 GiB 可用内存，不触发 swap，在 Ryzen 9 9955HX 上解码 9.1–14.7 tok/s。主要卖点是 AVX-512BW 四级寄存器 + L1/L2/L3 多列 tiling（prefill 25.0→44.36 tok/s，+77%）、一个 1.64 MB 的 Zobrist n-gram 自推测 drafter、/dev/shm 的 KV 快照（18.9–32.6 ms 恢复），代价是引入自定义张量类型 GGML_TYPE_Q2_0（type ID 40），未经补丁的 llama.cpp、Ollama、LM Studio 会直接拒绝加载。

Discussion: 最有价值的部分是几个人真的照着 README 跑了，结果都失败了：aappleby 在 Ryzen 7945HX 上测 Nemotron，说除了 prefill 更快，CPU 解码速度和原版 llama.cpp 差不多；ar-nelson 的 Xeon 被脚本判为「Tier A」，但 modchip 默认只装 Nemotron，手动装 DeepSeek 后先是张量形状不匹配报错，再用随包的二进制直接 Illegal instruction 崩溃，结论是「完全不知道怎么跑起来」。adrian17 质疑文档里的数字自相矛盾——76.87 GiB 其实是 unsloth IQ1_S 的 82.5GB，而被称作 IQ2_XXS 的量化实际有 91GB——并指出最终 GGUF 只有 unsloth IQ1_S 的 75%，还砍了注意力层精度、把每层 6 个专家降到 4 个，怀疑质量不可用。围绕 2-bit 量化吵得很开：一派引用 TUM 的量化可靠性论文称 4-bit 是性价比拐点、再低性能会显著下滑（也有人纠正该论文不覆盖当前主流的 QAT，不能一概而论），另一派说大模型吃得住激进量化，DeepSeek v4.1 Flash 在 2-bit 下仍可用，比在小模型上跑 4-bit 强。另有 kennywinker 与 senordevnyc 的长辩论：前者算出约 800 美元的 E5 工作站当量成本、质疑订阅的必要性，后者反驳说按「智能密度」折算后 Opus 5.5 级别的质量省下的人力成本远超每月 200 美元。几乎一致的共识是 README 是严重的 AI 生成「slop」，emoji 和术语堆砌到几乎不可读，反而要靠评论区才搞懂这项目到底在做什么。

Worth reading

  • aappleby: 实测者报告：在 16 核 Zen 4 + 96GB DDR5 上，Nemotron 的解码速度与原版 llama.cpp 基本一致，只有 prefill 明显更快，且 setup 里根本没有 DeepSeek 选项。
  • ar-nelson: 完整复现失败记录：readiness 脚本给出 Tier A，但 modchip 不安装 DeepSeek，手动加载报 ffn_gate_tid2eid 张量形状错误，随包的 llama-cpp 二进制直接 illegal instruction。
  • adrian17: 拆穿文档数字：76.87GiB 实为 unsloth IQ1_S 的 82.5GB，作者疑似混淆了 IQ2_XXS 与 IQ1_S，且「MoE pruning」其实指每层只跑 4 个而非 6 个专家。

entry.title: Writing as a thinking tool
entry.content:
#6 on HN · muratbuffalo.blogspot.com · 191 points · 65 comments · HN discussion

A blog post by Murat Buffalo arguing that writing is not the record of thought but the machinery of it, built around Manuel Blum's line that the only difference between a finite automaton and a Turing machine is 「paper and pencil」. He likens drafting to out-of-core execution: reviewing a paper he thinks he understands, then finds he grasped maybe 60% until he writes the review, and a 2018 post connecting Paxos and Nakamoto consensus became the seed of a research paper. His worry is LLMs: Bezos claimed a six-page memo cannot be written without clear thinking, but a model can now produce six pages with no thinking at all, which makes writing your own prose a widening comparative advantage. His advice: freewrite in bulk without judgment, then edit ruthlessly as if a stranger wrote it, keep prose plain (Strunk and White, Vonnegut), write for yourself, and put writing on the calendar instead of waiting for inspiration.

Discussion: The thread is broadly sympathetic and mostly extends the thesis to code: several engineers say the real work is understanding the problem and that the volume of code they ship in a year could be typed in a week, so letting a model write it removes the step where the design gets worked out. A cluster of commenters describes middle-ground workflows — have the AI critique your own draft rather than write it, or force it to explain and prove its output — while a stricter faction argues even AI feedback is a slippery slope away from your own voice. The sharpest disagreement is over the automaton analogy: a Turing machine with a finite tape is just a finite automaton, so the real ingredient is an effectively unbounded supply of paper, which one reply turns into practical advice to buy boxes of cheap pens and notepads rather than one nice notebook. A few dissenters push back on the whole premise — one says school-forced writing made them avoid notes entirely and they have learned everything without it, and another notes writing can become pseudo-rationalizing over-analysis, linking a PubMed study on the downside. Side threads wander into stationery (Rhodia 5mm grid pads, Uni-ball Jetstream SXN-210) and colour-coded note systems.

Worth reading

  • raincole: Points out the analogy is technically broken: a Turing machine with a finite tape is equivalent to a finite automaton, so the difference is unbounded space, not paper per se.
  • fcoury: Describes a personal skill that, after an agent writes a feature, replays the meaningful diffs and has him retype them by hand — slow, but used for critical work to imprint understanding.
  • baxtr: Counter-argument to the thread's consensus: for highly analytical people, writing can become a way to elaborate thoughts instead of testing them, leading to over-analysis and pseudo-rationalizing, with a PubMed reference.

entry.title: The Reconstruction of Torn Documents
entry.content:
#8 on HN · bundesarchiv.de · 65 points · 39 comments · HN discussion

A FAQ-style page from the German Federal Archives (Bundesarchiv) explaining the state of efforts to piece back together the roughly 16,000 bags of hand-torn Stasi files — 2,500–3,500 fragments per bag, an estimated 400–600 million fragments covering 40–55 million pages. The computer-assisted 「virtual reconstruction」 project run with Fraunhofer IPK since 2007 was wound down: scanning stopped in 2014, reassembly in 2016, and although the e-Puzzler software was demonstrated to work in principle in 2013 it never hit the target 80% automated reconstruction rate or became viable for mass processing, after about €6.5 million spent. The archive says the old contract is being terminated, a requirements catalogue and market survey will look for new vendors, and manual puzzle-and-glue reconstruction continues in the meantime.

Discussion: Much of the thread pushes back on the page's flat claim that shredded paper could not be reconstructed, citing the 2011 DARPA Shredder Challenge, the reconstructed shredded US embassy documents from Tehran, and the point that the material was only declared unrecoverable and then burned in 1991.
