A Crusoe newsroom post announcing that Google acquired its southeast Wyoming data center campus site, closing out Crusoe's pre-development work: site selection, government approvals, and a hybrid power strategy built with Tallgrass Energy that combines fuel cells, grid power and natural gas turbines, with a long-term plan for carbon capture through Tallgrass's regional CO2 sequestration hub. CEO Chase Lochmiller says Crusoe has more than 6 GW contracted and over 40 GW in its pipeline, and the post notes Crusoe is also developer of Google's campus under construction in Armstrong County near Amarillo. The release frames it as a completed handoff; the thread supplies the less flattering backstory.

Discussion: The dominant thread is that this was not a friendly handoff: one commenter cites Google's own announcement of a $17 billion Wyoming investment plus Bloomberg reporting that Crusoe was pushed aside after failing to sign customers including Google, with concerns about cost and schedule surfacing as early as June 2026, when Crusoe described the project as 「paused」. Several commenters frame Crusoe as a bitcoin miner that pivoted to AI neoclouds around 2024 and lacks decades of data-center experience, and one former interview candidate calls the engineering staff fine but the leadership 「very dodgy」. Others push back: Crusoe is lead developer on the 1.2 GW Abilene, Texas campus (「Project Ludicrous」) in Stargate, and CoreWeave made the same crypto-to-datacenter pivot successfully. The rest splits between an argument that already-built, already-powered sites (especially ones with brownfield room) are about to become extremely valuable, and skeptics who see the buildout as an accounting and loan-collateral game that will unwind — countered by the observation that the labs still rate-limit and impose quotas.

Worth reading

  • tristanj: Links Google's $17 billion Wyoming announcement and Bloomberg reporting that Crusoe was pushed aside after failing to land customers including Google, with cost and timetable concerns already visible in June.
  • alpb: Counter-argument to the 「no experience」 charge: Crusoe is lead developer of the 1.2 GW Abilene, Texas campus (Project Ludicrous) under Stargate.
  • rooftopzen: Skeptical take that Google may back out, comparing it to Nscale, and arguing demand is overstated by parties using data centers as loan collateral.

entry.title: Chomsky and the two cultures of statistical learning (2011)
entry.content:
#25 on HN · norvig.com · 121 points · 99 comments · HN discussion

Peter Norvig's 2011 essay responds to Noam Chomsky's remarks at MIT's 150th-birthday 「Minds and Machines」 symposium, where Chomsky dismissed statistical language work as success that merely 「approximates unanalyzed data」. Norvig restates five Chomsky claims — that engineering success is irrelevant to science, that data-gathering is butterfly collecting, that billion-parameter models are opaque, that a word-probability model can't capture language, and that statistics has been proven incapable of learning language — and answers each, arguing engineering success is evidence (not proof), that Shannon's Markov models are being straw-manned, and that Gold's 1967 theorem does not apply to natural language since Horning showed PCFG learning is possible. Along the way he gives worked examples, including that 「I before E except after C」 scores only about 0.753 accuracy on a trillion-word corpus versus 0.793 for the simpler rule.

Discussion: The thread relitigates the science-versus-engineering split: several commenters argue planes teach you little about birds, so LLMs — trained on millions of times a child's text and compute — are an impressive technology but not a model of human language acquisition. Others push back that Norvig answers this in the essay's opening, that successful engineering is genuine evidence a phenomenon is statistical, and that a newborn brain arrives with a rich evolutionary prior rather than a blank slate, making the sample-efficiency comparison unfair. A second disagreement is over how close the machinery is: backprop, self-attention and BPE versus spiking neurons, with some calling LLMs the only model that demonstrably produces competent language and others insisting similar outputs say nothing about similar mechanisms. On Chomsky himself, one camp calls him dogmatic and says his influence is waning while generative grammar's empirical findings survive; others defend the field's real discoveries and note that statistical learning and innateness are not mutually exclusive (citing Charles Yang and Lidz). The thread tails off into a stretch about Chomsky's friendship with Jeffrey Epstein, where most participants correct an unfounded accusation while calling the relationship a stain on his reputation.

Worth reading

  • theptip: Argues Norvig is not confused about engineering versus science — successful modelling is Bayesian evidence for a hypothesis — and that the sample-efficiency objection fails because an LLM starts pretraining with almost no prior while a brain inherits one from evolution, invoking predictive processing as independent support.
  • suddenlybananas: A linguistics-side rebuttal claiming Norvig misreads the field, singling out his suggestion that English is 「kinda」 pro-drop as unserious and comparing such critiques to mocking Galileo by pointing out that a feather falls slower than an iron ball.
  • mturmon: Points to newer work on the creative aspects of language use (CALU) and links a Substack essay by Michigan linguist Chandra Sripada plus his Mindscape interview arguing LLMs are an existence proof that open-ended, context-sensitive language can arise.

entry.title: What do the next 4000 emoji look like?
entry.content:
#26 on HN · jenniferdaniel.substack.com · 58 points · 46 comments · HN discussion

A Substack essay by Jennifer Daniel (who commenters note chairs or sits on the Unicode emoji subcommittee) arguing that emoji are repeating the 5,000-year history of writing: an inventory phase (the original 176 emoji in 1999, Unicode standardization in 2010, endless noun requests like 🌯 and 🦔), a rebus/polysemy phase (💀, 🍆, 🤡), and a grammar phase (🫠, 🥹, 🫡 used as tone markers). Her prediction is that the next 4,000 emoji shouldn't be more nouns but composable modifiers — directional ligatures, intensity diacritics, and Hangul/Chinese-style semantic compounds built on Zero-Width Joiners, the mechanism behind 😶‍🌫️.

Discussion: The thread is dominated by people who think putting emoji in Unicode at all was a mistake, on the grounds that it is slow, bureaucratic, subjective, and not a writing system — countered by the argument that emoji are now genuinely part of how people write, and that Unicode already includes non-writing things like ASCII control codes and the DOS/Commodore pictographs. A recurring side grievance is Han unification making it impossible to know which glyph an author intended. Another cluster proposes embedding small bitmaps or vectors in text instead of standardizing glyphs, which others reject on zooming, theming, caching, security and complexity grounds, and by pointing out that Unicode encodes characters, not fonts. Others complain that HN strips emoji from comments, that many of the article's own emoji did not render for readers, and that a garbled phrase (「loudly of ryongface」) reads like AI text — though the author turned out to be a human involved in the emoji approval process. There is no consensus, but a clear majority view that emoji-as-Unicode is an awkward compromise at best.

Worth reading

  • ninjin: A detailed argument that Unicode emoji have distorted the process (slow, subjective inclusion decisions, not really a script), that the inclusion was a necessary evil to bring Japanese carriers into Unicode, and that Han unification is Unicode's worst flaw — illustrated by the thought experiment of merging Latin, Greek, Cyrillic and maths glyph subsets.
  • chrismorgan: Pushes back on the essay's thesis: Unicode encodes what already exists rather than inventing new notation, and its modifier mechanism is too constrained technically for the kind of open-ended compositional system the article predicts.
  • negura: Argues the linguistic-history framing misses the business model: new emoji require full OS updates (iOS, Android pre-12), which makes them a driver of planned obsolescence and device upgrades.

entry.title: Show HN: Waymark – A workflow engine that compiles jobs instead of replaying
entry.content:
#28 on HN · github.com · 62 points · 18 comments · HN discussion

Waymark is an MIT-licensed open-source durable execution library from Pierce Freeman (icyfox) and mozgiii, positioned between Temporal/DBOS and plain Postgres job queues. Instead of replaying workflow code from the start, it parses a Python workflow's AST into an IR and lowers it to bytecode for a stackless VM, which a Rust core executes and snapshots to Postgres — so any code that compiles will run, and non-deterministic calls like time or uuid fail at compile time rather than runtime. Postgres is the only broker (benchmarks around 1,500 workflows/second), actions plug into FastAPI-style dependency injection, there's a built-in webapp on port 24119 and cron/interval scheduling; the authors explicitly warn against production use before 1.0.0 and say SQLite support and JavaScript are candidates for later.

Discussion: The thread is largely admiring. An ex-Pachyderm engineer argues the real insight is applying the Bazel/Nix pattern — a pure coordination language over sandboxed imperative components — to distributed workflows, and says a compiler-driven orchestrator would have solved his team's partial-cache invalidation problems (the author replies he already has an internal map-reduce and asks where caching broke). Several people ask for SQLite or .NET CIL support; the author says the DB layer is already plugin-shaped and easy to swap. The one real dispute is over async: one commenter calls the async-heavy API off-putting and predicts breakage from Python version and third-party coupling, and when the author says background jobs are better modeled as async, he pushes back that coroutines run on a single thread and that thread/process queues have worked for decades. Others counter that asyncio is the norm across Temporal, Hatchet and Dagster for IO-heavy distributed work, and point to asyncio.to_thread and aiomultiprocess for sync code; the author notes actions themselves can be synchronous.

Worth reading

  • msteffen: A former Pachyderm engineer says Waymark applies the Bazel/Nix pattern of a pure coordination layer over sandboxed imperative code, and that this architecture would have fixed his team's pipeline caching headaches.
  • icyfox: The author explains why durability matters for agents: each LLM and tool call becomes a checkpoint, sleeps can last hours, and every call gets a clean input/output contract for tracing.
  • whilenot-dev: A commenter answers the sync-code complaint concretely — use asyncio.to_thread, or aiomultiprocess if you want processes — and asks what low-level concurrency control sync workflows would actually buy.

entry.title: Sodium-ion batteries approach cost parity with LFP
entry.content:
#29 on HN · pv-magazine.com · 173 points · 80 comments · HN discussion

A pv magazine write-up of a Wood Mackenzie analysis arguing sodium-ion is the most promising non-lithium chemistry for stationary storage: 70+ GWh of supply agreements signed, cell-level cost parity with LFP expected from late 2026, and system-level parity only after 2030. Current global average is $229/kWh versus about $200/kWh for LFP, but sodium-ion is credited with 21% lower total cost of ownership over 20 years thanks to no capacity-expansion cycling and lower operating costs. BYD targets 30 GWh of sodium-ion capacity, CATL aims for over 1 GWh of shipments by the end of 2026, and policy is tilting the field — China exempts sodium-ion from a consumption tax until end-2028 while taxing LFP, the US imposes roughly 58% tariffs on Chinese storage cells alongside IRA 45X credits, and India offers a $1.25B incentive program.

Discussion: The thread splits sharply on safety: several people want sodium home batteries because they believe the chemistry is inherently safer, but margalabargala, backed by a linked paper, argues sodium thermal runaway is less violent yet more likely — especially at 100% state of charge — and that the off-gassed products are worse than LFP's hydrogen. A second running argument corrects a common misconception: lithium cells discharge fine at -25C, it is charging below 0C that destroys them via lithium plating, so the low-temperature advantage of sodium-ion is narrower than advertised. On cost, dzhiurgis and others call the article's $200/kWh LFP figure nonsense, citing cell prices of $30-50/kWh for storage and automotive grade, with others replying that the number mixes in pack, BMS, inverter and installation. The most consequential thread is about provenance: akamaka says the submitted article looked like an LLM-embellished rewrite of a CATL announcement with invented numbers, and HN moderator dang confirms the link was swapped to pv magazine from the original ievchina piece, which commenters archive because the site kept erroring out. A side debate mocks the counterfactual 「what if all fossil-fuel money had gone to batteries」 premise, with replies noting that petrochemical materials research underpins much of modern battery and semiconductor work.

Worth reading

  • margalabargala: Links a paper comparing chemistries and argues sodium thermal runaway is less dangerous per event than lithium but more likely to start, particularly when charged to 100% SOC.
  • dzhiurgis: Challenges the article's economics, saying automotive cells run around $50/kWh and stationary storage around $30/kWh, not the $200/kWh stated for LFP.
  • akamaka: Alleges the originally submitted article was an LLM-rewritten version of a CATL cost-parity story with fabricated figures — a claim the moderator implicitly confirms by swapping the link.

entry.title: Show HN: Tmux-restore saves tmux windows and agent sessions across reboots
entry.content:
#30 on HN · github.com · 28 points · 13 comments · HN discussion

tmux-restore 是 andrewboldi 开发的一款 MIT 许可工具，它封装在 tmux-resurrect 和 tmux-continuum 两个插件之上：它每分钟保存一次全部 tmux 状态，并在系统关机时再保存一次（Linux 上通过 systemd，macOS 上通过 launchd），恢复时会带回各个会话、窗口、分屏、工作目录和滚动缓冲区。它最大的价值在于让 agent 会话可以接续：一个小型适配器会到 Claude Code、Codex、Gemini CLI、opencode 和 pi 各自的会话文件里找出对应的 conversation id，然后保存一组命令，用相同的命令行参数恢复该对话。出于安全考虑，它只重新启动编辑器和监控程序；部署脚本、dev server 等则被重新输入到提示符处，等待用户按 Enter 确认，不会自动执行。安装方式是通过 curl 执行 install.sh，脚本会自动安装 tmux、TPM 以及所需插件。

Discussion: 最主要的疑问是，它比原版插件多做了什么：几位评论者已经在跑 tmux-resurrect/tmux-continuum（另一个人甚至为每个面板专门 fork 了 Zed），作者回应说，新增的部分是 agent 会话恢复，以及关机时保存这一层。一位评论者建议提供手动安装操作步骤，而不是只给出 curl | bash 一行命令。有人提出，用带休眠的 VM 是更简单也更完整的方案，但反驳意见指出，VM 仍然会为了升级内核而重启，而且升级库之后无论如何都要重启依赖程序。最实质的提醒是安全性问题：该工具会把屏幕缓冲区持久化到磁盘，因此任何留在某个 pane 里的敏感内容（例如密码）都会被捕获，并且每 10 分钟覆盖一次。

Worth reading

  • jauntywundrkind: 滚动缓冲区也会被保存，因此停留在某个 pane 中的密码或密钥会被写入磁盘，并且每 10 分钟覆盖一次；评论者原本以为只会保存布局和窗口名称。
  • b112: 反驳“休眠 VM”方案：VM 本身也需要为了内核升级而重启，而且升级库之后必须重启依赖这些库的程序，所以这并不能真正解决问题。
  • visarga: 评论者 fork 了 Zed，通过传递一个与单个 shell pane 绑定的 ZED_TERMINAL_ID 来恢复该 pane 中的 agent 会话；这种做法要作用于 10 个以上窗口、每窗口 1 到 4 个 agent pane 的场景。

entry.title: US FAA says it will phase out floppy disks from air traffic control by 2028
entry.content:
#1 on HN · reuters.com · 158 points · 138 comments · HN discussion

这是一篇路透社的报道（原文无法抓取，返回 HTTP 401，因此以下内容依据标题和评论转述）：FAA 宣布将在 2028 年前，把空中交通管制中仍在使用的软盘淘汰掉。评论者补充说，涉事系统是 IDS-4，运行 MS-DOS、使用 3.5 英寸软盘（有人指出它实际诞生于 1990 年代初，而不是新闻所说的 1980 年代），整个替换项目属于 EIDS 计划，预算被提到约 120 亿美元。官方给出的紧迫理由之一，是 10 月 13 日休斯敦乔治·布什洲际机场外一条光纤被挖断，导致数据服务中断并触发地面停飞。

Article not read: HTTP 401

Discussion: 讨论主要分成两种立场。一方以曾在 FAA 做过 NOTAM 数字化工作的承包商为代表：他认可 FAA 的安全风险管理（SRM）流程本身，但说它没有反向的制衡力量，常常变成硬性阻塞，审核委员会熟悉旧系统、不理解新系统，风险判断失真；反对者则认为航空规则是「用血写成的」，在事故率已经极低的情况下，任何变更本身都会引入风险，举证责任在提议变革的一方。另一条争论线围绕那条被挖断的光纤：多人最初嘲讽 FAA 没有备份，随即被纠正：断掉的正是备份线路，主线路当时在检修，属于「瑞士奶酪」式多重失效，有人据此论证需要三重冗余而非双冗余。关于软盘本身，多数人同意磁介质和驱动器早已停产、备件只能靠 eBay 拆机 scavenge，这种供应链风险本身就是安全隐患；但也有资深从业者强调，真正卡住升级的往往不是软盘，而是关键路径上那些无法升级的 1980/1990 年代老机器。不少人还提到，空管员至今仍用纸质飞行进程条和木钉，替换难度远超外界想象，并对「云端 21 世纪系统」的可靠性和政治化宣传表示怀疑。

Worth reading

  • bargl: 前 FAA 现代化项目参与者现身说法：SRM 流程严谨但缺乏制衡，曾因一位 80 多岁不愿退休、不理解现代系统的工程师而使项目长期卡死。
  • Jtsummers: 亲历者说明真正的瓶颈不是软盘而是关键路径上的 1980/1990 年代老计算机——去年才淘汰一套依赖 1990 年代中期机器、只能靠 eBay 拆件的系统。
  • skissane: 给出 FAA 的 EIDS 官方页面和 SysAtl 的 IDS-4 资料，指出 IDS-4 实为 1990 年代初的 MS-DOS + 3.5 英寸软盘系统，纠正报道中「1980 年代」的说法。

entry.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production
entry.content:
#2 on HN · nbcnews.com · 571 points · 1,276 comments · HN discussion

A Reuters story (via NBC News) reporting that Elon Musk said Tesla will wind down Cybertruck assembly at its Austin gigafactory around mid-2027, freeing capacity for the Cybercab robotaxi. US Cybertruck sales fell to 20,237 in 2025, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024, against Musk's pre-launch prediction of 250,000 a year; Musk called it the 「best vehicle Tesla has ever made」 and the shutdown the 「end of an era」. Analysts quoted (Andy Palmer, Felipe Munoz) argue electric pickups broadly flopped in the US and that the truck's stainless-steel wedge could never pass European pedestrian-impact rules, while Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill says the platform 「lives on through Cybercab」.

Discussion: The top thread is not about the shutdown at all: a owner-adjacent commenter describes a friend running his house off a Cybertruck for 14 days after Hurricane Helene by driving to a Supercharger to refill, which set off a long debate. Dozens of replies point out this is generic V2H/V2L, not Cybertruck-specific — Ford's F-150 Lightning did it first, and Kia EV9, Ioniq 5, BYD and even a Jeep 4xe can do the same — while others argue a $500–$8k propane or diesel generator is cheaper and more reliable when roads, chargers and grid are down. On the product itself, commenters split between 「glad someone took a swing」 (comparing it to the DeLorean, praising 48V, steer-by-wire and unpainted steel) and those who call it an ugly, impractical non-truck; a recurring argument is that price, not aesthetics, killed it — a $40–50k version would have sold — countered by the observation that $65k+ F-series trucks sell in far higher volume. A second recurring thesis is that the Cybertruck was really a low-volume testbed for Tesla's next-gen electrical architecture that got scaled up before product-market fit, and many use the news to question Tesla's future with only Model 3/Y left, a Cybercab still answering NHTSA questions, and BYD dominating outside the US. The Musk-politics angle is everywhere, with some commenters objecting that the thread's 「I don't like Elon, but…」 framing is itself tedious.

Worth reading

  • brightball: First-hand account of a Cybertruck powering a whole house through a 14-day post-Helene outage by shuttling to a Supercharger to recharge — the story that seeded the entire vehicle-to-home subthread.
  • crawshaw: Argues the ignored explanation is price: the truck was designed for an era of inflated, zero-interest-rate truck prices, and at $40k it would have found a much larger market.
  • x3haloed: A cancelled pre-order holder lists exactly why: delivered range came in far below the announcement, the price rose, the stressed-skin exoskeleton became glued-on panels, and Tesla's politics became a reason not to buy.

entry.title: First steps in bare-metal programming using UEFI
entry.content:
#5 on HN · kevinboone.me · 110 points · 7 comments · HN discussion

这是 Kevin Boone 撰写的一组系列文章的索引页，讲的是如何在 Linux 工作站上开发 UEFI 固件 PC 的裸机应用。目标读者是有经验的 Linux 开发者，但假定读者此前不熟悉 UEFI；系列内容包括所需工具、编译与链接、制作可启动的光盘或 U 盘，以及使用 Simple File System 协议做基本文件管理，其中已列出第 2 至第 5 部分。文章明确要求按顺序阅读，后篇依赖前篇。

Discussion: 评论整体比较正面：一位用 Zig 写 bootloader 的开发者说这份指南是很好的起点，但提醒 EFI 环境里的 UTF-16 字符串和各类「尖锐边角」让它和普通 Linux 开发相差很远。有人为这些怪癖提供了背景和补丁：指出 edk2-libc 可以补上缺失的 C 标准库，并说明 UEFI 的「Windows 味」源自 Intel Boot Initiative → EFI → UEFI 的演进过程。另一位资深评论者则强烈反对这种「沿用」的说法，认为 UTF-16 和 VFAT 在 1998 年和 2005 年就已经是不合理的选择。同一位评论者还提出 Multiboot2 可作为自己构建 PE32+ 镜像的替代方案，并分享了一个只用 289 行头文件、借助 LLM 生成的 UEFI 输入监视示例程序。

Worth reading

  • kragen: 用「传播疾病」这样的说法反驳官方对设计沿用的正面叙述，并逐项批评 UTF-16、VFAT 的历史选择，只承认 PE32+ 尚可辩护。
  • kragen: 提出 Multiboot2 作为替代路径（仍可调用 UEFI 服务），并给出自己用 Claude 生成 289 行 UEFI 头文件和 inputmon 示例、在 QEMU+OVMF 下运行的第一手经验。
  • the_panopticon: 指出 edk2-libc 可弥补缺少 C 标准库的问题，并以亲历者视角解释 UEFI 的 Windows 风格来自 Intel Boot Initiative/EFI 的演进，附上设计文档链接。

entry.title: We know 15k websites are infected. how do we tell them?
entry.content:
#6 on HN · scotthelme.co.uk · 72 points · 48 comments · HN discussion

Scott Helme of Report URI says his threat-intelligence crawlers have identified 15,579 sites — conservatively 135 million visits a month — running malicious JavaScript: Magecart card skimmers, ClickFix fake-captcha malware lures, iOS spyware exploits (DarkSword, Coruna) and redirects to phishing pages. The infection vectors he lists are WordPress-style direct compromise, infected third-party supply-chain scripts, XSS, and 「DeadTag」 (a group buying expired domains that sites still load scripts from). He publishes no site list, says security.txt uptake is low and most outreach emails go unanswered, and asks CERTs/NCSCs and buyers of commercial feeds to mail intel@report-uri.com; he has no scalable notification plan.

Discussion: The dominant suggestion is to hand the list to browser vendors and Google Safe Browsing so users get an interstitial — protecting visitors first and forcing owners to notice via traffic drops or complaints; several people note this is exactly how they discovered their own site was hacked, and one asks the obvious follow-up: why aren't these already flagged? A second camp wants the list published outright (a haveibeenpwned-style lookup, or a plain text file sorted by traffic), arguing this isn't 「responsible disclosure」 at all since the harm is already happening and secrecy only protects reputations; others object that a public list of known-vulnerable sites is a target list for attackers, and one warns that charging owners for details reads as extortion. The sharpest pushback is over the definition of 「infected」: a commenter argues that if third-party analytics scripts count, the blacklist would cover most of the web, while others reply that a visitor entering card details doesn't care whether the bad JS was first- or third-party. Contact-channel advice centers on whois, abuse@, admin@, legal@ and contact pages — with a side argument about whether GDPR or pre-existing privacy-proxy services killed whois — and small-site operators doubt any of it reaches a human. A few ask Report URI what detection tooling they use, and how they'd handle sites with no findable contact at all.

Worth reading

  • sublinear: Argues the 「infected」 criteria are dangerously vague — if a compromised third-party analytics script counts, a blacklist would take out most sites people use daily, since almost every site loads at least one third-party script.
  • athrowaway3z: Strong counter-argument: 「responsible disclosure」 is being misused — the sites are already infected, so publish the URLs with proof and auto-update as they get fixed, accepting the consequences.
  • testplzignore: Cuts through the disclosure framing with an analogy: responsible disclosure fits a pickable lock, not watching a house being looted from across the street — just put a text file on the blog.

entry.title: Blender's UI and Runtime: Much Faster Than GPUI
entry.content:
#7 on HN · github.com · 600 points · 244 comments · HN discussion

BUI 是一个把 Blender 界面层（控件绘制、交互规则、主题外观）抽出来做成独立 C 核心 UI 库的项目，提供 Python（tkinter 全量 API、Qt 风格、45 个 Blender 组件）、Rust、JavaScript/React/Svelte、C/C++ 和 Dear ImGui 绑定，无需安装 Blender 也不需要浏览器或 webview。README 声称按需重绘、空闲时 0% CPU，相比 gpui-fast 每帧少 2–4 倍 CPU、首帧约 5 ms，打包成单文件可执行程序为 6.3–6.9 MB，首次渲染约 70 ms、19 MB 内存。项目自述绘图代码是从 Blender 的 interface_widgets.cc 移植的 C 代码，仓库声明“完全由 LLM 编写，无人类手写代码”，并因源自 GPL 的 Blender 而只能以 GPL 发布；已知缺失无障碍支持、输入法和系统原生外观。

Discussion: 讨论明显分成两派：一方（最上面的评论）夸 README 第一行就说清了是什么、为什么该关心；另一方则认为整篇 README 是典型的 LLM 文风——「super duper fast」「4. The many ways in」这类措辞、大段与代码片段无关的截图，让人读几段就放弃评估，作者本人回应说他不是让 AI 生成，而是让 AI 从 Blender 里“删掉非 UI 逻辑”，并称“AI 擅长删除而非生成”。许可证是第二个焦点：多人指出 GPL 让这个库对大多数闭源或非 GPL 项目不可用，作者解释说因为派生自 Blender 源码，无法改成 LGPL，只有重写才行；也有人认为这对 Blender 这类应用合理，用来做通用库则是硬伤。技术可信度上，有人实测网页 demo 后逐条列出失败项（跨多个数值框拖动多选编辑、Ctrl+C/V、Shift 精调、UI 缩放、折叠面板、右键重置、Tab 切换、快捷键、提示气泡），作者承认网站上的示例只是 mockup 并随后更新；Rust GUI 作者则反驳「比 GPUI 快」的说法，给出自己移植 JS framework benchmark 的数据，显示 GPUI 在多数字幕场景落后于 Dioxus Native、Iced、egui 和 Slint。此外还有关于 Blender UI 本身好不好用（baby duck syndrome、3ds Max/Softimage XSI 之争）、是否需要原生控件和系统主题、以及 GIMP/Inkscape 是否该采用它的长串闲聊。

Worth reading

  • Lockal: 有人按 Blender 用户的标准逐条测试网页 demo，列出跨字段多选编辑、Ctrl+C/V、Shift 精调、UI 缩放、折叠、右键重置、Tab 跳转、快捷键加速键等十项失败，认为这更像是套了 Blender 皮肤的 imgui，而非真正的 Blender UI 移植。
  • nicoburns: Rust GUI 库作者贴出自己移植 JS framework benchmark 的实测表格：在 create 1k、update、select row、swap/remove row 等项上，GPUI 普遍比 Dioxus Native、Iced、egui、Slint 慢，直接反驳了“GPUI 最快”的前提。
  • ppmpreetham: 作者本人回应许可证质疑：因为代码派生自 GPL 的 Blender 源码，无法改用 LGPL，除非全部重写。

entry.title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash
entry.content:
#8 on HN · blog.google · 245 points · 192 comments · HN discussion

A Google DeepMind product post announcing Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, a video generation/editing model that now makes native 15-second clips (up from 10 seconds in 1.1), settable from 3 to 15 seconds in one-second steps. It claims stronger reference adherence and character/product consistency, multi-turn conversational editing of a clip, better lip-sync and multi-speaker dialogue, and a 30% price cut to $0.07 per second of 720p video, with general availability on the Gemini API and Gemini for business plus rollout in Flow, Google Vids, the Gemini app (Ultra subscribers) and Google Ads, with SynthID watermarking. Google also admits current weaknesses in fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics.

Discussion: The thread barely discusses the model: the top comments are a pile-on about how impossible it is to find, buy and use Google's AI products, with users citing mysterious payment errors, identity verification demands, Workspace accounts stuck on older models, crippled trial-plan limits and endless Cloud console steps — with OpenRouter, Vercel's AI Gateway and Antigravity as the workarounds people actually use. A smaller camp pushes back hard: the plans are just Google One subscriptions, OpenAI and Anthropic naming is no clearer, and their Gemini/AI Studio/GCP setups work fine, which prompted accusations of astroturfing from both directions. The handful of people who actually used the video model are more measured: a film-maker reports it has been live in Flow since the day before and that Flow's credit cost went up (18 credits for six seconds vs 10 for 1.1) even as the API got cheaper, and finds quality only marginally better; another long-time AI video maker says 15 seconds helps but the model still can't hold idiosyncratic character designs without first and last frames. Others flag naming confusion (Omni's 1.x numbering sits alongside Gemini 4) and note the page's own text-to-speech reads 「dropped the price 3%」 instead of 30%.

Worth reading

  • msabalau: A film-maker who used it in Flow the day before says the character-consistency claim is the real draw but that it costs more, not less, in Flow and is not obviously better in limited testing — and that creatives use Flow, not AI Studio or the API.
  • fuzzythrowaway2: Someone making AI video since early 2024 argues the core problem is unchanged: models still won't follow direction precisely, and without first/last-frame control, fat, ugly, muscular or non-human character designs regress to bland commercial looks.
  • msabalau: Concrete pricing correction from Flow: Omni 1.2 shows 18 credits for a six-second video versus 10 credits for Omni 1.1, so the 30% API cut coincides with a cost increase in Google's own creative tool.

entry.title: Size-It-Up (Game)
entry.content:
#10 on HN · magnitudle.com · 31 points · 12 comments · HN discussion

Size It Up 是 Magnitudle 出品的每日视觉尺寸估算游戏：每轮给出一个目标物体的剪影，玩家把它缩放至在已知参照物旁边看起来尺寸正确，锁定后揭晓误差。每天五轮，每轮满分 100 分，总分 500 分；误差越小得分越高。网站还附有每个剪影的素材来源与授权记录，以及「谁在玩」的排行榜页面。

Discussion: 主流意见认为玩法有趣，但参照物选得不好：有人说自己从没见过发电站涡轮转子，只能靠蒙，而像鸡蛋、篮球架、送货车这类日常物品就好得多；还有人指出某一轮直接给出了某台德国核电站涡轮的具体型号，一查就知道答案，反而让游戏失去意义。有人反驳说“这就是游戏的一部分”，也有人认真回应“美国中心”的批评——一位美国用户表示自己同样没见过猫鼬、袋熊或新生熊猫幼崽，认为这正是游戏的用意。多名手机用户反馈手指拖动只会平移、无法改变大小，一位用户给出正确操作：一根手指拿起物体，再加第二根手指缩放，并有人建议加入触屏操作说明。另有建议给每轮加个人形参照物，或做一版天体尺寸的变体。

Worth reading

  • xivzgrev: 批评参照物不可及：没有香蕉做比例尺的自由女神像和大本钟纯属瞎猜，建议改用鸡蛋对马桶、篮球架对送货车这类人人都知道大致尺寸的物品。
  • horsawlarway: 指出涡轮那轮尤其荒谬——尺寸跨度极大，而且给出具体型号后上网一查就知道答案，游戏就失去意义了。
  • slowcache: 给出手机端的正确操作：一根手指先把物体拿起来，再加第二根手指才是缩放。

entry.title: Rune: A native GPU-rendered Rust UI framework for macOS, Windows, Linux and web
entry.content:
#11 on HN · github.com · 96 points · 70 comments · HN discussion

Rune is a pre-release, MIT-licensed Rust UI framework from Anomaly (anomalyco) that ships its own renderer, text stack, layout engine and spring animations, targeting macOS, Windows, Linux and the web. Its pitch is agent-friendliness: every app can run headless, so a coding agent can render to PNG, dump the element tree and drive scripted input to check its own work. The README also states that the project does not accept pull requests at all — contributors are told to have their agent file an issue, which the maintainers' agents then act on, and users are told to pin a rev of dev because it is pre-release.

Discussion: The thread is split between interest in the headless/agent-testing angle and blunt skepticism about the project's provenance and substance. nicoburns opened with a ranked list of established Rust GUI crates by crates.io downloads — egui (30.3M total, 9.2M in 90 days), Iced, Slint, GPUI, Freya, Dioxus Native, Floem, Vizia — implying readers should use those instead, and several others asked what Rune offers over egui or GPUI. The no-PR policy drew the most argument: some see it as a prompt-injection nightmare where a crafted issue tricks the maintainers' agents into adding a backdoor, while others (bhouston) counter that vetting issues is an easier and safer gate than vetting obfuscated code in PRs; several commenters found the 「tell your agent to tell our agent」 framing depressing, noting SQLite and Lua also take ideas but not code, and one suggested beginners go elsewhere. A factual fight broke out over testing: one commenter claimed zero tests, others pointed to crates/rune-kit/tests, and the correction landed that the tests exist but do not run in CI (the README itself is widely described as written for agents, not humans). On a technical note, commenters defended GPU rendering on power-efficiency and transparency-composition grounds, and argued over whether 「native」 here means OS widgets or merely 「not Electron」 — with the consensus that Rune is the latter.

Worth reading

  • nicoburns: A hand-picked, download-ranked survey of existing Rust GUI crates (egui, Iced, Slint, GPUI, Freya, Dioxus Native, Floem, Vizia) with numbers, framed as reasons to skip this project.
  • bhouston: Argues that gating issues for malicious intent is easier and more secure than gating PRs, since obfuscated code is the easier place to hide a deliberate bug.
  • esafak: The key correction to the 「zero tests」 claim: tests exist under crates/rune-kit/tests but are not run in CI, despite the absence of test runs on the dev branch's commit history.

entry.title: Deus Ex
entry.content:
#13 on HN · filfre.net · 269 points · 132 comments · HN discussion

A long essay by Jimmy Maher on The Digital Antiquarian, part of his ongoing history of Warren Spector, reassessing Ion Storm's Deus Ex (June 2000) against its modern reputation as the most important game ever made. Maher argues the game's real lineage is Looking Glass's immersive-sim ethic — System Shock above all — and Spector's three-word pitch 「Problems, not puzzles」, while noting the compromises: a conventional twelve-mission structure, explicit skill-point character building, and less strict diegesis than System Shock. He also punctures lore: J.C. Denton's initials really do stand for 「Jesus Christ」, but only because Spector borrowed the name from a helpful friend he used to address that way, and the game's secret organization is FEMA.

Discussion: The thread splits into nostalgia, practical mod advice and an argument about the essay's politics. Several developers and longtime players push back on the article's framing: one says there is not enough hagiography around Deus Ex, not too much, and disputes the criticism of its three-choice ending as on-rails compared with System Shock's fifteen-second boss fight, while a professional game developer confirms the solo-creator myth is a real problem — fans credit one visible person for decisions he never made. Considerable energy goes to soundtracks (the UNATCO and Hong Kong themes get the most love, plus Michiel van den Bos's 2020 remixes) and to how to play it today: GMDX is widely recommended over the flashier Revision for a first run, with links to the browser port OpenDE, the DX-Rust reimplementation, and mention of a stalled official Deus Ex Remastered whose January launch was pulled after a poor reception. A commenter who says he rebuilt the browser port with co-op and ultrawide support in about four prompts argues AI will undercut remaster studios like Nightdive; others reply that rights, devkits, publishing deals and actual QA are the hard part. The sharpest disagreement is over Maher's claim that the game's 「wealthy bankers」 conspiracy tropes echo the Protocols of the Elders of Zion — some call the essay drivel for that, others defend the point, and one reader says the connection had simply never occurred to him before. Side threads recommend Prey (2017) and Dishonored as successors and swap discoveries about hidden branches, such as keeping Paul Denton alive and killing Anna Navarre on the plane.

Worth reading

  • retsibsi: Corrects the article's claim that the Twin Towers were left out of the skybox for polygon-budget reasons: according to Warren Spector, the artist simply forgot them.
  • glenstein: A substantive counter-argument to the essay's thesis — argues Deus Ex is beloved or unknown rather than over-mythologized, that its conspiracy curiosity is 90s X-Files rather than Alex Jones, and that System Shock's ending is no less on-rails.
  • iaaan: Explains the low-tech trick behind Paul Denton's survival: leaving through the hotel's front door before he dies keeps him alive, while exiting back through the window flags him as abandoned.

entry.title: Devvm.dev: One VM for every project
entry.content:
#15 on HN · devvm.dev · 32 points · 16 comments · HN discussion

devvm is an MIT-licensed open-source tool that spins up a per-project Linux VM — via Lima, using Apple's Virtualization framework on macOS and QEMU on Linux — pre-loaded with the toolchains your project's files imply and with a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex or opencode) running inside it rather than on the host. Its pitch is blast-radius containment for supply-chain attacks, leaked secrets, prompt injection and rogue agents: a default allowlist network tier through a host-side proxy that substitutes real credentials for placeholders, locked .git hooks/config on macOS, an optional --clone mode that works on a repo clone instead, and COW copies of a base image so later VMs start in seconds. It also supports docker/nix/desktop layers, custom layer setup scripts, --from container base images and devcontainer.json, and installs via Homebrew tap or a curl|bash script.

Discussion: The thread is split between genuine interest and fatigue with the growing pile of near-identical sandbox projects. Several commenters say they are building or have built the same thing (libvirt + cloud-init, or around smolvm), and multiple people — including one who built an agent harness on it — tout smolvm as the underrated alternative, though another dismisses Lima/krunkit as slow and unreliable outside colima. Security-minded readers like the kernel isolation and secret shielding, but the design gets pushed on two points: the rigid one-VM-per-directory assumption, which people say breaks gitops multi-repo or frontend+backend workflows, and unclear support for supplying your own image. Others object to the curl|bash installer and the 'trust us with your Claude login' flow, want it in package managers, and propose lighter Linux alternatives such as bubblewrap — countered by replies that bwrap is Linux-only, has sharp edges, and isolates far less than a microVM.

Worth reading

  • brkomir: Describes receiving a fake recruiter's zip containing a hidden .git directory with a hook that eval()'d a remote address, and asks whether devvm inspects or warns about hooks already present in a folder before starting.
  • mnahkies: Argues the one-VM-per-directory model is too rigid for real work — mounting a terraform/argocd/grafana gitops set, or a frontend and backend repo, into one VM — and says installing all tools on a COW base layer is cheap enough that auto-detection matters less.
  • benatkin: Clarifies the layering versus smolvm: devvm could run on top of smolvm, since it handles toolchain and agent setup inside the VM while smolvm only points at prebuilt images.

entry.title: Democrats launching congressional investigations into SpaceXAI, META and Apple
entry.content:
#16 on HN · washingtonpost.com · 31 points · 5 comments · HN discussion

The linked article is a Washington Post piece (dated Nov 6, 2026) whose headline frames corporate America facing a 「Democratic reckoning」 after courting Trump; the URL slug says the same. The article text could not be fetched (the read timed out), so its specific claims, the committees involved and the scope of the probes are not confirmed here — the title indicates incoming congressional investigations targeting SpaceXAI, Meta and Apple. Commenters add only that Democratic midterm wins could affect Elon Musk, pointing to Forbes coverage of that.

Article not read: The read operation timed out

Discussion: There is almost no discussion of the story's substance: with just five comments, the thread is entirely about getting past the paywall and sharing mirrors. One commenter asks for a link, another points to archive.is, and a third offers WallHop, noting it does not geo-block. The only on-topic contribution is a pointer to a Forbes article on what Democratic midterm wins could mean for Elon Musk's net worth, described as information on the SpaceX investigation specifically. No one in the thread reports first-hand knowledge of the probes, disputes the premise, or predicts outcomes, so there is no consensus beyond agreement that the Post's paywall is in the way.

Worth reading

entry.title: Kalshi court losses pile up as judges refuse to block state gambling laws
entry.content:
#17 on HN · arstechnica.com · 82 points · 65 comments · HN discussion

Ars Technica 报道，Kalshi 本周在两个联邦巡回上诉法院受挫：第九巡回法院拒绝全席重审，没有一位法官要求投票，维持了内华达州可禁止其体育博彩的三人合议庭裁决；第二巡回法院则维持地方法院判决，拒绝为纽约和康涅狄格州的执法发出初步禁令，并一并驳回了 Coinbase 针对康涅狄格州的同类上诉。阿肯色州总检察长 Tim Griffin 另在州法院起诉 Kalshi，称其向 18 岁用户提供赌博、未缴税也未取得牌照；此前犹他州总检察长已提起刑事指控。Kalshi 唯一的重大胜利来自第三巡回法院（4 月，新泽西州无权监管），但新泽西已请求最高法院审理，另有 39 个州和哥伦比亚特区提交了支持简报，CFTC 则反过来起诉了包括亚利桑那、康涅狄格、伊利诺伊在内的十个州。

Discussion: 评论区几乎一致不接受 Kalshi 的「swap 而非赌博」说法，争论焦点转向它和股票、期权、期货到底有何本质区别。一派认为两者都是对未知事件的押注，另一派（获更多支持）强调股票背后是真实企业、有 SEC 监管和内幕交易刑责，而预测市场没有标的资产、平台自己决定事件如何结算和赔率、还能自行做市，实质是「戴着格劳乔眼镜的赌博」。也有人指出这条界线本就模糊：期权和天气衍生品同样接近赌博，真正差别在监管强度与用途（风险管理 vs 娱乐）。关于为何挨告的总是 Kalshi，有人纠正说 Polymarket 2022 年与 CFTC 和解后退出美国，直到 2025 年底收购持牌交易所 QCEX 才回归，且其美国站不提供引发争议的体育盘。另有一支讨论转向最高法院：有人认为这最终是最高院说了算（优先条款、商业条款），也有人指出若州法在实质上禁止赌博，最高院未必能救 Kalshi。

Worth reading

  • dogmayor: 引用 Matt Levine 的 Money Stuff：Kalshi 甚至没有上线「Kalshi 体育博彩是否合法」这个合约，尽管它此前已上线过至少 16 个挂钩最高法院裁决的合约。
  • xenadu02: 详细论证预测市场缺乏股票那样的底层资产与约束：平台可自营、可随意增发合约、可单方面裁定事件结果，玩家无处申诉。
  • LordDragonfang: 纠正「只有 Kalshi 被告」的前提：Polymarket 2022 年退出美国、2025 年底才通过收购 QCEX 回归，且目前至少有三起针对它的诉讼。

entry.title: Perplexity launches AI agents for work
entry.content:
#18 on HN · perplexity.ai · 49 points · 37 comments · HN discussion

The linked Perplexity blog post announces 「teammates」, AI agents intended for complex, ongoing work rather than one-off queries. The article itself returned HTTP 403 and could not be read, so details such as pricing, supported models, launch date and concrete capabilities are not available here. Commenters describe the category as agent teammates with persistent memory.

Article not read: HTTP 403

Discussion: The thread is overwhelmingly skeptical about Perplexity's relevance: several commenters say they forgot it existed, ask 「who?」 or argue it has become a niche tool. A former subscriber says the service was made worse to save money, including silently switching users off the smarter model they had selected, while others say the early anti-hallucination pitch never worked reliably in practice. Countering that, daily users praise it as a clean, ad-free fact-finder and news summarizer, and one notes the company has users and revenue in the hundreds of millions and sees persistent-memory agent teammates as a genuinely useful direction. Much of the argument is about moat: one camp says there is none now that frontier labs have caught up and free Pro giveaways converted poorly, while another says brand and name recognition are themselves the moat and that a company with that revenue should not be written off. A side argument over whether Gemini is fumbling the third spot ends with one commenter saying Perplexity and Google are not competitors along any meaningful dimension.

Worth reading

  • jwr: A former subscriber says Perplexity has degraded its service to cut costs, including 「accidentally」 switching users from the smarter model they chose to a cheaper, dumber one.
  • wmchen: Argues that much of the early hype came from free Pro giveaways through telcos and banks, with near-zero conversion, and that Perplexity had no moat once frontier labs caught up.
  • Mattasher: A daily user defends it as a cleaner, ad-free alternative to Google for fact-finding and synthesizing local downsides, with memory that makes answers more personal.

entry.title: Anthropic IPO buyers see valuation as low as $1.1T
entry.content:
#24 on HN · bloomberg.com · 82 points · 198 comments · HN discussion

The Bloomberg article itself was unavailable (HTTP 403), so this rests on the headline and the submitter's link: prospective buyers in Anthropic's IPO are reportedly discussing a $1.2T–$1.3T range, with some sounding out values as low as $1.1T — down from earlier talk of $2T and then $1.5T. The thread treats that slide as the real story, arguing over whether any of those numbers is defensible.

Article not read: HTTP 403

Discussion: The most concrete pushback on the valuation came from people pairing revenue figures with it: one commenter notes Anthropic went from $9B ARR in Dec 2025 to $80B in Oct 2026 at ~85% gross margin, while others counter that this came with a roughly $160B net loss and an $80B hole in the first half of 2026 (a third replies that most of that is accounting charges from valuation marks, not R&D). A long-running subthread disputes the moat entirely — several developers say locally run open-weight models, chiefly Qwen 3.8 on Strix Halo hardware via the Gufo engine, have already displaced their paid Claude subscriptions, and that Chinese-derived models are already inside F500 stacks via Microsoft and Cursor; others argue compute, capital and frontier-model lead are the moat, and that enterprises won't buy from Chinese providers directly. A separate cluster of comments ignores the valuation debate to explain IPO mechanics to a self-described novice — how the offer price is set from institutional demand, that later trading doesn't change what the company raises, and why a small pop is the goal. Bubble analogies (tulips, Railway Mania, Pets.com) drew the standard correction that the technology survives while the over-investment doesn't, and the SpaceX comparison was fact-checked: SPCX priced at $135 in June 2026 and trades around $134, i.e. below its IPO price.

Worth reading

  • tarvaina: Puts the growth in perspective: Meta took from 2014 to 2020 to go from $9B to $80B revenue, while Anthropic did it in under a year — with the caveat that Meta's figures are trailing-twelve-month and Anthropic's are annualized run rate.
  • paulpauper: Corrects the recurring claim that SpaceX has held above its IPO price: SPCX was priced at $135 on 12 June 2026 and now trades around $134, so IPO buyers are underwater.
  • CharlieDigital: Argues F500s are already on Chinese-derived models, citing Microsoft-Decision-1 post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B and Cursor's Composer 2 built on Moonshot's Kimi.

entry.title: Living beyond the limits of survival: wood ants trapped in a gigantic pitfall (2016)
entry.content:
#25 on HN · jhr.pensoft.net · 145 points · 46 comments · HN discussion

A 2016 paper in the Journal of Hymenoptera Research (51: 227–239, doi 10.3897/jhr.51.9096) describing a “colony” of the wood ant Formica polyctena found in January 2013 inside an abandoned Soviet bunker in western Poland that once stored nuclear weapons. Workers from a large nest on top of the bunker fall through a ventilation pipe and cannot climb back out; the authors estimate roughly two million dead workers carpeting the floor in layers a few centimetres thick, and note the trapped group has produced no offspring, blamed on low but stable temperatures and scarce food. (Only the paper’s metadata loaded here, so details come from the abstract text quoted in the thread.)

Discussion: The thread is a mix of admiration for the paper and dark comedy about the setting: commenters were amused that the ants were discovered during winter bat counts by chiropterologists, and several read the trapped worker mass as a metaphor for communism or for office life. There is real disagreement over why the ants never reproduce — one line of argument says a queenless worker colony is a dead end, which others correct by quoting the paper, that queens or brood occasionally fall in but the cold prevents breeding. Others ask why the ants, which can walk on ceilings, don’t simply climb the pipe back out, and speculate the growing earthen mound might eventually reach the opening. A side debate about whether the USSR actually stored nuclear warheads in Poland gets a careful answer: the bunkers stored warheads or delivery-system components for forward deployment in a crisis, and Warsaw Pact states hosted tactical weapons routinely; elsewhere people argue over whether such Cold War spending was wasted or successful deterrence. Several note the story keeps resurfacing on HN, including a 116-comment thread in 2019.

Worth reading

  • alexey-salmin: Questions whether the lack of offspring is really about temperature at all, since a colony of only workers without a queen is a dead end.
  • sandworm101: Explains that “nuclear weapon bunker” could mean warheads forward-deployed in a crisis or non-warhead missile and aircraft components, so “no nukes in Poland” in peacetime can still be true.
  • neuroticnews25: Quotes the paper’s estimate of about two million dead workers and mocks the confident identification of a single Leptothorax head among them.

entry.title: MTG-I2 First Images
entry.content:
#26 on HN · eumetsat.int · 54 points · 8 comments · HN discussion

EUMETSAT published the first full-disc image from the Flexible Combined Imager on MTG-I2, launched 27 August 2026, captured on 20 October from geostationary orbit 36,000 km up, showing Europe, Africa and the Atlantic. An accompanying rapid-scan animation previews the operational service: a high-resolution view of Europe every 2.5 minutes, aimed at earlier warnings for fast-developing storms, hail, flash floods and wildfires. The satellite was built by ESA with Thales Alenia Space as prime contractor and is still in calibration; operational service is expected in Q2 2027.

Discussion: The thread is short and mostly practical rather than critical. One commenter wondered how feasible it is to capture such imagery at home, noting NOAA has retired its last LRPT/APT-capable satellites and that Russia's Meteor M2-3 and M2-4 at 137 MHz have grown flaky with age, though a simple dipole and cheap SDR used to suffice; a reply pointed to a recent write-up of a successful Meteor M2-4 reception using an SDRplay. Others asked where imagery is available in real time and were pointed to EUMETSAT's View product viewer, which one commenter called 「damn nice」. Two quick factual clarifications: yes, the satellite is geostationary. No real disagreement anywhere — plus the inevitable joke that the headline sounded like a trading-card-game release.

Worth reading

  • nightjar: Links a detailed 2026 blog post showing a real amateur reception of Meteor M2-4 imagery with a simple antenna and an SDRplay radio.
  • bertili: Points to EUMETSAT's View product viewer, where the imagery can be browsed in near real time.

entry.title: Microsoft is winding down Oracle deal to rent AI cloud capacity
entry.content:
#27 on HN · reuters.com · 53 points · 12 comments · HN discussion

A Reuters item (credited to Bloomberg) reporting that Microsoft is ending an arrangement under which it rented AI cloud capacity from Oracle; the article itself could not be retrieved (HTTP 401), so the details here come from the headline and the thread. Commenters supply the specifics: one says it covers Microsoft declining to renew capacity built on 2023-vintage A100 GPUs used for Bing, with the company preferring newer hardware in its own datacenters, and that Oracle can re-let those instances at spot prices. The implied question in the thread is whether this signals softening AI demand or is merely a routine hardware-refresh decision.

Article not read: HTTP 401

Discussion: The thread splits between bubble-skeptics and people who think the story is being over-read. The skeptics argue GPU capex is never one-off — each generation costs more and customers will always want newer or cheaper kit — so it is unclear how the buildout becomes profitable, with side swipes at bailouts and politics (CoreWeave said to be down 20% since the election). Against that, one commenter counters that the market has stayed irrational for long stretches, and another notes that customers are still lining up for capacity, though at what price is contested. The strongest pushback comes from a commenter who calls the story a nothingburger about expiring A100s and claims Oracle can re-rent them anyway, while a data-driven reply cites roughly $2.3T in aggregate hyperscaler remaining performance obligations (about $1T of it OpenAI and Anthropic, versus $0.5T in 2022, with Google up 390% year over year) as evidence the spending is an existential bet rather than pure mania — a case immediately challenged as ignoring circular financing. There is no consensus, but the more informed-sounding voices treat this as a hardware-refresh non-event while still doubting the tier-2 labs' ROI.

Worth reading

  • neural_thing: Calls the story a nothingburger: it is Microsoft not renewing 2023 A100 capacity behind Bing, and Oracle can re-rent those chips at spot prices.
  • keeda: Puts numbers on demand — ~$2.3T in hyperscaler backlogs, ~$1T from OpenAI and Anthropic, up from ~$0.5T in 2022, Google growing 390% YoY.
  • zamalek: One-line rebuttal to the backlog argument: it does not address the circular financing in the buildout.

entry.title: Dutch 'idealist' bank ASN blocks non-Google Android, including GrapheneOS
entry.content:
#29 on HN · github.com · 585 points · 378 comments · HN discussion

This is not an article but a GitHub issue in the PrivSec-dev banking-apps-compat-report repo, tracking ASN Bank's (part of de Volksbank) Android app against degoogled/alternative Android. It opened in 2022, when the app reportedly worked without Google Play services, then flipped to requiring GMS at login; the thread revived in November 2026 with EPI/Wero's written answer that Google Play Integrity is needed rather than Android hardware key attestation alone, because they want assurance on app binary, distribution channel and OS integrity. Commenters dug out that Wero's own support page states custom ROMs such as LineageOS or Pixel Experience cannot install the app, and that the Play Integrity call lives in ASN/de Volksbank code (nl.devolksbank.mobile.banking.security.data.wero.IntegrityRepository#requestIntegrityToken) with the token sent to de Volksbank's own servers.

Discussion: The thread splits between people who see this as normal risk management and those who see lock-in. The defence is liability: Dutch banks are on the hook for fraud losses they could theoretically have prevented, so they eliminate perceived risk cheaply; others counter that the same banks happily serve stock Android phones years behind on security patches, which suggests the motive is not really security. A technical fight dominates the back half — commenters argue EPI's claim that hardware attestation cannot prove app or OS integrity is simply wrong, since the attestation certificate carries the challenge, verifiedBootState, the verified boot key hash, and the app's package name plus signing digest, and GrapheneOS publishes its trusted key hashes in a signed JSON. There is disagreement about remedies: some want EU-mandated open banking APIs, others note PSD2/PSD3 is nominally open but gated behind licensing and feature-poor, and a few point out that the EU's own digital identity wallet also leans on Play Integrity. On the ground, commenters report Rabobank also blocks GrapheneOS (though some get it working via Aurora Store), ING only warns, Triodos still works, N26 blocks new signups but keeps existing users, and UK's Starling has fixed GrapheneOS breakage. The one recurring correction is that 「ASN」 here is the bank, not ASN.1.

Worth reading

  • microtonal: microtonal rejects uattest.net as a fix, calling Unified Attestation an effort by vendors with years-old kernels that has campaigned against GrapheneOS, and argues banks should simply trust a list of signing keys such as grapheneos.org/attestation.json.
  • microtonal: Corrects the claim that Dutch police cracked GrapheneOS: the reseller had built his own fork with MDM, lacked upstream security updates, and had likely compromised signing keys, so phones were unlocked over ADB.
  • skrebbel: Points out the inconsistency at the heart of the security argument: GrapheneOS is rejected while stock Android missing three years of patches is accepted, so the banks cannot actually believe this is real risk.

entry.title: Flawless UI-UX Skill 1.0.0
entry.content:
#30 on HN · github.com · 15 points · 22 comments · HN discussion

A GitHub release (v1.0.0) of 「flawless-ui-ux」, a portable design-guidance skill that installs into AI coding agents via `npx flawless-ui-ux@latest install` (or pnpm/bunx). The interactive wizard picks project or global scope and copies the skill into twelve supported hosts — Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, GitHub Copilot CLI, Claude Code, Kiro, Kilo Code, Antigravity, Pi, Grok Build, Devin CLI and DeepSeek Harness — deduplicating to five physical copies, with rollback on failure, and requires Node 22.12+. The release notes claim no measurable outcome: they explicitly say tests and host inventories do not establish WCAG conformance or design-quality results, and the article page itself mostly failed to render.

Discussion: The thread is dominated by one complaint: a project calling itself 「flawless UI/UX」 ships no screenshots, demos or example outputs, and commenters read that as a signal not to trust it — one wryly notes that this repo of all repos lacks screenshots, another says it could be excused for a private project but then why publish it. A second, deeper critique from reedlaw asks whether skills like this beat plain model training at all, arguing guidance such as 「links for navigation, buttons for actions」 is already known to decent models and mostly bloats context and anchors the agent on irrelevant keywords; a reply points to whichai.dev for side-by-side skill-vs-default frontend comparisons, but no one supplies direct evidence for this skill. On the constructive side, practitioners argue the real difficulty is agentic UX rather than look-and-feel: CharlieDigital describes a dedicated UX agent that reviews flows against the Laws of UX and cites specific laws to builder agents, and others agree that role- and objective-based agents beat long rule lists. Several commenters doubt any algorithmic formula for good UX exists, and a few question what is even discussable about skill releases in general.

Worth reading

  • reedlaw: Argues that skills like this may not beat what models already learned, and can hurt by bloating context and anchoring the agent on irrelevant keywords.
  • CharlieDigital: First-hand report that a separate UX-only agent reviewing flows against the Laws of UX (with citations to builder agents) improved autonomy more than general look-and-feel tuning.
  • hbn: Questions what readers are meant to evaluate in skill releases at all, given unread markdown files and no way to judge opinionated design decisions.

entry.title: Scriptable GeoDNS: Leaving AWS for Bunny
entry.content:
#31 on HN · vincent.bernat.ch · 41 points · 15 comments · HN discussion

Vincent Bernat explains moving his blog's geo-aware DNS from AWS Route 53 to Bunny DNS, which is nearly free (up to 500 domains) and runs user-supplied JavaScript on each query. He runs seven small NixOS VMs (Paris, Nuremberg, Ashburn, Singapore, San Jose, São Paulo, Sydney) and a script returns the two closest servers via Bunny's RoutingEngine.getClosestServer() helper, falling back to the second if the first is down. He documents the failure of an HTTPS/SVCB record (RFC 9460) approach — Chrome ignores records whose target is not 「.」 and Bunny doesn't return glue for the target names, forcing a second lookup — and settles on returning one server with a 2-minute TTL when the second is more than twice as far and over 1000 miles away. Rough edges remain: Bunny can't publish DS records (so the luffy.cx zone lives on deSEC and the ACME zone runs on Hickory DNS in Rust), the CDN lacks HTTP/3, and the closest-server helper is IPv4-only; the bill dropped from about US$5 to US$1 a month.

Discussion: The pricing comparison is the loudest thread: one commenter notes the NTP Pool serves roughly a million DNS queries per second at its hourly peak with a small old Go program called geodns, and says paying US$0.70 per million at cloud rates for ~11 billion queries a day would be ruinous for a volunteer project. Several people praise Bunny's scriptable DNS as underrated, and a sub-thread corrects the article's Terraform setup: CDKTF was deprecated in December 2025, though Bernat points to a community fork, CDK Terrain (cdktn.io), and others say LLM agents now make hand-written HCL less painful anyway. A sidebar debate asks why not anycast; a commenter with ten years at an anycast CDN explains the trade-offs — hop count isn't latency, you can't easily split traffic from one network across datacenters, and load management means withdrawing advertised IP blocks per site — while Bernat says self-run anycast is complex and BGP-close can be a continent away. One skeptic questions who this is actually for, since running a blog on seven servers worldwide isn't a realistic default; others just marvel at the setup and the post's interactive map and animations.

Worth reading

  • cortesoft: A decade of operating an anycast CDN: hop counts don't reflect real latency, traffic engineering needs constant monitoring and fake-path padding, and balancing a single network across sites requires withdrawing IP blocks per datacenter.
  • askbjoernhansen: Concrete scale counterpoint to the pricing: the volunteer-run NTP Pool handles about a million DNS queries a second at peak with a small Go program, which Route 53's per-query pricing would make unaffordable.
  • vbernat: Notes that CDKTF was deprecated in December 2025 and points to the community fork CDK Terrain at cdktn.io.

entry.title: Claude Code sends your email address to websites
entry.content:
#1 on HN · github.com · 978 points · 318 comments · HN discussion

A GitHub bug report (#107757) against anthropics/claude-code alleges that Claude Code was inserting the signed-in user's account email into the User-Agent header of outbound HTTP requests — e.g. my-session-slug/1 <my.name@example.com> — and that the reporter now receives dozens of scam and phishing emails a day. The reporter argues this should be removed from the harness entirely rather than made an opt-in/opt-out setting, calls it a goldmine for scammers, and says they are moving their company to Pi with OpenRouter. The thread becomes an argument about how it happened, how bad it is, and what Anthropic did about it.

Discussion: The top-voted correction reframes the story: the leak is mostly Claude obeying sites that ask bots for contact info in the User-Agent — SEC EDGAR's data API returns 403 to a default curl agent and 200 once an email is supplied, and Wikipedia and the EVE Online API have similar policies — so this is model-generated compliance with a website's request, not a networking layer stamping every request. Anthropic staff (mpoteat, then lydia_hallie) confirm the root cause: the account email was deliberately put in the model's context so Claude would stop hallucinating names for @author tags, and Claude sometimes volunteered it as a contact address when writing curl commands; they shipped a built-in by-default mod, cc-plugin-privacy, in 2.1.317 to prompt before web/curl calls containing the email, and promise the next release will remove the email from context altogether, while conceding it still does not stop Claude writing a script that leaks it silently. Many commenters are furious — over vibe-coded software shipping PII leaks, over a plugin being the fix, over the GDPR angle — while others push back that the exposure is narrow and that spam anecdotes are coincidence; a few users with per-service email aliases report zero spam, which supports the narrow reading. Practitioners add that the behaviour is broader than the account email: subagents stuffed names, company names and repo URLs into User-Agent strings, and the leak shows up whenever private data sits in a context the agent can reach, so several argue the only real fix is sandboxing and keeping private data out of context.

Worth reading

  • varenc: Shows with a reproducible curl demo that SEC EDGAR's API rejects a default User-Agent with 403 and accepts one containing an email, making Claude's behaviour a plausible attempt to comply rather than a hardcoded leak (though the SEC accepts most non-curl agents too).
  • lydia_hallie: Anthropic's lydia_hallie states the root cause — the account email was added to the model context to stop hallucinated @author names — and the timeline: mod in 2.1.317, email removed from context in the next release, stable channel still on 2.1.311.
  • sunaookami: Quotes the hidden system-prompt block that injects the user's email with instructions never to send it to unrelated services, illustrating how a prompt-level guard failed against curl-generated headers.

entry.title: MS Paint Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
entry.content:
#3 on HN · cve.org · 488 points · 178 comments · HN discussion

The link is the CVE.org record for CVE-2026-83844, which could not be rendered without JavaScript, so the details below come from the MSRC advisory text that commenters quote. That text describes an out-of-bounds read in Windows Paint that lets an unauthenticated attacker execute code by sending a crafted packet to an affected service over the network, with no authentication or user interaction required, rated CVSS 8.1 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N). Commenters report the fix as Paint version 11.2609.401.0, affecting builds from 11.0.0.0 up to 11.2605.91.0, and note it ships through the Microsoft Store rather than Windows Update.

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: The thread is dominated by one question: how can a bitmap editor be reachable over the network at all. A large skeptical camp argues the MSRC sentence about 「a specially crafted packet to an affected service」 is boilerplate dropped into every RCE FAQ entry — noting Microsoft's October batch had 59 「wormable」 CVEs sharing the identical wording — and that the real vector is almost certainly opening a malicious image file, or a hijacked outbound connection from the new Copilot integration, which would make the 「no user interaction」 and 「network」 ratings wrong or at least misleadingly transcribed. Others counter that Paint on Windows 11 is a rewritten Store app with layers, background removal and AI features, so it has real network code, and someone reports that a stock up-to-date machine shows no listening port, undermining the literal server reading. Practical complaints cut across both sides: Windows Update offered nothing and people had to open the Microsoft Store page for Paint to get the patched build, and version numbering (11.2605.91 vs 11.2609.401.0) is confusing enough that users can't tell whether they're fixed. Around the edges are jokes about Calc, Minesweeper and Solitaire CVEs next, Zawinski's Law, and a running thread of nostalgia for the old offline XP-era mspaint.exe.

Worth reading

  • 6thbit: Points out that 59 October CVEs shared the identical 「specially crafted packet / no user interaction」 boilerplate, so the Paint advisory may simply be miscopied, and links the Zero Day Initiative's October 2026 review.
  • akerl_: Argues the network-access sentence looks like placeholder FAQ text Microsoft inserts for anything tagged RCE, and stays skeptical until someone shows how Paint is exposed over the network.
  • greyhound1: First-hand report that Windows Update showed no fix and the patched Paint had to be pulled manually from the Microsoft Store.

entry.title: Pwn.college
entry.content:
#4 on HN · pwn.college · 121 points · 12 comments · HN discussion

This is the landing page of pwn.college, a free hands-on cybersecurity education platform maintained by hackers at Arizona State University that also powers much of ASU's security curriculum. Learners start with a 「white belt」 and work through dojos — modules on the fundamentals of computing, exploitation and networking — earning belts as they go, with community-made and educator-importable dojos plus CTF and wargame pointers for after the dojo. The page asks users not to publish writeups, walkthroughs or livestreams of challenge solutions so the material stays usable for university grading, and notes the infrastructure is open source while some module content (with solutions) is closed.

Discussion: The thread is small and almost uniformly positive, with most commenters trading nostalgia for earlier wargames: hackthissite.org, OverTheWire, SmashTheStack and OWASP WebGoat all come up. One commenter notes the site was 「hugged to death」 by HN traffic and another reports it is still reachable via a deeper link such as /welcome/welcome/. The only real disagreement is about the scoreboard: one reader points out the top scores shown are just 10, which is what you get for finishing the tutorial, and is corrected that each module has its own scoreboard, so the tutorial board simply maxes out at the tutorial's total — met with a joke that accepting that explanation is not a very hacker-like mindset. A commenter who appears to be one of the people behind the project says OverTheWire, which he used as class assignments, was a big inspiration for pwn.college, and another highlights that completing all the levels earns you an actual physical belt.

Worth reading

  • adamdoupe: Someone involved with the project says OverTheWire, which he used as class assignments, was a major inspiration for pwn.college.
  • unsnap_biceps: Explains that each module has its own scoreboard, so the apparently low top score of 10 just reflects the tutorial module's maximum.
  • MisterMunchkin: Notes the unusual incentive that finishing all levels gets you a real belt mailed to you.

entry.title: Nvidia Kubernetes Engine (NVKE)
entry.content:
#5 on HN · github.com · 67 points · 18 comments · HN discussion

A GitHub repository from NVIDIA's dsx-ai-factory org introducing NVKE, a preview-stage management plane that platform teams install to provision and lifecycle-manage Kubernetes clusters on their own NVIDIA GPU bare metal. A throwaway seed cluster stands up the management cluster; that plane then creates workload clusters through NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo, the only supported infrastructure provider at preview), Cluster API and a node agent, with nodes attesting via SPIFFE/SPIRE using their TPM. The README is explicit that it is not a distribution or a Cluster API flavour, and that preview builds ship with API authentication off and plain HTTP, no management-plane upgrade or backup/restore path, and FDE node images that offer no real data-at-rest confidentiality.

Discussion: The dominant reaction is that the README fails to explain the product: commenters call it an AI-generated data dump and say that after reading they are more confused than before, though one replies that the opening paragraph does state it. A technically substantive critique argues NVKE blends concerns that should be separate — Cluster API, Kamaji-style hosted control planes and gpu-operator — leaving only the kind-based management-cluster bootstrapper and the SPIFFE/TPM identity work as genuinely interesting. Others note plain Kubernetes already schedules GPUs and ask why a platform team with k8s or k3s would need this; one explanation is that it targets tenant-isolated clusters on NVIDIA's DSX reference stack, using NICo/BlueField for isolated networking and wipe-and-re-attest between tenants — mainly relevant if you want NVIDIA Cloud Partner status or end-to-end NVIDIA support. A large side thread is OpenStack nostalgia, with people reporting Kolla-Ansible plus Ceph deployments driven by Broadcom's VMware pricing, and the tail of the thread drifts into jokes about dating things 'before AI' (BAI).

Worth reading

  • QuentinM: Explains the actual use case: tenant-isolated clusters on NVIDIA's DSX reference stack with NICo/BlueField network isolation and host wipe-and-re-attest between tenants, mainly worth it for NVIDIA Cloud Partner status or full-stack NVIDIA support.
  • Yasuraka: Argues the project conflates Cluster API, Kamaji and gpu-operator, and that only the kind-based bootstrapper and SPIFFE/TPM integration are worth borrowing.
  • hedora: A pointed version of the confusion: if you already run a platform team shipping k8s or k3s, what does NVKE add — and is there Stripe integration for reselling clusters?

entry.title: From Linux to Wikipedia: How Volunteers Build the Internet
entry.content:
#6 on HN · thereader.mitpress.mit.edu · 46 points · 19 comments · HN discussion

这是 MIT Press 的 The Reader 上的一篇文章，它在本次抓取时返回 403，因此无法读原文；从标题和评论中的引文看，文章讨论的是「peer production」（同伴生产）：由志愿者协作构建的大型项目，比如 Linux 和 Wikipedia。评论者引用文章称，这类项目依赖多样化、通常并非金钱的激励，其运作方式违背了关于组织和经济生产的常规假设。

Article not read: HTTP 403

Discussion: 讨论几乎完全转向了怀旧和对科技商业化的批评：一种主流观点认为，早期贡献者的热情、技能和闲暇时间，被产品化、云化和现在的 AI 依次侵蚀。几位评论者指出，真正的门槛是「means」——每天能拿出八小时做志愿工作的经济条件，而这在当下越来越难以维持；另一个人则称之为「志愿者的活干好了、引来关注、带来钱、再被追钱的人优化掉」的循环。反对意见来自一位长期开源贡献者：修下水道这类粗活必须付钱，复杂社会无法只靠人情运转。争论的焦点是，金钱是否会消灭内在动机，还是说问题只在于不公平的剥削——比如大公司接手项目大赚而贡献者分文不得。帖子后段完全跑题：一位用户指控新账号是 AI 水军，结果自己被另一位评论者用账号年龄和 karma 反将一军，还有人指出对方的拼写错误正是为了躲避 HN 的 LLM 检测器。整体上没有共识，只有对「好的东西大多来自非市场动机」这一点的普遍认同。

Worth reading

  • komali2: 长篇论证：把金钱当作唯一激励是新的、错误的假设；销售竞赛的奖品是车而非现金，因为人们真正想展示的是能力与地位，而不是货币本身。
  • WalterBright: 最强反方：修下水道之类的脏活必须付钱，人不会白干；作者自称已为开源贡献数十年，并认为复杂社会无法只靠人情交换运转。
  • lakeviewterrace: 用账号数据反击 AI 水军指控——被指为机器人的账号只有 31 天、1515 karma，而指控者自己的评论同样没提供价值。

entry.title: I struggle to believe that AI R&D is ingenious
entry.content:
#7 on HN · lesswrong.com · 49 points · 14 comments · HN discussion

A LessWrong quick take by Arjun Panickssery arguing that current models show poor basic research judgment. Across side projects — a Scrabble engine, an Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe bot, formalizing philosophy proofs for an AI Philosophy contest, and judging eight Apart hackathon papers that scored 60–95% on Pangram — he says models miss the obviously important papers, run experiments with too little training data to distinguish anything, and chase trivial directions; Astra located a key Tic-Tac-Toe blog post but failed to recognize its relevance. His one clear exception is fast-feedback hill-climbing: repeated prompting pushed the SOTA on “listing all legal Scrabble moves” 10x, though the two big leaps came from his own suggestions. He also notes models write reports so opaque that interrogation is needed to learn what they actually did.

Discussion: Commenters split between “you're using them wrong” and “I've seen exactly this.” The harshest rebuttal is that the examples are not fundamental limits and that Opus 5.5 handles all four with context and direction, so the failures will simply be engineered away. Several practitioners report the same asymmetry from first-hand work — models faithfully implement any suggestion but propose bad ones themselves, get distracted, and miss the big picture; one quant-hedge-fund commenter agrees with the diagnosis yet still thinks models make his company roughly 2x more productive at R&D because they implement experiments fast. The most substantive thread argues the real bottleneck is scaffolding: performance degrades as context, task count, and subjective decisions grow, and a harness that forces one focused decision at a time works well, but agents are no help in building such harnesses. A side argument over creativity: one commenter claims models only produce probable outputs (and always the surname “Okafor”), which others dispute, attributing blandness to averaging over incompatible styles rather than an inability to be novel.

Worth reading

  • Gareth321: Argues the post reads like someone who tried a blank-prompt free ChatGPT, that Opus 5.5 handles all four examples, and that nothing described is a fundamental limitation.
  • nfw2: Describes models as a competent part of a digital brain but “a genius with severe ADHD and short-term memory loss,” and says performance degrades with context size, task count and subjective decisions unless a harness enforces one focused decision at a time.
  • skew-aberration: First-hand report with Fabel on non-AI ML models: perfect at implementing his suggestions, useless autonomously, though he suspects the fix is simply running hundreds of competing agents.

entry.title: Inkling 2 Small
entry.content:
#8 on HN · thinkingmachines.ai · 177 points · 63 comments · HN discussion

Thinking Machines (Mira Murati's lab) announced Inkling 2 Small, a mixture-of-experts model with 594B total parameters and 17B active, image input support, and variable effort, scoring 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. It is initially closed-weight on Tinker, with Apache 2.0 weights promised next week after external safety testing; the post claims top or near-top scores across agentic coding, vision, finance and long-context benchmarks against GLM-5.3-Flash, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, Muse Spark Open and Kimi K3. The demo they highlight is autoresearch: the model autonomously post-trained Qwen3.5-4B on Tinker for 4.5 hours at $426 of spend, more than doubling a time-series forecasting score, and they claim it beat their own researchers at blind wine identification (three wines from one photo, 19 of 20 trials).

Discussion: The thread is split between 「this is the first US open-weights model that is actually good enough」 and a hard-nosed price argument: several commenters point out it does not beat DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 on the headline coding benchmark and costs roughly 2-3x more, so for their workloads there is no reason to switch. A recurring counterpoint is sovereignty rather than capability — companies that distrust models trained in China will pay a premium for a US one, though a subthread immediately asks why anyone outside the US should trust American models either. Commenters also debate who is actually ahead in the US: one side notes US open weights lag the frontier much more than Chinese ones and predicts any near-frontier US lab gets acquired or closes up, while others argue open models always catch up within months. Side arguments cover Inception's Mercury 3 diffusion model (praised for speed, called 「brain dead」 without coaxing by skeptics, with one reply calling out a suspiciously new account shilling it), the model's size (one commenter reckons a Q2-Q3 quant needs two DGX Sparks), and the wine-tasting anecdote, which some read as a nice generalization demo and others as a pointless parlor trick. Notably, the benchmark tables show competitors winning several rows, which one commenter cites as unusually honest reporting.

Worth reading

  • Bolwin: Cites Artificial Analysis pricing for the model — $0.30/$0.03/$1 per million input/cached/output tokens and $1.18 cost per task, roughly double DeepSeek's.
  • a11r: Points out the benchmark tables visibly let competitors (GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi) win several rows, which makes the claimed wins over GLM 5.3 Flash more credible if they hold up outside benchmarks.
  • itkovian_: Claims the training run was done entirely in NVFP4 and that this is by far the strongest model trained at that precision, explaining the fast turnaround.

entry.title: Britain to make salary disclosure in job ads mandatory
entry.content:
#9 on HN · reuters.com · 26 points · 14 comments · HN discussion

A Reuters report (the article itself was unavailable, returning HTTP 401) on UK government plans to require employers to state pay — at minimum a minimum salary, or a range — in job advertisements. No details on thresholds, enforcement or timetable could be read from the piece, so the specifics come from commenters' understanding of the proposal.

Article not read: HTTP 401

Discussion: The thread is skeptical that mandated ranges solve anything: several commenters argue a wide £60-90k engineering band conveys little, and that publishing averages would be more useful but runs into privacy problems for small teams. One line of argument, from WalterBright, worries the rule will be gamed — employers re-scoping or inventing a slightly different job after interview to escape the advertised figure — and he predicts litigation and wasted money, while others counter that nothing prevents negotiation and that candidates can simply walk away. PaulRobinson, citing UK civil service experience where bands are already published, calls the 「actual salary = min(range)」 cynicism unrealistic in practice, arguing the effect is to cap the negotiable ceiling and narrow pay distributions rather than lower averages, and that this would help close demographic pay gaps for identical roles at identical companies.

Worth reading

  • PaulRobinson: First-hand comparison with the UK civil service, which already publishes bands: he says the floor-everyone-gets-paid argument doesn't match reality, but the policy will compress distributions and narrow demographic pay gaps.
  • Xenoamorphous: Asks the practical design question the law must answer — whether there's a maximum permitted spread, to stop meaningless 「£20,000 to £100,000」 ranges.
  • WalterBright: Raises the bait-and-switch loophole: companies sometimes craft a bespoke role for a candidate after meeting them, sidestepping the advertised posting entirely.

entry.title: The Hackintosh Reborn
entry.content:
