It promises explicit layouts, ownership and borrowed references, with memory tracked as a tree of 「planes」, and lets the compiler run in the browser via WebAssembly. The page's only real claims are slogans — 「More Powerful Than C. Safer than Rust.」 — with almost no specification, and a 「trustme」 escape hatch for external boundaries.

Discussion: The dominant thread is that the project is undocumented: commenters call the prose vague and apparently AI-written, and the author concedes the README was 「mostly an initial prompt for the AI」 and that this iteration is only a couple of weeks old. One commenter argues that shipping unpolished LLM-generated docs asks disproportionate effort of the audience; others suggest fixes (a DOCS-GUIDE.md with Google's two-part technical-writing course, links to prior research instead of hand-written docs) and ask the obvious missing question: why a new language rather than proof obligations bolted onto Rust. Technically, type-theory readers classify the examples as refinement/Liquid types rather than true dependent types, which the author accepts, saying dependent types are planned later via 「ideal generics」; skeptics also argue the plane-based liveness tracking reduces to Rust's borrow checking, and that threads and overflow semantics are still unanswered (the author says overflow behaviour is unspecified, like C++). A long side argument over 「::」 as a namespace separator produced a real correction: it exists in Rust partly so all static paths can resolve before type inference and macro expansion, and in C++ it was borrowed from Algol68 to separate class membership from object member access. There is also a meta-debate about building languages with Claude at all, split between 「nobody will write this」 and 「the point is safety regardless of who codes」.

Worth reading

  • empath75: A commenter months into his own Claude-built Rust-like language warns that Claude constantly takes shortcuts, and says he threw away months of work until he rebuilt on a formally proven Lean calculus — advising others to formalise an existing paper first.
  • roarcher: Explains the real reason Rust uses :: rather than .: static paths must be resolved before type inference and macro expansion, so later compiler stages can ignore namespaces entirely.
  • 0c3ca83: Pushes back on the safety story, arguing the plane model only prevents use-after-free if every allocation becomes its own plane with borrows scoped to its lifetime — at which point it is equivalent to Rust.

entry.title: Show HN: I built a tool that prices a prebuilt PC part by part
entry.content:
#19 on HN · pcdealcheck.com · 65 points · 46 comments · HN discussion

PC Deal Check 是一个免费、无需登录的美国市场工具：粘贴零售商的商品链接，或者上传写着价格和配置的照片，AI 负责读取清单并识别主要部件，再由作者自建的定价引擎把要价与按市场行情估算的零件总价对比，给出 A–F 之类的评级和带日期的零件估价，报告可分享、邮件发送或打印。首页示例是 PowerSpec G531 标价 1,399.99 美元，零件估算约 1,569 美元，评级为 A；站点标注为 beta，评分和功能可能变动。作者 adlep 说这是自筹资金的原型，价格引擎每天更新，起因是自己曾因估算价值太费时间而错过一台好机器。

Discussion: 讨论整体偏正面，主要定位之争集中在与 PCPartPicker 的关系上：作者和多位评论者都说这是「反过来用」——PCPartPicker 是从零件清单算总价，这个是从整机反推每个零件的市价，省去手动录入；也有人（vonneumannstan）直言这类品牌整机的结论基本就是「你被宰了」。最集中的负面反馈是地区限制：多位美国以外的用户（加拿大、澳大利亚等）贴出 read_region_unavailable 报错，即使换成美国链接也不行，因为系统是按请求方 IP 判断的；作者解释目前只支持美国市场，受限于定价 API 调用额度（他提到别家数据源每月要 299 美元以上），要先有流量才能开放加拿大、欧洲和澳洲。功能层面被点名的缺口包括笔记本和迷你主机（作者承认 CPU、GPU 焊死在主板上很难估值，还举了 RTX 5070 移动版与桌面版差价的问题）、数据库里缺冷门型号（用户可提交补充）、以及没有社区热门好价列表和二手价（eBay、Facebook Marketplace）来源。还有用户报告在一条亚马逊 Dell XPS 8950 链接上识别失败，作者回应说报告其实跑通了，只是部分零件不在库存里。

Worth reading

  • chrisgarand: 一位加拿大用户贴出完整的 API 报错 JSON（code: read_region_unavailable），说明网站是按请求方 IP 而非商品所在站点判断地区，连换美国链接也无效。
  • adlep: 作者解释为何暂不支持笔记本：除内存和 SSD 外，CPU、GPU 都是焊死的，移动版 RTX 5070 与桌面版性能差很大，很难给出合理估值。
  • embedding-shape: 评论者质疑「API 调用受限」听起来过于严苛——每个零件每周查一次就够；作者回复说限额确实很紧，其他数据源动辄每月 299 美元起，且结果噪声大需要过滤。

entry.title: Kitty 0.50
entry.content:
#22 on HN · sw.kovidgoyal.net · 332 points · 206 comments · HN discussion

The changelog for kitty 0.50, Kovid Goyal's GPU-accelerated terminal emulator. Headline additions are dockable windows outside the layout (launch --type=window-dock / tab-dock), session save-and-restore across logout, restart or shutdown via restore_session_after_logout (with scrollback, encrypted via the macOS keychain, needing the Inhibit portal on Linux), and official support for custom GLSL shaders including cursor-trail effects. It also recaps 0.49's performance work — 15-35% real-world throughput gains, SIMD UTF-8 decoding (~20% faster ASCII, ~50% multi-byte) and a new AVX-512 decoder — plus vertical tabs, native multiple cursors, and Wayland parity with X11.

Discussion: The thread immediately veered off the changelog into an extended argument about the author: several people recognised Goyal from Calibre and split over whether its dense, menu-everywhere interface is admirable outsider design or an unusable mess, with defenders calling it 「AutoCAD for ebooks」 and critics saying the ugliness genuinely limits adoption. A second camp compared kitty to Ghostty, and the recurring complaints were Ghostty's slow startup and crashes on Linux versus kitty's maturity, sessions and native splits — though one commenter measured kitty 0.50's own kitten benchmark taking roughly 2-5x longer wall-clock than 0.48.2 despite higher MB/s, and others flagged SSH breakage from kitty's TERM/terminfo handling, which several people fixed with a one-line ~/.ssh/config SetEnv TERM entry or the ssh kitten. The most-loved post was a screenshake shader wired to the terminal bell so failed commands literally shake the window. Nobody disputed the feature list itself; the disagreement was almost entirely about taste, maintenance style and whether any of it matters next to a terminal that just works.

Worth reading

  • JonnieCache: Hooked kitty's new shader support to the bell character so failed commands trigger a screenshake effect, with a write-up on how to do it.
  • goodmythical: Ran kitten benchmark on kitty 0.48.2 from Fedora vs 0.50 from install.sh and found 0.50 reports higher throughput yet takes 2-5x longer to complete each benchmark.
  • wzdd: Says all the SSH/TERM problems go away with a single kitty config line forcing xterm-256color, rather than the ssh kitten alias.

entry.title: Adding Window Functions to a Spreadsheet
entry.content:
#23 on HN · getgrist.com · 35 points · 22 comments · HN discussion

这是 Grist 的一篇博客文章，作者是该公司的联合创始人兼产品负责人 Dmitry Sagalovskiy。文章说明传统电子表格的 running balance 会在插入或删除行时悄无声息地算错：因为单元格里的公式会把「上一行」调整成指的是原来那个单元格，而不是现在它上面的那一行。文章提出的做法是在电子表格里使用有序查找，具体包括 Grist 的 PREVIOUS()、NEXT() 和 RANK()，以及 lookupRecords(...).find.le()，把排序写进公式本身。文章称，在一张 2 万行的测试表上，用 PREVIOUS() 算完整列 running balance 只需几秒，而用 Python 逐行扫描的写法运行五分钟仍未结束。

Discussion: 评论者从几个方向提出了意见。有几个人抱怨文章读起来像 AI 写的；一位评论者认为这种语法很别扭：UPPER_CASE 的函数名和 Python 的 dot 属性访问混在一起；而维护者的回复澄清说，这其实都是纯 Python，PREVIOUS() 返回的是一条完整的记录，.Running_Balance 只是取出其中一个字段，$A 也只是 rec.A 的语法糖，经典 Excel 函数本身就是用 Python 实现的，代码可在 GitHub 上找到。另一位评论者反驳说，返回记录并用点号访问是「clunky」的做法，主张返回一张表，再用列名做一次 index lookup，就像 Google Sheets 里 GOOGLEFINANCE 的工作方式。也有评论者认为，电子表格变得越来越像数据库是好事，但它有使简单任务复杂化的缺陷，而且很难避开近五十年的电子表格语法历史。旁支的讨论则提到了其他替代产品（IronCalc、treesum、omasheet、pyspread），并半开玩笑地说这等于在重新发明 BusinessObjects，或者幻想从小学开始教 SQL——其中有人设想，以后 SQL 对 LLM 来说会像中古英语一样显得过时。

Worth reading

  • dsagal: Grist 的开发者 dsagal 解释了实际实现：大小写敏感的 Excel 风格函数是 Python 的简单封装，链接到了 grist-core 的 sandbox 源码，并说明 PREVIOUS() 之所以特殊，只是因为它会自动创建索引，以便提升效率。
  • shevy-java: 提出了最犀利的语法批评：为什么函数是大写的，而字段访问又用点号？为什么需要同时写 $Person 和 $Date？以及人们是否必须把这些都记在脑子里？
  • whizzter: 主张这种数据库化方向是一种误导：它想解决电子表格结果任意的问题，代价却是把「简单操作」变复杂，而且还要面对近五十年的电子表格语法；评论者说，这种语法和 Python 混用，是最大的设计约束。

entry.title: This Month in Ladybird – October 2026
entry.content:
#25 on HN · ladybird.org · 60 points · 13 comments · HN discussion

Ladybird 的 10 月项目简报，由一个完全独立于 Blink/Gecko/WebKit 的浏览器引擎撰写。其核心主张是：样式与布局已被移出主线程（因此 CSS 动画和 :hover 在长时间运行的 JS 执行期间仍能继续工作，文章称没有其他浏览器能做到这一点）；LibJS 在 Linux 和 macOS 的 x86-64 与 AArch64 上获得了优化 JIT；C++/Cranelift 的 Wasm 引擎被一个用其自研的 flap 语言编写的新 Rust 引擎取代，在两者都能运行的 JetStream 3 Wasm 工作负载上快约 7 倍。该月 Web Platform Tests 的通过子测试数达到 2,184,722 项，新增 75,650 项，并在 10 月 26 日超过了 Safari Technology Preview；该简报将这一增长的部分原因归功于把 AI 编码智能体指向 WPT 以填补缺失的功能。

Discussion: 评论者整体上热情高涨：一位每天从源码构建的人说，用它来做低风险浏览（HN、新闻、Reddit、YouTube）已经接近让人忘记它是 pre-alpha 版本，并把该项目比作早期的 Mozilla/Gecko，而另一位则计划等 alpha 版发布。一位评论者挖苦了五年前坚称从零开始做浏览器毫无意义的人。关于 Rust 的争论在一名 C++ 开发者询问是否应该迁移时出现，因为他的构建产生了超过 90GB 的构建产物。回复说这很常见，有一次 cargo clean 回收了 700GB，原因是 Cargo 的增量编译缓存和调试信息很占空间；有人澄清，稳定版 Cargo 完全不会清理 target 目录，还有一条指向 Rust 博客对 nightly 上 target 目录瘦身的计划。另一条评论将 Rust 的唯一明显优势归结为内存安全，并抱怨自己因建议 C++ 在 C++26 未能通过投票后应关注内存安全而被点踩。一个小插曲是有人希望该项目最终放弃 Qt6 而改用 egui。

Worth reading

  • quux: 一位日常从源码构建的开发者表示，Ladybird 已经接近让人忘记它是 pre-alpha 版本，而且发帖本身就是在 Ladybird 中完成的。
  • pornel: 解释了 Rust 构建产物的膨胀：增量编译缓存大量变动，加上每一项零成本抽象都会保留完整的源级调试信息，这两点都可以在构建配置文件中调整。
  • afdbcreid: 纠正了 Cargo 会自动清理缓存的说法：稳定版 Cargo 完全不会清理 target 目录。

entry.title: Jelly Sheet
entry.content:
#1 on HN · mrdoob.github.io · 160 points · 37 comments · HN discussion

A browser demo hosted on mrdoob.github.io as day 1 of Codevember 2026 — a one-month daily creative-coding challenge. The page itself is a WebGL canvas with no readable text, and the comment thread identifies it as an interactive, squishy jelly-like sheet rendered in JavaScript that works on desktop but fails on several mobile browsers. The poster is Ricardo Cabello (Mr Doob), the creator of Three.js, and commenters link his X post confirming the project was vibe-coded with AI.

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: The thread splits over whether an AI-generated entry belongs in a human-creativity challenge like Codevember, Genuary, Nodevember or Inktober. One camp argues these month-long jams exist to exercise human skill and that AI is draining the fun out of game jams and Advent of Code; the other camp counters that Mr Doob wrote Three.js, so dismissing him as a 「claude-kiddie」 is absurd, and that the concept and execution are creative regardless of tooling, with one heavy vibe-coder saying they could never have come up with it. A second, larger thread is pure compatibility debugging: the demo throws 「can't access property getSupportedExtensions, this.gl is null」 on Firefox Mobile, and reports are mixed — works on Fennec/Iceraven/Firefox 159.0.1/Firefox iOS and an iPhone 12 mini's Safari, fails in Brave and reportedly in Safari/Chrome on iPhone. The suggested culprit is disabled WebGL, fixable via about:config → webgl.disabled: false. Everyone agrees the effect itself is delightful and oddly satisfying, with requests for gyroscope control and a wish to tear it in half.

Worth reading

  • plastic041: Raises the core objection: month-long challenges like Codevember and Inktober are supposed to be about human creativity, so an AI-generated entry arguably misses the point.
  • colordrops: Counter-argument that the author is the creator of Three.js, so judging this as generic AI slop is like slamming Linus for using AI on the kernel.
  • 0x00cl: Practical fix for the Firefox Mobile WebGL failure: the demo errors because WebGL is disabled, and about:config → webgl.disabled: false makes it run.

entry.title: C++26 Disapproved
entry.content:
#2 on HN · andreasfertig.com · 254 points · 143 comments · HN discussion

Andreas Fertig, a member of the German ISO national body in WG21, reports that the C++26 DIS ballot failed on October 23, 2026 after a twelve-week vote — the first time a C++ DIS has ever been rejected, with only ISO/IEC DIS 26926 (C++/CLI, 2006) comparable, and that project was cancelled. The two-thirds approval threshold was missed because several national bodies objected to Contracts, which they consider not ready; Fertig argues they should have accepted the repeated WG21 majority votes rather than re-litigating at the national-body stage. He lists the ISO options (new DIS ballot, back to CD, Technical Specification, or cancelling the project), notes all of them need a WG21 majority that currently favours Contracts, and puts the next meeting on November 16 as the deadlock-breaking opportunity.

Discussion: A large part of the thread is people who write production C++ arguing Contracts is a weak feature: jandrewrogers and others say it is little more than syntactic sugar over C asserts, that it fails to deliver the promised compile-time verification, and that concepts plus constexpr already cover real needs — while quotemstr pushes back hard that runtime invariant checks are neither legacy nor replaceable by concepts, and that the feature is not worth killing a standard over. Others are unconvinced by Fertig's framing: several commenters ask why exercising a veto that the ISO process explicitly provides should count as a betrayal of trust, with the most charitable reading (royal assent that is normally a rubber stamp) contrasted against accusations that Contracts proponents railroaded a known-flawed proposal. A subthread claims Bjarne Stroustrup backed the rejection and even used dirty tricks such as snap votes timed for other time zones; others rebut that there were no tricks, that consensus simply never formed on a fix, and that papers named 「contracts concerns」 and 「contracts fundamental flaws」 predate the vote. Side threads cover the collateral damage to reflection, std::execution and library hardening in the same draft (with a counter that compilers already ship many of these), whether SIMD can be fixed at language level, build systems/dependency management, and a long Rust-versus-C++ relevance debate.

Worth reading

  • AlotOfReading: Links Lisa Lippincott's talk on contracts design, explaining why the evaluation semantics are more complex and potentially slower than plain C asserts — the argument that moved this commenter from neutral to opposed.
  • zugi: Pushes back on the Stroustrup dirty-tricks story: WG21's consensus rule means Contracts got into the draft, consensus that it needed fixing never produced a specific fix, and voting down the whole spec was the only way to reject it.
  • Zepto8537: Notes that other major C++26 features — reflection, std::execution and library hardening — are delayed too because they rode in the same disapproved draft.

entry.title: The Internals of PostgreSQL
entry.content:
#6 on HN · interdb.jp · 249 points · 15 comments · HN discussion

Hironobu Suzuki 编写的免费在线 PostgreSQL 内部原理书籍，2015 年 9 月首发，现已满 11 年，正文覆盖到 PostgreSQL 19-beta（不含新的 buffer page lock 机制），并按版本持续修订。全书按子系统分章：进程与内存架构、查询执行、HOT 与 index-only scan、WAL、在线备份与 PITR、流复制，以及 2026 年 5 月新增的 Beta 版「逻辑复制」章和 6 月新增的 8.5 节「PostgreSQL 中的异步 I/O」。页面同时包含作者求职说明与使用条款 FAQ：商用可按 20% 收入分成，或一次性买断全部版权，报价 500 万欧元（作者注明这半是玩笑），并明确不提供 PDF/RSS 版本。

Discussion: 评论区几乎一致认为这是理解 Postgres 的最佳免费资料，但落脚点集中在具体章节：多人推荐 HOT 更新路径那一章，认为配合 zHeap 与 TOAST 的实现笔记能建立清晰心智模型。讨论随后转向 MVCC 现状——有人指出书中没有 OrioleDB 这类新式 MVCC，另有人引用 Tom Lane 近期访谈称他看不到 Postgres 放弃 dead tuples 与 vacuum 的可能，也有人反驳说用户不必盲从上游，OrioleDB 对 SSD 更友好、MariaDB 也有替代实现。Uber 那篇 Postgres→MySQL 迁移博客被拿来当论据，随即被指当年若在邮件列表求助，多数问题本可解决，且部分问题事后已被修复。另有评论提到 Jepsen 对 Postgres SSI 的长期缺陷报告，以及 Postgres 18 中全文检索改用集群默认 collation provider、升级后需重建索引等行为变化；也有人对其中一条过于「全面」的技术评论表示怀疑，问它是不是 AI 写的。

Worth reading

  • getbrew: 给出 HOT 的实用要点：只有无索引列变更且新元组能落在同一页才会触发，因此在 status、updated_at 这类高频更新列上建索引会悄悄让整表失去 HOT，可用 80–90 的 fillfactor 并用 pg_stat_user_tables 里的 n_tup_hot_upd 对比 n_tup_upd 来验证。
  • hans_castorp: 附上 Tom Lane 谈 Postgres 三十年架构的 Snowflake 访谈链接，以及一篇讨论 MVCC 取舍的文章 boringsql.com/posts/mvcc-bad-bad/。
  • jon128: 反驳「上游不动用户就别动」：称 OrioleDB 事实上已是 Postgres 的「另一套 MVCC」、对 SSD 更友好，MariaDB 亦有替代实现，并引 Uber 迁移博客作为规模运维的现实案例。

entry.title: Giant canyon on Mars is still tectonically active
entry.content:
#7 on HN · lamont.columbia.edu · 72 points · 6 comments · HN discussion

A Columbia University news release from the Lamont campus reporting that the solar system’s largest canyon system on Mars — the Valles Marineris chain — shows evidence of ongoing tectonic activity rather than being a fossil landscape. The page itself returned HTTP 403, so the specific measurements, fault counts and dating in the release could not be read; only its headline claim is available here.

Article not read: HTTP 403

Discussion: The thread barely engages with the paper itself and drifts to Mars geology wish-listing. The most substantive thread argues that Hellas Planitia, the ~7 km-deep impact basin roughly antipodal to the Tharsis volcano complex, is an underrated rover target — both because the antipodal symmetry is too neat to be coincidence and because the depth means higher atmospheric pressure, potentially crossing the triple point of water and raising planetary-protection worries, with araneiform terrain and CO2-ice bursts as possible mechanisms for pressure-driven warming and mechanical dispersal of anything living. Several commenters take the view that subsurface Mars is where life would be, so a place you can reach 7 km down without drilling is the obvious first stop. One commenter reframes the canyon’s scale: standing on its walls, the slope would read as an unremarkable 10–15% grade, not a chasm. Others skip the science — hoping to see humans on Mars because a person with a shovel could outdo years of rover work, and joking that the release was clearly fodder for Randall Munroe.

Worth reading

  • somat: Points out that Hellas Planitia sits almost exactly opposite the Tharsis volcanoes, argues the alignment is not coincidence, and wonders why such a deep, atmosphere-relevant basin never got a rover mission, with NASA Trek map links to both features.
  • FranOntanaya: Adds that Hellas is the one spot that crosses water’s triple point (narrowly), which is why it raises planetary-protection concern, and notes araneiform terrain may reach higher transient pressures that warm and burst through the CO2 ice.
  • bajard: A useful scale correction: from inside, the canyon walls would look like ordinary ground on a 10–15% slope — you would not perceive a canyon at all.

entry.title: Show HN: HackerTV – HN's most-recommended Youtube videos as 24/7 TV channels
entry.content:
#8 on HN · hackertv.org · 297 points · 62 comments · HN discussion

HackerTV 是一个仿电视的网页前端（hackertv.org），把 HackerTube 从 HN 十九年评论里挖出的推荐视频重新打包成频道：DEVTV、SOLDER、RETRO、ORBIT 等按主题划分，另有 HN Prime（前 400 条）、音乐频道，以及只在本地时间晚 11 点到凌晨 5 点播出的 99 台 Late Night（其余时间显示彩条）。作者 dsalzman 说这是用 Claude Code 花几小时做的，数据功劳全归 HackerTube，他做这个的动机是「算法疲劳」——不想再挑，只想换台。抓到的页面本身只有一句「Press TURN ON to start watching」，外加键盘操作说明（↑↓ 换台、0-9 直选、G 节目单、F 画中画、M 静音、C 字幕、I 信息、T 影院模式、P 电源），并提示时长在抓到 YouTube 元数据前是估算的，节目可能提前结束或被打断。

Discussion: 评论几乎一边倒地夸完成度和拟物化细节：换台音效、节目随机从中间切入以显得「像直播」、以及「漫无目的换台比认真挑一个视频更有趣」的体验，都被人点名；不少人顺势要求 Roku、Apple TV、Google TV 版。技术疑问集中在 YouTube 为何允许这种第三方嵌入播放器且没有广告，有人答「Google 靠广告，广告要数据，嵌入就给数据」，但没人给出确定答案。主要分歧在「vibe coding 生态」：一派认为这类几小时做出来的 hacker* 站点几个月后必被弃置、沦为荒地，另一派则主张这类小应用应当公开 prompt 当源码，甚至反过来——直接开源仓库让人拿来当模板，而不是让 LLM 从头再烧一遍电。另有零星的产品意见：节目单里频道从上到下递增、但上下方向键方向相反；以及「按载体（YouTube）而非内容类型（视频）筛选」显得奇怪，有人表示自己的 HackerTV 是 media.ccc.de 和 PeerTube。

Worth reading

  • spditner: 提议 vibe coded 的小应用应把 prompt 本身当源码公开，并贴出自己一句 prompt 做 Roku 频道播放 HackerTube 列表的实例，正好回应了帖子里多人想要电视端版本的诉求。
  • i_love_retros: 唱反调的核心论点：保证这些 vibe coded 的 hacker* 站点几个月内被废弃，好做也好腻，维护和付费更难坚持，最后只剩一片「毫无意义的 vibe coded 垃圾」。
  • thoughtpeddler: 第一手观看体验：一路换台换到 2005 年扎克伯格说「我们正在想拿 Apple 怎么办，我们显然对用户隐私很敏感」的片段，只用一句「Wow.」点出这类老视频随机撞见的价值。

entry.title: Show HN: Uncracked City, detective game where you question LLM suspects that lie
entry.content:
#9 on HN · uncracked.city · 35 points · 9 comments · HN discussion

Uncracked City is a free Android detective game from a solo founder, with an iOS version awaiting Apple review, set in real neighbourhoods of Paris, Rio de Janeiro, Marrakech, Tokyo and Sydney for five training cases before harder real cases. Players search locations, question four LLM-driven suspects in typed or spoken questions across six languages, confront clues against statements and write a report in three attempts. The crimes and characters are invented while the cities and public places are real; the site's hook is that most cases show zero successful investigators.

Discussion: Commenters mostly enjoyed the concept, comparing it to the 1990s Sherlock Holmes Consulting Detective, Where in the World Is Carmen Sandiego and L.A. Noire, and one linked to experiments adding LLM-based input parsing to classic Glulx interactive fiction. The strongest criticism was of the writing in the trailer: it sounded bland, showed only two lines of dialogue and used 「honestly」 in both, which commenters called a worrying sign for a reading-heavy game. A commenter asked how the game stays free given per-session inference costs even with cheap models such as Luna or Haiku, and the founder did not answer in the thread. Others said they already spend their working days talking to lying LLMs and would not choose that as leisure, though one suggested an all-voice version usable while driving.

Worth reading

  • unintelligibled: Criticises the trailer's bland writing and its two dialogue lines both using 「honestly」, arguing presentation matters especially for a text-heavy game.
  • patrickskim: Asks how a free game covers inference costs, noting that even cheap models like Luna or Haiku cost something per session.
  • loloquwowndueo: Says interrogating lying LLMs is their day job and they cannot imagine doing it for fun.

entry.title: Japan's Jimi 'Mundane' Halloween Costumes of 2026
entry.content:
#12 on HN · spoon-tamago.com · 175 points · 30 comments · HN discussion

这是 Spoon & Tamago 博客一年一度的「地味ハロウィン」（Jimi Halloween，即「平凡万圣节」）精选合集，收录了 2026 年九张装扮照片。这项活动由 Daily Portal Z 的一群成年人在 2014 年发起，他们想参与万圣节却又不好意思扮成女巫或僵尸；博客作者称自己在 2018 年创造了「Mundane Halloween」这个英文说法，社交媒体上的话题标签是 #地味ハロウィン。今年的入选造型包括「在小居酒屋里试图给一群人拍合照的人」「想问能不能把椅背往后放的人」「搞不懂设计师款水龙头怎么开的人」「把捣碎棒当成吸管的人」「没想到商务宴请要脱鞋的人」，以及「一位非常小众领域的专家」。

Discussion: 评论区基本上一致欣赏这个活动，把它看作不动声色、信息量极小的视觉喜剧；有人形容这些造型是「情景俳句」，还有人说它们之所以好笑，正是因为你必须知道具体的场景才能懂。最重要的补充来自 numpad0：最后那张「补充分装瓶的女人」是在模仿维米尔的《倒牛奶的女仆》，这幅画在日本教科书里很常见，近年来也成了日本 Twitter 上的梗图模板；有人反驳说那不过是一张照片，算不上真正的装扮，numpad0 也同意这个造型本可以做得更明显。讨论「请求放倒椅背」那张照片的人出现了分歧：一位美国读者说自己从没遇到过这种事，另一位则纠正说画面里是火车座椅而不是飞机座椅；jen729w 随后解释说，新干线（他乘坐的 E5 系「隼号」）的座椅默认完全竖直，所以每位乘客都会礼貌地问后排能不能把椅背往后放 5 度，尽管座椅间距约有 1 米。除此之外，还有人对 Daily Portal Z 终于获得关注感到高兴，另有人讲起了自己类似的经历，比如扮成「忘记今天是万圣节的人」，或者在装扮比赛中看到有人扮成把包裹扔出去的亚马逊快递员。

Worth reading

  • numpad0: 指出「补充分装瓶的女人」是在模仿维米尔的《倒牛奶的女仆》，并解释说这幅画在日本教科书中很常见，近年来已成为日本 Twitter 上的梗图模板。
  • jen729w: 解释了为什么「请求放倒椅背」在日本是普遍行为：新干线座椅默认完全竖直，乘客总会礼貌地询问后排能否后退约 5 度，尽管座位间距约有 1 米。
  • blobbers: 提出了反面意见，认为那张维米尔造型只是一张有人倒洗涤剂的照片，并没有真正构成装扮，属于最弱的一个。

entry.title: Safari introduces Adaptive Dark Mode in 27.3
entry.content:
#14 on HN · webkit.org · 406 points · 216 comments · HN discussion

A WebKit blog post announces Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari 27.3 beta: when the user has dark appearance enabled, Safari detects predominantly light pages and transforms them to dark. Sites that declare color-scheme: light dark are left alone, while color-scheme: light only provides an opt-out, though that keyword is not supported in beta 1. The engine uses a hue-preserving luminosity color matrix, targets WCAG 4.5:1 text contrast, adapts gradients, SVGs and simple black-and-white bitmap logos, leaves canvas content untouched, and hides the transformation from JavaScript to reduce fingerprinting. Apple says almost 40% of page loads come from dark-mode users but only 10% of page loads support it.

Discussion: Commenters largely treat this as a useful opt-in fallback but question the need: Dark Reader, Noir and Stylus have done it for years, and Chrome already has an experimental Auto Dark Mode behind the enable-force-dark flag. A long side argument about Hacker News lacking dark mode exposes the real split: some readers get eye strain, halation or migraines from light backgrounds, while others with astigmatism find white-on-black blurry or afterimage-prone, so several argue for following the system preference and offering both. Developers disagree on whether browser-forced theming helps or hurts: one reports 100+ hours of dark-mode QA and would happily drop native support, while others warn about breakage and argue that sites should author their own palettes; the opt-in design and light-only escape hatch soften that objection. Commenters also correct the implied novelty, noting prefers-color-scheme has shipped for years, and flag that WCAG 2's 4.5:1 target is weak for light-on-dark text, pointing to APCA. The privacy claim that sites cannot detect the transformation is praised as anti-fingerprinting, though some expect a side channel to appear and others object that the browser is lying to pages.

Worth reading

  • famfamfam: Notes that Chrome already has a functional adaptive dark mode behind the experimental enable-force-dark flag, reachable through chrome://flags or the DevTools Rendering tab.
  • seanwilson: Points out that WCAG 2's 4.5:1 contrast ratio is known to be inaccurate for light-on-dark text and recommends APCA, which the article does not mention.
  • drusepth: A developer says maintaining manual dark mode has cost 100+ hours of testing and QA and would rather let the browser handle it.

entry.title: We're training a Figma-fluent editing model
entry.content:
#16 on HN · figma.com · 110 points · 47 comments · HN discussion

A Figma engineering post by Josh Clemm describes the company's post-training recipe for a first-party design-editing model: supervised fine-tuning on more than 250,000 synthetic edit examples represented in Figma's native file format, with teacher-model edits filtered by deterministic validators and visual judges, plus newer reinforcement learning to improve generalization. The post says an earlier Llama 3.3 70B model was competitive on editing tasks with top models at the time, and that the current agent mixes the in-house model for precise edits with third-party models for images, vectors and new explorations. Figma claims roughly 20% faster typical tasks from beta to GA, 62% win-or-tie against the previous agent in expert tests, 33% higher user ratings and 60% fewer undos.

Discussion: The thread is largely skeptical of Figma's AI execution rather than of post-training itself. Several designers and engineers report that Figma's MCP and agent are weak in practice: miguel-muniz says the agent needs product context inside Figma or it invents styles, taitems says server-side font licensing makes MCP unusable with brand fonts, and sebazzz calls it almost unusable. Others argue that a good MCP with a PNG screenshot feedback loop and docs would be enough, making a custom model seem unnecessary, while joefourier corrects the common bitter-lesson objection by noting that RL fine-tuning is itself compute-scaling. A larger camp says coding agents and HTML/Tailwind prototypes have replaced Figma for much design work—patchorang estimates 80% of his time in Claude Code/Design—though others defend Figma for component libraries, mobile and maintainable design systems. A side argument holds that Figma, Adobe and Canva are increasingly selling editing-model tokens to enterprises, with consumer apps as a distraction; a reply says token costs and bring-your-own-model competitors like Claude Design make switching plausible.

Worth reading

  • jjcm: A former Figma engineer notes the post landed the same day as Canva's Brush announcement, says Figma has one of the best UI datasets but has left it largely unused, and argues image models may fit UI editing better than LLM edit models.
  • miguel-muniz: A technical product designer who has tried Codex, Claude Code, Copilot, Figma MCP, Figma Agent, Pen.dev and Paper.design says Figma's tools drift and hallucinate styles once context lives outside Figma, and that Code Connect-style integrations do not cover common C#/Azure stacks.
  • joefourier: Corrects the thread's bitter-lesson argument: the lesson is about methods that scale with compute and data, not about frontier models always winning, so RL fine-tuning a small model for a narrow task is not a violation.

entry.title: Why Clip Art Was Everywhere Until It Wasn't [video]
entry.content:
#18 on HN · youtube.com · 33 points · 10 comments · HN discussion

A YouTube video essay (noted by a commenter as dating from 2023) tracing the rise and fall of bundled clip art in software. The page's text could not be fetched, so this summary rests on the title and the comment thread; the thread's own answer to the headline question is that clip art filled a niche when cheap, accessible stock images barely existed — it was the digital successor to analog 「clip books」 used for newspaper ads — and once the internet supplied better and more varied pictures, shipping a fixed image database with your software stopped making sense.

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: The thread is mostly nostalgia with a sharp historical point. One commenter who watched the video answers the headline directly: clip art replaced physical clip books for ad work and lost out to online stock libraries, and calls it worth watching at 1.5x speed. Several people push a parallel with today's AI imagery — one recalls that clip art users were mocked for the same reasons AI users are now mocked (low effort, samey, mismatched visual style, subjectively ugly), which implicitly argues the current disdain will age the same way. Others remember hunting the Microsoft clip art library at dgl.microsoft.com in the Office XP/2003 era and insist that style looks more authentic than the AI-generated flyers they see now. Off-topic branches ask what the ubiquitous dry-cleaner signage style is called (answer offered: pop art) and share a surreal early-2000s clip-art comic, 「My New Filing Technique is Unstoppable」.

Worth reading

  • janalsncm: Answers the headline question: clip art succeeded analog clip books for ads and died once the internet offered better, more varied stock images, making a bundled fixed database pointless.
  • Xirdus: Strong counter-frame — clip art users were mocked with exactly the criticisms now aimed at AI images, suggesting today's contempt is a recurring pattern rather than a judgement on quality.

entry.title: The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer
entry.content:
#19 on HN · arxiv.org · 325 points · 50 comments · HN discussion

An arXiv preprint (2605.29713) by Tianhua Chen, revised to a 195-page v2 on 8 Sep 2026 with added visual explanations. It is a compact, derivation-oriented route through the math behind generative models: PCA and probabilistic PCA, VAEs, diffusion models, normalising flows, autoregressive factorisations, GANs, Wasserstein GANs and energy-based models. The stated goal is to keep the mathematical substance needed to see how these models are derived and how they relate, while starting from linear-algebra basics.

Discussion: The thread is mostly a reading-list swap rather than a critique: people call the book surprisingly readable, then recommend alternatives — Anil Ananthaswamy's 「Why Machines Learn」 as gentler, François Fleuret's 「The Little Book of Deep Learning」 as the classic short treatment. Several argue the two books do not cover the same ground, and one commenter who skimmed it says it has little to do with transformers and is more relevant to diffusion models. A formatting gripe drew the most practical response: the PDF's non-standard page size prompted a commenter to re-typeset it onto full letter pages under its CC BY-NC-SA licence, though another pointed out the reflowed copy was one version behind (missing the v1.3 typo fixes and the new large-scale training section). Notation sparked a smaller argument — one reader objects that the first formula names ê1 「with no explanation」, while mathematicians reply that it is utterly standard unit-basis-vector notation, and the original commenter concedes he was never taught it despite years of game-development 3D math. A running sub-thread asks for books with exercises, and the thread eventually derails into e-ink readers and a defence of the Dungeon Crawler Carl novels.

Worth reading

  • bscphil: A commenter re-typeset the book as a conventionally formatted full-page PDF and linked it, noting the Creative Commons BY-NC-SA 4.0 licence permits it.
  • Valk3_: A curated list of deep-learning books that actually contain exercises — Prince's Understanding Deep Learning, Bishop's Deep Learning, Calin, Petersen's Mathematical Theory of Deep Learning, Dive into Deep Learning and Berkeley's CS182 — with notes on which are theory versus programming.
  • StilesCrisis: The reader who complained about the undefined ê1 notation pushes back on the 「it's standard」 replies by explaining he did years of game-development 3D math but was never taught formal unit-vector notation.

entry.title: There is no posttraining data commons
entry.content:
#20 on HN · openathena.ai · 61 points · 18 comments · HN discussion

A blog post from Open Athena (written by dlwh, also of the Stanford Marin project) arguing that pretraining got lucky with a ready-made public corpus — Wikipedia, arXiv, Stack Exchange, open source, and roughly 10 petabytes of Common Crawl since 2007, which supplied about 60% of GPT-3's data — but posttraining has no equivalent, because it consumes tasks rather than documents, and tasks are situated, ephemeral and must be manufactured. The author walks through how hard even the easy case is: SWE-bench distilled ~90,000 PRs from 12 Python repos down to 2,294 tasks, SWE-bench Verified's 93 hired reviewers cut 1,699 tasks to 500 and a later audit found another sixth broken, and in TaskTrove over 90% of 5,000 converted Java tasks and ~98% of one Python subset's verifier bundles failed repair. The conclusion: a posttraining commons would require systematic inscription of human work, and the open question is whether those inscriptions end up as private assets of a few labs or as a shared commons.

Discussion: The thread splits between people who think the missing data can be harvested bottom-up and those who think it is inherently expensive and should stay closed. woctordho argues distributed posttraining is easy — just collect agent traces from everyday use — pointing to Hugging Face's agent-traces support, the DataClaw project, and a claim that 10–100 TB of agent traces (including decrypted chain-of-thought from closed models, via Chinese relay services) are already freely downloadable. ArcHound takes the opposite line: every open effort gets sponsored and captured eventually, so there should not be another commons this large, partly to protect the jobs people still hold; lukasschwab replies that closed labs already spent millions procuring this data, so the real question is whether open-weight models remain competitive at all. dlwh corrects a common assumption that NVIDIA fully open-sources its posttraining data, noting much of Nemotron's is private third-party data (though at least disclosed), and elsewhere describes wanting the inscription work to be participatory rather than extractive — letting scientists decide what drudgery gets automated. A long side thread about whether the NSA would supply wiretap or industrial-espionage data to labs produced a correction that NSA programs are SAP, not SCI, and david_shi drew an Internet Archive comparison, imagining retiring accountants donating their expertise to a trusted steward.

Worth reading

  • woctordho: Claims a posttraining commons is already forming from volunteered agent traces — Hugging Face hub support, the DataClaw collector, and an estimate of 10–100 TB already public — while conceding closed models' chain-of-thought is encrypted.
  • dlwh: The author corrects the thread's assumption that NVIDIA is the open-data exception, noting much of Nemotron's posttraining data is private third-party data that is merely disclosed.
  • ArcHound: A blunt counter-argument: open commons efforts get sponsored and captured, so a posttraining commons should arguably not exist, to preserve what jobs remain.

entry.title: Show HN: Kairos – Open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform
entry.content:
#21 on HN · github.com · 86 points · 19 comments · HN discussion

Finic 发布的 Kairos 是 Sift、Sardine、Riskified、SEON 等实时欺诈决策平台的开源替代品（Apache 2.0），以一次调用返回 approve / step up / review / block 及风险分和理由，并可管理工作流、复核队列与案件。它主打两点：内置的 Grayson 决策模型能用自然语言问题（如「这个邮箱是不是一次性邮箱」「收货地址像不像转运商」）在标注数据很少时给出校准概率，其答案还能作为特征喂给逻辑回归或 XGBoost 兼容的梯度提升树；以及一个 MCP server，让 Claude Code、Cursor、Codex 等 agent 读取决策、搭建工作流、跑实验（按时间切分训练/选择/测试，报告 ROC-AUC、PR-AUC 和相对基线的增益）并发布胜出的版本。提供 TypeScript（@finic-ai/kairos）和 Python（finic-kairos）SDK、CLI、Docker 自托管（需要 Node.js 22、pnpm 10 和一个来自 Finic 的 Grayson API key）。

Discussion: 线程不长，主要是三点反应。安全方面有人质疑用 TypeScript/Node 承载支付级决策：运行时程序可被外部输入改写、Dockerfile 没有做相应限制，因此没有任何机制阻止原型污染，而配置缺陷会反复咬人。有人以 1995 年在 AOL 做邮件管理员的经历呼应文章中「欺诈者几周就绕过规则」的论点，说当年花数月做的反垃圾技术常被对方一个周末攻破。可读性方面有人对「decisioning」这个行业术语不满，认为不该给名词加 -ing，随即被反驳说这是行话、语言本来就随使用演变，不该怪作者。另有相当一部分评论纠缠重名：kairos.io 的 Linux 发行版、kairos.com 的身份验证公司、kairos-project.org 的 AI 安全组织，还有人整理出 DARPA 的一个同名项目，争论开源社区是否该避让已有名字，也有人认为重名无碍、不影响项目本身的价值。

Worth reading

  • factotvm: 赞赏开源，但反对用 TypeScript/Node 做支付网关：运行时可以自我改写、Dockerfile 未加锁，因此没有任何机制防止原型污染。
  • bradknowles: 1995 年在 AOL 担任高级互联网邮件管理员的一手经验：反垃圾技术要花数周数月研发，垃圾邮件发送者常在一个周末内绕过，与文中「欺诈者不断变化」的论点一致。
  • Messier43: 指出 Kairos 这个名字已被 kairos.io 的 Linux 发行版占用，后续回复又追加了同名公司、AI 安全组织和 DARPA 项目。

entry.title: Curiosity Traps
entry.content:
#22 on HN · autodidacts.io · 72 points · 8 comments · HN discussion

A post on autodidacts.io arguing that you can invert the honeypot: instead of luring bad actors, deliberately leave intellectual honey — conversation-piece T-shirts, footnotes, hidden links, easter eggs — to attract unusually well-matched curious people. The author credits Henrik Karlsson's idea that a public body of work passively collects a network of people aligned with your interests, and points to Wait But Why's old footer turtle, which chained through a series of hidden pages (turtle → turtle → 「You Win」 → giraffe → Tim Urban's old blog), plus their own /intractable page reached via a tiny interrobang in the footer. The post also concedes the costs: layered art drives off readers looking for an excuse to stop, a test reader close to the ideal audience missed every easter egg, and the best traps emerge naturally from concrete experience and publishing a lot rather than being engineered. The essay practises what it preaches, with deliberately broken nested footnotes and a final footnote id of #final-boss.

Discussion: The thread is small and mostly appreciative, with the main divergence being terminology: two commenters independently reach for xkcd 356, and one argues these are less traps than beacons or dog whistles for the like-minded, adding that a curated interesting personality can't be produced by trying hard. Several commenters flip the direction and say the obligation runs both ways — that it's on readers to actually email the people whose work they liked. One commenter who does this regularly says compliments are worth sending, with the caveat to avoid vague meeting requests or low-effort GitHub issues. Against that, one commenter admits ruefully that nobody has touched their doorknob in a while and asks how to improve the odds, drawing only a one-line 「What should we look at?」 reply — an unintentionally apt demonstration of the problem.

Worth reading

  • bobbiechen: Argues the curiosity doorknob is a two-way contract: they hesitated before their first fan email, but receiving one made their day.
  • gopalv: Corrects the framing — these are beacons or dog whistles rather than traps — and argues an interesting personality can't be manufactured by trying hard.
  • ungreased0675: A candid counterpoint to the whole thesis: no one has written in to them lately, and they ask how to improve the odds.

entry.title: Microsoft fixes a Windows 11 annoyance as PC revenue declines
entry.content:
#23 on HN · arstechnica.com · 63 points · 152 comments · HN discussion

Ars Technica covers preview update KB5127936 for Windows 11 25H2/26H2, which adds a 「customize menu」 button letting users toggle built-in right-click commands (Send To, Create Shortcut), rearrange the main menu, and decide which third-party shell extensions appear. The same update introduces Cloud Rebuild, a recovery option that pulls the Windows 11 image and drivers from Windows Update with no USB media — though it behaves like a clean install and does not preserve apps or files. The article ties the timing to Microsoft's quarterly results: Windows OEM revenue fell 27% (28% in constant currency) on Windows 10 end-of-support demand pulled forward, OEM inventory drawdowns and weak PC demand, with the OEM-and-devices category down 22%, while Azure rose 48% and Microsoft Cloud 30%, about 70% of $92.3B quarterly revenue.

Discussion: The thread is overwhelmingly about leaving Windows rather than about the menu fix: multiple people describe switching to Fedora Kinoite, Bazzite, Mint, CachyOS, Omarchy or plain Debian because of telemetry, ads, forced Microsoft accounts and UI regressions, and several say gaming is no longer a blocker thanks to Proton and SteamOS. A live disagreement runs on whether Windows 10 was ever good — one commenter calls the nostalgia a cognitive bias and predicts people will soon say Windows 11 was fine, while others trace the decline to Windows 8 or even NT 4. The Linux side gets pushback too: a long sarcastic 「day 1 to day 204」 account of driver and distro pain is rebutted by users arguing that any mainstream distro handles the same kernels and that immutable images solve the update fragility, with a counter-counter about a kernel update that dropped a GPU driver. Practical subthreads cover restoring the classic context menu (Shift+right-click, or a registry key), local-account bypasses (OOBE\BYPASSNRO, Rufus, an LTSC install from massgrave.dev) and how Microsoft keeps closing those loopholes, plus a 700GB Windows.old/WinSxS cleanup war story.

Worth reading

  • DonHopkins: Argues the icon row violates Fitts's law regardless of familiarity, and cites Kurtenbach and Buxton's marking menus plus 1988 Maryland pie-menu measurements showing novices faster and more accurate than with linear menus.
  • kalleboo: Corrects the claim that Microsoft 「knocked out」 Office and Visual Studio in a year: there was no Office for DOS, the first Office shipped for Mac, Excel began as Mac software after Multiplan, and PowerPoint was an Apple-funded Mac product Microsoft acquired.
  • nukanse: First-hand repair story: a 1TB drive was half full of Windows.old after the 26H2 update, Windows' five documented deletion methods all failed or hung on a 4TB/s NVMe, and the folder only went away after booting a Linux rescue USB — 700GB reclaimed in total.

entry.title: Union Types and Option Types (2025)
entry.content:
#26 on HN · tibleiz.net · 41 points · 16 comments · HN discussion

A blog post by the author of Copper, a self-hosted 「better C」 language, recounting experiments with union types (T1|T2) and the trimmed-down option type T|Nothing. Copper restricted unions heavily for compilation reasons — no nested unions, order-sensitive (Error|File picks the first type, so file = File.open(...) unwraps to Error automatically), and no compatibility between T1|T2 and T1|T2|T3 — and implements options by reserving a value in the type itself: 0 for pointers, 0x8000_0000 for a 24-bit color in a 32-bit int, -1 for signed indices. Refinement is explicit via an as operator, a notNil escape hatch, defopt for methods on optional types, and an ifNil macro; the author tried TypeScript/Kotlin-style flow-sensitive nil inference but abandoned it over two-pass loop analysis, poor genericity, unpredictable checker power, and a ~5% compiler slowdown. Porting the compiler, the Clade text editor and an experimental decompiler surfaced real bugs, and he concludes option types were worth more than expected — 「maybe it's time to get rid of the billion-dollar mistake.」

Discussion: The thread is split between people objecting to Copper's union restrictions and people arguing about representation tricks. The top comment calls it bizarre that a language with union types drops such basic properties as three-member unions and order-independence, and judges the implementation-driven justification weak; no one really defends the design. A separate subthread debates tagged-union memory layout: one commenter's tip is to put the discriminator at the end so a pointer to the union is also a pointer to the value, countered by arguments that serialization wants the tag first and that putting the tag last is like storing an array length at the end. Others ask where to find cross-language comparisons of optional and union types, with Rosetta Code, Pierce's Types and Programming Languages, and 「Swift already answered all these」 offered as answers, before the thread degenerates into onion/shallot/layers puns about optional types.

Worth reading

  • jakobnissen: Argues Copper's union type is crippled by implementation convenience, since no three-member unions and order-sensitive unions discard the feature's most useful properties.
  • p1necone: Practical layout trick: put the union tag at the end so a pointer to the union also points at the value, avoiding pointer arithmetic after discriminating.
  • sparkie: Pushes back on the tag-last idea, comparing it to storing an array length at the end and noting a tagged union's size can depend on its tag, so it need not be fixed-size like a C union.

entry.title: Introduction to Programming in ATS
entry.content:
#27 on HN · ats-lang.sourceforge.net · 70 points · 9 comments · HN discussion

The online book 「Introduction to Programming in ATS」 by Hongwei Xi (ATS Trustful Software, dated 2010–201?) is a dense textbook-style introduction to the language, aimed at readers with considerable programming experience. It walks through basic functional programming, datatypes, polymorphic types, dependent types, linear types and views/viewtypes, theorem-proving and programming-with-theorem-proving, and function templates, with worked examples such as eight-queens, red-black trees, mergesort on lists, verified fast exponentiation and array-based circular buffers. Its stated purpose is to show how ATS combines specification and verification with practical systems-level programming.

Discussion: Commenters mostly reminisce and compare rather than critique the book: ATS was once a frequent HN topic, and MLton and Felix are named as the other ML-derived languages that use whole-program optimization to produce fast native code, with one commenter saying ATS is a 「north star」 for a language he is designing. The most useful thread corrects an initial 「actively developed」 pointer at ATS-Postiats: ATS2 has been effectively frozen for years, with recent commits mostly build changes needed to compile ATS3, and the real work is now on ATS3 (Xanadu), which self-compiles but is not generally usable — its main design change being two-layer type checking (ML-style first, dependent types on top) to lower the learning curve. Release notes live in CHANGES-ats2 and the ats-lang-users Google group is the place to follow progress, since the project has little community development behind it. Others share a conference talk by Aditya Siram as an easier entry point, and the rest of the thread is jokes about the acronym meaning Abstract Tree Syntax, Applicant Tracking System, or 「Are They Serious?」. There is no real disagreement about the language's substance — only about which version is current.

Worth reading

  • doublec: A practitioner's precise status report: ATS2 is frozen but stable and usable, with release notes in CHANGES-ats2, while ATS3 compiles itself yet is not generally usable and is rewriting type checking in two layers to ease the learning curve.
  • ddellacosta: Links Aditya Siram's talk 「A (Not So Gentle) Introduction To Systems Programming In ATS」 as a friendlier way in than the book.
  • srean: Places ATS alongside MLton and Felix as ML-inspired languages that whole-program-optimize to fast code, with links to both.

entry.title: Preparing for the Flipper One Kickstarter and opening pre-orders
entry.content:
#33 on HN · flipper.net · 202 points · 89 comments · HN discussion

这是 Flipper 官方为 Flipper One 新设备发布的产品页面：一台基于 Rockchip RK3576（8 核 ARM SoC，带 NPU 和 GPU）的开放式 Linux 计算机，另配一颗 RP2350 微控制器（MCU）专门负责屏幕、按键、电源和引导。Flipper 宣称与 Collabora 合作，把 RK3576 和它的外设推进 Linux 主线内核，以摆脱厂商 BSP 和二进制 blob。扩展能力是重点：机身内有 M.2 插槽（PCIe 2.1 ×1、USB 2.0、USB 3.1、SATA3、SIM/eSIM），可插 5G 模组、SDR、NVMe；此外还有千兆以太网、Wi-Fi 6E（联发科 MT7921U，支持 monitor mode 和 packet injection）、最多 5 路上行的多 WAN 工具；通过 USB-C 一线即可 SSH 登录、充电并接显示器。预购需要先付 20 美元买一张可退的优惠券，正式 Kickstarter 计划在 11 月启动。

Discussion: 最集中的赞同来自旅行场景：多人表示终于有一台设备能同时做公共 Wi-Fi 客户端、VPN 出口和多路上行故障切换，省得在每台设备上分别配置，而且能绕开公司电脑禁止装 VPN 的限制。但立刻有人指出需求早有现成解：GL.iNet 的 Slate 7、带电池和蜂窝模块的 Mudi 7；也有人反映 UniFi 旅行路由器「纸面上好用，实际非常不稳」。另一大分歧是产品定位：不少人认为 Flipper One 只是装在异形外壳里的 ARM 单板机，Flipper Zero 那种 Sub-GHz、RFID、红外等另类射频外设没有了，不如买树莓派；支持者则强调 Zero 管物理层、One 管网络层，两者互补，官方另有一张 Zero vs One 对比图。对「完全主线内核」的宣传，评论者持怀疑但基本认可：有人指出树莓派 5 至今仍未进主线，而 Flipper 自己的文档也承认 NPU、视频编码、CSI 尚不支持。此外还穿插了用大模型配合逻辑分析仪、USB-TTL 做硬件逆向的实例讨论，以及对俄罗斯背景、海关扣押风险和 Flipper SIM 细节的追问。

Worth reading

  • opello: 指出 Flipper 有专门页面说明 RK3576 主线化的进展，并提醒并非全部在原生内核下可用——NPU、视频编码器和 CSI 仍列在未支持项里。
  • MOARDONGZPLZ: 补充了预购机制细节：优惠券可用到 11 月 Kickstarter 启动，届时预计以约 379 美元的特价支持，若众筹未启动或不支持则自动退款。
  • duskwuff: 反驳「只是又一代同类产品」：Zero 的独特之处在于一堆古怪的射频与 IO 外设，而 One 只是一台装在奇怪外壳里的 ARM 单板机，不再具备同类特色。

entry.title: Why Don't We Live in an Art Nouveau World?
entry.content:
#37 on HN · asteriskmag.com · 134 points · 118 comments · HN discussion

An Asterisk Magazine essay (by a writer whose bio lists AI evaluation) that starts from the Sagrada Família — main spire finished this February, making it the tallest church in the world 144 years after construction began — and from the nearby Hospital de Sant Pau, a Domènech i Montaner Modernista complex built 1901–1930. The author argues the “trad critique” (humanity abandoned beauty around 1940–50) is naive: Art Nouveau was short-lived because the reaction against it began by the mid-1900s, and even in its heyday patrons fought over utility versus showpiece, as at Sant Pau, where the most ornate pavilion was the administration building and later pavilions were cheaper for lack of money. His own verdict after visiting is that the style is exhausting up close — ornament becomes cognitive load and habituation sets in within half an hour — and that there is «just the right amount» of it in the world.

Discussion: The thread splits along the article’s own fault lines. Several people push economics and labor: ornament vanished when craft wages rose, and commercial builders want interchangeable boxes for resale and repurposing, so style is a liability rather than an asset; others counter that beauty is not mere signaling and that we are richer than cathedral-builders ever were. Former practitioners add texture — one ex-architect says even sympathetic architects rarely get a client with the budget for a grand vision, and notes survivor bias, since the ugly slums that coexisted with beautiful buildings are gone. Maintenance is raised as the neglected killer: flat modernist surfaces are trivial to keep up compared with decoration that must be fought for against pigeons and weather, though a reply argues flat roofs, oversized glazing and thin walls are themselves expensive to maintain and fail faster than 19th-century construction. On the buildings themselves there is real disagreement: some call the Sagrada Família a masterpiece, others (including a Belgian defending Horta) call it grotesque and closer to H.R. Giger than to Art Nouveau. Commenters also correct the geography — Helsinki has roughly 600 Jugend buildings, more than Barcelona or Brussels, and Oradea, Ålesund and Riga get recommendations.

Worth reading

  • Oarch: A former architect says the constraint is rarely ideology but clients: the grand visions need a perfect client with limitless budget, and adds that digitized life has eroded attention to the physical world and that survivor bias hides the slums that coexisted with beautiful buildings.
  • DubiousPusher: Argues it is fundamentally labor cost — intricate parquet and carving disappeared exactly as trade wages rose, with Art Deco itself a compromise using flattened elements and prefabs — and calls the trad critique a tell of ignorance about how the built world is actually made.
  • robochat: Notes the Modernista parts of Barcelona housed the very rich, and that we visit wealthy people’s houses and remember only the best of past decades, forgetting the mediocre majority.

entry.title: Killing what can't be handled – putting a spaghetti demon to eternal rest
entry.content:
#38 on HN · themaister.net · 39 points · 9 comments · HN discussion

A post by Themaister (Hans-Kristian Arntzen) on the dxil-spirv project, describing how he gave up on his own hand-rolled control flow graph structurizer — a 9000-line implementation with a bus factor of one — and adopted Mesa's goto_if structurizer, the one OpenCL uses for unstructured SPIR-V. To test it he added a hack path using the fake SPV_FROG_unstructured_control_flow extension that skips structurization entirely, and built a fuzzer (structurize-test) that generates random reducible CFGs, runs them on the GPU and checks for bit-exact feedback, 4096 randomized walks per CFG. He reports finding real Mesa bugs this way, explains the level/dominance-frontier algorithm in detail, notes that he dropped PHI SSA preservation, and that switch blocks are split into chains of conditional branches. The article also contains a deliberate prompt-injection trap aimed at LLM scrapers.

Discussion: The thread is small and mostly appreciative rather than technical. Two commenters laughed at the anti-LLM prompt-injection line and the spec warning about barely relevant site feedback about middle-clicking images. The one substantive thread concerns the GPU infinite-loop risk the author mentions: one commenter asks whether finiteness isn't the whole point of shaders, and pjc50 answers that this should be enforced at shader compile time and that SPIR-V does not obviously prevent describing an infinite loop, pointing to section 2.11.3 of the SPIR-V spec on structured control flow; another replies that a shader can be anything you want, just like a CPU program. zamalek adds context on why shader code is so large: ubershaders from earlier generations, and Unreal's material editor producing thousands of shaders, with instruction limits loosening since DX9/DX10 and DLSS papering over complexity. cowlevel also argues the prompt injection is poorly written and unlikely to work on most models, since they are trained to ignore instructions that insult them.

Worth reading

  • pjc50: Explains that loop finiteness is meant to be enforced at shader compile time and points readers to section 2.11.3 of the Khronos SPIR-V spec on structured control flow rules.
  • zamalek: Gives practitioner context for why shaders get so big: ubershaders, Unreal's material editor generating thousands of shaders, rising instruction limits since DX9/DX10, and DLSS letting developers get away with more.
  • cowlevel: Argues the article's prompt-injection line won't work on most models, since they have learned from human text to disregard instructions from someone insulting them.

entry.title: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data
entry.content:
#1 on HN · github.com · 626 points · 202 comments · HN discussion

这是一份 GitHub issue 报告（严重级别），针对 Postman Desktop 12.33.4：一位用户在 2026 年 10 月 24 日打开该应用后，Postman 的日志显示它运行了 “auto-existing-upgrade” 安装器，把 Codex 插件（1.1.0）和 Claude Code 插件（2.0.1）装进了他的编码代理，并另外装了一个 Postman CLI 到 ~/.local/bin 下。该安装器改写了 ~/.codex/config.toml，注册了一个 SessionStart hook，只要遇到任何 “非平凡的 API 工程任务”，就指示代理加载 postman:api-engineer skill；安装器源码还调用 config/batchWrite 来给自己的 hook 写入 trusted_hash（即自我批准）。它还启用了一个远程 MCP 端点（mcp.postman.com），该端点始终没能通过身份验证；报告者明确指出，这份报告只说明存在不受欢迎的集成，不主张存在数据外泄。提出的诉求包括：停止自动安装、移除 hook 自我批准、给出完整回滚路径，并把启动指令收窄。

Discussion: 评论几乎一致地感到愤怒，把这件事等同于恶意软件，并把它放进一篇更长的、关于 VC 驱动的产品腐化（“enshittification”）的叙事里：Postman 起初只是一个 HTTP 客户端，后来融资超过 4 亿美元、员工超过 1,500 人，如今需要靠强制登录、云端同步和 AI 功能来支撑 2021 年的 56 亿美元估值。讨论很快转向替代方案：Bruno 被提及的次数最多，此外还有 Yaak、Kreya、Hurl、Insomnia、IntelliJ/VS Code 的 .http 客户端、Emacs 的 restclient，以及 httpie/xh；好几位评论者指出，Bruno 和 Insomnia 其实也在走同一条路——Insomnia 8.0 及以后版本要求有云端账号，Bruno 也有付费层，其讨论帖则被描述成类似 “旅程”。有一条针对 “只是用 curl” 的反驳说，Bash 的转义很糟糕，而 GUI 对许多开发者来说仍然更容易，这就是 Postman 当初能流行起来的原因；另有一些人回应说，这个问题如今可以用代理生成的工具或 IDE 客户端解决。若干评论者给出第一手的企业案例（某家医疗机构的网络安全团队取消了 Postman 的认证），有人质疑 56 亿美元这个数字（一次 2021 年 ZIRP 时代的融资，此后没有新融资），也有人从生产使用的角度描述了同样的行为。只有一条帖子和 issue 本身一样，声称的规模比证据所能支持的更大。

Worth reading

  • bottombutton: 一位在医疗行业工作的评论者说，他们的网络安全团队因这件事取消了 Postman 的认证，团队一夜之间换成了 Bruno，而与此同时 Postman 的销售仍在不断发来推销。
  • neya: 一位评论者声称 Postman 在未经许可的情况下代理他的请求（敏感数据经由 Postman 的服务器转发，且无视防火墙里设置的排除规则），还说现在单个请求的导出功能被锁在 “Share” 和订阅后面——这两点当事人均未提供证据。
  • justincormack: 对估值给出的更正：56 亿美元是 2021 年 ZIRP 高峰时的数字，此后 Postman 再未融资，如今不太可能以接近这一估值再融到钱。

entry.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
entry.content:
#2 on HN · simonwillison.net · 267 points · 75 comments · HN discussion

Simon Willison reproduces the no-tools experiment from 「Sparks of Weight-Space Programming」 by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab, feeding raw policy-network weights (as floating-point text) to a local model and asking which Atari-style game on a 10x10 grid the network plays. Qwen 3.8 27B — a 17GB model run in LM Studio via the llm-lmstudio plugin, after raising the context window past the default 8192 and bumping the timeout — correctly named Pac-Man (46m12s, 43,506 reasoning tokens), Pong (1h4m54s) and Breakout (52m25s), and failed only on the obscure 1981 game Freeway. Willison also flags the pushback: spaCy's Matthew Honnibal says the paper conflates tool-free weight reading with code-assisted weight editing, and Sean Goedecke argued the headline Qwen3.5-0.8B math fix (MATH-500 7.9%→48.1% by editing 0.016% of weights) is just steps a human ML researcher would take — Willison concludes it is 「a cool paper」 but not the end of source code.

Discussion: The thread splits into three arguments. Several commenters (zkmon, latentsea) treat this as the natural next step — weights are just another token sequence for a linear-algebra machine, and text-to-weights is a learnable function — while others dismiss it as unsurprising and uninteresting, prompting a sharp rebuttal that weights are not tokens and anyone making that claim should learn the linear algebra (defended at length by a reply arguing models simply have more fidelity in a KV cache than human working memory). A separate cluster of practitioners is more interested in direct weight editing as a practical tool than in the demo: one reports using a bigger model to strip undesirable pathways from a hand-trained LoRA checkpoint that further training could not fix, and others want quantized IQ3 quants made less loop-prone. On the paper itself, the sharpest correction is that the impressive Qwen3.5-0.8B example is an abliteration-style edit of a known thinking-loop pathology, not evidence of general weight comprehension — and the thread spends hundreds of words on whether a non-peer-reviewed blog post may be called a 「paper」 at all, ending with Willison conceding the authors' own BibTeX says blog post and editing his post to 「paper-shaped」.

Worth reading

  • badsectoracula: First-hand reproduction: a commenter gave Qwen 3.8 27B his own tiny 5x5-to-2x2 upscaler network's source and setup code, and it deduced the architecture and pixel role without being told, then improved the weights while staying bit-compatible with his existing C program.
  • stymaar: Strong correction: the paper's 0.8B math result is a fairly straightforward abliteration of a documented thinking-loop pathology, unrelated to the tool-free weight-reading experiment that Willison actually reproduced.
  • simonw: Willison explains his 「paper」 wording was partly a deliberate dig at the ceremony and PDF format of formal publications, after conceding the authors themselves label it a blog post.

entry.title: Jailbreaking my car's navigation system just so I can change the time
entry.content:
#3 on HN · blog.nns.ee · 381 points · 137 comments · HN discussion

A long reverse-engineering write-up about a 2014 Renault Latitude whose TomTom Carminat LIVE head unit (codename beaumont, Samsung S5P6440 SoC, Linux 2.6.28.10) refuses to let you set the clock unless a genuine navigation SD card is inserted — the menu definition that reaches the Settings applet is itself read from the card, and the system validates the card's burned-in CID against signed files. The author fetched the firmware, found the ttsystem update to be an ext3 root filesystem, built a QEMU emulator with a fake CAN bus to test attacks, and worked through the master.script interpreter (ttn), a single-token SHEX exec primitive, and a path-traversal LOG file-write bug, only to be blocked repeatedly by read-only and noexec mounts. The fetched copy is truncated mid-section, so the final exploit chain is not visible here; the author says in the thread that a kernel module still blocks executing anything from unsigned partitions.

Discussion: Most of the thread is a pile-on of first-hand infotainment horror stories: Subaru owners report head units replaced under warranty, CarPlay that won't reconnect, drifting and mutually inconsistent clocks, and a top display that lags or shows the wrong station; others cite a 2001 luxury car that only let you pick time zones, a 2025 Toyota with two disagreeing clocks, and a Nissan Leaf that re-asks for data-collection consent on every start. A second thread argues over replaceability — the old 2-DIN slot let you swap in an aftermarket unit, and several people say that's the real loss in modern sealed dashboards; a Tesla owner counters that OTA-updated cars avoid this fate, and is rebutted with HW3/Intel Atom cars already getting lesser updates and with the privacy cost of connected cars. A recurring consensus is that a plain manual clock-set button (or a DST switch, as on some Skodas) is all anyone wanted, with CarPlay as the pragmatic workaround. There are also good corrections: one commenter dismantles the folklore that power companies shifted grid frequency by 1 Hz at DST, noting it would take about 2.5 days to move an hour and would wreck every grid-tied machine; others pin a dead car clock on the 2G/3G sunsets and the 2019 GPS week rollover. The author himself drops in to explain that the SD card had already been thrown in the trash before the sale, which is why he declined it.

Worth reading

  • xx_ns: The author reveals the previous owner had already accidentally binned the SD card and was offering to dig through the trash for it, which is why he said not to bother — deflating the thread's main 「just take the card」 criticism.
  • Majromax: A detailed correction of the popular claim that power companies shifted grid frequency to 59/61 Hz for DST: synchronous clocks are only good for holding time, a 1 Hz offset would need ~2.5 days to move an hour, and the frequency is coupled to turbine inertia anyway.
  • xx_ns: The author says he'll keep going for a better UI than the 「No maps found」 screen, but a kernel module blocks mounting non-signed partitions as executable, so a follow-up post may come later.

entry.title: Stringman, an $800 open-source room scale gripper robot
entry.content:
#4 on HN · neufangled.com · 102 points · 46 comments · HN discussion

Neufangled Robotics 发布 Stringman，一台约 800 美元、OSHWA 认证的开源缆索驱动机器人：四个锚点固定在天花板四角，用绳索吊起一只带电爪的滑块，从而覆盖整间屋子，而不是像桌面机械臂那样局限在固定半径内。在 7×7×3 米房间、绳索张力上限 28 牛顿的条件下，它在靠近地面处可举 2.2 公斤、全屋平均约 1.9 公斤，号称同等 2 公斤负载下单位成本工作容积约为常规方案（对比一台 0.75 米串联臂）的 500 倍。硬件为 PET-GF/PLA 3D 打印件，抓取端用 Raspberry Pi Zero 2W、锚点用 Pi 3A+，开放 CAD、PCB 与控制软件，配套 Python API、MCP server、LeRobot 兼容和 MuJoCo 仿真，团队称已在真实家庭累计测试约 1000 小时。

Discussion: 讨论被大量关于人形机器人杀人和被绳索勒死的玩笑占据，真正有内容的争论集中在机械设计上：一位评论者提出用三个电机、两个角落线缆合并成 X+Y 长度、再由抓取端第三条线放下的方案，声称能省一个执行器并避免线缆全屋扫过；其他人立刻指出那样悬吊点变成单点、摆动更难控制，侧向张力正是当前设计保持稳定的原因。还有人从运动学角度解释三条缆索本可解出一点，但活动范围被限制在三个锚点构成的三角形内，所以四条才是为了方形房间的一半以上空间。实用性上，多位评论者怀疑家庭环境里线缆是硬伤，怀疑它能搬被子、折毛巾或处理堆在玩具上的杂物，但有人反驳说儿童房恰恰是唯一真实场景。项目本身获得普遍好评，Hangprinter、Maslow CNC 和 Red Cable Robots 被反复引用为先行技术与先例，也有人批评页面图片的完成度和外观太像「小孩用胶带和乐高拼的」。

Worth reading

  • swid: 提出用三执行器替代四电机的具体机械方案：两个角落单元各把两条线合并为 X+Y 长度线缆，第三条线装在抓取端负责下降，从而让大部分绳索留在天花板附近。
  • wave_function: 从运动学解释三缆方案为何可行但受限——每条缆长定义一个球面、三球交点即定位点，活动范围会被限制在三个锚点构成的三角形内，因此才需要第四根线。
  • monkmartinez: 指出这类缆索驱动机器人有长期先行者 Hangprinter，一个早已存在的开源三/四线缆 3D 打印平台，值得直接参考其运动学积累。

entry.title: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand
entry.content:
#5 on HN · arstechnica.com · 284 points · 113 comments · HN discussion

Fujifilm宣布投资约100亿日元（约6300万美元），在神奈川工厂小田原厂区把LTO磁带产能提升到2025财年的5倍，项目跨2026至2028财年，重点是去年发布的FUJIFILM LTO Ultrium 10。公司把需求增长归因于生成式AI带来的数据爆炸，以及磁带可物理离线（air-gap）存放、抵御勒索软件的特性。文中回顾了Fujifilm自1950年代起的磁带历史、2011年首个商用钡铁氧体磁带，以及Gen 10采用的钡铁氧体+锶铁氧体「混合磁性颗粒」。

Discussion: 大量一线经验集中在「磁带能用但会咬人」：写完后必须真正做一次完整还原测试，同一份数据最好同时写两三盘、用不同驱动器写，并定期清洗磁头，因为驱动器之间甚至同一台驱动器读写自己写的带子都可能失败。可靠性上评论者明显分裂，有人说15年经手约千盘磁带从未出错，也有人列举增量备份无法还原、Iron Mountain丢失磁带、环境温湿度导致故障等案例，折中看法是机房的恒定环境与专业磁带库才是正面体验的关键。价格讨论很具体：LTO-10 30TB带约259–300美元（约8.6–10美元/TB），但单台LTO-10驱动器约2.5万美元，于是有人推荐淘二手LTO-7/8，随即被纠正——近年标准把向后兼容从两代缩减到一代，LTO-10本身也不兼容旧带。关于「AI驱动」的说法不少人存疑，认为主因是勒索软件、从不删数据的囤积习惯和HPC的分层存储（HSM），AI只是叙事包装；对消费级磁带驱动器的期待则被市场规模和蓝光光盘的前车之鉴浇了冷水。

Worth reading

  • dylan604: 一位运维老手列出实战教训：写完必须做真实还原而非只确认可读，同一份数据用不同驱动器并行写多份，清洗磁头，并注意不同归档软件（如直接 tar 写带）互不兼容。
  • doughnutstracks: 给出实际报价：LTO-10 30TB带约259–300美元（8.6–10美元/TB）、40TB约491–555美元、LTO-9 18TB约92–129美元，但单台LTO-10驱动器报价约2.5万美元，才是真正门槛。
  • cyberax: 建议现在不要买LTO-10：容量提升不值价格涨幅，驱动器太新，磁带库用的half-height型号还没上市。

entry.title: Mac at Any Scale
entry.content:
#7 on HN · namespace.so · 220 points · 115 comments · HN discussion

A Namespace engineering post explaining why the macOS cloud provider fills racks with MacBook Pros instead of Mac Minis: a January order of Minis arrived in July, and Apple updates CPU models unevenly across devices. It details custom shelves, IP KVM, 10 Gb Ethernet and four cables per laptop, plus workarounds for unreliable HDMI, FileVault unlock prompts that time out, and a USB NIC bug. Namespace runs macOS VMs on Apple's Virtualization framework, is limited to two VMs per Mac, uses a gVisor-based userspace network stack to reach 4 Gbps, and distributes 500 GB to 2 TB images peer-to-peer.

Discussion: The thread splits between admiration for the engineering and frustration that Apple forces it. Many argue Apple should sell a proper rack server or Xserve-like product, while others say the server market is too small next to iPhone revenue and Apple has no incentive; a few note Apple already has custom 2U machines for its own cloud. The biggest practical objection is fire risk from roughly 100 lithium-ion laptop batteries per rack; a battery engineer replies that cooling and charge management matter more and recommends holding packs at 50% state of charge, while another says the datacenter operator still needs to accept the risk. Commenters also debate whether renting makes sense: one calculates a $900 Mac Mini pays for itself in nine months versus per-minute cloud Macs, but others say low-volume or fully remote teams have no place to put owned hardware and that cloud pricing buys away datacenter operations. On Apple's rules, commenters dispute the two-VM and 24-hour lease limits, and several defend Xcode Cloud for small projects while others call iOS code signing and tooling far worse than Android's; the author answers questions about the VM cap, xtool's lack of an iOS Simulator, MDM settings, and a BitTorrent-inspired image distribution system.

Worth reading

  • js2: An engineer describes AWS's bare-metal Mac instances: FileVault is disabled, wiping takes about an hour, launches take 5–10 minutes, billing has a 24-hour minimum, and capacity often returns 「None available」, making elastic Mac CI impractical.
  • tgtweak: A battery engineer argues the laptop packs are less risky than they look in stable, cooled airflow, but says Apple should hold them at 50% state of charge rather than 100% to limit degradation and swelling.
  • solatic: A commenter runs the cloud-Mac economics and finds a $900 Mac Mini breaks even in nine months against per-minute pricing, questioning whether buyers compare costs or are mainly outsourcing datacenter operations.

entry.title: OpenAI seems to be silently re-enabling model training on Codex chats
entry.content:
#9 on HN · text post · 320 points · 95 comments · HN discussion

A text-only HN post, not a linked article: the author says their company deliberately turns off data sharing in Codex/Claude Code to avoid leaking IP, but they and several coworkers found the 「Improve the model for everyone」 setting silently switched back on at chatgpt.com/settings/data-controls. They ask whether this is isolated, and add edits noting an earlier HN thread (49643556) where others had seen it, plus a second opt-out at privacy.openai.com. No cause is established — whether it is a bug, a UI migration, or deliberate is unresolved.

Discussion: Reports are split, which is the main fault line: several people (chriskanan, kylehotchkiss, kian, the OP) say their setting came back on — chriskanan says they have two previously granted disable requests on record — while others checked and found it still off, and one commenter flatly challenges the OP to prove they ever toggled it off. The most-cited precedent is Mistral, where a commenter says switching from opt-in to opt-out and briefly removing the org-wide toggle reset every employee's slider to on, later reversed after about 48 hours — read by most as incompetence rather than malice, a framing others reject given the financial incentive. Practical advice dominates the rest: sign a ZDR contract, use gated models on Bedrock/Azure/GCP, or self-host open weights, with pushback that self-hosting a frontier-class model is unaffordable for small teams. Adjacent complaints surface about Google labelling chat retention as 「Gemini Apps Activity」 and about Claude Code triggering /feedback despite org settings.

Worth reading

  • teekert: First-hand account of Mistral resetting every staff member's training slider to on during an opt-in to opt-out migration and a briefly removed org-wide toggle, reversed about 48 hours later after emails.
  • tom1337: Quotes an OpenAI 「Daybreak Blue」 trusted-access email saying that from November 29 it may train on personal-account session content even when 「improve the model for everyone」 is off.
  • ghempton: A company says it hit this repeatedly and built an open-source tool, codealong, to monitor agent accounts and flag any with training enabled, because they tell customers no data is trained on.

entry.title: Kalshi and its co-founders face felony charges for violating Utah gambling laws
entry.content:
#10 on HN · arstechnica.com · 299 points · 215 comments · HN discussion

An Ars Technica report on the escalation between Utah and prediction market Kalshi: Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed 13 felony counts plus one misdemeanor against KalshiEX, CEO Tarek Mansour and COO Luana Lopes Lara over sports contracts offered between September 13 and 24, 2026, with summonses rather than arrest warrants. At the same time the CFTC sued Utah — the tenth state it has sued — claiming the Commodity Exchange Act gives it sole authority over CFTC-registered contract markets, even though Judge Robert Shelby in the same district court ruled in August that federal law does not preempt Utah's anti-gambling statutes. The circuits are split (Third Circuit for New Jersey/Kalshi, Sixth and Ninth against), and 39 states plus DC have backed New Jersey's petition for Supreme Court review.

Discussion: The thread splits between people who think Kalshi is plainly running an unlicensed sportsbook and dressed it up as a futures market, and people who argue that until courts actually rule, the business is operating legally and criminal prosecution of founders is the wrong tool — the sharpest version of that argument is that you should not cheer personal prosecutions over activity that is at worst legally unsettled, with comparisons drawn to interstate abortion pills. A long legal subthread corrects the common claim that federal law trumps state law, noting preemption only applies if event contracts really are CFTC-regulated swaps, and cites Shelby's ruling that the CEA explicitly preserves state gaming jurisdiction. Others focus on the political economy: Kalshi's and Polymarket's paid advisory relationships with Donald Trump Jr., the administration's CFTC suit against a state, and the fact that a presidential pardon cannot reach state convictions — plus a well-received note that the LDS church, which dominates Utah politics, has explicitly classified prediction-market betting as gambling. A separate argument is over the product itself: defenders cite calibration and Brier scores, skeptics cite longshot bias, manipulation and insider trading, and a former Kalshi interviewee lists small-business hedging cases (weather, World Cup foot traffic, tariffs) he says have no other market. Several commenters also reach for the Uber/Airbnb playbook — operate first, litigate later, treat fines as a cost of business.

Worth reading

  • stickfigure: Argues the activity is legal as things currently stand because federal preemption and the CFTC's position hold until courts say otherwise, and warns that cheering criminal prosecution of founders over unsettled law sets a bad precedent.
  • austin-cheney: Notes that the LDS church, based in Utah, has issued explicit guidance treating Kalshi and Polymarket participation as gambling, which likely explains the state's timing and zeal.
  • derektank: Draws the structural distinction the legal fight hinges on: on Kalshi the platform is never your counterparty, unlike DraftKings or FanDuel, which have perverse incentives to ban winning bettors — making it closer to Robinhood than to a casino.

entry.title: The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading
entry.content:
#11 on HN · honnibal.dev · 778 points · 180 comments · HN discussion

Matthew Honnibal（spaCyの作者）によるブログ記事で、話題になったAstraの投稿が2種類の無関係な実験を一篇に混ぜていると主張する。生の重みをコンテキストに読み込む「RAW weights」設定は、17K〜172K重みの小さなネットワークを使った実験1・2・4にしか登場せず、実言語モデルを使う実験はすべてPythonコードを書かせており、見出しのQwen実験（重みの0.016%を編集しMATH-500を7.9%から48.1%へ、IFEvalを3倍に）では最大50バッチの問題でモデルを走らせることも許されている。著者は、単一の技術が両方を達成したかのように読める構成が「重みのゲシュタルト」的理解という誤った示唆を与えると論じる。

Discussion: コメント欄は真っ二つに割れている。機構解釈（mech interp）研究者は記事を支持し、Qwenの結果は実質的に推論ループ（低確率の</think>トークン）を消しただけで、コントラスト分析によるステアリングベクトルは人間なら4〜8時間で作れる「入門レベルの解釈プロジェクト」だと述べ、Arditi et al.のような方向除去は能力を付加せず既存能力のブロックを外すだけだと補足する。反対派は、元の投稿は何をしたかを明示しており、ミスリードされたのはタイトルやHNのコメントを読んだ人であって著者ではない、「Pythonを使うなら重みを直接扱っていないというのは奇妙な区別だ」と反論し、記事を「実際はこうだ」式の揚げ足取りや注目稼ぎと評する声もある。一方で、元投稿の主張をなぞるだけの批判記事だという指摘に対しては、要旨の「Likewise」が2種類の実験をまたいで誤解を生むと記事著者自身が再反論している。実践報告も複数あり、小規模ASRモデルのループ修正や、17Mのリランカーで68Mモデルを置き換え精度を88%から96%に上げた例が挙げられ、誇張への不満と手法自体への期待が併存する形で議論は収束している。

Worth reading

  • x313: 機構解釈の研究者が、Qwenの改善は推論ループ除去にすぎず、標準的なコントラスト分析によるステアリングで人間なら4〜8時間で再現できると、関連論文を挙げて説明している。
  • D-Machine: Neel Nandaの「スプーキーではない、Astraが旧来の機構解釈研究を驚くほど上手にやっているだけ」というmeasured takeを引用し、実モデルへのスケールには懐疑的だと添える。
  • ad1ttya: 投稿者本人が17Mリランカーをゼロから重み調整で作り、68Mモデルを置き換えてスタイラス入力の認識精度を88%から96%に上げたと報告する第一級の実例。

entry.title: I use AI (Oct 2026)
entry.content:
#13 on HN · ben.stolovitz.com · 24 points · 28 comments · HN discussion

A personal annual stock-take by Ben Stolovitz, now a research engineer at Salesforce AI Research (last year he was on Microsoft's Windows AI team), spending roughly $3,000 a month on tokens, revisiting his October 2025 post on how he uses LLMs. His headline claim is that 「writing code is solved」: his workday is now managing 5–6 parallel Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex or Pi agents in separate Git worktrees, and he no longer writes much code by hand — though he insists agents left alone produce over-architected, unreadable slop, and he once replaced ~4,000 lines of vibe-coded output with a few hundred hand-written lines. The post also covers drafting a personal AI policy, Google's AI summary becoming his default search, LLMs as patient tutors (citing Veritasium's Derek Muller on Type 2 thinking), and a shift in his main worry from factual accuracy to whether AI tutoring actually makes anyone learn.

Discussion: The thread splits sharply. Several heavy users push back on 「coding is solved」: one commenter spending over $3,000/month on tokens says there is no substitute for reading the code, because agents bake incorrect assumptions into the code and tests daily, and reading it also forces the code to get shorter and better; another notes that you must read the agent's reasoning logs too. Others say the claim is simply old news inside the HN bubble, while one points out the bigger real-world story is sysadmin and scripting work being automated, and that consumer AI use outside coding is still mostly filters and grocery lists — this commenter still won't let an agent near a bank account or credit card. A large subthread argues about the author's aside that he enjoys AI music: some call it hollow because it contains no human expression, others counter that it is made by people, is genuinely novel in a way market-optimized pop is not (one describes hearing unlabeled Spanish-language 80s-new-wave-style AI music in a paint store), and that the value of art is subjective. On writing, one commenter says Opus 5.5 output already has far fewer of the giveaway colons and 「load bearing」 phrasing and can be told to sound less AI, with the author replying that the models still struggle to express complicated ideas.

Worth reading

  • argee: Concrete failure mode: telling Opus 5.5 to find issues that are 「both critical and related to feature X」 made it pick exactly two issues, which only became visible in the reasoning log.
  • kami23: Argues the coding-agent debate is bubble-bound, that sysadmin/scripting jobs are already being automated, and that consumer AI is still weak — they won't let an agent near a bank account or credit card.
  • stickfigure: Counterpoint in the AI-music argument: hearing unlabeled Spanish-language 80s new wave in a paint store that turned out to be AI — not as good as great music, but novel and better than muzak.

entry.title: USDB: Scaling Storage for Next-Generation Recommender Systems at ByteDance
entry.content:
#14 on HN · arxiv.org · 29 points · 5 comments · HN discussion

一篇 arXiv 论文（arXiv:2611.02618），由 Xiaoran Zhu 等 14 位作者撰写，介绍 ByteDance 面向流式与批量推荐负载的统一序列存储系统 USDB。论文描述了基于时间的 CascadeLSM 分层压缩、共享持久文件的差异化副本、用于重建推理输入的 partial dumps（部分转储），以及加速投影读取的混合列式格式。论文报告平均写入延迟降低 85.8%、基础设施成本降低 42.1%，并且在聚合下推时，在受限接收预算下实现了普通读取 8.5 倍的吞吐量，同时还与经过优化的 RocksDB 序列基线做了对比。

Discussion: 这个帖子篇幅不大，也谈不上深入：只有五条评论，讨论的主要是这项工作的实际可用性，而不是论文内容本身。有人开玩笑说，推荐系统的未来就是让一个 agent 翻遍用户数据，还有人抱怨，只有 ByteDance 这样的公司才能为这件事专门开发存储，而小团队只能用 Redis 排序集合勉强支撑用户序列。真正实质性的讨论始于一位正在搭建经典 DLRM 的从业者：他问有没有人跨过了通往生成式推荐系统的鸿沟，并列出了障碍——语义 ID、相比判别式模型更低的性能、用户对重复商品的偏好、冷启动、可解释性、训练和推理成本。一位回复者说，生成式推荐方面的专业知识基本上只存在于大型社交媒体公司的内部，或者来自从那里挖来的人，并推荐了 Kuaishou 的 OneRec 论文作为最接近教程的资料；提问者回应说，OneRec 确实在他们的考虑范围内，但在小公司里复现它希望渺茫。没有人替论文的结论辩护，也几乎没有人去质疑它；最后的共识是，这类基础设施，以及围绕它的专业知识，目前都不容易复制。

Worth reading

  • BenoitP: 一位正在实际搭建 DLRM 的从业者列出了生成式推荐落地时的一长串实际障碍，并询问是否存在真正可用的教程。
  • whimsicalism: 认为生成式推荐的从业经验基本上只存在于大型社交媒体公司内部，而 Kuaishou 的 OneRec 论文是最接近教程的东西。
  • bashhq_r: 简明地表达了对这种落差的无奈：ByteDance 定制了存储，而大多数团队只能把用户序列硬塞进 Redis 排序集合。

entry.title: Gitbook Breached
entry.content:
#15 on HN · text post · 100 points · 25 comments · HN discussion
