这是一条 Hacker News 文字帖：用户 punchmesan 就 GitBook 的可用性问题提交了支持工单，收到的回复是一份安全事件通知，而此前并没有任何正式的客户通告或数据泄露通报。GitBook 称自己在 11 月 2 日欧洲中部时间（CET）19:00 遭到一次「使用 AI 智能体的复杂且有高度针对性的攻击」，攻击者借此获取了基础设施凭据；可能被访问的内容包括 Git Sync secrets、GitBook API token、第三方 API token，以及访客向 GitBook Assistant 提出的问题。GitBook 替换了全部凭据，并作废了每个客户的 API token，同时表示没有证据表明用户内容被修改。

Discussion: GitBook 的 CTO 现身评论区，确认了攻击事件，并表示团队正全天候处理、服务正分阶段恢复——多位评论者称赞这次对外沟通做得干净利落。最大的争议点是「AI 智能体」的说法：怀疑者指出，日志很难区分 AI 与人类操作者，还有人指责 GitBook 是在「问责洗白」，用一个听起来无法防御的攻击者来推卸责任；CTO 反驳说，这次攻击的节奏与适应能力远超他们以往应对的人类攻击，并承诺会发布完整的事后复盘。实际层面，评论者称赞 GitBook 主动作废了 token，而没有把这件事留给用户；有一些抱怨是关于两个状态页面（gitbookstatus.com 与 gitbook.com/status）给出不一致的信息，以及安全事件页面加载了 11 个第三方域名。零星杂音包括一条 2FA 界面在开启后不刷新的 bug 报告，以及一条对 GitBook 团队多年前关停 friendco.de 的旧怨，CTO 对此道了歉。

Worth reading

  • MrZander: 质疑把攻击归因于 AI 智能体的依据：究竟哪些日志能把 AI 和人类攻击者区分开？
  • SamyPesse: GitBook 的 CTO 回应「问责洗白」的指责，称这次攻击在节奏和适应能力上远超他们以往应对的人类攻击者。
  • eddythompson80: 指出 GitBook 的安全事件页面连接了 11 个第三方域名。

entry.title: Writing seen in PHerc. 306B, for the first time in 2000 years
entry.content:
#16 on HN · scrollprize.substack.com · 85 points · 12 comments · HN discussion

A Vesuvius Challenge post by Paul Henderson and Federica Nicolardi awarding a $50K First Letters Prize on PHerc. 306B, a papyrus scroll carbonized in the AD 79 eruption, excavated at Herculaneum in the 1750s and micro-CT scanned at the ESRF in Grenoble last year. Liam Warner, a freelance software engineer from northern England with a spare RTX 4090, and Nicola Bodill, an MA student in Latin and Ancient Greek at the University of Sydney, made 10+ characters readable in a 4 cm² area, enough to make the reading τὸ δι᾽ αὑτὸ αἱρετόν (“that which is in itself desirable”) very plausible — an expression with parallels in Aristotle, Sextus Empiricus and Philodemus' On Anger. The work also settles that 306B is the upper part of the split scroll, and it came out of 25 submissions, several of which recovered 7, 8 or 9 characters and fell just short; 20 more scanned scrolls remain unread, and the $800K Grand Prize for reading 70% of a whole scroll is still open.

Discussion: The thread is short and almost entirely admiring rather than critical — nobody disputes the reading or the method. The most-upvoted comment reaches for the Human Genome Project as a model, hoping for the same geometric ramp-up from a couple of percent to completion, and notes that tens of thousands of scrolls may still await scanning. A subthread adds a sober correction to the romance of the 1750s excavators preserving the rolls: many were partly destroyed by early attempts to physically unroll them, and an unknown number were allegedly burned for heat after being mistaken for logs. Others invoke Clarke's third law and note how often experts declared the scrolls unreadable, and one commenter jokes that they initially parsed “306B” as a model parameter count.

Worth reading

  • jiehong: Points out that the story of careful preservation is partly myth — quite a few scrolls were damaged or destroyed by early physical unrolling attempts.
  • runeb: Adds that an unknown number of the scrolls were allegedly burned as firewood during early excavations because they were mistaken for ordinary logs.
  • embedding-shape: Asks how many experts over the years called reading the scrolls impossible, quoting Clarke's law that a distinguished elderly scientist saying something is impossible is very probably wrong.

entry.title: Antimony: CAD Software Evolved from Lisp Machines and Not Drafting Tables (2015)
entry.content:
#18 on HN · mattkeeter.com · 72 points · 31 comments · HN discussion

Matt Keeter 介绍了 Antimony，这是一个基于节点图的实体建模 CAD 工具，它采用 Python 3.x 脚本和函数式表示（由前缀字符串构成的数学表达式）来描述形状，而不是用传统绘图桌的隐喻。其节点通过有向无环图连接，更改会自动向下游传播，可以导出 2.5D 高度图和 .stl 文件做 3D 制造，当时提供 Mac 预编译包，Linux/Mac 源码在 GitHub 上，被自评为 beta 级稳定性。文章还谈到它脱胎于 MIT 比特与原子中心的个人级 CAD/CAM 工作流程。

Discussion: 作者本人（mkeeter）现身评论区，指出这其实是 2015 年的旧文，自己从 2016 年前后已逐渐减少维护，但有一个更活跃的分支叫 stibium，且「因为是 2026 年」所以大量借助了 LLM。有资深 CAD 用户反驳标题的「Lisp 机」框架，指出 AutoCAD 的 AutoLISP 已内建四十多年，Lisp 风格在行业里并不新鲜。讨论很快转向代码式 CAD 与 GUI 参数化 CAD 之争：反对者（如 CyLith）认为 CSG 操作会不可预测地改变拓扑，无法可靠引用结果的边或组件，参数化一改就全盘崩溃，因此 OpenSCAD 类工具只能算玩具；拥护者则说它在某些维度上远比 GUI CAD 强大，能快速构建复杂模型。多人推荐 FluidCAD（作者亲自现身），认为它把 GUI 操作与等效的代码操作结合，还带约束式 2D 草绘器和时间线；另有评论者列出 OpenSCAD 新版 RC、PythonSCAD、CadQuery、Build123D 等生态，并追问如何在纯构造式几何里做倒角和圆角。

Worth reading

  • mkeeter: 作者 Matt Keeter 确认这是 2015 年的文章，自己 2016 年起基本停止维护，指向活跃分支 stibium，并坦言其大量使用了 LLM 辅助。
  • seemaze: 指出 AutoCAD 的原生 AutoLISP 已存在四十余年，标题中「Lisp 机而非绘图桌」的说法颇具反讽意味。
  • CyLith: 从原理上批评代码式 CAD：CSG 会不可预测地改变拓扑、无法稳定引用结果中的边和组件，参数化后问题呈指数级放大。

entry.title: Study estimates 75% of NFL players who died over 15-year span had CTE
entry.content:
#19 on HN · nbcnews.com · 194 points · 132 comments · HN discussion

An NBC News report on a JAMA Network Open study led by Yorghos Tripodis of Boston University's Alzheimer's Disease and CTE Center. The researchers combined 396 donated brains—93% of which showed CTE—with death records for 1,966 other former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023, then corrected for the roughly fivefold higher donation rate among players with cognitive decline. They estimate about 1,760 of 2,360 former players, or nearly 75%, had CTE, and about 27% had dementia; the authors stress these are estimates because CTE can only be diagnosed after death.

Discussion: The thread is dominated by parents and former players saying they would not let children play tackle football, with many arguing the damage is cumulative from youth and high-school play rather than something that begins in the NFL. Several commenters push back that youth football is not the NFL and that all sports carry risk; one former high-school and college player cites injury and concussion statistics and warns against extrapolating professional data to children. Proposed fixes range from banning tackle below college and expanding flag football to eliminating contact practices, redesigning the line of scrimmage, mandating Guardian Caps and adopting rugby-style tackling. Commenters also dispute whether the sport can be made safe without becoming unrecognizable, and some note the headline's 75% is a modeled estimate while 93% of the donated brains showed CTE.

Worth reading

  • ggreer: ggreer links the JAMA Network Open paper and explains the selection-bias correction—donation rates for cognitively impaired players ranged from 1.8x to 4x—while noting the sample is too small to compare positions.
  • wdr1: A former high-school and college player argues against extrapolating NFL CTE data to kids, citing football and girls' soccer injury and concussion rates and asking where risk-taking should stop.
  • 1970-01-01: Points out the buried lede: the study's quoted researcher says most head impacts happened in college, high school and youth football, not the NFL.

entry.title: Could a modern chess engine on a Pentium have defeated Kasparov in 1996?
entry.content:
#20 on HN · nicholas.carlini.com · 362 points · 157 comments · HN discussion

Nicholas Carlini bought a 200 MHz Pentium Pro with 64MB of SIMM RAM (a machine that cost roughly $4,000–5,000 in 1995–96) and ported Stockfish to it, booting a custom hypervisor off a 1.44MB floppy and exposing the engine over HTTP via a Realtek RTL8139C so readers can play it. His tuned, 32-bit, ≤64MB build is estimated at ~2846 Elo at 1 second/move, 3109 at 10s and 3180 at 30s, extrapolated to ~3300 ± 87 at classical time controls — far above Kasparov's ~2800. He also back-ported modern search, SPSA/Texel tuning and NNUE into 1996's Crafty 11.13 (1999 Elo at 1s on the Pentium, 2383 at 10s), and in a 100-game match the modern engine on 1996 hardware beat original Crafty on a modern Ryzen 78–17–5. His headline claim: +720 of the +1335 Elo gained over Crafty comes from better programming, not faster hardware. The code was written by LLMs (Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, GPT-6), disclosed partway through the post.

Discussion: The thread splits into three arguments. One camp attacks the article's aside that grandmasters consider roughly as many moves as amateurs: strong club players report that GMs on stream plainly examine more branches and deeper lines, while others dig up the actual source — Adriaan de Groot's 1946 think-aloud study, plus a modern replication showing masters and intermediates evaluated 145 vs 139 positions in one test position — and argue the point is about pattern-recognition pruning and not re-analysing the same lines, not raw node counts. A second dispute is whether the algorithmic gains can be separated from hardware at all: several commenters note NNUE and Stockfish's distributed Fishtest testing regime were only possible with modern compute, so the +720/+1335 split is post-hoc bookkeeping. Corrections and nitpicks are plentiful: the article's jab at the Pentium MMX being 「better-in-almost-every-way」 is wrong (the Pro was the first P6 out-of-order core; MMX was a souped-up P5 in a different market segment), and the board diagrams list human vs Pentium regardless of colour, confusing readers trying to follow the games. A large subthread drifts entirely to video codecs — whether AV1/HEVC could have streamed over ISDN in the 90s, 8088 Domination on an IBM PC, and why voice calls still sound bad. Broad agreement on the core thesis: software/algorithmic progress is a large and underrated multiplier on top of Moore's law.

Worth reading

  • ketzu: Traces the 「GMs consider as many moves as amateurs」 claim to de Groot's 1946 study and quotes a modern replication with actual numbers (145 vs 139 positions evaluated; mean depth 4.1 vs 3.3), while noting masters search faster rather than wider.
  • orac81: Points out that a 100 MHz Pentium running Chess Genius already beat Kasparov in a 1994 Intel Grand Prix game, with links — undercutting the framing that this was unprecedented for commodity hardware.
  • vhcr: Argues the article's programming-vs-hardware split is artificial: NNUE training and Fishtest-scale tuning could not have been done on 1996 hardware, so much of the 「algorithmic」 gain is really hardware-enabled.

entry.title: Tiny Basic for Arduino
entry.content:
#21 on HN · dilshan.github.io · 49 points · 12 comments · HN discussion

A project page for a lightweight BASIC interpreter aimed at mid-range Arduino boards and MCUs, pitched as letting you write, edit and run BASIC programs directly on the hardware without a PC IDE. It advertises hardware I/O, math and bit-manipulation built-ins plus minimal dependencies for portability. The page itself is mostly feature copy — it gives no benchmarks, version number or source link — and, as commenters note, it only actually targets 32-bit ARM Cortex-M boards, not the classic 8-bit AVR Arduinos.

Discussion: The thread splits between people who find the exercise charming and people who question its usefulness next to MicroPython and CircuitPython on the same hardware. One camp points out the lineage: the Parallax BASIC Stamp has been a BASIC-programmable microcontroller since the 1990s, though a reply counters that at roughly $80 back then — about $160 in today's money — it was a closed, expensive system, nothing like a modern Arduino. Others flag that the comparison board, the Arduino Due, is 14 years old and overpriced, and that RP2040/RP2350 boards beat it easily. The most useful correction is that the title oversells compatibility: only the 32-bit ARM Cortex-M Arduinos are supported, and for cheap RP2040/RP2350 hardware people recommend MMBasic or Geoff Graham's BASIC for the Pico and Pico 2. A sub-thread mocking the idea of needing an interpreter to run an interpreter was answered by the poster himself, who clarified that Python is used only at build time and the shipped interpreter is C compiled to a binary.

Worth reading

  • Surac: Notes the title is misleading — only 32-bit ARM Cortex-M Arduinos are supported, not the 8-bit boards people picture — and recommends MMBasic for cheap RP2040/RP2350 hardware.
  • AlexeyBrin: The poster (AlexeyBrin) corrects the 「interpreter to run an interpreter」 complaint: Python is only used during the build phase, while the actual interpreter is written in C and runs as a binary on the Arduino.
  • k310: Digs up the original Tiny BASIC lineage, linking Dr. Dobb's Volume 1 #5 from 1976, the 8080 source on GitHub, and the Wikipedia history page.

entry.title: Google will turn off search for schools that reject AI
entry.content:
#22 on HN · nytimes.com · 370 points · 286 comments · HN discussion

A New York Times report (the article itself returned HTTP 403 and was only reachable via archive links posted in the thread) on Google's education policy for K-12 accounts. Google education VP Chris Phillips is quoted saying 「Search and A.I. are deeply integrated」, so schools that ban AI features lose Google Search entirely and students instead see a message blaming the school; the companion Google blog post says access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search will be off for K-12 student accounts until administrators explicitly enable them, presented as giving schools control. The dispute in the thread is whether that is a genuine opt-in or an offer with no AI-free option.

Article not read: HTTP 403

Discussion: The thread is overwhelmingly hostile: the top commenters call it coercion and textbook tying, repeatedly invoking the US v. Microsoft precedent over 「Windows and IE are deeply integrated」, and several compare Google to tobacco companies hooking children young. Defenders argue Google cannot practically ship a non-AI search — ranking has been machine-learned for over a decade — and that AI summaries are often higher signal than the SEO-spam top ten, with some saying their non-technical relatives now prefer chat interfaces. That is countered by a flood of first-hand reports of confidently wrong summaries (one commenter cites an oumi.ai finding that overviews contradict their cited sources about 10% of the time and calls 10% far too low), and by the argument that reading and evaluating results is precisely the skill schools teach. A parallel thread is about dependency rather than AI: a tutor notes their high school blocked DuckDuckGo and forced Google, and people point to Google Classroom and Chromebooks as the real lock-in, with Kagi, DuckDuckGo (including its noai.duckduckgo.com entry point, whose lifespan commenters doubt) and Brave offered as exits. There is also a meta-argument after moderators swapped the submission's NYT link and title for Google's marketing blog post and then reverted it.

Worth reading

  • ceejayoz: The submitter quotes the article directly to rebut the 「it's just opt-in」 defence: schools can toggle AI, but off means no Search either, so the choice is bundled.
  • runarberg: A former high-school tutor reports DuckDuckGo was blocked on school networks and Google was the only option, which undercuts the 「schools can just switch」 answer.
  • smallerize: Cites an oumi.ai study finding Google's AI summaries contradict the sources they cite about 10% of the time, the concrete number the reliability debate keeps returning to.

entry.title: Show HN: HackerChurn – which SaaS tools HN wants to cancel
entry.content:
#23 on HN · hissingkitty.com · 56 points · 21 comments · HN discussion

HackerChurn is a small site by drewlem that scans a sample of public Hacker News comments from the past three years for mentions of software it tracks, classifies sentiment, and ranks tools by how many complaints they drew. The fetched page is mostly a set of ranked categories with complaint themes rather than readable names — security breaches and weak encryption, disruptive updates and poor testing, price rises, lock-in and intrusive AI, overblocking, slow queries — and the underlying tool names only surface through the comments. The author says the scoring is rough math on the ratio of negative to positive sentiment, and in-thread cites Datadog sitting at #51 with 13 complaints.

Discussion: The dominant objection is that raw complaint counts measure popularity, not badness: several commenters argue a widely used tool inevitably collects more complaints than a niche worse one, and ask for normalization by user base or for positive and neutral mentions to be counted too; the author concedes this and says each row now links to every comment counted as a complaint. The sharpest criticism is about sentiment attribution — one commenter checked the first CrowdStrike item and found an informative post that merely mentioned the product, then sampled more and called the list a crapshoot not worth trusting. Others expected GitHub at the top and were surprised by its absence, noting HN negativity does not match GitHub's reported record month for new organizations, which the author attributes to noise diluting the ratio. Side threads ask whether networks like LinkedIn and RealPage belong beside products, flag Datadog's absence as the one real surprise, and report that review submission was erroring under load before the author pushed a fix.

Worth reading

  • halflife: A commenter checked the top CrowdStrike entry and found it was an informative post that merely mentioned the product, then sampled several more and judged the negative-sentiment classification unreliable.
  • AznHisoka: Counter-data point: despite HN's hostility to GitHub, October was reportedly its best month ever for new organizations signing up, per Bloomberry data.
  • tmpz22: Datadog is named as the most surprising omission, since its high-touch sales, fat margins and IPO pressure are exactly the pattern the list otherwise captures — the author replies it is only #51 with 13 complaints.

entry.title: Practice speaking Japanese with real YouTube videos, graded line by line
entry.content:
#25 on HN · jivx.com · 46 points · 14 comments · HN discussion

JIVX is a web tool that takes a Japanese YouTube video and turns its lines into sentences you type or say, each one graded, or lets you practice with a video someone else already added. The page is mostly a catalogue of pre-processed videos (variety channels, podcasts, comprehensible-input channels, a Zelda playthrough) each tagged with sentence counts by JLPT level, from N5 up to N2. No explanation of the grading mechanics, pricing or wait times appears on the page itself.

Discussion: The thread splits into two conversations. The on-topic critique is skeptical: one commenter pasted in a video, was told there was a 26-minute wait, and could not work out what YouTube had to do with the product; on trying it he found it was not conversational practice at all but translation exercises — a Japanese sentence the video's speaker said, its English, and you translate it back — with no context making it a response to anything. Others asked whether pitch accent is annotated, and asked for German, Spanish and anime versions instead. The other half of the thread is a digression on gender-coded speech: a commenter's anecdote about a stay-at-home dad in Japan who picked up 「female」 Japanese from spending his days with Japanese mothers drew detailed replies on 女らしい (onnarashii) speech — intonation, politeness level, word choice and particles — with people noting the same happens to men who learn Russian from women or English from Southern moms, and that onnarashii usage is fading outside hospitality. A final subthread asks for an offline Japanese conversation chatbot; one commenter recommends Mistral's Voxtral 3 but distrusts LLM Japanese generally (only DeepL produces passable translation), another says he built one himself from Vosk, Gemma in Ollama and Kokoro TTS.

Worth reading

  • 1317: After actually trying it, this commenter says it is not speaking practice at all but decontextualised translation drills based on lines some YouTuber happened to say, and he does not see the point.
  • traceroute66: Explains the linguistic substance behind the thread's gender-speech anecdote: 女らしい speech is a bundle of intonation, politeness level, word choice and particle choice, historically rooted and now mostly confined to formal and hospitality contexts.
  • JoeDaDude: A commenter who wanted an offline Japanese conversation partner describes the stack he built: Vosk STT with vosk-model-ja-0.22, Gemma via Ollama with a custom tutor model card, and Kokoro TTS with the jf_alpha voice and unidic dictionary.

entry.title: DiscImageStudio: burn visible artwork onto CDs, DVDs and Blu-ray discs
entry.content:
#3 on HN · github.com · 158 points · 35 comments · HN discussion

DiscImageStudio 是一个以 GPL-3.0-or-later 授权的开源项目（.NET 10），把一张普通图片转换成符合 CD、DVD 和单层 BD-R 25 GB 物理层约束的数据，刻录后光盘数据面会呈现肉眼可见的图案。Windows 端提供 WPF 图形界面与一键刻录（基于系统自带 IMAPI2，仅接受空白盘），Linux 和 macOS 只有实验性 CLI，可离线导出 ISO / RAW / WAV+CUE；实现参照 ECMA-394、ECMA-267、ECMA-359 与 ISO/IEC 30190，CD 交织部分移植自 arduinocelentano 的 CDImage。项目还附了一套盘片标定流程，声称把可确定的盘面物理参数精度从 10^-6 提升到 10^-14，并用三次轨距拟合修正十字线弯曲。作者明确警告即时刻录为实验功能，只应用可报废的盘片。

Discussion: 讨论很快变成了光盘盘面打印技术的怀旧串：LightScribe、Yamaha 的 DiscT@2、2007 年的 Labelflash 以及 Neato 贴纸标签都被翻出来。对 LightScribe 的实际效果存在分歧——有人回忆每次要 20–30 分钟、成品在正常光线下偏淡、还不如记号笔；也有人反驳说慢归慢，纯黑白文字和线稿只要调好对比度就很清楚。一位做过 BSidesSF CTF 题目的人分享了第一手经验：他让人从 CDDA 原始 PCM 反推刻录后的盘面图像，花了数周才搞定，因为测定 pre-groove 几何极其敏感，他始终没能做出足够可靠的标定流程，因此对有人做成这件事表示佩服。关于图案与数据能否共存，有人指出同一区域不能兼作两者，但盘内圈放数据、外圈闲置区放图案是可行的。另有一支支线在争论项目里随处可见的动漫少女立绘是否令人反感，以及现在还有没有厂商在生产光驱。

Worth reading

  • bmenrigh: 作者做过同类 CTF 题：从原始 PCM 模拟刻录盘面，花了数周，卡在盘片 pre-groove 几何标定的敏感度上，最终没能发布可复用的标定方案。
  • sourweasel: 纠正「图与数据能否兼得」的疑问：同一区域不能既存数据又成像，但内圈数据加外圈闲置区画图是可行的。
  • sam1714: 对 LightScribe 的反面一手评价：每遍 20–30 分钟、盘片更贵，烧两遍后在实际光线下仍偏淡，家用还不如记号笔。

entry.title: Show HN: Hacker Times, a New York Times-inspired version of Hacker News
entry.content:
#4 on HN · hackertimes.ca · 206 points · 67 comments · HN discussion

一位名为 polpenn 的开发者制作的 Hacker News 前台页面重制版，按报纸版式排版：包括报头、分节、带摘要的稿件，以及真实的 HN 评论数；该站点每小时更新一次。链接页面本身是一份“已保存版次”，日期为 2026 年 11 月 3 日（星期二），并用带插图的大版式呈现了当天的 HN 报道——例如 MIT CSAIL 对 GPT-6 Astra 修改神经网络权重的研究、Karpathy 的 HackerTube，以及 Robert Haas 将 PostgreSQL 发布延迟归因于 AI 辅助发现的缺陷。该站点没有新增报道；它的主张只是呈现方式：把 HN 的链接列表重新包装成一份可阅读的报纸。

Discussion: 最尖锐的质疑是关于目的：如果报纸的价值在于报道和编辑，而这个项目只是重绘界面，那么为什么不做一个浏览器扩展，直接在原页面改写，而要单独维护一个每小时更新的站点？好几位评论者指出，此前已有不少同类作品存在——thefrontpage.dev、times.hntrends.net、hackernewstimes.com，以及 2020 年一个获得 627 分的 paper-HN——并认为在动手做之前应该先用 AI 智能体检索先前作品；另有人反驳说，为自己重新做一遍没什么可耻。熟悉前作的评论者提到，thefrontpage.dev 在几周前坏掉了，这也印证了此类项目往往会被弃置。视觉和字号设计本身也受到批评：一位排版评论者称，把 Georgia Bold 放在 55px 字号上做标题是错误选择，而 Google Fonts 上有大量更好的衬线字体；另有人认为，移动端的版式更像 Slashdot，而不是《纽约时报》。反复出现的玩笑围绕付费墙（“我觉得付费墙好像没有生效”），另有多条评论抱怨“Manufacturing Consent”字体的说明文字读起来太像 LLM 输出。管理员 dang 为这个项目辩护：HN 本来就不是一个统一的“自我”，社区还在慢慢摸索如何使用这些工具，而像这个站点和 Karpathy 的 HackerTube 这样的生成式站点看起来不错，没有那种一眼可见的 LLM 同质化感。

Worth reading

  • emaro: 列出了五个同类的 Hacker News 报纸化项目，其中包括一个来自六年前、曾经在 HN 上获得 627 分的作品，并附有搜索链接。
  • dang: dang 从版务角度回应“HN 对 AI 生成内容自相矛盾”的指责：HN 并非一个统一的自我；社区还在边做边学；这个站点和 HackerTube 都避开了 LLM 容易产生的同质化感。
  • muglug: 一位排版评论者认为，标题选用 Georgia Bold、以及 55px 的字号都不合适，并指出 Google Fonts 上有大量更好的衬线字体。

entry.title: European RISC-V Industrial Computing Initiative
entry.content:
#5 on HN · erici.eu · 61 points · 24 comments · HN discussion

ERICI is a newly founded, non-commercial European initiative (initiated by Yuri Zaporozhets in Ravensburg) proposing a reference software stack for RISC-V industrial computers, arguing that RVA23 silicon — the profile ratified in October 2024 that makes hypervisor and vector extensions mandatory — now exists but the industrial machine built around it does not. It specifies layers: an HFI BIOS (GPL-2.0, based on U-Boot), the mr-bml bootloader (GPL-3.0), the gRouvr partitioning hypervisor and QSOE (Apache 2.0), with real-time and Linux partitions isolated via IOMMU on a Skimmer microkernel or seL4. The site lists two existing RVA23 boards as examples — T-Chip's edge mini PC and Milk-V's board, both using SpacemiT K3 with 8× X100 cores up to 2.4 GHz, up to 32 GB LPDDR5 — and says the partitioned stack has been demonstrated on a K3 PicoITX board but not yet on those products.

Discussion: The thread is mostly skeptical about the framing rather than the technology. Several commenters ask what problem this actually solves, noting industrial machines already run for decades; the answer offered is that modern software churn plus the risk of political sanctions on ISA licensing makes vendor-neutral openness newly valuable. Others point out the awkward contradiction that the only RVA23 hardware cited is Chinese (SpacemiT K3, in T-Chip and Milk-V boards), making a European initiative read as promotion of Chinese appliances — a commenter notes the reference stack is verified on exactly that silicon. The most concrete counter-argument is the European Processor Initiative as precedent for an EU chip effort that amounted to little, though a reply cites EPI's SiPearl Rhea1 (80 Neoverse V1 cores, selected for the Jupiter exascale machine) as real output. A separate thread mocks the site's AI-generated copy and layout, with some defending it as harmless for a technical landing page and others finding the repeated 「the silicon is here, the industrial computer isn't」 construction tiresome; one early comment's reference to 「CPEU」 was never explained.

Worth reading

  • ShadowOfThePit: Asks the central question plainly: industrial machines already run 30+ years, so what is this initiative actually fixing beyond generic FOSS advocacy?
  • hollowonepl: Argues it is ironic for a European initiative to promote Chinese computer appliances, given that Chinese vendors are the only ones making this silicon today.
  • 0l: Cites the European Processor Initiative as a precedent for an EU chip initiative that went nowhere, linking its Wikipedia page.

entry.title: Resisting Cognitive Surrender
entry.content:
#8 on HN · knlb.dev · 127 points · 43 comments · HN discussion

A working-notes essay by knlb (October 2026) arguing against 「cognitive surrender」 — accepting agent output without thinking — which he calls fast, low-effort and seductive but prone to suboptimal decisions and quiet technical debt. He describes Gell-Mann amnesia with agents (in awe where he lacks expertise, then watching the agent fail to create a directory), complexity explosions in projects that shipped hundreds of thousands of lines, and the erosion of mechanical sympathy, citing The Ironies of Automation (1983). His remedies: a personal 「vibe limit」 for change complexity, conscious triage of what to delegate, a four-column PR view (diff, agent commentary, his own notes), stacked 「make the change easy, then make the easy change」 diffs, an AGENTS.md rule forbidding direct edits, debugger sessions, and shell harnesses that explain obscure flags.

Discussion: Several commenters largely agree but push further: one proposes a hard architectural boundary between agent-written and human-written code, like Shopify's platform APIs that let third-party code be a big ball of mud without corrupting the core, and others describe review collapsing into rubber-stamped LGTMs, verbose machine-written codebases, and contributors quitting rather than work alongside 「mindless robots」. The sharpest exchange is about review drift — that no single PR is ever rejected for making code 1% less understandable, so the loss compounds, with one commenter correcting the arithmetic to 0.99^100, a 63.4% decline. Against this, a self-described FAANG-ish commenter argues quality simply doesn't matter in the market: production issues up ~40% year over year while engagement and user numbers keep growing, a claim another commenter rejects as both bad engineering and commercially self-defeating. A recurring counter-argument is that the essay is copium that will evaporate as models improve — one predicts the author will 「just send it」 within six months and lists Karpathy and Primeagen as following the same trajectory, though a reply insists Primeagen actually walked back toward a middle ground. Others report the pressure is managerial rather than enthusiastic, note real improvement in model reliability since August, and suggest vibe-coded prototypes that get thrown away are a legitimate use.

Worth reading

  • cowlevel: Argues the real damage is bias, not error: every merge that degrades understandability by 1% still gets merged, and after 100 such merges the codebase is incomprehensible even though no reviewer made a mistake.
  • nurettin: First-hand account of the model-improvement curve: statistical errors persisted into January, were gone after August, and instruction-following is now the main remaining problem.
  • willtemperley: A GIS practitioner describes foundational, intricate libraries being copied and relicensed by vibe-coders, with the key maintainer now on indefinite strike — a concrete cost of the quality-indifference argument.

entry.title: Toit v2.0.0
entry.content:
#9 on HN · toit.io · 13 points · 5 comments · HN discussion

The Toit blog announces v2.0.0 of Toit, a language for writing scripts on a computer and applications on microcontrollers such as the ESP32, after more than four years of alpha, 2,000+ commits, 500,000+ lines changed and 200+ alpha releases. Toit started closed-source at Toitware, was open-sourced, and has been carried on by volunteers since Toitware shut down in 2024. The release was unblocked by the last planned breaking change — peripheral APIs now accept pin numbers directly instead of requiring gpio.Pin objects — while a formatter, compiler resolution improvements and more architecture support remain as open PRs for later releases; other additions include Arm EC618 and most ESP32 variants, a unified toit command, a rewritten package manager, mixins and firmware envelopes.

Discussion: The thread is tiny, so there is no real debate — mostly clarification. One commenter quotes the project's own one-liner (a readable syntax, an efficient runtime, good tooling, free and open source, volunteer-maintained), which prompted another to say that even after reading that blurb and more of the homepage he still had no idea what Toit actually is — a complaint about positioning rather than the release itself. The most substantive reply supplies credibility instead of explanation: the people behind Toit are the original V8 VM team from Chrome, so they know their stuff. Nobody in the thread reports running v2.0.0 or pushes back on the release.

Worth reading

  • skrebbel: Says the project's own description and homepage leave him unable to tell what Toit is — an implicit critique of how the project explains itself.
  • jacobgorm: Notes that Toit's creators were the original V8 VM team at Google, vouching for the technical quality behind the language and runtime.

entry.title: Scaling Git at OpenAI
entry.content:
#12 on HN · openai.com · 192 points · 108 comments · HN discussion

OpenAI's engineering post introduces Pando, a new Git backend for its monorepo that keeps the standard Git protocol and client but replaces the storage layer. Pando gives up repository-wide point-in-time consistency (using causal consistency, with only per-ref serializability) and stops generating a unique packfile per client, instead reusing immutable packfiles recorded as ref versions in blob and metadata stores. OpenAI says this cut median push latency by nearly 5x and now serves close to a petabyte of Git data per day, after reliability had at times dropped below 90%.

Discussion: A large camp treats the post as evidence of agent-driven slop rather than engineering progress: commenters ask what work could justify petabyte-scale Git traffic and argue that agents produce bloated code, endless fix commits and redundant documentation. Others push back that cheap code expands the set of worthwhile projects, that agents benefit from version history as much as humans do, and that Git being unusable for Google- and Meta-scale monorepos predates the AI era entirely. Several note this is roughly the fifth to seventh such post in a year (Cursor, GitHub twice, Anthropic, GitLab, Entire), and wonder how much the designs converge on ideas Google and Meta have used for a decade. Concrete criticism targets the post itself: one commenter building a code forge says there are no throughput or concurrency benchmarks, and another asks how streaming packfiles to blob storage without unpacking them can be safe against misbehaving clients and agents. A recurring side thread praises the write-up for being detailed and free of marketing hype, and skeptics and defenders split over whether LLM-written code volume is an asset or a liability for future maintenance.

Worth reading

  • pksunkara: Points out the post has no benchmarks — no pushes per second or concurrent pusher counts — from the perspective of someone building a competing code forge.
  • cadamsdotcom: Asks how Pando can validate a pushed packfile while streaming it to blob storage without unpacking, and whether that amounts to trusting the client, especially with agent-driven pushes.
  • skydhash: Argues Git is sufficient for the Linux kernel, FreeBSD, QEMU and Firefox; it broke at Google and Meta because of org-wide monorepos, and now a different assumption — that you want version control rather than a rolling snapshot log — is breaking.

entry.title: Self-Employed? Solopreneur? NIST Has a Cybersecurity Guide Just for You
entry.content:
#14 on HN · nist.gov · 199 points · 54 comments · HN discussion

NIST has published Cybersecurity White Paper 50 (CSWP 50), Small Business Cybersecurity: Non-Employer Firms, a lay-language rewrite of NISTIR 7621 aimed at the more than 28 million U.S. businesses with no paid employees. It maps selected actions from CSF 2.0 — backups, patching, changing default router passwords — to a rationale, first steps, and later-stage practices, plus worksheets and three hypothetical use cases involving a lawyer, an artisan and a consultant. NIST says no prior cybersecurity knowledge is assumed.

Discussion: The thread is split between readers who say the paper is still not written for novices — starting with the title 「Non-Employer Firms」, which no small business owner uses — and defenders who say the PDF defines phishing and MFA, links to deeper CISA resources, and avoids talking down to readers. Critics also complain the guide is buried behind the news page and an academic-looking landing page, requiring extra clicks busy owners will not make; one defender counters that the download is two clicks away. A separate and much louder argument erupts over the document's use of 「SI」, which several commenters read as 「Super Intelligence」: some call it a political shibboleth or federal mandate that undermines the paper's credibility, while others defend NIST as one of the few trustworthy technical publishers. Practitioners add concrete advice — inventory what is valuable, delete data you do not need, keep secrets out of email, use Signal — and one commenter argues solo operators inevitably need a trusted IT consultant, lawyer and accountant rather than a document. The rough consensus, if any, is that NIST's material is solid and worth reading, but that this package does not reliably reach the non-technical audience it claims to serve.

Worth reading

  • nomilk: Argues the title and framing defeat the lay-language goal: small businesses do not call themselves 「Non-Employer Firms」 and most do not know what NIST or a white paper is.
  • philosopherNoob: Objects to the document's use of 「SI」 as misplaced jargon that puts a fancy algorithm on a pedestal instead of grounding it for ordinary readers.
  • mmooss: Offers detailed practical advice for non-technical owners: inventory valuables and threats, avoid storing what you do not need, keep passwords and client data out of email, and use Signal.

entry.title: Show HN: ReBirth 338 in Browser
entry.content:
#15 on HN · margeux.com · 15 points · 6 comments · HN discussion

这是一个 Show HN 发布，把 Propellerhead 在 1997 年推出的经典软件合成器 ReBirth RB-338（模拟 Roland TB-303、TR-808、TR-909）搬进了网页，地址是 margeux.com/rb338.html。链接页面几乎没有可读文本，因为它依赖 JavaScript 运行，所以下面这些内容来自标题和评论区：评论者根据大量文件名中出现「wine」判断，这个项目实际上是在浏览器里用 boxedwine（Emscripten 编译的 Wine）运行原版 Windows 程序，也就是把 x86 模拟叠在上面。

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: 讨论主要围绕技术实现和加载性能展开。flohofwoe 指出，这个页面加载了大量看起来完全相同的 .js 文件（例如 rb338/boxedwine-firefox-20261103.js，像是 Emscripten 的 JS 胶水文件），此外还加载了两个 100 MB 和 150 MB 的大文件，在 50 Mbit 的网络上首次启动等待很久；他认为重复下载同一个文件看起来像 bug，应该可以大幅优化。有人追问实现方式，认为是 boxedwine 模拟 x86；有用户报告在 Firefox 115.44.0esr 上无法运行，未得到回应。另有评论者说，ReBirth 相关的 Facebook 群组里最近涌入大量「vibe-coded」的克隆和移植，并推荐了 rb.varyform.info 作为其中较好的一个。整体氛围是「90 年代音乐复兴」的怀旧热情，没有形成明确共识，只是对首屏加载和兼容性有共同的抱怨。

Worth reading

  • flohofwoe: 指出页面把同一个 Emscripten JS 垫片重复下载了几十次，外加 100 MB 与 150 MB 两个大包，在 50 Mbit 网络上首启动极慢，怀疑是 bug。
  • skrebbel: 推荐 8bitbubsy 的原生 Fasttracker 2 克隆（16-bits.org/ft2.php），称其完成度很高且「不是 AI 生成的」，唯一缺憾是没有 Space Pigs 主题。
  • thm: 提到 ReBirth 社区正涌现大量 AI 辅助编写的克隆与移植，并给出其中较好的一个：rb.varyform.info。

entry.title: Shrinking NixOS RAM footprint and resource requirements to the bare minimum
entry.content:
#19 on HN · lowendspirit.com · 49 points · 5 comments · HN discussion

A LowEndSpirit forum write-up by AnthonySmith documenting how he cut a NixOS 26.05 KVM guest template for his VPS host TierHive from 288MB idle to 96MB idle on a 512MB VPS, and from a 896MB rebuild to a 371MB peak. The methods are mostly kernel cmdline and config surgery: sysctl.vm.mem_profiling=never, kfence.sample_interval=0, initcall_blacklist for ksm/tpm, transparent_hugepage=never (the single biggest win, ~52MB at 2GB), blacklisting or /bin/false-ing unused virtio drivers, a trimmed kernel modules tree (162MB to 45MB on disk), dropping systemd-resolved/timesyncd/oomd, socket-activated sshd, zram plus aggressive swappiness, and Boehm GC tuning for Nix evaluation. He notes release jumps (26.05 to unstable) still OOM at 512MB and usually need a second run.

entry.title: SLAC researchers find proof of altermagnetism, a new magnetic phase
entry.content:
#22 on HN · www6.slac.stanford.edu · 69 points · 8 comments · HN discussion

A SLAC-led team reports in Science (29 October 2026, D. Jost et al., DOI 10.1126/science.adv3196) experimental confirmation of altermagnetism, a third magnetic phase beyond ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. Using circularly polarized X-rays on the ID32 beamline at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, they measured a chiral scattering signal in manganese telluride (MnTe) — left- and right-handed beams scattered differently — which a conventional antiferromagnet cannot produce; the experiment ran in 2024 and was repeated in early 2025. The claimed payoff is spintronics: altermagnets have zero net magnetization like antiferromagnets (so stray fields cannot flip bits) but, like ferromagnets, can carry spin-polarized currents that make the state readable.

Discussion: The thread is short and mostly appreciative rather than technical. One commenter asks the obvious question — how altermagnetism differs from antiferromagnetism, given that the net-zero moment was supposedly the defining trait — and the only answer offered is a pointer to the paper's abstract; a follow-up admits the abstract and intro left them with more questions than before, while another replies that the writing is clear enough for almost anyone to grasp the difference. One poster links the Science publication directly and notes the phase's quasi-particle, the altermagnon, makes a great band name; others praise the article's prose about chirality as 'spiral staircase' physics, and one quips that 'this is huge if true.' No one in the thread reports first-hand experimental work, and the closest thing to consensus is that the result sounds significant and is worth reading the paper for.

Worth reading

  • ortusdux: Posts the direct Science DOI link to the underlying paper, plus the observation that 『Chiral Altermagnon』 would make a good band name.
  • clilog_d: Raises the central conceptual question the article leaves fuzzy: if net-zero magnetic moment defines antiferromagnetism, what actually makes altermagnetism a separate phase?
  • buildbot: Reports that reading the abstract and introduction did not resolve the confusion — a useful signal that the popular account may not settle the distinction either.

entry.title: Show HN: I built a little browser game to practice Vim commands
entry.content:
#24 on HN · hjkl.duy.run · 20 points · 14 comments · HN discussion

hjkl (hjkl.duy.run) is a free, no-account browser game by dh1011 for drilling Vim commands. You pick skills — text objects like ci" ci' ci( diw daw, repeat edits, jumps like 12G gg G ctrl-o ctrl-i — and then make small real edits in an in-browser Vim editor: each skill gives two guided edits, two prompted edits and two independent edits, and any valid edit that reaches the target text passes. Type :help in Normal mode for the commands available; it needs a desktop browser with a physical keyboard.

Discussion: The thread is mostly positive, with practical quibbles and several concrete corrections to the teaching. glibg10b argues the game teaches suboptimal habits: for the ciw examples ce is easier with the cursor on the word's first letter, and where dw works the game drills vlllld instead; they also note Ctrl-A/Ctrl-X (increment/decrement the first number after the cursor) and fY would beat the game's t:t: approach, and report a simulator bug — Ctrl-V then j then Ctrl-A on a column increments only the cell under the cursor, where real Vim would increment all of them. Others complain about input friction: one user is annoyed that the site itself can't be driven by keyboard and requires the mouse between exercises, another suggests Vim motions should select the next exercise in the sidebar, and a third notes the skill grid cells aren't clickable as a whole. There are also feature requests — jumbled rather than grouped challenges, and an in-browser vim.golf — and one commenter says plain everyday Vim use, not games, is what made commands stick; author dh1011 replies to several threads promising the undo prompt, keyboard navigation and full-cell clicks.

Worth reading

  • glibg10b: Detailed Vim critique: ce beats ciw here, dw shouldn't be taught as vlllld, Ctrl-A/Ctrl-X and fY are simpler alternatives, plus a concrete visual-block Ctrl-A bug where the simulator only increments one cell.
  • sponno: A user is annoyed that the site itself cannot be operated by keyboard and forces a mouse between exercises.
  • alabhyajindal: Requests jumbled challenges instead of all 「fix a typo」 first, and suggests the game could become a browser version of vim.golf.

entry.title: The SEC Should Block Anthropic's IPO to Protect the Public
entry.content:
#25 on HN · techpolicy.press · 318 points · 236 comments · HN discussion

这是 Tech Policy Press 上的一篇评论文章，作者是 Matt Scherer（Open Markets Institute，也是《Brace for Impact》一书的合著者）。文章主张，SEC 应当阻止 Anthropic 上市，直到它提交连续两个季度经审计的财务报表。文中指出，Anthropic 账面上有约 960 亿美元现金，却背负着约 8950 亿美元的合同义务；其中至少 5820 亿美元是不可撤销的，分别欠 Amazon、AMD、Broadcom、Google 和 Microsoft。2026 年的业绩尚未经审计，而且第三季度营收增长明显放缓，因此文章认为，价格战、需求疲软、开放权重模型的竞争，以及每个 1 GW 约 310 亿美元的数据中心成本（该公司已签约 15 GW，自称最终需要 20–25 GW），会让这些义务无法履行；而一旦这些股票被纳入指数基金和 401(k)，普通投资者就会承担损失。

Discussion: 最大的分歧在于 SEC 的角色：是一手把不合格的注册文件挡在门外，还是只要求充分披露、然后交由市场判断。不少评论者纠正了文章的前提：S-1 通常必须包含经审计的财务报表，非 GAAP 指标也很常见，第三季度的数据是后来通过修订补充进去的，脚注本来就是招股书的一部分，而文章把“藏在脚注里”当成了大问题。另一条主线是指数纳入带来的风险：有人说，巨型 IPO 一上市就以高排名直接进入指数，普通指数持有人只能吃到下跌的损失；但另一些人指出，S&P 500 要求上市满 12 个月、并且连续四个季度盈利为正，而 Russell、CRSP 等指数虽然会更早纳入，却按流通市值加权，所以被动资金被迫买入的规模远没有想象中大。文章引用的“职场 AI 使用率从 2025 年夏季的 46% 降至 33%”被查出来源很弱：数据来自《经济学人》引用的一项 Jon Hartley 调查，而 2026 年的原始数据在互联网档案里也找不到；同时，人口普查局的数据显示 2026 年的使用率呈上升趋势。此外，还有人围绕“是否该替投资者做决定”争论：一方认为，让养老金和散户替内部的投资者接盘并不公平；另一方认为，剥夺投资者买入或做空的机会才是真正的家长式作风。

Worth reading

  • simonw: simonw 查到了这句统计数据的出处：是《经济学人》2026 年 7 月的一篇文章引用了 Jon Hartley 等人约 2.4 万人的调查；他指出人口普查局的方法在 12 月改动过，但 2026 年的数字一直在上升，而该调查“33%”所依据的 2026 年原始数据在互联网档案里根本没有保存。
  • hannasanarion: hannasanarion 找到了原论文（SSRN 5136877），指出“AI 使用率下滑”只出现在附录四张图中的一张，作者自己都没有评论这个下降，而且整份调查几乎没有涉及 Claude、Copilot 或 Microsoft，因此很难用来得出“AI 要熄火”的结论。
  • JumpCrisscross: JumpCrisscross 直接反驳“财务数据只是口头保证”的说法：在美国，几乎所有通过 IPO 上市的公司都必须提供经审计的财务报表（Regulation S-X 的要求），审计意见就写在 S-1 里；他认为，这轮讨论暴露出财经网红在传播金融知识的盲区。

entry.title: Polyend releases the Tracker firmware source code
entry.content:
#26 on HN · polyend.com · 122 points · 38 comments · HN discussion

Polyend has released the firmware source for the original Tracker, Tracker+ and Tracker Mini on GitHub, alongside a 「Tracker Community Edition 1.0」 build that owners can flash, modify and redistribute. The update adds SD-card streaming of long samples (even on the original Tracker), dedicated micro-move and volume fields so both step FX slots stay free, a plugin system in the Sample Editor with six bundled effects/generators and a plugin SDK, two new synth engines (CHIP and DIRT) plus a synth SDK for Tracker+/Mini, wavetable envelopes and LFOs, faster project load/save, tighter MIDI clock, and a browser-based theme/font designer. Polyend says a recovery system guards against bricking, and that devices broken by custom firmware fall outside warranty but can still be sent in for paid out-of-warranty repair.

Discussion: The thread is overwhelmingly positive and treats the move as an industry trend rather than a one-off: commenters tie it to the viral success of M-VAVE's open-firmware FM-1, to existing efforts by Synthstrom (Deluge) and Mutable Instruments, and to LLM-assisted reverse engineering that has lately produced custom firmware for gear like the Model:Cycles, Cobalt8 and LXR-02. Several argue Polyend is partly getting ahead of the modding scene and partly handing maintenance of older hardware to the community, and one points out the release is not just source code but a feature drop plus plugin/synth SDKs. The one real disagreement is over Polyend's repair offer: one user calls the explicit acknowledgement of bricking risk and willingness to service units groundbreaking, while a European reply says paid out-of-warranty repair is completely normal there and that in the EU a vendor must prove custom firmware caused a fault before denying a warranty claim. A long tangent about Ableton going open source ends with a rebuke to someone calling it overpriced junk, and the rest of the thread drifts into M8 and Dirtywave comparisons, hardware alternatives like Renoise, and hope for alternative hardware running the firmware.

Worth reading

  • knvlt: A user describes using an LLM to mod a Modal Cobalt8 — adding Curtis/303/Steiner-Parker filters, Braids oscillators, granular delay and a Karplus-Strong effect in two days — while stressing it proves ease of access, not skill, and that they still pay for gig-stable gear.
  • embedding-shape: Challenges the framing of Polyend's repair offer as groundbreaking: paid out-of-warranty service is routine in Europe across Elektron, Novation, Korg and Yamaha, and EU warranty denial requires the vendor to prove the custom firmware caused the fault.
  • gregsadetsky: Notes that Erika Synths recently open-sourced the LXR-02 firmware too, and that they ported it to WebAssembly — the link is posted in a reply.

entry.title: V100 SXM2 pinout and NVLink reference
entry.content:
#30 on HN · github.com · 31 points · 5 comments · HN discussion

A GitHub reference kit from pigeon-labs-stack aimed at an eventual open-source carrier board for NVIDIA V100 SXM2 modules. It curates 800 canonical connector contacts (400 on connector A for PCIe, power and control; 400 on connector B for NVLink and management), two- and four-GPU NVLink connection tables with exact B-side pads, lane directions and polarity, plus three connector-only KiCad 10.0.7 starter projects and a PDF workbook. The author stresses it is a reference pre-release, not a qualified board: no regulator, power-control or clock circuitry, and each V100 still needs an external 156.25 MHz differential NVHS clock on B/E20 (±) and a 100 MHz PCIe clock on A/E7 (±); the original reverse-engineering is credited upstream and licensed CERN-OHL-W-2.0 / CC BY-SA 4.0.

Discussion: Two commenters had already tried this themselves: one mapped connector A by hand in Feb 2024 and got partway into an SXM2-to-PCIe interposer, and points to Facebook's Big Basin JBOG schematics from Open Compute — itself derived from NVIDIA's DGX-1 reference design — as filling gaps and explaining the form factor and OpenPOWER-like pinout. Another did similar work from OCP documents and server schematics but gave up after renting an 8×V100 machine and concluding it was poor for LLM inference. That pessimism drew a direct counter from an owner of four V100S cards, who runs them as PCIe variants over 25 Gbps Ethernet with RDMA and reports DeepSeek V4.1 IQ2_XXS at 80–100 t/s and a Qwen model at 200 t/s single / 450–550 t/s aggregate, arguing the cards have more headroom than commonly assumed because their compute is just enough to keep the VRAM busy. A final commenter is simply glad the link was reposted after his own submission sank, noting the V100 is one of the few still semi-affordable GPUs.

Worth reading

  • devbug: Says he hand-mapped connector A in Feb 2024 and links Facebook's Big Basin JBOG schematics from Open Compute, derived from the DGX-1 reference design, as a source that resolves gaps in this project's pin data.
  • bitexploder: First-hand benchmarks from an owner of four V100S cards on 25 GbE with RDMA: DeepSeek V4.1 IQ2_XXS at 80–100 t/s, a Qwen model at 450–550 t/s aggregate, arguing the cards are underrated for local inference.
  • Gracana: The counterweight: having done similar OCP-based reverse engineering, he abandoned it after renting an 8×V100 server and finding it disappointing for LLM inference.

entry.title: Skill to Create Product Videos
entry.content:
#32 on HN · github.com · 97 points · 27 comments · HN discussion

aaitor/skill-video-studio (v1.0.1, MIT) is a local video-production workspace driven by a Claude Code project skill called /devrel-video: Playwright CLI scripts capture real browser interactions along fixed beats, HyperFrames composes title cards, browser frames, chapters and CTAs, and FFmpeg handles mastering, ffprobe QA, contact sheets and thumbnails. Optional layers include six local music styles, narration-driven timing, EN/ES subtitles, and bring-your-own presenter footage or LatentSync avatars on a private SSH GPU host; it needs Node.js 22+, FFmpeg and Chromium, and the author notes offline CI only checks sources, not the full render stack. Argomaniz frames it as a fix for the part of shipping he always neglected: manuals, demos and support content, admitting the skill won't do distribution for you.

Discussion: The premise landed well — several commenters agreed that promotion feels like an unpaid obligation and that self-promotion rules on Reddit and Lobsters make it worse — but the demo video itself took most of the fire: the narrator gets cut off around 11 seconds, the four-on-the-floor kick is too loud with heavy sidechain compression, and the drums drift out of sync. The bigger argument was about skills as a concept: one commenter called them overblown hype, 「just words added to your context」, and said speech-to-text would serve people better, while others countered that a skill is worth writing for your own corporate style and sales workflow. A side-by-side test of the same product video with and without the skill produced nearly identical results, which the tester offered not as an attack but as a reminder to check whether the model already does the job unaided; another commenter noted that having Claude rebuild the UI rather than record it makes the whole interface animatable. Multiple people already run similar pipelines — fal.ai avatars at about $2 per demo, ElevenLabs voiceover, filmcraft-cli, iOS simulator capture — and one warned that recent major Playwright CVEs make patching important.

Worth reading

  • jjcm: Posted with/without-skill videos of the same product that look almost identical, arguing models are now good enough that a skill's value should be measured, plus a warning about major Playwright CVEs.
  • zeroq: Strong skeptic take: skills are overhyped because they are just words in the context window, more useful to non-technical users than to engineers.
  • TomGarden: Notes concrete flaws in the author's own example output: voiceover cut off and drums rushing out of sync with the rest of the music.

entry.title: Intel stock collapse worsens as $3.5T chip rout spreads
entry.content:
#34 on HN · finance.yahoo.com · 196 points · 151 comments · HN discussion

A Yahoo Finance markets piece by Jared Blikre (with an AI-assistance disclosure) reporting that Intel fell about 9% on Monday, Nov. 2, after its worst session since 1974 on Oct. 30, when a weak forecast knocked nearly 29% off the shares — leaving Intel worth less than half its Sept. 30 value. The rout was broad: Micron, Sandisk, Seagate and Western Digital fell 6-8%, Marvell dropped on its $115B Lumentum acquisition, and chip/memory names have lost roughly $3.7T in market value since Oct. 6 (the HN headline says $3.5T), with Nvidia down about 16% over that span. The article quotes bulls calling the selloff 「kitchen-sinked」 and Jeff Hirsch noting chips rose in all eight midterm cycles since 1994, while flagging AMD's earnings as the next test.

Discussion: The biggest thread is about whether Intel still matters. One camp says the scale of the move — down ~50% in a month though still up ~50% year-over-year — is meme-stock behavior for a company running most of the world's PCs and servers; others push back that Intel's x86 share is closer to 60% and falling every year, AMD took the datacenter crown, and ARM hyperscaler silicon is encroaching. A second thread argues over whether Intel's fate matters to shareholders: several posters note the US government now holds equity and that a national-interest rescue can nationalize the company while wiping out common stock, while others insist the fabs and advanced packaging are strategically indispensable and Washington will not let them go. A striking subthread is insider testimony — a self-described ex-Intel senior principal says the problem is a decade of brain drain and pay too low to hold talent (not just leadership), corroborated by another ex-engineer, though others cite Panther Lake and Arc GPUs as evidence Intel's engineering is still capable. On the numbers, commenters compare Nvidia's blowout quarter ($96B revenue, $60B profit) to Intel's $16.5B/$3.3B, and note Intel's forward P/E of ~31 is roughly AMD's but far above Nvidia's; a few correct the framing that Intel's fabs are its weakness, arguing the 「5 nodes in 4 years」 catch-up largely worked and the fab business is now the crown jewel but lacks external customers.

Worth reading

  • poxy22: A self-described former Intel senior principal engineer rejects the leadership-only explanation: a decade of brain drain and underpaying engineers meant the technical problems simply could not be solved, and Intel engineers 「suck」 — including himself.
  • Tuna-Fish: Argues there will still be a company making chips in Intel's fabs in 5-20 years because it is in the US national interest, but that this says nothing about common shareholders, who are typically wiped out when strategic firms are rescued.
  • quickthrowman: Puts hard numbers on the Intel-vs-Nvidia divergence: Nvidia's Q2 2026 revenue was $96B with $60B profit at ~75% gross margins, against Intel's $16.5B revenue and $3.3B profit.

entry.title: C64 Basic Dungeon Crawler: Stairs, Levels and Levelling Up (Part 11)
entry.content:
#35 on HN · retrogamecoders.com · 74 points · 12 comments · HN discussion

这是 retrogamecoders.com 系列教程的第 11 部分，讲解在用 BASIC 编写的 Commodore 64 地牢爬行游戏中加入关卡进度。代码被拆成 INITPLAYER（每局只运行一次，使角色在关卡切换时保持生命值、属性、金币、钥匙和魔法）和 BUILDLEVEL（每层重建地图）；游戏现在有 5 层，每层必须收集全部圣杯才能使用楼梯，圣杯数量按 INT(LV/2)+1 计算（第 1–2 层为 1 个，第 3–4 层为 2 个，第 5 层为 3 个），楼梯随机放在四个角落房间之一，并且始终位于开放房间中央。升级会加上等于体质一半的生命值，偶数等级加 1 点力量、奇数等级加 1 点敏捷，一个 * 药水增加 50 点魔法，上限为 100；作者指出这些数字有意做得粗略，并预计之后需要一阶段难度与数值平衡调整。

Discussion: 讨论很快转向技术问题：classichasclass 指出这些代码无法在真正的 C64 上运行——BASIC 2.0 没有标签，而且 STATS 会与保留的状态字 ST 冲突——因此它只能在网站提供的自定义在线 IDE 中运行，该 IDE 会添加行号、重命名变量并做分词。krige 表示同意，说看到没有行号的 GOSUB 就是一个明显的警示信号。其他人则为这种做法辩护：sbuttgereit 记得 1980 年代 C64 BBS 软件使用类似的「编译器」来适配过大的程序，sedatk 补充说，那个年代的杂志往往提供打字辅助工具，这样就能发布纯文本清单，而不是 PETSCII 乱码；后来有评论者指出这个工具是 RGC Basic，一个用 C 写成的类似 Commodore BASIC 的解释器，并带有现代便利功能。旁支讨论指向同时期的替代作：leoc 提到 1984 年 Usborne 的书《Write Your Own Fantasy Games》（Howarth 和 Evans 著），the_af 更正了其 Google Drive 链接为请求权限，并链接到 Usborne 的免费编程书籍页面和一篇平淡的评论。EmX_3000 感叹很少有家用电脑拥有真正为其硬件调校的 BASIC，并指出 C64 场景至今仍是最活跃的复古社区，Someone 则回应说，ROM BASIC 是成本与上市时间的取舍问题；teddyh 回忆说，1983 年的地牢爬行游戏 Sword of Fargoal 是用真正的 Commodore 64 BASIC 写成的。

Worth reading

  • classichasclass: 指出这一清单无法在真正的 C64 上运行——BASIC 2.0 没有标签，而且 STATS 与 ST 状态字冲突——并解释说它只能用于网站的自定义编译式 IDE。
  • harwoodr: 确认该工具是 RGC Basic，一个用 C 写成、遵循 Commodore BASIC 风格并带有现代便利功能的解释器。
  • sbuttgereit: 第一手回忆称，1980 年代 C64 BASIC 的 BBS 项目同样使用「编译器」优化，以适配过大的程序。

entry.title: Show HN: I've updated my Linux System Call website and API
entry.content:
#37 on HN · syscall.sh · 219 points · 52 comments · HN discussion

syscall.sh 是一个按架构整理的 Linux 系统调用参考网站兼 API，作者 guitmz 在 2020 年首次发布，这次大幅更新。网站现在覆盖 27 种架构，带有内核版本选择器（Linux 3.3 到 7.3），列出系统调用号、参数、寄存器和进入内核的指令，并标注每条系统调用首次出现和何时被移除；每种架构的数据还以纯 JSON 形式提供，例如 /x64/syscalls.json，另有 API 位于 api.syscall.sh/v2。所有数据都由生成器直接扫描内核源码中的系统调用表和 SYSCALL_DEFINE 宏得出，简短描述取自 man-pages 项目和 liburing，前端每周通过 cronjob 从 API 重建。

Discussion: 评论区整体很正面，有人正在学 aarch64 汇编，称其“很方便”，也有人反馈网站在自己机器上会打乱显示效果。最实质的纠正是：x86_64/x32 上系统调用号放在 eax 而非 rax，高位被忽略；作者承认这个错误并说自 5.14 起内核只读 eax，会补上说明，而纠正者又贴出 lore.kernel.org 的补丁链接指出内核在此问题上反复过几次。不少人对“为什么同一套 Linux API 的系统调用号各架构不同”感兴趣，作者和他人解释系统调用 ABI 是架构相关的、号码是 90 年代各移植维护者各自分配的、如今已成冻结 ABI，riscv 等新架构干脆不实现 open/fork，libc 会转调 openat/clone。还有一段争论围绕“约 400 个系统调用是否真的算 400 个不同调用”：一方认为 read/pread、pipe/pipe2 等只是同一功能的变体，另一方坚持系统调用号是客观且唯一有意义的计数，并用 ioctl 子命令上千、io_uring 把许多调用合并成一个入口、以及 Windows ntos 约 490 个系统调用来反驳；adrian_b 估计 x86-64 上有 450 多个，其中约三分之一已过时、另三分之一极少使用。有人建议给已废弃的调用加提示横幅（如用 pipe2 替代 pipe），作者则提到可以增加“相似系统调用”区块，并透露打算整理公开自己写的 CLI 工具。

Worth reading

  • bkallus: 指出 x86_64 和 x32 的系统调用号实际放在 eax 而不是 rax，rax 高 32 位会被忽略，作者确认并更新文档。
  • ozgrakkurt: 实用建议：用 echo '#include <sys/syscall.h>' | gcc -E -dM -xc - 在本机核对真实系统调用号，因为 LLM 给出过错误常量；同时提到 Chromium 的旧系统调用表。
  • guitmz: 解释各架构系统调用号不同的历史原因：90 年代各移植开发者自行按添加顺序编号，随后冻结成不可更改的 ABI，且 32/64 位类型差异本就要求不同变体。

entry.title: Too Expensive to Exist
entry.content:
#40 on HN · mapwriting.substack.com · 37 points · 5 comments · HN discussion

A personal essay on the Substack Mapwriting about a $12-a-night private campground in Texas, an hour and a half from the author's home, that is ending individual camping and day-use trail access in October 2026 because the owner can no longer afford rising liability insurance. From there it widens into an angry sweep: state park campsites booked out past Christmas, over 95% of Texas land in private hands, a 25-acre wood near his childhood home fenced and clear-cut by an owner afraid of wildfire liability, pushes to transfer federal land to states, the 211-mile Ambler Road mining corridor in Alaska, and the argument that growth, Jevons paradox and cost disease make every such loss permanent.

Discussion: The thread is small and mostly sympathetic. One commenter sorts the complaints into three buckets — insurance-industry rent-seeking, ennui, and symptoms of rising population density — and argues supply and demand apply to space as much as anything, though he insists he is not relitigating Malthusianism. Another immediately rejects that framing, defining Malthusianism as the claim that some people must be poor because reproduction outruns productivity and that gains get absorbed by population, then counters that food production has outpaced population and birth rates are falling, recommending Henry George's Progress and Poverty as the better account, where land scarcity rather than reproductive instinct creates poverty. A third observation is that the essay's repeated word is 「impotent」: the sentiment is widespread among ordinary people but absent from leaders, whose networks are correlated with the wealthy and insulated — they are the last to hear about campground insurance rates. The most substantive reply comes from a Texas native who says the state has no interest in funding community resources; he cites Fairfield Lake State Park, where the state could have bought land it already leased cheaply from a power company that closed its plant, complete with staff and infrastructure in place, but let it fall into private hands. He also corrects a common assumption that the Rockies' and Sierras' public land is geographically inevitable, noting it came from deliberate local and municipal campaigns. One commenter found the piece more stream-of-consciousness than expected from the title but agreed with it anyway.

Worth reading

  • hingler36: A Texan recounts how the state declined to buy Fairfield Lake State Park from the power company that leased it the land, despite having staff and infrastructure ready, and argues public land in the Rockies and Sierras was won by concerted local campaigns, not geography.
  • skew-aberration: Pushes back on the Malthusian framing, arguing productivity growth has outpaced population and fertility is falling, and points to Henry George's Progress and Poverty for a land-scarcity explanation of poverty.
  • rafterydj: Notes that the essay's recurring word is 「impotent」 and that leaders are structurally the last to hear about costs like campground insurance because their networks correlate with wealth.

entry.title: Ask HN: Does anyone have a contact with Cleveland-area Ham club?
entry.content:
#41 on HN · text post · 131 points · 21 comments · HN discussion

这是一条 HN 求助帖，不是链接文章。发帖人 stockresearcher 说，自己家里有一大批无线电设备需要搬走，否则就会被扔进垃圾箱，其中很多还是全新的；他填写了 Cuyahoga Amateur Radio Club 网站的表单，但怀疑没有人会看，于是来 HN 找人牵线。发帖人后来更新说，通过这个帖子已经联系上俱乐部的人，虽然不能保证结果，但「避免进垃圾填埋场的最好机会已经出现了」。

Discussion: 回应的重点几乎全是帮忙：有当地火腿（Radio2034）建议同时联系 Case Western 的 W8EDU 俱乐部，并留下邮箱；也有人表示会把帖子转给认识的无线电爱好者。Archive.org 的 jonah-archive 借机提醒，他们运营的 Digital Library of Amateur Radio Communications 已经收录超过 25,000 件资料，欢迎捐出纸质文献和 ephemera，但不收硬件。讨论还延伸到「这种帖子为什么能上首页」：有人认为 HN 本来就偏爱火腿相关的极客历史，而且发帖时间对美国用户有利；也有人调侃火腿像「精灵森林里的德鲁伊」，稀有、有文化共鸣，还容易拿到免费赞同。另有枝节讨论如何追查一位祖父在 1940–80 年代的呼号历史，建议查学校图书馆和县图书馆的旧缩微胶片。

Worth reading

  • Radio2034: 当地火腿 Radio2034 建议联系 Case Western 的 W8EDU 俱乐部，并表示愿意直接帮忙牵线。
  • jonah-archive: Internet Archive 的 jonah-archive 介绍 Digital Library of Amateur Radio Communications，称其已收录逾 25,000 件资料，可接收纸质无线电文献。
  • Radio2034: 给追查祖父呼号的人提供具体方法：查学校俱乐部档案、校图书馆和县图书馆数字化的旧缩微胶片。

entry.title: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
entry.content:
#1 on HN · rikiyat.github.io · 612 points · 178 comments · HN discussion

这是一篇关于「Weight-Space Programming」的博客文章，作者称 GPT-6 Astra 能直接在上下文中读写神经网络权重，而不需要梯度下降或优化器。实验包括：仅凭原始权重识别四个 PPO 网络各自训练的是哪个游戏、识别 DDPM 生成的形状、只看中间四层判断 7.2M 参数小语言模型的训练语言（Python/罗马字/英语），并找出 induction head。最引人注目的是改 Qwen3.5-0.8B：Astra 定位到导致推理死循环的权重方向，只改 0.016% 的权重，MATH-500 从 7.9% 升到 48.1%，IFEval 提升约 3 倍；此外还从零写出 MinAtar 三个游戏的网络，击败训练 1 亿步的 PPO。

Discussion: 评论区一半是震惊，一半是「意料之中」。怀疑派认为这类能力更可能是 OpenAI 为递归自我改进（RSI）专门训练出来的，且预训练语料里本就散落着大量权重文件和可解释性文献；乐观派则强调单次前向推理就胜过上亿步 PPO 实在反常理，并猜测注意力机制在权重上做了类似 PCA 的投影。多位读者给出了关键修正：Qwen 的数学提升并不是「教会它数学」，而是消除了层 15/19 MLP 写入的一个「循环方向」，与 Arditi 等人 2024 年关于拒绝方向的研究同源，投影只能移除行为、无法新增能力；同样方法用在本来就不循环、单纯数学差的 Gemma 3 270M 上则完全失败。还有人称过程其实允许了 50 轮批量迭代并在下游任务上评估，与「无环境反馈」的说法有出入。规模是最大的共识性疑虑：一个数万亿参数的模型去修 0.8B 模型，能否递归到自己身上、上下文容量是否够（有人估算 1M 上下文最多编辑约 20B 的 fp4 模型）都未经验证；不少人顺带担心权重供应链完整性和去审查（abliteration）风险。

Worth reading

  • l9o: 指出 Qwen 原本就会数学，只是 96 个答案里有 85 个撞到 token 上限陷入死循环，Astra 修的是循环而非补齐知识，且对不循环的 Gemma 3 270M 无效。
  • augment_me: 认为所谓数学飞跃本质是移除激活空间里一个导致循环而非收敛的方向，属于已知的 Arditi et al. 2024 技术，可替代 LoRA/GRPO 类后训练，但无法注入新知识。
  • Wheen: 提醒这是数万亿参数模型在优化 8 亿参数模型，没有任何证据表明它能用同样方法改进自身。

entry.title: Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise
entry.content:
#2 on HN · text post · 294 points · 202 comments · HN discussion

Subvocal 是由 The Subvocal Company（YC F26）的 Aarush Yadav 和 Arnav 创办的项目：它用一副眼镜向面部发射低功率射频，这种射频能穿过舌头、嘴唇和软腭，被无声的口型动作调制，再通过云端模型解码成文字，延迟通常低于 500ms。团队称原型在 20 句校准后，词错率可到约 5%，并且因为射频能看到口腔内部，闭着嘴做「内部言语」也能工作。影片里的测试者通过 500 副预购、200 美元折扣销售，目标 Q1 2027 出货，目前只支持英文，解码在配套 app 或云端完成，也要求联网。团队还说自己试过 EMG、IMU、唇读和 mmWave，最后才转向这种射频方案。

Discussion: 评论区整体非常热情，大量评论引用科幻作品，如《Ender's Game》《Speaker for the Dead》的 Jane、《1984》的 speakwrite 和《The Whispering Earring》，说自己等这类技术等了二十年。最集中的批评针对官网：好几个人滑了半天都不知道这是眼镜，看不到「how it works」到底怎么工作，讨厌必须滚动触发的动画，FAQ 只说不使用相机，却不说用什么；创始人逐条回应称会改，并修好了 Safari 鼠标滚轮无法滚动的问题。另一大争论是打字与说话的效率：创始人称大多数人打字 40–50 WPM，说话 120–200 WPM，说话更自然；但多位重度听写用户反驳说，口述内容充满填充词、更不精确，代码和符号仍然只能靠键盘，有人认为 prompt 质量因此下降。有人指控官网图片疑似 AI 生成，产品可能根本不存在，是骗局；dang 出面反驳，指出预购新品本来就还没有成品，技术是真的，创始人也在评论区做了大量技术答疑。还有关于 RF 长期贴着面部是否安全、是否会被用于监视、能否装在处方镜片上、为何不做成项链、发箍或耳塞的讨论；创始人说安全经过验证，射频只在主动听写时开启，也承认远程窃听难度很大。

Worth reading

  • aarushyadav: 创始人解释为何放弃纯唇读方案：语音有 40 个音素，但外部可见的视位只有 12–15 个（P 和 B 在镜头里几乎一样），因此 Auto-AVSR 的 17% 词错率已经触及该模态的信息论上限，没法做到产品级。
  • aarushyadav: 关于把硬件装在笔记本或桌上，创始人说同一频段的射频在那么远的距离会被强烈衰减，改用 60GHz mmWave 又只能看到视位，而且空间分辨率只有约 5cm×5cm，因此目前做不出能架在桌面的版本。
  • dang: 面对「AI 生成图即骗局」的指控，dang 反驳说预购的新硬件本来就没有成品，帖子里有大量技术细节和开发中的影片，把「还没做完产品、在忙技术」说成诈骗是站不住的。

entry.title: Launch HN: Momentic (YC W24) – Agents that catch bugs by using your app
entry.content:
#3 on HN · momentic.ai · 72 points · 51 comments · HN discussion

Momentic, founded by Wei-Wei and Jeff (ex-Robinhood, Retool, WeWork, Qualtrics), launched 「Mo」, a hosted QA agent that autonomously explores web, iOS and Android apps to find bugs instead of generating Playwright/Selenium scripts. The post claims Mo found 269 bugs with 19.3% recall at 84% precision and $2.67 per bug in 60-minute runs against Gitea, Metabase, Twenty and Saleor (1,396 human-labeled bugs), versus Codex at 86 bugs / 6.2% recall / 86% precision / $0.80 per bug, Claude Code at 59 bugs / $4.2% and Devin at 27 bugs / 1.9%. The linked page is mostly a marketing landing page of feature announcements (CLI, auto-heal, MCP integration, plain-English YAML tests, hosted Android emulators, SOC 2 Type 2), with $250 of free Mo spend for new signups.

Discussion: The dominant thread is the moat question: several commenters argue a custom harness gets swallowed by the next frontier model, and two say they built comparable exploratory-testing setups in-house in weeks; the founders counter that general models still verify their own work badly, that multi-browser/mobile infra and knowledge-base maintenance are the real work, and that custom harnesses have in fact gained ground (Devin, AI code review). A second cluster is confusion over the headline metric — code commenters read $2.67 vs $0.80 per bug as 「Codex is better and cheaper」, and the team answers that recall is the metric that matters in QA since a missed bug ships broken code, conceding precision is marginally worse. Pricing drew fire: one commenter coined BYOA (bring your own agent) and complained about paying for yet another proprietary token pool, and the founders replied that no off-the-shelf model configuration met their performance bar, leaving BYOK as a possible future. On the practical side, a user reported Mo failing to install their iOS app because hosted simulators run iOS 26 while the app requires 27 (a founder said a fix was in progress), and a skeptic who has actually run parallel Playwright agents defended the difficulty of stateful exploratory testing and DOM grounding. The benchmark harness is MIT-licensed and the team invited competitors to submit results.

Worth reading

  • Arkada: Argues from experience that 「just point Opus at localhost with Playwright MCP」 collapses on stateful apps — the coding agent burns its context on DOM selectors and misses bugs like a demo's 2.5h→25h inflation on refresh, and resource leases for parallel sub-agents are real orchestration work.
  • jeffan: Co-founder Jeff explains why there is no bring-your-own-key option: vanilla models plugged into the harness were not Pareto-optimal for element grounding and visual understanding, so they built tuned custom agents — but BYOK stays on the roadmap as open models improve.
  • brahyam: A user's firsthand failure report: Momentic could not install their iOS build on the hosted simulator (app needs iOS 27, infrastructure is on 26), a concrete limitation a founder acknowledged in reply.

entry.title: US boy names that became girl names and vice versa
entry.content:
#4 on HN · namedaisy.com · 150 points · 153 comments · HN discussion

namedaisy.com 对 1936–2025 年美国社会保障局的全国婴儿姓名档案进行了分析，在 5,536 个足够常见、可供评估的名字中，有 125 个发生了显著变化，其中 54 个符合严格定义的性别转换。42 个名字从以男孩为主变成以女孩为主，仅 12 个走了相反方向。更值得注意的是转换由谁推动：42 个转向女孩的名字中有 34 个主要因为女孩使用率上升，而 12 个转向男孩的名字中有 9 个主要因为女孩使用率下降；换句话说，无论转向哪边，变化最大的通常都来自女孩。转向女孩的转换往往发生在名字人气新高时（42 个中有 32 个），而转向男孩的转换常发生在名字几近消失之后，例如 Joan 在 2001–2005 年转为男性名时只有 1,435 名婴儿使用，而它的峰值是 74,477。

Discussion: 评论区的主流观察是：女孩名字更“动态”，并且存在文化上的不对称。有评论者指出：“女性采用传统男性事物”已成为常态，而男性采用传统女性事物（比如男人穿裙子）仍会被当作异装或跨性别。也有用户觉得这个观察成立，但指出这正说明“女性”被当作“异常”的文化标准。另有人质疑原文“同样模式”的说法，认为在反方向上的“同样”应该是男孩使用率上升，而不是女孩使用率下降。最实质的修正来自语言背景：Jan 在荷兰语与中欧、东欧是 John 的男性形式，而 Jean 在法语中是男性名，在英语中则是女性名，因此数据中部分“性别翻转”其实是不同来源、不同发音的同拼写名字被混合在一起；有评论者进一步解释，这更像是新的、流行的女孩名叠加在一个低基数的传统名字之上，并以 Arya（《权力的游戏》）、Paris（Hilton）、Stevie（Nicks）等流行文化触发为例。此外，多名评论者批评原页面的可视化配色对色盲不友好、图表难以阅读，其中一人干脆做了替代版。

Worth reading

  • ecshafer: 指出 Jan（荷兰语、中欧的 John 男性形式）与 Jean（英语女性名，也是法语男性名）是不同来源的名字，不能直接算作性别翻转。
  • casta: 一位名叫 Daniele 的意大利男性开发者说，自己在美国因为名字被反复加入女性技术社群，甚至被以“团队女性占比超过 50%”为卖点的公司招募。
  • xnx: 评论者认为原页面的可视化太差，于是自己重做了一个替代版本（alwaysleaveanote.com）。

entry.title: Egoless Mathematics in the AI Era
entry.content:
#5 on HN · terrytao.wordpress.com · 27 points · 15 comments · HN discussion

A guest post on Terence Tao's blog, written by Karthik C. S., Amit Sahai and Jie Xue, arguing from a Platonist position that mathematical truths exist independently of the people who discover them, so AI-made discoveries should not threaten mathematicians' sense of worth. It argues that the anxiety is really a symptom of a prior mistake — measuring intellectual life by outputs, citations and prizes — and proposes 「egoless mathematics」 as an ideal that could reconcile pro-AI and anti-AI factions in the field. The post's own AI usage statement credits GPT Astra 6.0 and GPT 6.1 Sol for drafting help, and Tao notes it was converted from another file format using AI.

Discussion: The thread is largely skeptical. The sharpest objection, from j2kun, is that the essay reduces to 「people don't matter; all that matters is truth」 and that policy decisions should not be built on that value — he follows up by asking a Platonist commenter why his children should bother learning math rather than just prompting an AI. A counterweight comes from abstractbill, who left academia after a math PhD and says he has grown steadily more Platonist, finding it beautiful that alien mathematicians and their AIs must rediscover the same results; the reply from rubikscube09 is simply that discovering things with your own brain is fun. Several commenters attack the essay's practicality rather than its metaphysics: anarticle notes that in publish-or-perish academia credit is essentially the only reward and research budgets are already thin, so egolessness reads as an impossible luxury. The AI-usage disclosure draws the most visceral reaction, with one commenter reading the acknowledgemen as tonally close to a prayer to a machine god, and another linking a satire about a dystopian Lean-and-LLM future for mathematics that he says tenured people are literally pushing for.

Worth reading

  • j2kun: j2kun reads the essay as arguing that people don't matter and only truth does, and warns about the policy conclusions that follow from treating that as a shared value.
  • anarticle: anarticle argues egolessness is unaffordable in an academy where credit is the only currency and research budgets are already stretched, asking what researchers get instead.
  • delusional: delusional singles out the GPT Astra 6.0 / GPT 6.1 Sol acknowledgement as reading like a prayer to a machine god, and says it is a moment to ask what is actually going on.

entry.title: Show HN: Warsaw in voxels – An interactive 3D map of the city centre
entry.content:
#6 on HN · p.migdal.pl · 124 points · 25 comments · HN discussion

A Show HN release by the author (stared) of a browser-based voxel city explorer for central Warsaw, built with open data: OpenStreetMap for buildings, streets, sidewalks and tram tracks, GUGiK/Geoportal LiDAR for building heights and trees plus aerial imagery for colours, and Warsaw's city tree database for individual tree species and seasonal foliage. It lets you change date, time of day and weather, fly around, and click pedestrians to walk the streets in a Dungeon Keeper-style trick; the code is on GitHub under stared/warsaw-vibe-voxel. The linked page is a JavaScript app with no readable text, so this is based on the post and comments.

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: The dominant complaint is performance: several people with dedicated laptop GPUs (a 3080 Ti mobile on Windows 11/Chrome, another unnamed) call it near-unusable, one reporting ~30fps in the profiler but frame times of about 120ms with large gaps between updates, and a mobile user says Safari reloads the page under the load. The author defends the tradeoff, saying he balanced features against toggles, optimised for desktop first, and has ideas like rendering only a small area at 1m³ voxels and the rest as grey 8m³ blocks. Accuracy drew sharp criticism: a commenter familiar with the area says the Old Town and Plac Zamkowy are badly butchered, with wrong colours, too many storeys and the castle looking like a grey blok — answered that the Old Town is not in the map at all, which several others confirm, noting only a fragment of Śródmieście is covered. Commenters also ask for live transit and traffic overlays, and note it would beat text-and-picture tables as a local-news interface; the author says extending coverage is easy with the AI tooling he used, but the polishing — jagged geometry, disconnected streets, floating tree crowns, wrecked-looking bridges — is the slow part. Several others simply praise it: the autumn trees, golden-hour light and landmark labels, and one Android Firefox user finds it responsive.

Worth reading

  • jesse__: Concrete performance data: ~30fps in the profiler but ~120ms frame times with big gaps, on a 3080 Ti mobile.
  • radicality: A Warsaw local says the Old Town and Plac Zamkowy look wrong — wrong colours, far too many storeys, the castle rendered as a grey residential blok.
  • stared: The author explains that expanding coverage is fast with Opus 5.5 on open data, but manual polishing of jagged geometry, disconnected streets and broken bridges is what takes the time.

entry.title: If you love a website, back it up
entry.content:
#7 on HN · blog.mistys-internet.website · 222 points · 52 comments · HN discussion

A post by someone who works in web archiving (on blog.mistys-internet.website) about teapuppies.com, an Ochaken anime/toy fansite that had been online unchanged since around 2005 and then disappeared, with its domain now serving online gambling ads. The author argues personal archiving is not just for the Internet Archive and walks through ArchiveWeb.page (Chrome extension and standalone app), the Browsertrix crawler (the only paid tool, seven-day trial, open source and self-hostable) and the WARC/WACZ formats, plus ReplayWeb.page for embedding a saved site in a page — demonstrated with a full archived copy of teapuppies hosted at teapuppies.mistys-internet.website. Disclosure: most of the tools are made by the author's employer.

Discussion: Commenters broadly agree and trade stacks: SingleFile for one-page saves, ArchiveBox for multi-format archival, Linkding plus SingleFile, Karakeep, Hister, Obsidian Web Clipper, plain wget -mkpnp for static academic sites, and print-to-PDF. The main friction is with server-side tools: several long-time ArchiveBox users say capture queues fill with failed scans, maintenance becomes a chore, and Cloudflare/AI-bot blocking makes server-initiated crawls impossible — prompting one commenter to write a browser-side tool (recueil) precisely so captures happen in a real session. A counter-argument holds that saving whole pages mostly preserves junk, so the better goal is to extract and keep the information (ebook, text) rather than the HTML; others counter that readability-style extraction tools handle the filtering. Others raise practical obstacles the post skips: anti-AI-bot mitigations, hard drive prices for hoarders, and the fragility of trusting a single cloud folder like Dropbox. Sentiment is that link rot is inevitable and community/personal mirroring is the answer, with a long side thread arguing about whether LLMs will end up rewriting the historical record.

Worth reading

  • szszrk: A multi-year ArchiveBox user reports queues full of failed scans and nothing successfully captured for several versions, and argues simpler web-clipper style captures fit real use better.
  • phendrenad2: A strong counter-argument: the modern web is mostly CSS/JS/tracking junk, so preserve the information itself (an ebook or text) rather than schlepping hundreds of gigabytes of HTML.
  • whartung: Raises an obstacle the article ignores: anti-AI-bot and Cloudflare-style mitigations may block CLI and app-based crawlers, even if browser extensions get through.

entry.title: Ask HN: Who is hiring? (November 2026)
entry.content:
#8 on HN · text post · 117 points · 94 comments · HN discussion

This is Hacker News's monthly Who is hiring? thread — a text post, not a linked article — where employers post open roles directly; the November 2026 edition drew 94 comments (54 shown here) and 117 points. The boilerplate asks posters to state location, mark REMOTE or ONSITE, restrict themselves to one post per company and only if they are personally at the hiring company, and points readers to aggregators like gethnjobs.com and hnwork.app plus the companion Who wants to be hired? thread. The listings are overwhelmingly small startups and Series A–D companies, with a heavy tilt toward AI agent and LLM work, and roughly a dozen explicitly name Rust.

Discussion: There is essentially no debate here — it is a listings thread, and per the posted rules commenters are asked not to reply to job posts to complain. What the set of posts reveals is the current market shape: AI/agent roles dominate (Curai's clinical agents, Mastra's agent framework, Juro's Operator agent, Helmsted, Pond AI, Mesmer's software factories), and Rust shows up repeatedly as a rewrite or greenfield language (Postscript rebuilding its platform in Rust, Voluntas' 100% Rust trading firm, Paradromics' embedded Linux stack, bracehealth). Remote remains the default but with strong regional carve-outs (US-only for most, EU-only for others, CET-only for eventfirst), while a notable cluster insists on onsite: Reducto and Pond AI in SF, Mesmer in Berlin, Tandem Health in Stockholm, Monumental in Amsterdam. Pay transparency is now near-universal, with listed bands running from CNIO's €45–65k public-sector sysadmin role to Thunder Compute's $250–325K base plus 0.1–0.3% equity, and a visible minority of posts are sales or GTM roles rather than engineering (Mastra, CreativeLens, Revnode's commission-only 20%, Charly's GovTech AEs).

Worth reading

  • cpeterson42: Thunder Compute (YC S24) gives unusually specific numbers for a C++ GPU-hypervisor systems role in SF: $250–325K base, 0.1–0.3% equity, and a profit-sharing pool with $3.3M currently tied to gross-profit milestones.
  • mslzed: Zed Industries describes what the $42M went toward — an operation-based version control system at delta.dev that tracks edits at granularity and gets folded into the editor for agent and teammate collaboration — while hiring backend cloud and product design.
