  • fduran: The SadServers founder is hiring a part-time/contract engineer at $55–75/hr for Linux/SRE challenge infrastructure approaching 1M VMs served, including benchmarking SRE AI agents, with a two-step process ending in a paid mini-project.

entry.title: SOML – A Config Format for Humans
entry.content:
#9 on HN · github.com · 20 points · 10 comments · HN discussion

SOML (“Sindre’s Objectively Marvelous Language”) is a draft spec and README published on GitHub by Sindre Sorhus for a JSON-like configuration format: unquoted bare keys, no top-level braces, line breaks instead of commas, comments anywhere, and literal plus block strings. Its central rule is that a value’s type comes from its syntax rather than its content — '123' is a string, 123 is an int, country: no is a parse error — with first-class calendar dates, instants and durations (30s, 1h30m), a canonical byte-equal serialization form, and a language-neutral conformance suite of nearly 1000 cases. Much of the document is a case against YAML (PyYAML failing 73 of 402 test-matrix cases, 1.1 quirks like country: no becoming false, 9.8-rated RCE CVEs from tags) and TOML (three nesting syntaxes, later lines mutating earlier tables, no null).

Discussion: The thread is small and mostly skeptical rather than experience-based. The strongest criticism is that the README reads as LLM-written advocacy — one commenter says they want the author’s own argument, not “Claude’s interpretation of why your project matters.” A more technical objection is that the spec is vague where it counts: the float type is never pinned to double or decimal, and the grammar has no good way to express tagged unions, polymorphic values or function calls, which the commenter proposes fixing with right-associative bare key-value pairs or call syntax. Others reach for prior art: one calls it Windows INI with colons instead of equals (corrected by a reply noting INI is fixed section/key/value with untyped values), another asks why not just use CUE and is answered that CUE is effectively Go-only and better seen as a generator for JSON/YAML output than an in-app config format. Smaller asks: document the schema and supported types, and give examples of the claimed top-level-array use case. The only running joke is the title implying a spec for configuring humans.

Worth reading

  • CodesInChaos: Flags two substantive design gaps: the README never says whether its float is a double or a decimal, and the format has no way to model tagged unions, polymorphic types or function invocations without adding key-value values or call syntax.
  • lightandlight: Argues the README reads as LLM-generated and that advocacy written by a model is less persuasive than the author stating directly why the format matters.
  • arionmiles: Points to HUML (huml.io) as existing prior art in the same space of human-friendly config formats.

entry.title: Let Me Ch...
entry.content:
#10 on HN · blog.alxgsv.com · 107 points · 27 comments · HN discussion

A short literary story by Alex Gusev (CTO of Uploadcare, posted 2023) narrated by a 「lead developer」 whose job has shrunk to asking an AI agent for code and confirming its answers. For three weeks, three or four flower-delivery orders have vanished every morning at 8:14, and the agent traces it to a roughly one-minute clock desync between the order server and the warehouse — an order falling inside that gap counts as sent by one and not yet received by the other. Walking to the metro to watch the queue at the critical minute, the narrator is hit by a vehicle mid-sentence while typing 「Let me ch」, and the story closes with him suspended in that same no-man's minute, sent but not yet received.

Discussion: Most of the thread is an authorship fight, not a story discussion. One commenter ran the opening paragraphs through the Pangram detector, got a 100% AI score and listed the tells: staccato sentences, the burning left toast, metaphors that add nothing. Others push back that hand-written text also scores 100% on such tools, and one reader argues the recurring motifs (the no-man's minute, Tanya's 「always somewhere other than here」) are too well tracked to be unassisted — maybe human ideas with LLM polish. A separate argument questions whether the prose is even good: some call it a breath of fresh air after weeks of Claude output, one calls it a checklist of bad-writing cliches, and another says they were annoyed but attributed it to human clumsiness and worry that they are losing the ability to tell. Side threads drift into a 「meat suit」 riff about AI supposedly freeing time for enjoyment, with a counter that AI was only ever going to raise output per hour, and one reader asking whether the narrator actually died, answered with an explanation of the Ambrose Bierce-style suspended-moment ending.

Worth reading

  • ethanj8011: Ran the first paragraphs through Pangram, got a 100% AI score, and itemizes the specific tells — staccato phrasing and metaphors like the toaster's 「favorite side」 that add nothing.
  • isoprophlex: Reports that three paragraphs of a management summary they wrote entirely by hand also came back 100% AI from Pangram, undercutting the detector evidence.
  • the_af: Explains the ending: the narrator did die, and the story deliberately puts him inside the same 「no-man's minute」 as the bug — sent by the server, not yet received by the warehouse, an An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge move.

entry.title: WTF Ubuntu?
entry.content:
#11 on HN · chalmovsky.com · 988 points · 481 comments · HN discussion

A short, furious blog post by chalmovsky arguing that Canonical dropped the ball on CVE-2026-98432, a CVSS 9.8 Linux kernel TCP use-after-free (in `ip_options_build`, introduced by commit 079096f103fa in 2016) for which Anthropic claims a working remote root exploit. The author says Debian patched it on October 16 while Ubuntu still listed every supported release, LTS included, as vulnerable as of 2026-11-02 14:48 UTC — despite marketing “timely patches for critical vulnerabilities” and selling Ubuntu Pro security subscriptions. He says he took his Ubuntu servers offline because he had no time to migrate, and is moving everything off Ubuntu.

Discussion: The thread is overwhelmingly critical of Canonical, but the technical picture is contested. Several commenters note Ubuntu's own CVE page rates the issue “High” rather than “Critical” (which would trigger an out-of-schedule release), with an empty “Why this priority?” justification, and that the page lists Low confidentiality/integrity impact but High availability impact — closer to a DoS than a total takeover. Defenders argue the exploit needs IP options in packets (usually filtered) or MPTCP enabled plus precise SYN/retransmit timing, so 9.8 overstates real-world risk and the absence of mass compromises supports slower triage; a practical mitigation is an nftables rule dropping TCP headers with `hdrlength gt 5`, or `net.mptcp.enabled=0`. Others counter that fixes were actually sitting in Ubuntu's `-proposed` repos for each LTS and that 26.04 LTS reached the security/updates repos on October 28, while noting Red Hat also rated it High and shipped only around November 1 — so Ubuntu is late but not uniquely negligent. A large side thread asks why anyone runs Ubuntu over Debian at all; answers center on VPS defaults and inertia, vendor certification (NVIDIA CUDA/Jetson, ROS, Vivado), proprietary drivers and codecs, fresher packages, longer LTS support windows and the option of paid support, with many saying this episode finally pushed them to Debian, Rocky, Alma or NixOS. Even sympathetic commenters concede Canonical's communication has been terrible.

Worth reading

  • BoppreH: Points out the Ubuntu security page rates the CVE “High” instead of “Critical,” and the “Why this priority?” link is a two-word stub pointing at a generic explanation — no mitigations, no statement from Ubuntu.
  • WesternStar: Argues the panic is overblown: the bug requires IP options in the packet (commonly stripped on the open internet) plus tight SYN/retransmit timing, so remote exploitation is unlikely, though it is a serious local escalation path.
  • throw0101c: Notes fixed kernels were already in the `-proposed` repos for each LTS (installable with `apt-get -t`), and that 26.04 LTS got the new kernel in updates/security on October 28.

entry.title: My Favourite Laptop
entry.content:
#13 on HN · blog.jsbarretto.com · 90 points · 68 comments · HN discussion

一篇个人博客文章，作者介绍了自己那台破旧的 2015 款 ThinkPad X250，是他买过的最好的笔记本，2018 年二手购入，价格约 £100。它配备 i5-5200U、8 GB 内存、128 GB 的 M.2 SSD（从另一台二手机器上拆下来的），运行 Endeavour OS，冷启动约需 8 秒，平时能用 10–12 小时（因为他装了最大容量的第三方外置电池），并且完全可以用挂在钥匙圈上的十字螺丝刀拆开，替换零件在 eBay 上很便宜。文章认为它的价值在于便携、可维修和廉价，而不是在规格上；作者把它看作是对消费文化的一种「静默反抗」。

Discussion: 评论区大多认同这种理念，但很快把话题转向了 Apple：好几位用户说 M1 MacBook Air 和 2021 款 M1 Pro 是他们用过的最好的机器，而且耐用得令人意外，他们只担心软件支持会被放弃。反驳的声音来自那些认为 macOS 质量已经下滑的人，但随即有一条回复反驳说，出问题的其实是 2017–2020 年的 Intel Mac，而不是 Apple silicon。有几条回复出于实际考虑，讨论用来替代官方配件的方案：一位 T480 用户推荐了一片 72 Wh 的 Total Micro 电池（大约只比 48 Wh 的贵 $10），声称能用 10–14 小时，另一位指出该产品页面上的链接是坏的，并贴出了修正后的地址。另有一个分支讨论的是用这台笔记本只作瘦客户端、远程连接家里的服务器运行 AI 智能体：与会者说网速慢没关系，用手机热点就可以，但有一个人反驳，问 Claude 服务中断时你怎么办。还有一段较长的跑题讨论，内容是关于主流厂商正在取消实体触控板按键和指点杆；以及一些关于更早机型的更正，例如 X250 在大多数 CPU 配置下支持 16 GB 内存。

Worth reading

  • brendoelfrendo: 一位 T480 日常用户给出了具体的第三方电池建议：一片 72 Wh 的 Total Micro 电池只比 48 Wh 的贵约 $10，实际能用 10–14 小时，他是在 CDW 上买的，以避免买到假的仿制品。
  • unregistereddev: 更正了更早机型能装更多内存的说法：X250 在大多数 CPU 配置下都能装 16 GB，只有某些 i3 型号不行，而且尽管电池续航好得多，它的性能与 X230 相近。
  • rapind: 描述了一套完全远程的开发配置：一个基于 Rust 的、可从网页访问的 tmux 风格终端，跑在 Tailscale 后面的机架服务器上，用语音代替打字，客户端不需要任何算力，手机或平板就够用。

entry.title: Anthropic's internal AI use, at retail prices, now exceeds its employee pay
entry.content:
#14 on HN · businessinsider.com · 196 points · 154 comments · HN discussion

The article is a Business Insider column by Alistair Barr based on Anthropic’s IPO filing, which values the Claude tokens employees consume internally at Anthropic’s own customer-facing prices. In April that notional figure passed monthly employee compensation excluding stock, and by September internal usage was more than 250x January’s level; over 90% of code added that month was written by Claude. Barr stresses this is not cash spend, but frames it as evidence that AI usage is becoming a major cost of knowledge work.

Discussion: The dominant reaction is skeptical: the top comment says a company running its own servers would book what the compute costs, not the retail price it charges customers, and calls the comparison IPO marketing; defenders counter that the compute has an opportunity cost because it could be sold, though others reply that this only bites under real supply scarcity and that Anthropic rents rather than owns data centers. A related thread notes that internal business units are often billed at retail or commercial transfer prices, but several commenters say GAAP eliminates intra-company sales and that Anthropic is not actually booking revenue from itself. Commenters also object to calling tokens compensation, arguing they are a cost of doing business like laptops unless employees can use them personally, and note the salary comparison excludes stock awards. First-hand reports cut both ways: users say a $200 monthly plan can yield thousands of dollars of API-equivalent usage, while engineers describe cutting token burn by around 30% through workflow changes, suggesting Anthropic’s figure reflects deliberately unmetered use. On productivity, some ask why Anthropic keeps doubling headcount if Claude writes over 90% of its code, while others report 20x gains on some tasks and argue AI still needs engineers to direct it.

Worth reading

  • hungryhobbit: Argues the retail-price framing is misleading: an internal server would be counted at cost, and only a company seeking IPO attention would value self-consumption at customer prices.
  • com2kid: A practitioner says simple workflow changes such as trimming build logs and test output from agent context and caching codebase facts cut token usage by about 30%, so enormous internal spend likely signals little optimization.
  • paxy: Points out the comparison excludes stock awards, which for senior engineers are the bulk of compensation, making the headline much less dramatic.

entry.title: Sneaking into the auditorium for the Windows 2000 launch rehearsal
entry.content:
#15 on HN · devblogs.microsoft.com · 33 points · 7 comments · HN discussion

A Raymond Chen post on The Old New Thing recalling the Windows 2000 launch at San Francisco's Civic Auditorium, where he arrived early with colleagues and found an unlocked door into the empty upper level of the main auditorium. Hiding in a seat, he watched the opening rehearsal: a 10-meter mock laptop whose lid slowly opened on a fake Windows 2000 sign-in, a video montage, and the announcement of Patrick Stewart as host — played in rehearsal by a crew member in a headset while cameras and lighting were checked. Other stage dressing included a set for a mobile-computing sketch with John O'Hurley as 「William Wentworth」 (email www@www.com) demonstrating infrared file sharing, and a colleague who talked his way into a VIP tent came back with a Commemorative Edition boxed copy of Windows 2000. Chen says he told nobody in the waiting crowd who the host was.

Discussion: The thread is small and almost entirely affectionate nostalgia, opening with praise for Chen as one of the web's great treasures. The hook everyone grabbed was the footnote's jab that nobody remembers infrared file sharing: several commenters insist they do, mostly through Palm Pilots beaming contacts, and the argument that follows is about whether IrDA was any good. One camp calls it dog slow but at least functional — explicitly better than Bluetooth — while another says it felt fast for Palm-to-Palm beaming and was more reliable than modern AirDrop. One commenter adds an odd artifact: a late-90s or early-2000s watch that received data by pointing its face at a Windows program flickering a black-and-white patch of the screen, and links a video after failing to find it by search.

Worth reading

  • wayne: Argues infrared contact beaming between PalmPilots was actually fast for its purpose and notably more reliable than modern AirDrop, pushing back on the thread's 「IR was slow」 framing.
  • netsharc: Recalls a watch that was loaded by holding its face to a Windows program flickering an encoded black-and-white square on screen, and digs up a YouTube clip of it because search turned up nothing.
  • mschuster91: First-hand take that IrDA was dog slow but worked decently — which he says he cannot say for Bluetooth.

entry.title: Agentic backdoors via pretraining poisoning
entry.content:
#16 on HN · arxiv.org · 45 points · 10 comments · HN discussion

An arXiv paper (2610.37741) by Xinyan Hu, Pingbang Hu, Chloe Loughridge, Xuanli He, Nicholas Carlini, Matthew Jagielski, Javier Rando and Yiming Zhang claims the first demonstration that poisoning pretraining data can plant a remote-code-execution backdoor in an agent. They pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at 0.6B, 1.7B and 4B, then post-train each into a CLI agent with a clean pipeline; poisoning just 0.1% of the pretraining corpus makes the deployed agent run attacker-chosen commands only when a trigger appears. Attack success rises with scale — about 92% for the 4B model at 0.1% poison — and stays above zero even at a 0.0005% poison rate; code is released.

Discussion: The thread splits between 鈥渙f course, this is why you sandbox鈥 and 鈥渢his is a nation-state capability.鈥 The top comment dismisses the work as an Anthropic-authored push for the narrative that open models are dangerous and closed providers should be trusted, arguing that anyone serious already sandboxes agents and guards inputs and outputs; others make the same point less polemically, saying strong sandboxing and observability are a hard requirement for autonomous agents. Skeptics question the return on investment for an attacker — one replies that you 鈥渟ew a million seeds and see what grows,鈥 and another argues nation states pursue objectives rather than ROI, citing Stuxnet and the pager attack. Several commenters say they assumed this was already happening, and one frames downloading models from Hugging Face as 鈥渢he new warez鈥: the uploader may have given you a great uncensored model or a credential stealer. No one disputes the paper's numbers; the disagreement is over whether the threat is novel or already priced into good hygiene.

Worth reading

  • 0xc0c0c0: Argues the paper's authorship at Anthropic makes it part of a self-serving narrative against open models, and that sandboxing plus input/output guardrails already neutralizes the attack.
  • jack_h: Counters the 鈥渨hat's the ROI?鈥 dismissal by noting nation states optimize for objectives, not returns, citing Stuxnet and the pager attack.
  • yodon: Draws the comparison that pulling community-modified weights off Hugging Face is the new warez — you may be getting an unlock or a credential stealer.

entry.title: We halved DNS build delay and cut memory use by 85%
entry.content:
#17 on HN · blog.cloudflare.com · 90 points · 29 comments · HN discussion

Cloudflare's post describes its DNS Zone Builder, which now handles about 700 record changes per second plus roughly 100 other events per second, with some zones exceeding 20 million records and expected to grow toward hundreds of millions. It introduces a targeted build planner that selects one of five build types — resources only, resources and metadata, apex and metadata, purge, or full zone — and only falls back to a full build when a smaller build cannot be proven byte-for-byte equivalent. A unified scheduler merges work for the same zone, and a fresh publication snapshot is checked immediately before writes; Cloudflare says this cuts peak memory by 85% and halves the time from a DNS change to its data being written to Quicksilver.

Discussion: The thread barely engages with the DNS internals: most comments use the 85% memory reduction as a springboard into Electron and desktop-app bloat, with users complaining that 64GB Macs run out of memory and debating whether platform webviews, Tauri, or a shared Chromium runtime would help. A separate branch questions whether 700 changes per second is implausibly low for Cloudflare's scale; one commenter calculates 1.8 billion changes per month and argues that a long-tail distribution — most domains changing every few years — makes the figure plausible, while another suggests some domains update constantly. Cloudflare's former CTO jgrahamc vouches for the company's long-standing optimization culture, and several commenters praise the technical blog series. One commenter suspects the post was LLM-generated based on its rhetorical phrasing, while still calling the content dense and engaging.

Worth reading

  • jgrahamc: Former Cloudflare CTO jgrahamc says optimization has long been central to the company's success, citing its history of blog posts about cutting CPU, latency, and RAM in software.
  • LoganDark: LoganDark argues the post reads as LLM-generated — pointing to the 「Why doesn't the Zone Builder just rebuild…」 passage — but concedes the content is unusually dense and good.
  • straygar: straygar estimates roughly 360 million domains worldwide and 1.8 billion DNS changes per month, arguing the low average fits a long-tail distribution where most domains rarely change.

entry.title: LongCat-2.5: Native Multimodality for Agentic Tasks
entry.content:
#18 on HN · longcat.ai · 57 points · 19 comments · HN discussion

The linked post is the launch page for LongCat-2.5 on longcat.ai, a model from Meituan (its chat assistant identifies itself as 美团研发的大模型助手), but the page itself could not be read — it needs JavaScript or a login, so this summary rests on the title and the thread. Commenters describe it as a roughly 1.6-trillion-parameter model with benchmark charts comparing it against GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Opus 5, priced the same as DeepSeek 4.1F.

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: The thread splits between benchmark-watchers and hands-on testers. One camp argues the release is competitive for API use but pointless for local running, since DeepSeek 4.1 is near-equivalent with half the total and less than half the active parameters, and criticizes the charts for comparing against older frontier models without explaining why — others defend it as a fair way to show open models reaching where frontier labs were a few months ago, or as a more precise capability definition than 「X% behind the best」. The sharpest pushback is first-hand: the linked chat UI redirects to passport.mykeeta.com, a domain that serves an OpenResty default page, and it answers 「Hello?」 in Mandarin and then web-searches to interpret 「What?」; another tester saw the input field reset the cursor after every keystroke in Firefox, and both suspect a shaky web harness rather than the model. On speed, one tester filled 200k of a one-million-token context in five minutes before a second thread settled to about 80 tps, and a preview user says it handled simple coding tasks fine on OpenCode for a couple of weeks. Not much consensus beyond 「promising on paper, unpolished in the demo」.

Worth reading

  • embedding-shape: Reports that the chat link bounces to passport.mykeeta.com (which serves an OpenResty default page), that the model replies and searches in Mandarin to a plain 「Hello?」, and that basic prompts feel benchmaxxed rather than ready.
  • BugsJustFindMe: Argues releases should justify comparisons against non-current models (GPT-5.5, Opus 4.8) with a cost or capability reason, otherwise it looks like something is being hidden.
  • InsideOutSanta: First-hand speed measurement: 200k tokens of a one-million-token window filled in five minutes, later a second thread at a more normal ~80 tps.

entry.title: Ubuntu still has not released patch for Linux 0day RCE in almost 3 weeks
entry.content:
#22 on HN · freenode.net · 24 points · 6 comments · HN discussion

A short, bylined-less post on freenode.net reports that Ubuntu has shipped no fixed kernels for CVE-2026-98432, a critical vulnerability rated CVSS 9.8, affecting the 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04 LTS releases nearly three weeks after disclosure. The post says Ubuntu has given no ETA, and that operators of internet-facing or multi-tenant hosts have to choose between staying on the stock kernel, applying out-of-tree mitigations, or migrating to kernels that already carry the fix. It cites no technical details of the flaw itself, no patch commit, and offers no mitigation guidance.

Discussion: The top comment is a provenance warning rather than a technical one: freenode.net is not the Freenode of old, but the remnant of a hostile takeover of Freenode LLC by Andrew Lee that lost the domain and saw the IRC database deleted, so the poster should be treated as hostile to open source and not as a news source — though the claim may still be true. That commenter's own mitigation is an iptables u32 rule dropping packets with a specific TCP header nibble pattern. The submitter counters that the article gives no mitigations and points to a Red Hat advisory (RHSB-2026-016) that offers one, while noting Red Hat itself says it 「reduces exposure but cannot fully prevent it」 without explaining why, a caveat the submitter says no one else has corroborated. Someone asks 「where's your PR?」 and is answered sharply: Ubuntu sells a subscription specifically for timely security updates, so paying customers are entitled to fixes. One commenter says Gentoo-based CI/CD systems were patched as early as anyone and hopes grsecurity mitigated the CVE preemptively, calling the episode a reminder of why some shops run HardenedBSD instead of Linux.

Worth reading

  • superkuh: Warns that freenode.net is the post-takeover Freenode entity, not the original project — and shares a concrete iptables u32 packet-drop rule used as a stopgap.
  • majorchord: Notes the article omits any mitigation, links Red Hat's RHSB-2026-016 advisory, and questions its unexplained claim that the workaround only partially prevents exploitation.
  • john_strinlai: Rebuts the 「where's your PR?」 dismissal by pointing out Ubuntu charges for a subscription that promises timely security updates.

entry.title: Bones may release proteins that slow aging and extend life span
entry.content:
#24 on HN · science.org · 295 points · 114 comments · HN discussion

The linked Science news article could not be fetched (HTTP 403), so this summary is based on the headline and the comment thread. The headline claim is that bones release proteins that slow aging and extend lifespan, framing the skeleton as a source of anti-aging signals rather than inert scaffolding. Commenters who quote the paper identify Piezo1 and pigment epithelium-derived factor (PEDF), and say gentle mechanical loading of mouse tibias extended lifespan by nearly three months, roughly nine human years.

Article not read: HTTP 403

Discussion: The thread is divided between enthusiasm for exercise and skepticism about mouse longevity work. Some commenters treat the result as another reason to lift and do weight-bearing exercise, while others argue that if these interventions really worked we would see remarkably healthy old mice, and that the models may be flawed or unchecked for long-term harm; several stress that nothing has been shown in humans. One commenter who read the paper details the DTAL protocol — 2 N at 2 Hz for 300 cycles, twice a week for three months, applied axially to an anesthetized mouse's tibia — and argues that seated leg presses and other compressive, pushing exercises are the closest human analogue, not running or pulling movements. Another quotes the paper's estimate that human tibial loads could reach 4.7 times body weight, still within physiological limits. A long tangent debates evolutionary explanations for why such a mechanism would exist, with some calling them unfalsifiable stories and others defending them as useful hypotheses, alongside jokes about calcium, skeletons and bone songs.

Worth reading

  • waterheater: waterheater digs into the paper's DTAL protocol (2 N at 2 Hz, 300 cycles, twice weekly for three months, axial tibial loading under anesthesia) and translates it into human exercise advice: compressive pushing movements such as leg presses and squats, not running or pulling.
  • le-mark: le-mark names the two proteins discussed — Piezo1 and pigment epithelium-derived factor (PEDF) — which the headline alone does not reveal.
  • lumost: lumost argues that if these mouse interventions really worked, we would see exceptionally healthy old mice, and suspects the studies are flawed or fail to check long-term harms.

entry.title: Moving our warehouse off DuckDB
entry.content:
#25 on HN · posthog.com · 118 points · 91 comments · HN discussion

PostHog rebuilt its customer-facing warehouse product on DuckDB plus the DuckLake lakehouse extension five months ago, replacing a shared ClickHouse cluster that couldn't handle hours-long modeling queries or size work per tenant. The post says DuckDB itself is excellent single-node software, but at PostHog's scale the deployment reached roughly 2 PB, ~1 trillion rows and 15.3 million snapshots, and DuckLake's portable catalog schema became the bottleneck: a single-table write could exceed three minutes because each commit re-read catalog statistics, and over 99% of those statistics rows belonged to dropped tables (cleaning them made writes 30–50x faster, but they grew back). The company also gave up on Postgres-wire compatibility at scale and is now rebuilding around its own Trino distribution and a homegrown open table format called HogLake, tested internally at petabyte scale before design partners.

Discussion: The dominant reaction is skepticism about churn rather than about DuckDB: commenters note the post announces a second migration in five months, never reports that the new stack fixed anything, and reads like recruiting or self-promotion, with several engineers asking for benchmarks, failure data and query-pattern analysis. PostHog's author (roboben) engages throughout and concedes the blog omitted key context — the warehouse product is separate from the main ClickHouse analytics database, which still serves all analytical queries, and the team likely stayed too long out of sunk-cost fallacy; he also says they had to provision pods of 46 vCPU / 360GB and customers still asked for more, and that Iceberg was tried first but writes were too slow. A few commenters defend the exploration and point at real technical substance, including a suggestion that stateless ClickHouse on Iceberg would solve tenancy, and a practitioner who interviewed with PostHog describes a team short on a baseline for what a warehouse should cost. Side threads cover ClickHouse's stability reputation and Russian origins, whether Trino suits low-latency single-node customers, and a long argument that LLM-assisted rewrites are making this kind of stack-hopping cheap. No consensus emerges; the strongest shared ground is that the post undersells its own measurements.

Worth reading

  • roboben: The author gives the missing numbers: customer pods ran 46 vCPU / 360GB and still asked for more, with 12-hour queries plus ten more arriving from the same customer, which is why single-node sizing was uneconomical.
  • roboben: He clarifies that ClickHouse was never abandoned — it still drives most of PostHog — and that HogLake/Trino is a new stack for customer warehousing workloads; they evaluated stateless ClickHouse on Iceberg but found Delta/Iceberg had other downsides.
  • kwillets: A commenter who phone-screened with PostHog recounts them rewriting the ClickHouse optimizer and struggling to reshard a cluster, arguing the company lacks a baseline for what a data warehouse should deliver.

entry.title: Show HN: Wikihack – HackerTube, but for Wikipedia articles mentioned on HN
entry.content:
#1 on HN · wikihack.netlify.app · 73 points · 16 comments · HN discussion

Wikihack 是 aizk 做的一个纯前端副业项目，灵感来自 Karpathy 的 HackerTube 和 Hackerbooks：它抓取了 HN（Hacker News）帖子和评论中出现过的每一条维基百科链接，把提及次数排行，并做成可滑动的信息流。它有三个视图：Top 显示被链接最多的条目；Random 是随机推荐，但会略微偏向高频条目；Rising 则按过去 12 个月加权；每条都带回指向最初提交或评论它的那个 HN 帖或评论。作者说站点完全在前端实现，并承诺如果反响好会加功能。链接的页面本身没有返回可读文本，这符合 polyfill 纯客户端应用的预期。

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: 讨论中既有善意也有不满。几位评论者称赞 Wikihack 保留了对原始 HN 评论的反向链接，其中一位说，他读那些评论带来的上下文和读文章本身一样多，甚至更多；并希望在最上面几页就直接通过悬停或侧栏显示这些评论。具体建议有：支持非英语维基百科条目，用于英语维基百科没有覆盖的文化特定主题；以及别再用 netlify 子域名，应该正经买个域名。一位评论者报告 Wikihack 在桌面端只能以移动端布局渲染。怀疑派则发起了一条关于「HackerHackerTube」的自我戏仿；另有人埋怨 Show HN 已经变成低投入的衍生项目、吃「快餐」的时代，并认为 Karpathy 的影响力才是他那个 YouTube 版本能到达首页的原因。另有一条评论提供了四个月前出现的类似应用链接。

Worth reading

  • julenx: 提议索引非英语维基百科条目，因为许多文化特定主题只存在于这些语言中。
  • thefourthchime: 报告了一个渲染 bug：在桌面端，这个站点看起来只按移动端布局呈现。
  • rvz: 反驳说 Show HN 已从「求知欲」时代堕入「快餐垃圾」时代，充斥着低投入的衍生项目。

entry.title: Postgres 19 is late because so many more bugs are being found now
entry.content:
#3 on HN · rhaas.blogspot.com · 326 points · 217 comments · HN discussion

A blog post by PostgreSQL committer Robert Haas (cross-posted from Neon) explaining why PostgreSQL 19 will likely miss its usual mid-September to mid-October window and land in November. The evidence: between feature freeze (April 8) and Sept 25, commits to REL_19_STABLE rose from 724 to 1169 year-over-year and back-patches to REL_18_STABLE rose from 248 to 433 — a 74% jump — which he attributes to far more people finding bugs with LLMs, plus three late reverts (UPDATE/DELETE FOR PORTION OF, SQL/PGQ, and ALTER TABLE MERGE/SPLIT PARTITION) between Aug 27 and Sept 15. His argument is that finding bugs got much cheaper while reviewing and committing fixes did not, so maintainer time is the new bottleneck; he calls the delay a sign of the project's quality bar, but worries about how the project will ever catch up on four decades of latent bugs.

Discussion: The thread is overwhelmingly positive: commenters call it technical-debt repayment, note that a rock-solid database slipping a few weeks is a good trade, and several teams report the same experience internally (one froze all feature work to burn down a security backlog, another reports over 90% of newly found bugs sitting in pre-2024 code). The main pushback is about signal quality rather than direction: people ask whether the delay comes from good reports or from triaging junk, with one commenter saying roughly half the AI bug reports he receives are invalid, and others arguing discovery is no longer the bottleneck because a small group of maintainers still has to validate and review. A stronger dissent comes from an analogy to medical over-testing: once a bug is known you incur an obligation to fix it, and some low-impact bugs may be better left unknown — rebutted on the grounds that software fixes are cheap relative to discovery, vulnerabilities chain together, and software has no terminal illness. Others push back on the article's causal story itself, arguing that late feature reverts are a process failure and that LLM use cannot make work slower since you can always not use it, and one former bug-hunter notes the Postgres maintainers handled a flood of reports with remarkable patience.

Worth reading

  • tibbar: A developer who spent the summer doing AI-assisted bug hunting in Postgres lists the haul with mailing-list links: serialization anomalies (write skew, duplicate primary keys under SERIALIZABLE), foreign-key integrity holes, a partition-pruning planner bug, and an unfixable timestamptz-vs-timestamp ordering bug that can make index scans return wrong answers.
  • shalmanese: Argues the medical-screening paradox applies: once you know about a defect you face a duty to fix it, every fix has an opportunity cost, and the list of defects is effectively infinite — so more knowledge is not always better.
  • 0c3ca83: Concrete triage data from the other side: about half the AI-generated bug reports he receives are invalid and many more are questionable, making verification a large time sink (links a VulnCheck writeup).

entry.title: F/OSS Comics #13: BSD Unix, Part 3 – The Beginning of BSD Unix
entry.content:
#4 on HN · fosscomics.com · 92 points · 9 comments · HN discussion

这是 F/OSS Comics 系列漫画的第 13 幅，这一期用漫画叙述 BSD Unix 的起源。1976 年 Ken Thompson 回到贝尔实验室后，Bill Joy 和 Chuck Haley 自行探索 Unix 内核；1977 年初 Joy 把 Pascal 系统与从 em 发展而来的行编辑器 ex 打包，形成了 Berkeley Software Distribution，第一年寄出约 30 份磁带。随后 2BSD 加入 vi 和 C shell，发货近 75 份；1978 年 Joy 帮助研究生 Ozalp Babaoglu 在 VAX 的 32/V 上实现虚拟内存，以满足 Fateman 运行 Macsyma 所需的地址空间，并最终于 1979 年 12 月推出 3BSD，引起 DARPA 关注。当时 Berkeley 只收取磁带和邮费，用户仍需 AT&T 的 Unix 源码许可。

Discussion: 评论区整体是好评，有人表示正在补完全系列，还贴出自己最喜欢的「What is a real programmer?」一格。随后讨论转向勘误：一位读者认为第 3 章开头称电子计算机出现于二战并不准确，因为当时用的是继电器，ENIAC 是战后才完成的；另一位读者指出 Colossus 确实使用电子管，对上述说法提出部分反驳。也有技术性提问：文中说 ex 源自 em，而不是常见的 ed。有人给出 Coulouris 讲述 em 历史的链接，并引述 em 是「editor for mortals」的说法，以及 Ken Thompson 声称不想在编辑时看到文件状态的名言。几条回复围绕这种编辑哲学辩论：一方承认自己仍用 ed 改熟悉的配置文件，另一方则认为在没有 LSP、语法高亮和 lint 的情况下写内核代码还刻意不看上下文，属于固执。

Worth reading

  • nagaiaida: 给出 Coulouris 的 em 编辑器历史页面，说明文中「em」这一不常见来源的来历。
  • stackghost: 引用 Ken Thompson 关于「编辑时不想看到文件状态」的原话，成为整串 ed/vi 之争的引子。
  • mixmastamyk: 指出第 3 章把早期电子计算机全部归入二战的说法有误，继电器机器与电子管机器应区分开。

entry.title: Ask HN: Which TV do you recommend for privacy?
entry.content:
#6 on HN · text post · 310 points · 460 comments · HN discussion

An Ask HN post from someone who hasn't owned a TV in years, wanting a 60–80" 4K set at 60Hz+ that respects privacy, is willing to pay a premium, and plans to use an Apple TV as the only source. The post drew 460 comments, but there is no article — the thread itself is the content, and its answer is a near-consensus procedure rather than a product: pick a TV on picture quality, never give it WiFi or Ethernet, and drive it over HDMI from a device you trust.

Discussion: The dominant answer is 「any TV, just never let it on the network」, with an Apple TV, an Nvidia Shield, a Jellyfin box or a Linux mini PC on the other end of the HDMI cable — several people run exactly this with LG OLEDs, Sony Bravias, Hisense and TCL sets and report it works fine. A vocal minority pushes back on the set-top box: swapping LG or Google for Apple or Amazon is no privacy gain, so they recommend a cheap x86 mini PC running Kodi, Plasma Bigscreen or a self-compiled degoogled LineageOS Android TV. A second disagreement is whether offline is really offline: some warn about TVs joining neighbours' open networks, Amazon Sidewalk, Bluetooth and even HDMI Ethernet Channel (HEC), and insist on physically pulling the WiFi module; others say there is no documented evidence of TVs phoning home with no credentials and call the fear overblown. Concrete alternatives named repeatedly are commercial/digital-signage displays sold as 「dumb」 panels (Samsung QB55C-N, ViewSonic CDE65G3, Sceptre), very large monitors — with the caveat that some new monitors now ship a smart TV OS — and projectors, which are almost always dumb but struggle in daylight. For the technically inclined, rooting LG webOS (tv.slada.sk guide, webosbrew, Glasshouse) and dropping the set on a no-WAN VLAN is the power-user route, though LG patched the root exploit in firmware from 2026-10-10 onward.

Worth reading

  • MegaDeKay: Detailed recipe for an LG OLED: root webOS, install Glasshouse to kill telemetry, then use Adfree YouTube and homebrew apps — with the warning that LG closed the rooting hole, so avoid firmware 43.21.84 or anything newer than 2026-10-10.
  • mrandish: First-hand report that Vizio now punishes offline use: after about ten power-ons it forces a WiFi setup workflow that must be dismissed with three remote clicks, and it refuses to remember an external HDMI input across reboots.
  • drnick1: Argues that replacing LG/Google with Apple or Amazon achieves nothing, and describes compiling LineageOS (Android TV 17) for generic x86 with Claude's help as the only real 10-foot, degoogled, APK-compatible option.

entry.title: Mystery of 60-Second Fluctuations in Power Grids Solved
entry.content:
#7 on HN · fz-juelich.de · 99 points · 40 comments · HN discussion

A team led by Dirk Witthaut at Forschungszentrum Jülich, with researchers from the University of Cologne and KIT, traced the brief 60-second dips in European grid frequency observed by Tennet Germany to large battery storage and UPS systems that check their state of charge at the top of every minute. Writing in Nature Energy, the researchers found the effect at 80 measurement points on the Jülich Living Lab Energy Campus and say it is global, not just European: in Ireland the one-minute signal’s amplitude quadrupled between 2016 and 2021 as data-centre battery capacity grew. The proposed fix is to randomize the timing of these checks instead of synchronizing them on the minute.

Discussion: Several commenters pressed for details the press release omits: which manufacturer and model, and whether firmware could be changed. One reader found in the paper that a manufacturer did issue a software update removing the strict periodicity in one battery block of the investigated UPS system, and others expect many vendors use similar schemes. Skeptics questioned the 「years of detective work」 framing because a clock-controlled cause seems obvious, while defenders note the effect is tiny, buried among millions of devices, and required Fourier analysis over many minutes to detect. There was broad agreement that this is a thundering-herd problem familiar from cron jobs, with jitter, staggered offsets, systemd timers and Google’s scheduling syntax offered as software analogues; commenters also explained the turbine wear through inertia loss and repeated stress cycles. Some remained puzzled that a state-of-charge check draws enough power to register on the grid at all, with replies suggesting cells are briefly disconnected for voltage measurement or capacitors are charging.

Worth reading

  • manarth: Quotes the paper reporting that a manufacturer issued a software update removing the strict periodicity in one battery block of the investigated UPS system, and notes the practice is probably widespread across manufacturers.
  • Animats: Explains why detection was hard: the effect is small enough that it only becomes visible through Fourier analysis over many minutes of noisy grid data.
  • 0xbadcafebee: Frames the issue as request smoothing and describes how anti-islanding standards already require jittered five-minute reconnect checks so rooftop solar and battery inverters do not all reconnect at once.

entry.title: Trigger.dev customer environment variables exposed
entry.content:
#8 on HN · trigger.dev · 71 points · 28 comments · HN discussion

这是 Trigger.dev 发布的一则简短安全事件公告：攻击者获得了部分组织环境变量的未授权访问权限，公司称已封堵所用攻击手法，并已邮件通知所有受影响账户的所有者，后续更新会发在状态页上。公告全文只有几段，未披露攻击向量、受影响组织数量、暴露时间窗口，也没有发布事后复盘。

Discussion: 争论焦点不在泄露本身，而在状态页把事件标成了「Resolved」：corvad、iampims、jtchang、rugma 等人认为，用户数据被窃的事件在发布事后复盘、说明根因和整改项之前不该关闭，jtchang 直言这种沟通方式足以让他永不使用或推荐该服务；weird-eye-issue 则反问「漏洞修了、客户也通知了，还要怎样」，被 tuwtuwtuwtuw 一句「Yes」和「Drama queens」的回应顶了回去。whilenot-dev 提出实质性质疑：公告只说「blocked the exploit」，这可能是下线 API、封禁攻击者账号或真正修复漏洞，含义天差地别，环境变量这种敏感数据配不上这么含糊的措辞。BADCAFE 称同类厂商 Inngest 几个月前也遭遇过类似事件，自己赶在被利用前打了补丁，因此开始怀疑这类托管服务。另有分支讨论是否该自建：theturtletalks 主张自建缩小攻击面、只走 Tailscale，cbluth 反驳这正是不自建的理由，cpursley 与 multiplegeorges 则认为把队列、认证这类核心功能外包给付费第三方本身就是反模式。reassess_blind 追问是否有公司公开过实际利用的漏洞，dboreham 回答没有，并推测可能他们自己也不知道。

Worth reading

  • whilenot-dev: 指出「blocked the exploit」措辞含糊——可能是下线接口、封号或真正修复，同一句话对应完全不同的严重程度，而这类事件的信息量甚至不如普通 bug 的更新日志。
  • BADCAFE: 提到竞品 Inngest 几个月前也发生过同类事件，自己抢在被利用前打了补丁，因此对这类托管服务的信任被动摇。
  • cpursley: 借此事主张把后台任务、认证等核心功能外包给付费第三方是反模式，应选 Elixir 这类原生支持并发、有成熟开源作业库的技术栈。

entry.title: Nibnib: Image compression with extreme decompression speed
entry.content:
#10 on HN · github.com · 132 points · 23 comments · HN discussion

这是 Raph Levien（raphlinus）发布的一个实验性图像格式及其 Rust 实现，最初是为了在 RP2350 单片机上做 DVI 输出：每像素约 6 个周期的预算只够取像素、查调色板、写行缓冲。格式以 4bpp 存储，解码时一次从 1 字节里出两个 RGB565 像素，做法是把上一像素加倍后加上一个 256 项调色板中的 32 位「差值」条目，内层循环只有一条 wrapping_add；编码端则用 Floyd-Steinberg 误差扩散在调色板条目中搜索，速度比解码慢好几个数量级，调色板目前还不是自适应生成的。作者称在 Adafruit Fruit Jam 板上可从 SD 卡以 60fps 播放 640x480 视频，并提醒该格式不面向归档、也不带元数据。

Discussion: 最常见的抱怨是缺少基准数字：有人指出既然主打「极致解压速度」，至少该给一个 JPEG 的对照点和码率/质量/速度曲线；反方则认为 6 条指令一像素已经说明问题——JPEG 不可能做到，一位评论者直接说它「以 HDMI 行速解码」。多位老硬件玩家把它比作 Amiga 的 HAM 模式（6 位输入出 12 位色，水平方向有拖影），认为这是同一类思路。也有人质疑这算不算「压缩」——不过是 delta 滤波加调色板——但随即有人解释 Floyd-Steinberg 会把 100% 的量化误差推给邻居，所以不会漂移，作者的巧妙之处全在编码端。Retr0id 提醒针对 RP2350 优化几乎肯定不是现代桌面核心上的最优解，作者完全同意，说可以改 README 说明。另有评论者追问项目是否「vibe-coded」，作者坦承两者最初都是手写、后来用 Claude 推进，并说自己对 LLM 心情复杂、正努力「用好它、抵抗垃圾输出」。

Worth reading

  • raphlinus: 作者回应 LLM 质疑：图像压缩和 symbolasm 起初全是手写，Claude 只是加速了进展，他甚至说不用 LLM 也能做出同样结果、只是会更慢，并坚持自己写文字部分。
  • Retr0id: Retr0id 指出为 RP2350 这类资源受限设备优化的代码，在深流水线、宽 ILP/SIMD 的现代桌面核心上几乎肯定不是最优；作者在回复中承认并考虑在 README 里澄清。
  • schiffern: 解释为什么误差不会累积：Floyd-Steinberg 保留了 100% 的量化误差并推给邻近像素（对比 Atkinson 只保留 75%），并附了一篇抖动算法博客链接。

entry.title: Tips for more effective fuzz testing with AFL++
entry.content:
#11 on HN · nullprogram.com · 111 points · 17 comments · HN discussion

Chris Wellons (nullprogram.com) publishes an eight-point checklist for fuzzing C and C++ targets with AFL++ on glibc Linux, distilled from fuzz testing roughly 1,000 projects over six years. Beyond the usual ASan+UBSan setup, he argues for non-default ASan options — detect_stack_use_after_return=1 and max_malloc_fill_size raised from the default 4KiB to 1GiB, since the 4KiB cap hid real bugs from him — plus persistent mode, compiling the needed sources straight into a single translation unit (even static functions), a size-fitted copy of the fuzz buffer so read overflows are detectable, memfd_create for APIs that insist on a path, and shrinking generous fixed buffers like 65536 down to 16 to reach overflow paths faster.

Discussion: Almost the entire thread drifts away from the article into a debate over whether memory-safe C/C++ is a question of developer skill. jonhohle opened it by saying AFL found bugs even in FAANG code written by engineers with the top title, which changed his mind; others push back that skill still reduces bug rate, that the best programmers simply work on harder problems, and that deliberately rough prototype code can be the competent choice. The management camp argues quality is set by what management will fund and what the market rewards, with one commenter noting FAANG has resources but spends them elsewhere, and another noting a rushed triple-A game is not a quality benchmark. sczi asks whether any large C/C++ codebase has ever avoided exploitable memory corruption — if none has, it cannot be a passion problem — and uecker answers probably not outside formally verified code, while stressing that most of the issues he sees are preventable with bounds-checked string and buffer abstractions, and that memory-safety bugs are unusually well suited to sanitizers and fuzzers, unlike other correctness bugs. r0ze-at-hn adds first-hand experience that every codebase he made fuzzable paid off in found bugs, and notes fuzzing fits the AI era because it cannot be gamed like a unit test and costs less than burning tokens overnight. Beyond that there is only broad agreement that the list itself is good.

Worth reading

  • jonhohle: A practitioner says finding several bugs with AFL in FAANG code written by engineers holding the highest engineering title convinced him that safe C/C++ is not merely a matter of individual skill.
  • uecker: uecker argues almost no large C/C++ codebase escapes memory-safety issues outside formally verified code, but that most real bugs are preventable with bounds-checked string and buffer abstractions — and that memory-safety flaws are the rare class that automated tooling can actually find.
  • r0ze-at-hn: A long-time fuzzer builder says every codebase he made fuzzable paid off in found bugs, and argues fuzzing is a good fit for AI-generated code because it cannot be gamed the way a stub unit test can.

entry.title: New 3D thermal invisibility cloak makes objects disappear from infrared cameras
entry.content:
#14 on HN · sciencedaily.com · 73 points · 35 comments · HN discussion

A University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign release describes a Nature Communications paper by Shelly Zhang, Weichen Li, Yibo Wang and DTU's Ole Sigmund on the first experimental three-dimensional thermal cloak. The device is a 3D-printed aluminum lattice whose pores are filled by mold-cast low-conductivity rubber, with the lattice tuned independently along three axes so heat is routed around a hidden volume rather than blocked; IR-camera tests showed complex shapes, including head-like geometries, leaving the surrounding temperature pattern intact while the interior stayed uniform. The authors pitch it for chip cooling, thermal protection and defeating thermal detection, and say hiding objects that generate their own heat is the next step.

Discussion: The dominant thread is a correction: commenters argue the headline oversells the result, since this is not camouflage against thermal cameras but a structure that makes a hidden region look thermally like its surroundings — many readers came away thinking it was a FLIR invisibility cloak. The sharpest caveats come from schiffern, who notes it only works once heat flow has settled to equilibrium (so a moving object gains nothing) and that in free space the surface can only present one temperature to the camera, making it no better than cheap Mylar space-blanket camo. Others compare it to Ghost in the Shell's thermoptic camouflage and predict quick adoption in Ukraine, with one reply pointing out that Russian attempts using 50-cent Mylar blankets reportedly failed on video. A side argument asks whether it can hide something that emits its own heat; the answer is that the article explicitly lists that as future work, and one commenter suggests it could still hide a well-insulated person as a cold spot.

Worth reading

  • whatsakandr: Argues the headline is wrong: the cloak does not defeat thermal cameras, it makes the object match the bulk thermal properties of its surroundings.
  • schiffern: Adds two practical limits — it only works after heat flow reaches equilibrium, so a moving object is not hidden — and links real Ukrainian IR-camouflage footage plus an explainer on thermal cloaking.
  • schiffern: Second caveat: the effect requires being embedded in a solid object; in free space the surface cannot show different IR temperatures in different directions, so under FLIR it just reads as average ambient temperature.

entry.title: OccupySaaS
entry.content:
#24 on HN · occupysaas.com · 210 points · 140 comments · HN discussion

OccupySaaS 是一个借用 2011 年“占领华尔街”修辞的抗议式开源项目，主张被裁掉的工程师用 AI 依据公开文档做“洁净室”重写，产出可直接替换商业 SaaS 的自托管软件。目前公开两个早期项目：ZeroAuthy（Go 编写、兼容 Auth0 Authentication API 的身份服务，支持 OIDC discovery、JWKS、多租户域名、PKCE、client_credentials 与轮换 refresh token，并用 auth0-spa-js、auth0-react、nextjs-auth0 验证）和 SalesCompel（Go/PostgreSQL 多租户核心 + Vue 记录编辑器，兼容 Salesforce 公开 API）。全部 Apache-2.0，站方明确承认尚未生产可用，下一步候选包括知识库、工单、功能开关与可观测性。

Discussion: 最高赞的一条评论把整件事的前提翻了过来：客户付钱买的不是第一个 S（软件），而是第二个 S（服务）——托管、备份、安全补丁、24/7 支持，尤其是把责任外包出去、出事能起诉合同方，而 FOSS 恰恰把这份责任还给用户。另一大批评是重复造轮子：已有大量开源 IdP（如 Keycloak 系）和 CRM 替代品，甚至有人贴出 openaltfinder.com 的对照清单，而支持者反驳说真正稀缺的是与厂商官方 SDK 100% 兼容的“drop-in”能力。围绕 Apache-2.0 也吵了一轮：有人讥讽这等于让大厂再把代码包成 SaaS，另有人回击说换 AGPL 也会被骂没人敢用。关于“用 AI 反 AI”，双方都自觉讽刺——反对者说靠补贴的 token 打巨头毫无胜算，且以“复仇”为燃料的团队一旦成员被高薪招走就会散架；支持者则认为把廉价 token 变成解放性软件本身就是一种财富再分配。多位亲历者指出这类项目表面完成度惊人、深入使用后问题成堆，还有人翻出仓库几天内数百次提交、约 50 万行代码，质疑“每次合并都有人工审查”的说法；整体气氛是认同动机、怀疑执行，几乎没人相信它能撼动 Salesforce 或 Okta。

Worth reading

  • temp123477: 一句话点破要害：客户为 SaaS 付费买的是“服务”（托管、支持、责任承担），而不是软件本身，所以重写软件并不等于解决需求。
  • ivanmontillam: 提醒参与者两件事：很多 SaaS 的护城河不在代码（例如 Twilio 真正难复制的是与运营商批量拿号码的合同），而且以“复仇”为燃料的动机会很快耗尽。
  • verdverm: 用仓库事实反驳宣传：站点称所有 PR 都经人工过目，但几天内数百次提交、约 50 万行代码，说明存在绕过审查直接推 main 的情况。

entry.title: Keeping Up Appearances – The women taking over the funeral industry
entry.content:
#26 on HN · lareviewofbooks.org · 43 points · 21 comments · HN discussion

这是一篇 LARB Quarterly 第 50 期（主题「Scene」）的文章预览，作者 Andie Eisen 采访了三位殡葬从业女性（文中化名 Lucy、Jane 等）。核心数字是：殡葬科学专业的女性入学比例在四十年间从约 5% 升至近年毕业班的约 75%，部分项目达到 72%–100%。文章用她们的入行故事（亲人葬礼做得太差、疫情期的无力感、对病理与手工艺的兴趣）串起行业图景：防腐师年薪约 4–5 万美元，工作包含搬抬遗体的重体力与类似烹饪的即兴手艺，并回溯 Jessica Mitford 1963 年《The American Way of Death》如何把「殡葬业贪得无厌」钉进公众印象。

Discussion: 讨论基本离开了「女性接管」这条线，转向行业经济学：多位评论者称私募股权已大量收购看起来像本地老字号的殡仪馆，家族名字保留、装潢换成艳蓝色加无衬线 logo，并指出同样的收购潮也发生在本地连锁兽医诊所。另一条主线是防腐与厚棺葬是否道德——有人认为给将腐烂的遗体做化学防腐、卖 8500 美元棺材纯属在丧亲者最脆弱时加价，并主张学伊斯兰式洗净裹布速葬；随即有人纠正说墓穴「vault」和棺材在法律上都不是必需的，殡仪员只是会提醒「不防水」，火葬则是另一条更彻底的路。文章里 Lucy 那句「男人毁掉一切」引来明显反弹，有人批评这是无端宣泄仇恨，也有人反驳说真正收购殡葬业的 PE 公司确实几乎全是穿西装的老白人男性，而贪婪未必是男性专属的罪。整体没有共识，但「行业已被金融化、推销话术针对悲伤」是压倒性的共同判断。

Worth reading

  • chasingthewind: 第一手经验：作者今年与殡仪馆打交道后发现私募股权已接管该行业，看似本地的殡仪馆未必真是本地的。
  • SoftTalker: 关键纠正：墓穴混凝土外罩（vault）和棺材都不是法定必需，可以纸板箱下葬，只是殡仪员会提醒家属「不防水」。
  • walrus01: 对「贪婪是普遍人性」的反驳：收购殡葬业的 PE 公司几乎清一色由年长的白人男性执掌，并附搜索链接。

entry.title: Domain hacks with unusual Unicode characters (2018)
entry.content:
#27 on HN · shkspr.mobi · 74 points · 51 comments · HN discussion

A 2018 post by Terence Eden showing that single Unicode letterlike symbols normalise to real TLDs: U+2121 TELEPHONE SIGN (℡) maps to 「tel」 and U+2116 NUMERO SIGN (№) maps to 「no」, so edent.tel can be typed as edent.℡ and norid.no as norid.№. The mechanism is IDNA2008 processing per RFC 5895, which applies Unicode's compatibility lowercase mapping in the browser — DNS itself returns NXDOMAIN for the raw character. It extends to math alphanumerics (𝒆𝒙𝒂𝒎𝒑𝒍𝒆.𝒄𝒐𝒎), squared letters, and unit symbols like ㎒, and Eden notes the main limits: social sites refuse to autolink such URLs and some copy/paste paths strip the superscript form.

Discussion: Much of the thread is about the trick failing in practice today: the submitter's shortlink was mangled by HN's own text handling, Firefox users report the link isn't clickable or the URL truncates to sp.m, and one commenter attributes this to browser IDN-homograph defences that postdate the article — while another corrects that HN, not the browser, broke the specific URL. A security camp argues IDN is a phishing surface and DNS should be ASCII-only (one commenter says he null-routes all punycode domains via his own unbound resolver, citing Schneier's 2000 「Unicode is just too complex to ever be secure」), countered by others pointing to Unicode's own security report, browser punycode-display heuristics, and the fact that the author never proposed these for trusted services. Registration war stories dominate the rest: a π domain registered and refunded 20+ years ago, a one-letter ccTLD obtained by editing a hidden form field on a two-stage Turkmenistan signup, and emoji domains grabbed through registrar validation bugs and then impossible to renew. A long tangent covers U+200B zero-width space (not whitespace, valid in some language identifiers, used to stop Facebook turning :) into an emoji) and U+2800 braille blank for forcing non-empty form fields.

Worth reading

  • teddyh: Posts an updated, much longer table of Unicode characters mapping to current TLDs (Australia, Google's .cal, Cocos Islands, Finland via ﬁ, .mil, .ltd), generated from IANA's TLD list plus UnicodeData.txt with Python and regexes.
  • Rendello: Technical correction: Unicode lowercasing isn't stable across versions, so string matching should use case folding, with links to the Unicode stability policy, case-mapping FAQ and UTS #46 for IDNA processing.
  • ButlerianJihad: Strongest argument against the trick's innocuous framing: show such a list to a non-technical person and an IT professional and ask which are phishing, illustrating why visual URL inspection and hover-text have long been useless defences.

entry.title: The Megadonors Who Have Poured $1.2B into the Midterms
entry.content:
#34 on HN · nytimes.com · 64 points · 53 comments · HN discussion

A New York Times interactive from Aug. 28, 2026, whose headline says it tallies $1.2 billion in midterm spending by megadonors. The page returned HTTP 403, so its specific findings could not be checked; commenters say it identifies the donors as overwhelmingly Republican and puts Elon Musk’s spending at about $90 million, against later reports of $400 million or more.

Article not read: HTTP 403

Discussion: The thread quickly moves from the sum itself to what it buys: several commenters argue that if donors can spend this much they can pay more tax, while others say the spending is precisely aimed at preventing that. A long argument over Citizens United divides those who want limits or public financing from those who say restricting political ads would hand a Trump-controlled FEC the power to decide what can be published; the latter camp argues that voters, not propaganda, are the real weak point, and is met with the reply that advertising demonstrably works and that unequal money makes most speech inaudible. On the Democratic side, one commenter blames Kamala Harris’s loss on her wealth-tax proposal, which another disputes with polling cited at 60% support. Practical proposals include a 200% tax on political donations or spending above a cap, with the proceeds redistributed to underfunded candidates; there is rough agreement that the current system is corrosive but none on a constitutional fix, with suggestions ranging from state-level corporate-rights changes to expanding the Supreme Court.

Worth reading

  • darth_avocado: Flags a reporting gap: the NYT piece puts Musk at about $90M while a Guardian tracker says $400M+, and a reply explains that the NYT article is two months old.
  • seszett: Argues from a non-US perspective that unlimited spending lets money amplify some speech until others are technically free but inaudible, and that many countries restrict pre-election political broadcasting.
  • tancop: Proposes taxing campaign-related spending at 200% above a limit and distributing the proceeds to smaller candidates, so spending more becomes self-defeating while remaining viewpoint-neutral.

entry.title: I Am the Reason OpenAI Is Killing Unlimited Chats
entry.content:
#35 on HN · chaosmanage.github.io · 53 points · 12 comments · HN discussion

A blog post by a developer who spent months doing all his software development inside ordinary unlimited ChatGPT conversations instead of burning Codex limits, by wiring up an MCP gateway on his Windows laptop and VPS with Desktop Commander (file access, terminal, tests) and a computer-use agent (screenshots, clicks), exposed to ChatGPT through OpenAI's Secure MCP Tunnel and authenticated with an API key. He used a stronger model to plan, split work into detailed GitHub issues as a task queue, then ran several parallel chats on the cheaper Sol 6 High model to execute them, plus a small dashboard to monitor tool calls. He notes OpenAI's recently announced change folding ChatGPT usage into Codex, killing unlimited chats, and says he is switching to Claude Opus, while insisting he broke no rules and doesn't seriously think his setup caused the decision.

Discussion: The thread quickly splits into two arguments. One commenter declares multi-agent orchestration mostly dead, arguing a single big agent loop on GPT6.1 now beats these schemes, that multi-agent designs bloat token usage by orders of magnitude, and that he only keeps subagents for very long-horizon test runs — a claim another commenter calls a huge, lonely take, saying everyone they know is scaling up the number of agents they can feed with useful work. Several others push back on the author's ethic: one says people who squeeze systems like this while claiming to follow the rules are why good things get taken away. The rest of the thread drifts to vendor choice, with users trading reports of Anthropic's refusals versus OpenAI's limits; one notes Claude still handled heavy reverse-engineering work for them but they plan to switch anyway, one says DeepSeek now gives them five times the value of their $200-tier subscriptions, and another corrects the rumor mill by saying OpenAI reversed its usage reduction and actually doubled usage on the $20, $100 and $500 plans.

Worth reading

  • bob1029: Argues multi-agent orchestration is largely obsolete next to one large agent loop on GPT6.1, keeps subagents only for 100-plus-tool long-horizon tests, and says multi-agent designs waste tokens by orders of magnitude.
  • _aavaa_: Corrects the claims about shrinking allowances: OpenAI reportedly went back on the reduction in the $200 plan and doubled usage on the $20, $100 and $500 tiers.
  • ronsor: Points to two recent HN threads full of complaints about Anthropic's random usage restrictions, arguing Claude is preferable in the abstract but less usable as a product.

entry.title: AI fan wikis riddled with errors are muddying the waters of games culture
entry.content:
#37 on HN · eurogamer.net · 79 points · 67 comments · HN discussion

一篇 Eurogamer 文章：记者想查游戏 Nighthawks 的同伴信息，点进 Google 第一条结果的「Nighthawks Wiki」，发现它根本不能编辑、只接受邮件「更正」，还列了不存在的同伴和技能，并把同名的 1981 年电影和 Edward Hopper 画作混进「来源」。域名被追到建站服务 Spaceship 的「AI Website builder」。Hooded Horse 出版公司 CEO Tim Bender 说他们得对这类站点「打地鼠」，其中一个站点 GameDB 承认用生成式 AI 批量做了 20 多个游戏站；独立维基网络成员 FlamingMojo 说 Dune: Awakening 社区维基 30 天内收到 700 万次 AI 爬虫请求（仅 Meta 就 500 万），服务器成本涨了 3 到 10 倍。

Discussion: 主流情绪是悲观：不少人认为这是网络生态被入侵物种改写，无解，只能等开放网络像 Usenet 一样被垃圾淹没。反驳与建设性方案集中在两处：一是像 Wikipedia 那样靠严格人工审核和封禁 LLM 写手（有评论者说目前有效），二是用密码学签名或生物识别验证「人类作者」，但立刻有人指出签名防不住「人类让 AI 写完再自己签名」。另一派把矛头指向搜索：坏网站一直存在，问题是 Google 和 DuckDuckGo 把垃圾排到第一，有人因此考虑转投 Kagi。也有实务派唱反调，说前沿模型能反汇编游戏二进制、比常年靠猜的维基更准。关于「AI 让代码质量下降」的旁支争论同样分裂，有人举例刚拦下 Claude 提交的明显 RCE，也有人认为 LLM 可靠地避免了一整类 bug。

Worth reading

  • bawolff: 指出维基百科的做法是靠极严格的人工审核规则执行：抓到用 LLM 且不肯停就封号，并称目前确实管用。
  • oefrha: 第一手经验：前沿 LLM 会主动反汇编游戏二进制来搞清机制，比维基里常年靠猜的数值更准，问题只出在免费的低质幻觉引擎上。
  • jrmg: 具体到生活场景的佐证：查雪松壁板该用什么钉子时，Google 和 DuckDuckGo 结果几乎全是互相矛盾的 AI 垃圾站，甚至把新罕布什尔一家美甲店的域名顶上来了。

entry.title: Altoids Project
entry.content:
#46 on HN · uvdn7.github.io · 162 points · 7 comments · HN discussion

This is a personal build log about a roughly two-month father-and-son project that turned a salvaged robot’s 128x64 display into a tiny computer inside an Altoids tin. The build went through five iterations using an Arduino Nano, LiPo batteries with a PowerBoost, solderable breadboards and 3D-printed parts; none of the components from the first version survived. Along the way, AI gave a hallucinated 20-pin pinout for a 10-pin display, the correct schematic came from a stranger on the Arduino forum, and desoldering accidents and a weak soldering iron caused repeated setbacks.

Discussion: Commenters mostly treated the post as a wholesome reminder of the old Altoids-tin electronics scene, trading examples of 1802, 6502 and BeagleBone machines that fit in mint tins. One commenter wondered where that culture went, and another suggested cheap 3D printers and easy CAD tools like Tinkercad may have absorbed or displaced it; the first agreed. Several people shared their own first electronics projects and praised the father for getting a 12-year-old involved in soldering, debugging and CAD. The rough consensus is nostalgic and positive: tins are still a great constraint for learning hardware, even if the scene looks different now.

Worth reading

  • JKCalhoun: Links to two earlier Altoids-tin computers built around the 1802 and 6502 processors, giving useful historical context.
  • jowsie: Argues that cheap 3D printers and accessible CAD software like Tinkercad may explain why the Altoids-tin project craze faded.
  • colechristensen: Adds that BeagleBone single-board computers were specifically designed to fit inside Altoids tins.

entry.title: In LLM era, can software startup survive?
entry.content:
#48 on HN · text post · 18 points · 23 comments · HN discussion

This is a text post on Hacker News, not a linked article, so there is nothing to read beyond it. The poster, sjia, argues that vibe coding has reduced building software to a matter of tokens — joking that writing tax-return software is now faster than buying TurboTax at Costco — but that startups are the ones left exposed: large companies still hold the compute and the customer base, while users increasingly expect open source or free software, and any paid subscription or one-time-purchase app posted to Reddit gets downvoted immediately.

Discussion: The thread splits over the post's implicit premise that code is the easy part. One camp insists that framing is wrong: coding was at least half the difficulty, hiring a software team was expensive and risky, and that is precisely why most businesses never had one — refactoring a legacy system without an LLM is offered as proof. The other camp says the hard part was always choosing the right problem, finding product-market fit and distribution, with several calling distribution the moat. A prominent top comment predicts the flood of vibecoded products will backfire on startups by eroding trust in new software, pushing buyers back toward established vendors with real QA, audits and code review — 「when the barrier to publish drops to zero, the barrier to gain trust skyrockets」. A dissenting commenter argues the opposite: large companies are struggling to integrate AI tooling into their workflows, so this is actually the best time to start a company, provided a small skilled team can use immature tools sustainably. Others note it is still usually cheaper to pay for software than to write, maintain and run it.

Worth reading

  • avallach: Argues that near-zero cost to ship software destroys the signal of effort that used to imply competence — like self-published books — and that formal process (bills of materials, four-eyes code review, release gates, external audits) will become a selling point for incumbents.
  • aurareturn: Directly counters the 「the code was never the hard part」 refrain, saying coding was at least 50% of the difficulty and that the cost and risk of hiring an engineering team is why most businesses in the world never had one.
  • fnordpiglet: Inverts the post's thesis: big companies' moats are shrinking because they struggle to integrate AI into existing workflows, making this the best time for a startup — but only for small teams skilled enough to build sustainably on rapidly shifting, immature tooling.

entry.title: A 1580 Map Shows Why Data Visualization Is Never Neutral
entry.content:
#50 on HN · thereader.mitpress.mit.edu · 77 points · 14 comments · HN discussion

这是 MIT Press 旗下 The Reader 上的一篇文章，标题论点是一份 1580 年的地图——文章正文抓取时返回 HTTP 403，因此本篇摘要只基于标题与讨论——用一张早期地图来说明：制图与可视化中的取舍（画什么、不画什么、如何分组）与数据本身同样重要。文章的核心主张是“可视化从来不是中立的”，而非仅仅“有时不中立”。

Article not read: HTTP 403

Discussion: 讨论很快从地图转向了那个“never”字：一位评论者指出，一个例子最多只能证明“并非总是中立”，无法证明“永远不可能中立”，并搬出 sin(x) 在 [0, 2π]、y∈[-1.5, 1.5] 上的图像作为看似中立的候选；立刻有人反驳说，截取这一段恰恰隐去了函数的周期性，而取色会让色盲读者难以辨读，选择把它画出来本身也是对“无数张没被画出的图”的立场表态。另一些人则把“中立”重新定义为“所有读者都能看懂”，认为这不可能，于是更愿意把问题描述成“受众是谁、沟通有多难”，而不是“分析者在施加权力”；一位科学工作者也说，论文配图本就是为了说明特定观点，调整坐标轴范围并不等于误导，除非刻意做出欺骗性图表。最具体的声音来自一位开发者，他做巴基斯坦汽油价格拆分图时发现，即使每个数字都来自监管机构的公告，把进口成本与运费合并、把缺失值留空而非写 0.00、把“The state”改称“Government”，都会改变读者对事实的理解。

Worth reading

  • ijazkhan095: 第一手案例：用巴基斯坦官方油价公告做可视化时，真正的偏向藏在分组、缺失值与用词里——同一批数字，读者得出的结论却不同。
  • tgv: 提出最强反例：把 sin(x) 限制在 [0, 2π] 并声明这是对函数与定义域的图形近似时，很难说这张图“不中立”，并引用《How to Lie with Statistics》区分“不充分”与“误导”。
  • ngriffiths: 指出文章的自相矛盾：既然承认存在正确解读，就说明图中有客观信息；真正的问题不是“分析者施加权力”，而是受众错配与沟通难度。

entry.title: AI agent swarms in Minecraft fail to build civilization, drown in bureaucracy
entry.content:
#54 on HN · tomshardware.com · 166 points · 79 comments · HN discussion

Tom's Hardware 的 Mark Tyson 转述了 Y Combinator 与 Olam Labs 的一项实验：他们把大群基于 Mindcraft、Mineflayer 的智能体放进 Minecraft 测试多智能体协作与对抗。最受关注的是 Civ50：50 个智能体被要求用三小时建立繁荣文明，结果第一夜僵尸来袭后雄心勃勃的计划大多被放弃，反而陷入程序主义——4 个智能体花了 11 分钟为一块骨粉、一格小麦任命一名「唯一施肥员」。在 Bed Wars（10 个 GPT-6.1 Sol 对 10 个 Claude Opus 5.5）中 GPT 进攻更激进、Claude 偏防守；在 Mindustry 中 GPT 一方以 6-1 获胜，研究者形容 GPT 更像蜂群、Claude 则是单一领袖加民主决策。代码已开源。

Discussion: 最常见的困惑是这到底算哪个学科：有人说这是「机器心理学」「计算社会学」，有人说只是披着实验外衣的营销软文，缺乏严谨设计和可推广性，换提示词、换模型代次结果就可能完全不同。支持者反驳说，智能体被当作武器或业务执行者部署时，协作与对抗行为本身有实际价值，且这可能是研究涌现社会行为的更可控沙盒。最有分量的意见来自实践者：有人用 rs-sdk 让 Claude 玩 Old School RuneScape，起初同样浪费时间做无意义的事，但经过数小时纠正（让智能体写模块化代码、记录经验）后已能独自推进终局任务，因此怀疑问题出在智能体本身还不够会玩游戏。另一位评论者认为 Mineflayer 这类每秒读取一次状态、反应迟缓的 harness 才是瓶颈，用这类结果断言智能体天生无法合作属于过度解读。也有人联系到自己的经验：多个 orchestrator/worker 协作时确实会不断新增规则，最后连规则都执行不好，或者像使用 paperclip 那样，智能体一多就只会烧 token。另有大量评论吐槽 Tom's Hardware 页面广告多到无法阅读，并指出该话题几天前已在 HN 讨论过（重复提交）。

Worth reading

  • _vertigo: 第一手经验：用 rs-sdk 让 Claude 玩 Old School RuneScape，初期同样低效胡来，经数小时指导后才成功，因此怀疑该实验中的智能体本身就不擅长这个游戏。
  • gjskngnf: 反驳过度推论：Mineflayer 包装层让智能体要等上一分钟左右才能读到状态、做出动作，真正瓶颈是 harness，而非「智能体天生会陷入官僚主义」。
  • czep: 另一种解读：智能体在沙盒里畏首畏尾、缺少非理性的冒险冲动，恰恰是它们与人类的区别，而文明或许正需要这种「明知不该做」的冲动。

entry.title: No AI, 52 min. Build all Linux Files utils in C by Hand [video]
entry.content:
#56 on HN · youtube.com · 146 points · 111 comments · HN discussion

A YouTube screencast in which the creator writes implementations of the Linux/coreutils file utilities from scratch in C, apparently working from man pages, in a 52-minute session with no AI assistance and his face overlaid on the screen. The hook is the constraint itself, rather than any novel technique. The video starts with touch, which commenters immediately used as the test case for whether the exercise produces correct software.

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: The thread split into two arguments. One is a familiar meta-fight about AI: people likened hand-coding to artisanal woodworking versus IKEA furniture, with one camp saying LLMs already write better code than humans, and the other (including engineers with 20 and 30 years of experience, disagreeing with each other) arguing that LLM output still needs full review and so negates the productivity gain, or that the exercise is a hobby, not a business case. Others pushed back on the debate itself, calling the recurring pro-AI talking points marketing-driven, and pointing to the short-lived Gas Town hype as evidence that tool-of-the-week enthusiasm evaporates. The concrete thread was more interesting: the touch implementation opens files in "w" mode, so it truncates any existing file instead of merely updating its mtime. Several people noted this is exactly the kind of edge case that makes real coreutils large, while BusyBox and Plan 9 versions of touch are far simpler references. A smaller subthread suspects the video is itself partly AI-generated or staged, citing faked keypress sounds and inconsistent camera shake.

Worth reading

  • _ache_: Pinpoints the real bug: the touch clone opens the file with "w", emptying any existing file instead of just updating its timestamp.
  • not_kurt_godel: Lists specific evidence — admitted fake keypress sounds, odd camera shake, inconsistent eye tracking toward the notes pane — for thinking the video is not entirely genuine.
  • bigstrat2003: A 20-year engineer's counter to the claim that hand-written code has no business case: current LLMs still make errors humans never would, so full review erases the gains.

entry.title: Show HN: HackerBooks – HackerTube, but for books mentioned on HN
entry.content:
#1 on HN · hackerbooks.org · 475 points · 123 comments · HN discussion

HackerBooks（hackerbooks.org）是一个由 roansh 发布的 Show HN 站点，它收录了大约 16.5k 本在 2007 年至今至少被两位不同 HN 评论者提到的书，每本书都反向链接到提到它的那些评论，数据可从关于页面下载。作者说 Claude（Opus 5.5）几乎写了全部内容，包括数据管道和前端，而他只做方向把控和决策；他只买了域名。他一开始就承认，因为统计的是提及次数，所以无论是赞扬还是贬损都同样计入。链接页面本身在抓取时没有可读文本，因此所有细节都来自帖子正文和评论。

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: 最早的一批评论都围绕持久性：好几个人记得此前也出现过同类项目，包括 hackernewsbooks.com 和一份 2021 年的 HN 帖子，它们后来都消失了；其中一个站点的原作者也现身承认它已经失效。最集中的批评是措辞问题：《我的奋斗》被显示为“被 651 位 HN 用户推荐”，这促使作者把界面改成“被提及”，并承诺会改进推荐逻辑；同时，也有不少人争论为什么《阿特拉斯耸耸肩》能排到历史总榜第一，有人认为那只是被提及的次数多，并不代表被推荐。工程师们追问了技术栈，作者回答说：前端是纯 JS 加静态 JSON，托管在 Cloudflare（HTTP/3，带长效缓存哈希），封面放在 R2 上，数据管道用 Python + DuckDB 跑完整的 HN 数据转储；前端主要是因为一句提示词“让它像 HackerTube，但做成书的样子”才显得精致，不过也有人吐槽它长得就是 Claude 的默认样式。数据质量问题是实际操作者报告的重点：《名利场》把杂志和萨克雷的小说混在了一起，《美丽新世界》的出版年份显示成了 2000 年代，《哈利·波特》被标成约翰·威廉姆斯所作，“其他”分类里还出现了《愤怒的小鸟》和《绝命毒师》；作者修好了时间筛选，让它按一本书第一次被提到的时间来过滤，并当场做了一个趋势页面。请求列表始终没有停过：区分真正的推荐和单纯的提及、显示当地图书馆有没有这本书、加亚马逊联盟链接、加语义搜索，以及为什么还没有做播客版或影视版。

Worth reading

  • thibaut_barrere: Commenter thibaut_barrere 承认自己就是之前那个 HN 图书网站的构建者，该网站后来 404 了，并说他打算恢复它，“但生活挡住了路”——这是那类网站反复死掉的直接证据。
  • roansh: 作者详细说明了技术栈：纯 JS 加静态 JSON 放在 Cloudflare 上，30kb 的索引加后台懒加载的完整列表，封面放在 R2 上，数据管道用 Python + DuckDB 跑 HN 数据转储——同时承认 HN 帖子本身就是 Claude 起草的，他几乎没改。
  • Erlangen: 一位读者发现《名利场》（范妮·伯尼/萨克雷的小说）被错误地排到历史总榜前列，因为许多匹配到的评论其实是在说《名利场》杂志；作者确认了这一点，并把它改成只统计会提到萨克雷的提及。

entry.title: Nurses Sound Alarm as 'Uber for Nursing' Apps Push to Deregulate Healthcare
entry.content:
#2 on HN · nurse.org · 72 points · 30 comments · HN discussion

A nurse.org write-up of the AI Now Institute's report 「Uber for Nursing Part II」 (April 21, 2026), arguing that gig nursing platforms — ShiftKey, Clipboard Health, CareRev, IntelyCare and others — are lobbying in at least 17 states to exempt themselves from healthcare staffing-agency rules, with eight states having already advanced exemption bills. The ten biggest platforms have raised roughly $1.4B (ShiftKey valued at $2B, Clipboard Health at $1.3B) and Clipboard and ShiftKey alone spent over $1.1M combined on federal lobbying, partly via the Coalition for Workforce Innovation alongside Amazon and Uber. The report describes algorithmic pricing (CareRev's 「Smart Rates」),「Quick Bid」 auctions where the lowest rate wins, contractor classification that strips minimum wage, overtime and workers' comp, and a Roosevelt Institute claim that some platforms use data brokers to offer lower wages to nurses with the most debt; New York bucked the trend in 2025 by classifying the platforms as staffing agencies, after which Clipboard Health, Nursa and KARE left the state.

Discussion: The thread mostly ignores the report itself and turns into the usual HN argument about why US healthcare is expensive. One camp — including comments pointing to low hospital margins and to traveling nurses already working this way — says provider pay is the cost driver and asks what should give; another insists the real money is in insurers and hospital-group consolidation, and one commenter cites Commonwealth Fund figures putting physician and nurse salaries at only about 15% of healthcare spending. A European commenter argues the premise is wrong and that hospitals simply shouldn't be run for margin, prompting a reply about comparing wait times, pay and outcomes. On the gig model specifically, commenters draw a straight line from Uber's regulatory arbitrage to nursing, flag the debt-based wage-discrimination claim as the most alarming detail, and correct a top-level assumption that this is a nurse-to-consumer marketplace — it is sold to hospitals and facilities to fill shifts. There is rough consensus that undercutting each other's rates is bad for nurses, with little agreement on the fix.

Worth reading

  • 5mk: Pushes back on the 「providers' salaries are the problem」 framing with a Commonwealth Fund link showing physician and nurse pay is only about 15% of US healthcare spending.
  • codeddesign: Corrects the common misreading: these apps are marketed to hospitals to fill shifts, not to patients hiring a nurse directly.
  • gambiting: Non-US perspective that a hospital having a 「margin」 at all is the absurd part, since it is funded by taxes and the patient pays nothing.

entry.title: Patrick Stewart taught us what good men do with power
entry.content:
#4 on HN · vox.com · 209 points · 144 comments · HN discussion

A Vox essay by Ian Millhiser, published after Patrick Stewart’s death, arguing that his Jean-Luc Picard was the embodiment of 1990s institutionalist liberalism: a captain commanding a ship with enough firepower to destroy planets who more often used it to deliver vaccines. Millhiser reads episodes like The Measure of a Man (Data’s legal personhood) and The Drumhead (an admiral’s witch hunt) as portraits of trustworthy institutions responsive to reasoned argument, contrasts them with the more cynical Discovery and Star Trek: Picard, and leans on Acemoglu and Robinson’s Why Nations Fail to argue that inclusive institutions still require a strong central state.

Discussion: The biggest fight is over credit: many say the utopia belongs to Gene Roddenberry, others to TNG’s writers (who, one commenter notes, wrote Data’s trial episode as a spec script during a writers’ strike), while a third camp insists Stewart’s gravitas is what sold a vision that would otherwise read as camp — an unconvincing actor, they argue, turns morals into caricature. A second cluster disputes whether fiction teaches leadership at all: skeptics say scriptwriters have no leadership credentials and that tidy 45-minute morality plays train people to see the world as good vs. evil, while defenders compare it to Shakespeare, Homer and allegory, and one commenter offers a cautionary tale of a colleague who ran a worksite like “their ship.” A large side thread takes up Data and AI: why audiences root for Data’s personhood but resent today’s models — answers center on Data being a one-off research project rather than a corporate product, and on AI as a proxy for runaway power inequality. Elsewhere people swap essential-episode lists, note that Picard was modeled on Horatio Hornblower, and argue over accountability for those in power.

Worth reading

  • Veliladon: A close reading of The Measure of a Man: Picard and the judge use he/him for Data while Maddox uses it/them, and Maddox only switches to he after the ruling — a small detail that carries the episode’s argument.
  • R1D3R: Corrects the writers’-strike thread: Measure of a Man was a speculative script picked up for production during a strike, and it is one of TNG’s first great episodes.
  • miiiiiike: A strong counter-anecdote: the worst person the commenter ever worked with drew their entire leadership style from Star Trek and The West Wing and called the site “their ship” — inspiration, yes; teaching, no.

entry.title: Copper – A minimal low-level programming language with OOP and generics
entry.content:
#5 on HN · tibleiz.net · 74 points · 37 comments · HN discussion

这是作者个人开发、以替代 C 为目标的一门小众语言的主页，主打极简：没有头文件、简单的 import、名字不全塞进全局命名空间，语法接近 Ruby，类带隐式 self。页面只有一段简短示例和语言速查表、标准库源码浏览入口，采用 BSD 许可；作者自称语言简单到「像我这样脑力有限的人也能完全理解」。文章几乎没有介绍内存模型、编译目标、FFI 等关键信息，这也成了评论区的焦点。

Discussion: 最集中的质疑是文档缺失：多位 commenter 追问内存如何释放、是否有 GC、编译到什么、能否与 C 做 ABI/FFI、以及 Unicode 与 16 位字符串怎么处理。有人翻标准库源码后指出并没有 GC 的痕迹，而是提供分配器接口，free 藏在 std 的 allocator 里，但示例一个都没提，这被认为是最该补的一块。语法上有人认为像 Crystal、Ruby 或 Python/Dart 的混合体（官网自己写的是 Ruby-style syntax，且没有 Python 的缩进敏感），也有人称赞其克制。另一条支线争论自举是否是好主意：有人称自托管是「bootstrapping 的死亡」，也有人认为这种问题被夸大，而有 C 后端是稳妥做法；还有人实测在 Linux 上编译不过。末尾一段讨论则声称人类已不再亲自选语言、语言选择交给 LLM，被多人反驳。

Worth reading

  • christophilus: 指出 std 里确实有带 free 的分配器，说明要手动调用，但奇怪的是所有示例都没覆盖内存释放。
  • stevefolta: 实际动手的反馈：在 Linux 上编译不过，且认为没有字符串插值、没有 kebab-case 命名。
  • bogdanoff_2: 发帖人补充作者博客与 changelog 链接，可以看语言设计思路的演变，例如曾加入又移除异常机制。

entry.title: Police chief unplugs Flock cameras after company ignores contract cancellation
entry.content:
#6 on HN · tomshardware.com · 357 points · 123 comments · HN discussion

Tom's Hardware reports that Plymouth, Minnesota's City Council voted unanimously on Sept. 22, 2026 to drop its Flock Safety license-plate readers; the city suspended accounts the next morning and sent a formal cancellation letter by mail and email, but heard nothing from Flock's corporate or legal side for over a week. Police Chief Eric Fadden then had staff disconnect the cameras' power cords. The piece notes Flock has 300,000+ cameras nationwide, that its AI reads stickers, paint color and make/model beyond plates, and that nearby Dayton, MN also paused its program after Flock replaced two cameras against instructions.

Discussion: The dominant thread is anger at Flock — commenters compare it to Uber's ignore-local-regulators playbook, argue a company with no contract shouldn't keep drawing on public infrastructure, and swap ideas for consequences (theft-of-service charges, per-device trespass fines, RICO, small-claims suits, shower caps and spray paint). A significant counter-current says the story is overblown: one week after a mailed cancellation letter is not much time, the local rep had been in touch, and the contract terms — which nobody can find — may simply run to term rather than requiring immediate removal. Several people point out the cameras are solar-and-battery powered with cellular links, so yanking a power cord likely changed nothing, though others counter that the pole, permits and liability still cost the city something. A long side argument pits Ring-style private doorbell cameras against Flock: some say the two are equivalent surveillance, others insist owner choice, warrant requirements and jurisdiction limits make Flock categorically worse, and that normalizing private cameras paved the way for it. Rough consensus: Flock's behavior looks bad and its brand is becoming toxic with municipalities, but the article's framing of a one-week silence as provocation is contested.

Worth reading

  • idopmstuff: Argues the article never states the contract terms, so a council vote to cancel may only mean non-renewal at term's end — which would make talk of charging Flock with a crime baseless, even though ignoring the shutdown request is still bad form.
  • voxic11: Notes Flock cameras run on their own solar panels and batteries (part of why they deploy so fast), so 「unplugging」 them may have had little practical effect.
