  • lifeisloving: Claims police departments denied Flock funding on budget grounds suddenly receive mysterious ~$1M federal grants, and that Flock installs free of charge on promissory notes — arguing it behaves like a government surveillance program dressed as a startup.

entry.title: Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it
entry.content:
#7 on HN · terrytao.wordpress.com · 64 points · 76 comments · HN discussion

A guest post by Frank Calegari on Terence Tao's blog arguing that OpenAI's October 6 release of over 700 research papers was a watershed: AI can now make genuine contributions across many areas of mathematics, even if those papers are badly written, sloppy about attribution, and in some cases wrong. Calegari compares the moment to the classification of finite simple groups — announced by Daniel Gorenstein in 1983 (with the quasithin case finished two decades later by Aschbacher and Smith) — which solved the field's famous problem and thereby cooled interest in it, and he argues mathematicians should respond by valuing problem selection, structural understanding and broad programmes, and by using hiring and journal acceptance rather than rhetoric to reward that. He also warns that the arXiv is filling with rushed AI-assisted papers chasing priority while the Leiden declaration is honoured 「in name more than in spirit」, and tells tenured senior mathematicians that if they fear being scooped by AI they are not being ambitious enough.

Discussion: Commenters largely accept the framing that results matter less than digestion — choosing problems, understanding proofs, and drawing others in — with several comparing mathematics to software engineering where writing the code is now the cheap part. The sharpest disagreement is about who gets to play: one commenter notes that solving major problems currently costs roughly $10–22 million in API spend, which would make mathematical credit a function of capital rather than talent, while others argue the shift is simply craft turning into industry, and a counterpoint holds that mathematics has no internal profit motive, so this industrialisation is entirely exogenous and imposed by companies. A long subthread fights over Lean: whether 700 machine-checked proofs should count as solved, whether a Lean bug could be responsible (most think a bug that fakes 700 diverse proofs is implausible, but mis-specified statements and human-written formalisations are the real risk), and whether any of it addresses understanding. Sceptics predict professional mathematicians have little future, and that AI will beat humans at any problem including choosing them, while others insist mathematics is about machinery and comprehension and that no AI has yet produced a genuinely new conjecture or paradigm shift; several defend Calegari against charges that his periodic-table analogy is naive.

Worth reading

  • georgemcbay: Points out that at roughly $10–22 million in API costs per major result, credit for AI-assisted breakthroughs becomes a function of funding, giving well-capitalised but weaker mathematicians a structural advantage.
  • pfdietz: Claims several of the OpenAI proofs have already been accepted and dissected, that nobody seriously doubts the quasi-Riemann Hypothesis result, and that the 11/12-constant proof was an unexpected combination of known techniques that human mathematicians' narrowness had missed for 20 years.
  • QuesnayJr: A careful rebuttal: the classification of finite simple groups arguably cuts against Calegari's thesis, and the possibility he ignores is that a machine may also be better at forming conjectures — at which point there is no human role left.

entry.title: Proving and improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs
entry.content:
#8 on HN · arxiv.org · 84 points · 43 comments · HN discussion

An arXiv paper by Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun that turns the Platonic Representation Hypothesis into a theorem for Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures. It proves that JEPAs trained separately on different modalities learn the same representation up to a rotation when their positive pairs are good views of one scene, and argues that next-token prediction is a JEPA with bad views, which is why language models align with vision only at scale. Experiments spanning 145k captions and 940M web images produce an alignment scaling law: good views need 42 times fewer samples, a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with DINOv2 and CLIP image encoders better than language models up to 72B parameters and better than CLIP's text encoder, and one rotation turns separately trained encoders into a captioner scoring CIDEr .838 on COCO.

Discussion: Commenters split between finding the hypothesis profound and finding it a restatement of the obvious: one calls it an optimal dimensionality-reduction claim, another says it matters because it could let smaller models be trained, and a third recasts it as compressed data representations and classifier decision boundaries. Much of the thread drifts into philosophy, asking whether two internally consistent but incompatible world models could exist, with politics, religion and human tribes as examples, and whether objective reality or human judgement decides which representation wins. Technical objections are raised and partly answered: big-endian versus little-endian is not a counterexample because it is equivalent up to rotation or permutation, while a lossy mapping such as INT16 to FP16 is where compatibility gets interesting, and a physicist notes that coordinate choices are task-dependent before conceding that the paper defines its claim narrowly enough. The sharpest critiques concern scope and evidence: one reader suspects the theorem covers one architecture across modalities rather than human minds or arbitrary models, another asks how JEPAs could obtain web-scale good views instead of the unstructured corpus that makes next-token prediction work, and a third reports that every example in the paper's Hugging Face demo is mislabeled. A smaller camp is bullish on JEPAs, citing a text JEPA matching Qwen2.5-3B and 7B with fewer samples, while another subthread complains that theory papers dress standard math in hype terminology.

Worth reading

  • suddenlybananas: Questions whether the theorem really supports the broad PRH claim, which was meant to cover different architectures and human minds, not just one model family across modalities, and suspects strong assumptions do the work.
  • dominotw: Reports that every example in the paper's Hugging Face demo has a wrong caption, such as a cake described as a sheep sitting on it.
  • theptip: Asks whether JEPAs can assemble a web-scale supply of good views, since next-token prediction's advantage is mining unstructured web text.

entry.title: Bidirectional charging during grid outages
entry.content:
#9 on HN · jefftk.com · 57 points · 71 comments · HN discussion

Jeff Kaufman argues that using an EV as a solar-charged home backup — the car charging from panels when it is sunny and powering the house when it is not — is nearly impossible to buy today. He walks through the options: GM's V2H bundle is a discharge-only mode that ends when the grid returns, Ford's Charge Station Pro is no longer sold (the F-150 Lightning is discontinued), Kia's Wallbox Quasar 2 cannot charge and discharge at once, and Enphase's bidirectional charger is only 「targeting volume production beginning in Q4 2026」 and depends on automaker enablement. The only working path he finds is Tesla Powershare with a Cybertruck and a UL 1741-listed solar system on the backup panel, so he will likely install a smaller emergency-only battery instead.

Discussion: The thread splits away from bidirectional charging into a long batteries-versus-generator argument. One camp (bob1029 and allies) says batteries cannot ride out a week-long hurricane outage that requires continuous 5-ton HVAC — roughly 800kWh, or near half a million dollars — while a low-RPM generator on an automatic transfer switch costs about 15% of that and is 「undefeated from an engineering perspective」; others counter that this describes only the Gulf Coast, and suggest running AC only during solar production, downsizing loads, or using thermal mass. Several practitioners give real numbers: 18kW of solar plus 30kWh of batteries running a 5-ton AC indefinitely while the sun shines, backed by a generator-driven charger; and a winter ice-storm calculation of 600W furnace draw at 30% duty, about 4.3kWh a day, or roughly $10k for a week on cheap 4.8kWh batteries. On the article's actual subject, the consensus is that the blocker is standards and vertical integration: commenters say the microgrid interconnect device has no standardized control protocol, NACS/J3400 omits bidirectional power, and warranties plus California's 70%/75% battery-capacity law make automakers cautious. A UK commenter who spent a year trying to buy a V2H install with effectively unlimited budget found no vendor willing, and reports that exporting to the grid (V2G) is easier to arrange than powering your own house; others correct the article's currency by noting Tesla enabled Powershare V2H on new Model 3 and Model Y from October 1, though it needs a Powerwall 3.

Worth reading

  • amluto: Explains the root technical blocker: islanded V2H needs a microgrid interconnect device, and no vendor has standardized its control protocol, so only vertically integrated Tesla can make it work within its own products.
  • 1dom: First-hand report of a year spent trying to set up bidirectional charging in the UK, offering vendors a blank cheque and case-study rights, with no one willing — and notes V2G through Octopus-style tariffs is paradoxically easier than V2H.
  • qwerpy: First-hand experience riding out a five-day Pacific Northwest windstorm outage on Cybertruck Powershare, including topping the truck up at a neighbor's house and with a natural gas generator.

entry.title: Seoul Viosys begins production of rare-earth-free white light emitter
entry.content:
#11 on HN · semiconductor-today.com · 94 points · 15 comments · HN discussion

A Semiconductor Today report on Seoul Viosys (with parent Seoul Semiconductor) starting mass production of WICOP 3, a white LED that uses no rare earths, no package, and no silicone, plastic or lead frame — white light comes from gallium nitride alone, and chips can be as small as 10µm. The first production part is a 25µm x 10µm chip emitting 0.015lm at close to 100lm/W (target 200lm/W within two years), which the company says costs about half as much to make as a conventional white LED; mass production starts in Q4 2026, aimed at AR glasses and short-reach optical links for AI data centers, with Omdia cited forecasting a $60bn market within five years.

Discussion: The dominant thread is materials supply, not photometry: commenters note gallium is the catch, since China produced 99% of primary low-purity gallium, prices have roughly 10x'd in a decade and doubled in the past year, and Western production was abandoned largely for environmental and cost reasons — though Rio Tinto's Quebec pilot plant, due to ramp in 2027, is cited as a concrete counterweight. Others push on color quality: fitting inside the CIE white region says little, and a spiky spectral distribution will look bad in real use even if the chromaticity point is ideal, so people want a spectrograph. On the AI framing, the mood is skeptical but not dismissive — better, cheaper, higher-bandwidth data transmission has value regardless of the trend, with one commenter comparing it to startups bolting 「blockchain」 onto pitches in 2017. Separately, the original linked article turned out to be AI-written slop that garbled the company name as 「Biosys」; a moderator swapped in the Semiconductor Today piece and banned the site, and others noted the V/B confusion is a natural Korean transliteration artifact.

Worth reading

  • Animats: Rare-earth-free doesn't mean supply-chain-free: China made 99% of primary low-purity gallium, and the price is up 10x in ten years and 2x in the last year, citing USGS and Strategic Metals Invest data.
  • wyager: A good CIE chromaticity coordinate is not enough — a spiky spectral distribution will still render colors badly in real-world lighting, so a spectrograph is the number that matters.
  • wiml: Flags that the original article was riddled with AI-generated errors (company is Viosys, not Biosys) and guesses the real innovation is a multi-wavelength, multiple-quantum-well structure.

entry.title: Novellas with Groff
entry.content:
#12 on HN · movq.de · 79 points · 30 comments · HN discussion

A blog post on movq.de dated 2026-10-31 about writing novellas with groff. Commenters note that the author skipped the usual ms macro package and wrote his own macro set, and that he uses a small Perl script to translate Markdown-ish markup into groff macros. From the passages quoted in the thread, the post also discusses how world-building and proofreading long stories get hard, and mentions writing about 40k words in 10 days (the article itself could not be fetched, so these details come from quote snippets in the comments).

Article not read: [SSL: TLSV1_ALERT_DECODE_ERROR] tlsv1 alert decode error (_ssl.c:1147)

Discussion: The thread is mostly writers who code comparing their own setup: a coders' editor for prose, Emacs plus a Makefile plus Pandoc, Typst for near-instant Markdown to PDF, WeasyPrint with print stylesheets, Google Docs exported to Markdown and kept in Git, or Scrivener. Several people joke that the real function of a bespoke typesetting pipeline is to avoid writing, one describing elaborate Containerfile-and-Makefile machinery as essential work on the critical path, and the author-adjacent posts get teased for it. Others supply groff lore: that roff grew out of Multics RUNOFF and was effectively Unix's first killer app, that O'Reilly typeset its books with troff macros and Tim O'Reilly co-wrote Unix Text Processing, that Donovan and Kernighan's Go book used groff, and that 9front's Stanley Lieber still typesets fiction with troff -ms. On whether tooling matters, one camp says top writers keep a fixed routine because muscle memory triggers writing mode, citing George R. R. Martin on WordStar 4.0 on an offline DOS machine; the rebuttal is that he is the world's most famous case of writer's block and that sheer word count is a poor metric anyway. There is rough agreement that groff is underrated for publishing and that nobody should let the pipeline replace the prose.

Worth reading

  • tosti: Points out the notable part of the post: the author uses groff without the ms macros at all and wrote his own macro package.
  • staplung: Sketches the lineage from Multics RUNOFF to roff, arguing roff was Unix's first killer app (used for patent applications at Bell Labs) and is now largely displaced by mandoc on the BSDs.
  • 2b3a51: Adds that Tim O'Reilly co-wrote Unix Text Processing (Dougherty and O'Reilly, 1987), now free, with a recreated source repo on GitHub that compiles with only one font-path fix.

entry.title: Lenovo's 'encrypted' fingerprint USB is just an unencrypted SD card in a case
entry.content:
#14 on HN · reddit.com · 265 points · 99 comments · HN discussion

The submission is a Reddit r/technology thread about Lenovo’s ThinkPlus fingerprint USB drive (the FU100), marketed as AES-256 encrypted hardware but found on teardown to be an ordinary SD card in a case — the fingerprint sensor only switched the USB connection on, and nothing on the card was encrypted. The underlying reporting, which commenters trace back through Tom’s Hardware and HackingPassion to a Binary Ninja talk and slide deck, describes an AI-assisted follow-up that turned up a backdoor and hardcoded keys (including a “123456” credential) in other “secure” USB products. Commenters date the flaw to August 2025, note CVE-2025-13453 was issued in early January, that the product was announced in 2019 and sold only in China, and that the researcher’s presentation was in March.

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: The thread splits between reading this as outright fraud and as ordinary corporate incompetence: one camp says no security review could have passed this and Lenovo knowingly shipped a lie, while others argue box-ticking middle management and credulous marketing explain it without malice, and predict no consequences. A long sub-thread argues hardware versus software encryption: one side says free-software crypto on a normal stick is the only thing you can audit, the other that a properly built secure element or TPM genuinely adds brute-force resistance and lets a 6-digit PIN stand in for a 256-bit key, which is what actually brought full-disk encryption to non-experts. Several practitioners describe mandated encrypted drives at work (IronKey, Apricorn Aegis Padlock) and defend them for policy compliance and disaster recovery, while others point out the original IronKey was cracked and that BitLocker’s key escrow and YellowKey-style bypasses mean vendor promises are thin. Commenters also doubted the product existed at all until others found listings on Lenovo China’s ThinkPad site and AliExpress, and a side argument broke out over whether the Reddit link, Tom’s Hardware, or the original talk should have been submitted, plus whether a semicolon in a subheading signals AI authorship. Rough consensus: don’t trust unverifiable in-device encryption, and don’t trust Lenovo with secure hardware.

Worth reading

  • sllabres: Recalls being issued an IronKey under a Homeland Security grant, notes the original IronKey was later cracked by Unciphered in an attempt to unlock Stefan Thomas’s 7,002 BTC (worth $235M then), and links Lenovo’s own Chinese spec page for the drive.
  • forgotpwd16: Cuts through the “did this ever exist?” skepticism with a listing on Lenovo China’s ThinkPad store, after others found only AliExpress and Alibaba pages.
  • icpmoles: Corrects the widespread claim that potting the board would have made it secure — the slide deck shows the device was in fact potted in epoxy, so that defence was already tried.

entry.title: One-minute frequency disturbances from synchronization in power systems
entry.content:
#15 on HN · nature.com · 89 points · 35 comments · HN discussion

A Nature Energy paper (the nature.com URL is s41560) showing that grid-frequency time series from five continents — from Iceland's ~400,000 customers to the 400-million-customer Continental European synchronous area — all carry a narrow, persistent oscillation with a period of exactly one minute, phase-coherent over years. The authors attribute it to clock-synchronized control software in digitally controlled devices, especially battery UPSs and battery energy storage systems, whose periodic self-tests (documented as once per minute in commercial manuals) create synchronized demand peaks that propagate up through voltage levels; the frequency typically peaks at the start of each minute and then sags. The amplitude has grown in several grids, is linked to wear on hydropower turbines, and has prompted stricter load–frequency control rules; the observed deviation is around 1.5 mHz.

Discussion: Commenters treat it as a textbook thundering-herd problem: the top thread notes that gear designers deliberately avoid meshing gears with non-coprime tooth counts, and argues for staggering timer start-up with random jitter (and testing power-cut/reconnect scenarios, which resynchronize everything) — with a sub-thread nitpicking the exact randomization math and jitter granularity. Several point at everyday culprits: cron jobs, NTP clients (public NTP servers see spikes on minute marks from admins cronning ntpdate), and systemd's RandomizedDelaySec. There is real disagreement about the mechanism: one commenter doubts that many different UPS makes and models would run minute-periodic self-tests and proposes injection locking instead, and another suspects the cause is generic cron-style minute-precision scheduling rather than UPS firmware — both answered with the paper's own text plus vendor manuals stating 「battery circuit testing 1 x per minute for 1 sec」 and 「carried out automatically every 60 sec」. A side argument about weaponizing synchronized multi-megawatt data-centre loads to destabilize a grid is shot down on the grounds that megawatts are noise and grid resonance shifts moment to moment, with a rebuttal that hyperscale sites exceed 100 MW and the target is a local generator's controller, not a grid-wide resonance. Elsewhere, an electrical engineer complains that equipment is routinely shipped without staggered start-up logic for inrush current, and one commenter corrects the venue to Nature Energy.

Worth reading

  • the8472: Cites the paper's manufacturer confirmation and two UPS manuals that literally specify battery testing once per minute, tying it to NTP-synchronized clocks.
  • bob1029: Pushes back on the UPS explanation — too much coordination across makes and models, continuous rather than periodic — and proposes injection locking between physically coupled devices.
  • idiotsecant: Argues the proposed synchronized-load attack is unworkable: multi-megawatt swings are noise to a plant, let alone a grid region, and there is no fixed resonant frequency to push against.

entry.title: Frontier Airlines Likely Breached
entry.content:
#16 on HN · reddit.com · 108 points · 28 comments · HN discussion

The linked item is a Reddit PSA thread in r/frontierairlines, posted as users reported receiving scam emails containing complete booking details; the page itself could not be fetched, so the specifics come from the title and discussion. The implication is that reservation data was accessed or enumerated, though the thread contains no official confirmation from Frontier.

Article not read: page had almost no readable text (probably needs JavaScript or a login)

Discussion: Commenters split between seeing a broad security reckoning and doubting that breaches change corporate behavior: one argues companies just pay occasional class-action settlements, another says Sony Pictures survived, while others cite Jaguar Land Rover’s months-long shutdown and companies such as Zeabur and OSGrid that folded after attacks. The most concrete theory ties the emails to Amadeus, the GDS provider Frontier uses, after reports that an Amadeus endpoint had exposed passenger data since 2023; others note a similar Norwegian Cruise Line incident and wonder about shared customer-service software. A competing explanation is narrower: abuse of Frontier’s flight-status lookup to enumerate active itineraries, since a full breach would offer more lucrative options than better phishing. An AppSec veteran says most infosec work is liability paperwork and that adding staff would not have improved actual security, while a red-teamer using open-weight models argues alignment efforts will not stop capable attackers. There is rough agreement that regulation and headcount alone are not the fix, but no confirmation of the breach vector.

Worth reading

  • Mountain_Skies: An AppSec veteran says about 90% of the infosec work he saw was compliance paperwork to limit liability, and that tripling headcount would not have improved actual security.
  • bronco21016: Notes that several Asian airlines have notified customers of Amadeus-related breaches and that Frontier contracts with Amadeus for distribution, making the GDS a plausible common vector.
  • varenc: Argues the incident is more likely abuse of Frontier’s flight-status lookup to enumerate itineraries than a full breach, because a complete compromise would support more lucrative attacks than card-stealing phishing.

entry.title: Show HN: OmniDiff – Opensource, super fast, content aware Git difftool, in Rust
entry.content:
#18 on HN · github.com · 69 points · 26 comments · HN discussion

OmniDiff is Marko Ivankovic's AGPLv3 Rust diff tool (v0.3.0 at posting) that picks a diff algorithm by file type: 25 languages parsed with tree-sitter grammars, plus structural diffs for XML/plist/SVG, images (pixel- and frame-level), PDFs, archives (zip/tar/xz, including nested ones and Java class listings), fonts (glyph-by-glyph), and Windows/X11/Hyprland cursors. It claims 99.95% of code changes are handled robustly and 98.8% diffed with content-specific algorithms, and reports p50 4.2ms / p90 35.1ms / p99 177ms over 2,302 fixtures on a Core i7-1370P laptop, with the slowest at 482ms. The approach was derived from sampling 2,000 real diffs from the 7,400 Gentoo-packaged repositories, solved by hand; the same corpus drives CI. Install paths are cargo, a Homebrew tap, a signed apt repo, Nix flakes, and Arch/Gentoo recipes in packaging/.

entry.title: Show HN: I rebuilt my old canvas 3D library as a small WebGL 2 library – phoria2
entry.content:
#19 on HN · kevs3d.co.uk · 53 points · 8 comments · HN discussion

Kevin Roast 发布了 phoria2，这是对他 2013 年的 phoria.js 的一次重写——当年那个库用 canvas 2D context 画 3D，如今改成 WebGL 2 渲染器。这个库的目标是图表、带标签的场景、仪表盘和产品查看器：PBR 材质、instancing、点、线、标签、拾取、阴影、粒子以及 glTF 模型；没有运行时依赖，以纯 ES modules 分发，只在有内容变化时重绘，并配有面向人类和编码 agent 的选项校验（每条错误都会给出修复方式）。MIT 授权，通过 npm install phoria2 安装，另有一个 React 示例。

Discussion: 反应以肯定为主，集中在性能：有几位评论者说即使在手机上，demo 也稳定跑在 120 FPS，bricks demo 特别逗。一位前端开发者（Arkada）说，他没想到一个 3D 库内置了图表原语——timeseries、heat-colored hour/day surface chart 和 tiled dashboard——并指出按需渲染对开着许多图表的交易仪表盘很重要；他接着追问，在实时流式图表中 tween 对几何缓冲区更新的表现如何，作者没有给出回答。另一位（taylor-tg）想看到与 Three.js、Babylon 的对比文档，并反馈多数 demo 里的悬停交互在移动端表现不佳——点击后状态不会持续（Fennec/Android 17）——还表示愿意为此提交 contribution。唯一明显的分歧是 thrance 问为什么用 WebGL 2 而不是 WebGPU；Lerc 反驳说，WebGPU 目前在各个平台上还不可靠——有些 Linux 上，Firefox 不默认开启它，Chrome 也会时不时崩溃。

Worth reading

  • Arkada: 指出让这个库与众不同之处——内置 timeseries 和 surface 图表原语，再加上按需渲染，对长时间开着的交易仪表盘很关键；并追问流式数据下 tween 更新 buffer 的性能。
  • taylor-tg: 报告在手机上稳定 120 FPS，但指出移动端悬停/点击状态消失得太快（Fennec on Android 17），并提出愿意提交修复，同时希望有与 Three.js、Babylon 的对比。
  • Lerc: 务实反駁转向 WebGPU 的呼声：他试用过，它在各平台上仍不可依赖——Linux 上的 Firefox 不默认开启，Chrome 也频繁崩溃。

entry.title: Radiation Map of the World
entry.content:
#22 on HN · radiaverse.com · 90 points · 30 comments · HN discussion

Radiaverse is a website that aggregates public GPS-tagged dose-rate readings from owners of RadiaCode scintillation detectors into one shared hexagon map. Users publish tracks from the RadiaCode app, optionally anonymously, and the site adds community-described areas, photos and clips, with privacy measures including private-by-default tracks, a one-day publication delay and exclusion of GPS points worse than 15 metres. It highlights country coverage leaderboards and notable locations such as the Goiânia caesium-137 scrapyard and a 61.63 μSv/h hotspot in Fukushima.

Discussion: The top comment argues the site is not really a radiation map of Australia: it is a handful of handheld click-counter tracks, while Geoscience Australia offers a decades-long, calibrated 256-channel survey using a 40-litre crystal pack, with gridded data available for download. Several commenters found the map hard to interpret because the colour scale changes with zoom, apparent hotspots trace back to uncalibrated or drifting devices, and readings seem to rise with dwell time or poor ventilation. One observer added that recorder behaviour matters enormously, since some people walk normally while others place detectors directly beside granite or cast-iron fixtures; another countered that these devices are not sensitive enough for radon or cosmic rays to matter and are effectively uranium and thorium detectors. Others were put off by an 18-plus terms-of-service overlay before they could browse, and described the visible data as sparse and mostly green. Commenters also noted missing well-known high-background areas such as Ramsar in Iran and beaches in Kerala, and wondered why Germany appears to have near-complete coverage, jokingly attributing it to German nuclear anxiety.

Worth reading

  • defrost: Contrasts Radiaverse's few handheld tracks with Geoscience Australia's calibrated 256-channel, 40-litre crystal survey of the entire continent, and links the gridded data.
  • Karliss: Observes that readings vary with recorder behaviour, including people placing detectors next to granite or cast-iron light fixtures rather than simply walking.
  • Stitch4223: Criticises the changing scales and meaning while zooming, and suspects some tracks come from uncalibrated or over-sensitive devices.

entry.title: Parchment Paper History: How We Got Paper Perfect for Baking (2019)
entry.content:
#25 on HN · tedium.co · 8 points · 9 comments · HN discussion

A Tedium feature tracing baking parchment from the Apicius cookbook's reference to parchment through the 1847 process by French scientists Jean-André Poumarède and Louis Figuier, which treated plant-based paper with a cold sulfuric acid bath to imitate animal parchment. It then follows the modern product: Dow Corning's 1945 founding to find consumer uses for silicone, a 1955 patent filing that describes silicone-treated vegetable-fiber parchment as a separating medium, a 1957 fruitcake recipe recommending silicone-lined paper, and the FDA's 1979 GRAS designation for silicates. The piece also argues, via a Twitter poll in which 36% of respondents first remembered parchment paper in the 2000s, that baking parchment only became a household staple recently — a claim the thread pushes back on.

Discussion: The thread is small and mostly a correction session rather than a discussion of the history. One commenter says flatly that parchment paper was already widely used in kitchens well before the 2000s, undercutting the article's premise that it is a recent arrival. The rest of the thread is a fight over a single top-level claim that the real TL;DR is PFAS: others point out the article never mentions PFAS and attributes the non-stick property to a silicone coating on cellulose, and when the claim was repeated, commenters noted a TL;DR should describe the article and that the 1847 invention predates PFAS synthesis by roughly a century. A minor sub-thread asks whether parchment paper differs from butcher paper and is answered with a quick search rather than expertise. No one with first-hand baking or materials experience weighed in, and no rough consensus formed beyond rejecting the PFAS framing.

Worth reading

  • Sharlin: A commenter disputes the article's framing that parchment paper is a recent kitchen staple, saying it was widely used well before the 2000s.
  • wasabi991011: Rebuts the PFAS claim on chronology: the article dates parchment paper to 1847, nearly a century before PFAS were synthesized.
  • sudobash1: Notes the article never mentions PFAS at all and attributes baking parchment's release properties to a silicone treatment.

entry.title: Show HN: Point your camera at a landscape to learn about its geology
entry.content:
#26 on HN · outcrop.rocks · 110 points · 31 comments · HN discussion

Outcrop 是一款 iOS 和 Android 应用，通过相机把地质图叠加到真实地貌上：Live 模式会标出取景框下方是哪种岩石单元、标出山峰和湖泊，轻点任意位置就能读取该处岩石的名称、年代、成分和成因。在岩石单元的页面上，还可以查看你脚下从地表往下的岩层柱状剖面、化石记录，以及一块岩石形成时它所在的位置——把地图变成那个年代的地球，就可以看板块如何漂移。其他功能包括可离线下载的旅行区域地图、美国境内的 Quaternary（第四纪）地质与土壤图层，以及一个与作者早先的 Flyover Country 应用（提供飞机舷窗视野解说）相呼应的姊妹应用。作者说它在 Google Play 上线，在 TestFlight 上处于 iPhone 测试阶段，并承认自己还没能在明尼苏达州以外测试过多少地形。

Discussion: 回复大多是赞赏：有人说自己和 9 岁的孩子花了两小时探索 “Where it formed”（它形成于哪里）这个功能，还有人称赞 Quaternary 和土壤图层对缺乏基岩出露的中西部很有用。作者积极回应反馈，并承认了几个合理的建议：把时间滑块翻过来，让过去在左、现在在右；保持当前地点居中；叠加经纬网；增加网页版本（他说 AR 依赖 ARCore/ARKit，但有可行性）；以及增加 ASTER/Landsat 的矿物学叠加层，他说此前从未听说过这个数据集。若干条帖子属于缺陷报告而非功能请求：有人无法在 Play Store 搜索中找到该应用（后来直接给出了商店链接，才解决），某人手机上的 TestFlight 要求输入安装码，一位使用老旧 Doogee 设备的用户收到 “tracking did not start”（跟踪未能启动）的提示，最终确认原因是该手机无法进行 Live 所需的运动跟踪。有一处实质性纠正由作者本人作出：一位用户以为某条河流有 4.6 亿年历史，作者澄清，这么古老的是河床下方的岩石，他正在考虑如何让这一区别更清楚。

Worth reading

  • headsupernova: 作者纠正了一处误读：显示出来的年代属于河床下方的岩石，而不是河流本身，他正在考虑如何把这个区别表达得更清楚。
  • RobotToaster: 这份 Live 跟踪问题报告被证明是硬件限制造成的：测试者使用的 Doogee 手机显示该设备无法进行运动跟踪，而不是应用本身的缺陷。
  • lightedman: 一位野外工作者建议把 ASTER 和 Landsat 数据叠加在地质图之上，用来显示浅表的矿物学信息；作者此前没有见过这个数据集，表示会研究一下。

entry.title: Understanding Email Encryption
entry.content:
#29 on HN · fastmail.com · 103 points · 22 comments · HN discussion

Fastmail 官方博客的一篇科普文，逐层拆解邮件加密：连接层的 TLS 1.3 与 PKI/证书透明度（CT），服务器之间的机会性 TLS（Fastmail 自 2009 年入站、2010 年出站支持）及其可被中间人降级的缺陷，以及用来补漏的 MTA-STS 和 DANE。文章明确表态：Fastmail 当下选择 MTA-STS 而非 DANE，理由是 DNSSEC 运维复杂且故障会长时间滞留缓存（举了 2023 年 10 月 Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 根区签名过期、2023 年 5 月新西兰 .nz 密钥轮换导致数天中断）。后半部分讲静态加密（BitLocker/LUKS）的边界，以及 Proton Mail、Tuta 那类零访问加密在密文仍可被入站截获、元数据与主题不加密、浏览器端解密代码可被篡改等方面的局限。

Discussion: 评论整体认可文章质量，但补了不少漏洞和反例。有人指出文章谈 OpenPGP 时漏掉了 Proton 等已支持的 WKD（Web Key Directory），它不依赖「信任网」也能自动加密。Signal 的易用性被反复争论：一方引用 2016 年研究称 28 名计算机系学生中 21 人无法建立并维持安全连接，另一方纠正说该研究考的是能否比对安全号以防中间人、而非日常加密本身，且 Signal 这些年 UX 已大幅改进，不过也有人反驳说把双方安全号合并成一个大数字反而更不直观。真正有杀伤力的是一线数据：一位自托管者说八年间没遇到一台拒绝 STARTTLS 的服务器，只碰到两张主机名写错的证书，说明强制加密已相当可行；另一位则指出校验目标 MX 证书但对方没有 DNSSEC 或 MTA-STS 时，你根本不知道那台 MX 是不是攻击者的。最尖锐的一条实测批评是针对 Fastmail 自己：它对外发邮件并不强制 MTA-STS，入站也只有约 0.2% 的域名启用，并给出了查询结果与探测到的 testing 模式策略文件。另有评论质疑「WhatsApp/Signal 自动加密」的说法过于自信，认为无可复现构建就无法证明实际加密，建议改提 Delta Chat 和 SimpleX。

Worth reading

  • 8organicbits: 实测指出 Fastmail 对外发信不强制 MTA-STS、入站仅约 0.2% 域名启用，并贴出 parquet 查询结果和探测到的测试中策略文件，呼吁官方补文档和仪表盘校验。
  • cubesnooper: 自托管者八年强制校验证书并拒绝降级：没有一台服务器拒绝 STARTTLS，只有两张主机名错误的有效证书，其中一张报告后即修复。
  • mmooss: 纠正那条 Signal 可用性研究的解读：论文考的是用户能否比对安全号以抵御中间人，而不是能否完成端到端加密，多数用户日常零成本即安全。

entry.title: Landline phones will switch off across Britland in 100 days, no extensions
entry.content:
#30 on HN · theregister.com · 72 points · 50 comments · HN discussion

The Register reports that Openreach, BT's network arm, has written to communications providers warning that the legacy PSTN phone network will be retired on 31 January 2027 and that the deadline will not slip again. Anything still hanging off copper — plain phones, point-of-sale terminals, fire and security alarms, TeleCare pendants — risks disruption; households without fibre can be moved to SOTAP, where exchange-side kit keeps an old analogue line working as before. Openreach's James Lilley says the easy migrations are done and the remainder are complex critical connections, while analyst Paolo Pescatore and Age UK's Caroline Abrahams complain that public awareness is low and providers must chase vulnerable non-responders themselves.

Discussion: The dominant objection is power: POTS is fed from exchange battery banks that run for days, whereas a fibre ONT plus router dies with the mains, and several Britons report that Openreach stopped shipping battery backup with newer ONTs altogether (one Canadian says Bell did the same), while Verizon's alternative is a box of 12 D-cells. A sizeable camp calls this nostalgia: almost nobody owns a corded phone any more, the copper plant is decaying for lack of users, and money is better spent on hardened cell sites, deployable towers and satellite SOS — to which others reply that much of rural California and rural Britain has no mobile coverage at all. A subtler point raised is that POTS carried legally enforceable quality-of-service obligations while VoIP and cellular are 「best effort」, though several commenters correct the implication that 「best effort」 is meaningless — it is a legal standard with teeth, and California's CPUC applies service-quality rules to all of it. One rural commenter deflates the alarm with first-hand detail: they were told they had switched over, but are actually on SOTAP, with analogue phones, CLI and exchange-provided power all still working. A running side thread mocks the headline's 「Britland」, which most readers had never encountered and which some say made them click purely to find out where it was.

Worth reading

  • gumby: Explains the reliability crux: POTS lines are powered from huge -48V battery banks in the exchange office, whereas a router's backup battery is unnoticed and unserviced, so it is dead within a year — exactly when an emergency call is needed.
  • zh3: First-hand report from a rural UK line that was declared 「switched over」 but is actually on SOTAP: analogue handsets, CLI and exchange-fed power still work, so in their frequent power cuts the phone still functions.
  • jordanb: Argues the real change is regulatory, not technical: POTS carried legally enforced quality-of-service obligations with penalties, while VoIP and cellular are 「best effort」, giving the phone company a way to shed that liability.
